# ☙ THE EIGHT BOOKS ON ASTRONOMY
## BY JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS THE JUNIOR, A SICILIAN OF SENATORIAL RANK, DEDICATED TO MAVORTIUS
### Lollianus; recently reclaimed from countless errors by the astrologer NICOLAUS PRUCKNER.
<note>original: "V. C." (Vir Clarissimus), a formal title for a person of senatorial rank in the Roman Empire. The title of the work is "Mathesis," though here titled "Astronomicon."</note>

#### TO THESE HAVE BEEN ADDED:

**CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY** of Pelusium and Alexandria, four books on astrological effects <note>original: ἀποτελεσμάτων (apotelesmatōn)</note>, which they call the **<term>Quadripartitum<note>Literally "The Four-Part Book," Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology, also known as the *Tetrabiblos*.</note>**

**One book on the significations of the fixed stars.**

**The <term>Centiloquium<note>A collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note></term> by the same author.**

->FROM THE ARABS AND CHALDEANS:<-

**One book of one hundred Aphorisms by HERMES,** the most ancient astrologer.

**The <term>Centiloquium<note>A similar collection of 100 aphorisms attributed to a figure named Bethem.</note></term> of BETHEM.**

**Another book by the same author on the Planetary Hours.**

**The propositions of ALMANSOR the Astrologer to the King of the Saracens.**

**One book on <term>Elections<note>The branch of astrology used to determine the most auspicious time to start an activity, such as a journey or a war.</note></term> by ZAHEL the Arab.**

**One book by MESSAHALAH on the nature of the Sphere and the Stars, and how they operate in this world.**

**Three books by OMAR on Nativities.** <note>A work regarding birth charts and the destiny of individuals.</note>

**Five books on Astronomy by MARCUS MANILIUS,** a most eloquent poet.

**Lastly, an introductory booklet by OTTO BRUNFELS on the definitions and terms of Astrology.**

->BASEL, FROM THE WORKSHOP OF JOHANNES HERWAGEN,<-
->IN THE MONTH OF MARCH, IN THE YEAR 1533.<-

# TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED AND LEARNED MAN, OTTO
## BRUNFELS, DOCTOR OF MEDICINE, NICOLAUS
### PRUCKNER SENDS GREETINGS.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'R' depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or ruler) seated at a desk or throne, enclosed within a decorative rectangular border.</image-desc> You seem to me to be doing exactly the right thing, most learned OTTO, in having invested your labors so far that nothing could be found lacking in you regarding that circle of disciplines which the Greeks call <term>the encyclopedia<note>original: ἐγκυκλοπαιδείαν (enkyklopaideian). Pruckner is praising Brunfels for his "all-around" education.</note></term>. I say this to mention nothing, for the moment, of your all-encompassing knowledge of languages, which you allowed yourself to acquire for this sole purpose: that it might be of use to you, and of benefit to the rest of us—that is, the more unrefined. Indeed, your most painstaking scholarly works speak for themselves, even if we remain silent, and they make it plain to almost the entire world just how much you have achieved and how much you have excelled.

How truly you must be congratulated now as a Physician—and a most excellent and great one at that—since as soon as you realized that the "sum of all things" (if I may say so without offense) was missing from your medical practice—namely, Astrology itself—you learned it through such great, tireless labor and sweat. Without astrology, I would consider all Medicine to be not only maimed, but truly worth nothing. Who is there who would not know this, provided they weigh the whole matter? Nor are you accustomed to listen to those who judge this art—noble in itself—as if it were unnecessary, or even not conducive to the physician’s work. Yet we are forced to see every day so many crises of life, so many deaths, and so many funerals of "patients" (as they call them), arising solely from the neglect—not to say contempt—of Astrology. It is as if that old <term>adage<note>A common proverb or saying.</note></term> against Physicians were once again finding its place: "More have perished by the hand of Physicians than by the sword." For how many people are there who do not see that we are being thrown into a thousand dangers of life through their ignorance? Who does not see the truth of what is commonly said: "Only Physicians are permitted to kill without punishment"? I wish it were as false as we all hope, and as false as we are forced to see it is true, to our own great misfortune.

I would not say this—nor would I wish the fair-minded reader to interpret it otherwise—as if I were ill-disposed toward Physicians themselves or toward Medicine itself; far be it from me! Indeed, let it be far from me, as one who admires and honors it more than others, especially if it is <term>guided by astrology<note>original: ἀστρολογῆται (astrologētai). Pruckner borrows a term from the Roman architect Vitruvius to describe a practice informed by the stars.</note></term> (to use a Vitruvian word). Because medicine excels all other arts, I am far from disapproving of it or marking it with a "black coal" <note>An ancient Roman idiom meaning to condemn or mark as unlucky.</note>. For what is better, what is more conducive or useful to man himself, than the very knowledge of things? "Happy is he," as the Poet <note>A reference to the Roman poet Virgil: *Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas* (Georgics 2.490).</note> pronounced, "who was able to know the causes of things." 

Nor do I dwell on those who anxiously dispute over the primacy or excellence of professions. While each person holds onto his own stubbornly and grants little to another, they often stir up great tragedies over "goat’s wool" or "the shadow of an ass" <note>Proverbial expressions for debating over trivial or worthless things.</note>; the more foolish they are, the more they think themselves prudent. 

But I return to the Physicians, who seem to me especially deserving of reproach because they neglect Astrology—an art primarily necessary for the healing craft—with such zeal. They are content only with what this or that <term>quack<note>original: Agyrta, a traveling performer or street-healer.</note></term> or charlatan has babbled at random or foolishly devised. In the meantime, they are so addicted to their chosen authority that they follow them in the Pythagorean fashion, saying: <term>"He himself said it,"<note>original: αὐτὸς ἔφα (autos epha). A Greek phrase referring to blind appeal to authority, famously used by the followers of Pythagoras.</note></term> when they have nothing else to answer. For instance, a certain physician of "first rank" (as he seemed to himself) recently said that he valued one **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> more than all other Physicians, whether ancient or modern; he honored him like a parent and wished to die with his Avicenna. Thus, it is no wonder if they despise Astrologers, since they grant so little even to their own peers.

Truly, it is a stupid, even impudent and daring deed, to criminalize a matter which you do not understand. Certain "shadowy" theologians do the same thing: neglecting the Word of God, they rail against the liberal arts from the pulpit, forbidding "water and fire" <note>A Roman legal formula for banishment or total social exclusion.</note> not so much to the arts themselves, but to their professors. First, they say the science of the stars is vain; second, that predictions are trifles and <term>elections<note>The practice of choosing the best time to start an undertaking based on the stars.</note></term> are sacrilege. They blather such nonsense as: even if it were mostly true, not all stars are known; the state of the heavens is different now than it was of old; the authorities do not agree; and similar rubbish. Do they not seem to you to be performing their duty uprightly? Is it not an extraordinary kind of arguing? Is it not a worthy and noble demonstration? Who could break such a firm and solid force of argument...

<summary>In this dedication to the physician Otto Brunfels, Nicolaus Pruckner argues that medicine is incomplete and even dangerous without astrology. He criticizes physicians who blindly follow authorities like Avicenna and theologians who dismiss the celestial arts without understanding them.</summary>
<keywords>Otto Brunfels, Nicolaus Pruckner, medical astrology, iatromathematics, Avicenna, criticism of physicians, theology and astrology, liberal arts, Vitruvius</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from Nicolaus Pruckner to Otto Brunfels. The previous page established Brunfels's reputation as a polymath and began the argument for the necessity of astrology in medical practice.</meta>

...to break down, and who could dissolve such an inexplicable method of proof and this Gordian knot <note>A metaphor for an intricate or unsolvable problem, famously "solved" by Alexander the Great cutting it with a sword.</note>. Just as with these things and others like them, so too can every single art—even Theology itself—not be rejected on such grounds. For who has ever known every herb, plant, and tree? Who has thoroughly investigated the powers of all things? Do many things not still lie hidden? Or is Theology therefore vain because we still do not know many things about God, about the angels, and about many other matters? Indeed, how much discord and dissension is there among theologians? It can therefore easily be perceived how much "erudition" those men possess who thus expose their own ignorance to the world; that is to say, these are unskilled men who think nothing is right except what pleases them, and they think everyone who does not agree with them is insane. 

But we have neither thrown away the spear nor the shield; the matter is still in safe waters, it stands secure. Let that fury burst, let everyone grumble if they wish—I will say what I feel: that **Astrology** is a certain part of **Medicine**, and not the smallest part at that. This has been proven by experience, as can be seen in <term>elections<note>The practice of "electing" or choosing the most astrologically favorable time to perform a specific action, such as a surgery or administering medicine.</note></term>, which he who neglects will, I know not in what manner, truly heal the sick. I could provide many examples of this matter where, because the choosing of the proper time was neglected, the sick were brought into the peril of their lives. 

In these very days, a certain man was suffering from that disease which is called a hernia, or rather a <term>hydrocele<note>original: "hydroccele"; a type of swelling in the scrotum caused by fluid buildup.</note></term>. A surgeon arrived who strongly held the stars in contempt and did not wish to be taught. He began the treatment and applied the scalpel while Taurus was rising <note>In traditional medical astrology, the sign of Taurus governs the throat and neck, but more importantly, specific "unfortunate" timings for surgery were determined by which sign the Moon or the Ascendant occupied.</note>. At that time, its rulers, Venus and the Moon, were "unfortunate" (to speak in the manner of the astrologers). Virgo held the <term>sixth house<note>In an astrological chart, the sixth house is traditionally associated with illness and infirmity.</note></term>, in which the Moon was also falling away from the angle and the house. Saturn presided over the tenth house, but was himself opposite to the house. Venus, the lady of the horoscope, was joined to Mars <term>partially<note>original: "partiliter"; meaning the planets were at the exact same degree, a "perfect" or very strong aspect.</note></term>, on the line of the tenth house, which belongs to the Physician in this matter. 

What good would you predict here, most learned **OTTO**? Would you not judge that there would be future danger from Mars, and specifically because of the Physician? But you ask: what happened? Immediately on the fifth day, he departed this life. What I had previously said privately to certain friends was found to be true. This is something I have proven not just once in others as well. Who, then, will deny that Elections are a most necessary thing for the Physician and suited for human use? 

Moved therefore by this matter, and wishing to consult the interests of many, I have gladly taken this burden upon myself: that after having thoroughly read **JULIUS FIRMICUS** <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer whose work "Matheseos libri octo" was a primary source for Western astrology.</note> and emended him as far as was permitted, I thought he should be published anew. Since you have now attained your long-merited Laurel <note>A reference to Brunfels receiving his doctoral degree in medicine.</note> and come forth to us as a new Doctor—may it be happy and auspicious—I also wished, for the glory and fame of your name, to dedicate to you the now-reborn **FIRMICUS**, as if he were new and restored to his proper splendor. We have added, furthermore, the principal authors who are by no means to be despised in this matter, so that you might have at hand those whom you could most safely follow.

->May you look upon this, our boldness, with a kind and fair mind.<- 
->At Benfeld, in the month of March, in the year of our restored<-
->salvation, 1533.<-

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the actual technical manual by Otto Brunfels, moving from the philosophical defense of astrology in the preface to specific terminology and definitions. It establishes the basic vocabulary of the "sidereal science" for the reader.</meta>

# ON DEFINITIONS AND TERMS
## A LITTLE BOOK ON ASTROLOGY BY OTTO BRUNFELS.

**Astrology** is the knowledge of the actions and significations of the stars and the heavens; in Latin, it is called the **sidereal science**.
**Dioptrics**, a part of Astrology, investigates the distances of the Sun (☉) and Moon (☽) and other stars through the use of instruments. <note>From the Greek 'dioptra,' an ancient astronomical sighting instrument.</note>
**Meteoroscopy**, a part of Astrology, seeks out the differences in elevations and the distances of the stars.
**Gnomonics**, a part of Astrology, teaches the theory of shadows and sundials, doing so by means of the ancient **gnomon**. <note>The gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>
An **Aster** is a single star, as Macrobius says.
An **Astron** is a sign composed of many stars, which we call a **constellation**. Thus, stars are indeed individual, such as the five **Wandering Stars** <note>The planets</note> and others which, not mixed with others, move alone.
**Sydera** <note>Constellations</note> truly are those which are formed into some sign by a composition of many stars, such as Aries (♈), Taurus (♉), Andromeda, Perseus, the Crown, and whatever types of various forms are believed to have been received into the heavens.
The **Horoscope** is the sign which is ascending. <note>In traditional astrology, the 'horoscopus' refers specifically to the Rising Sign or Ascendant, not the entire chart.</note>

-> GREEK NAMES OF THE PLANETS <-

$\hbar$ **The Shining One** <note>original: "φαίνων" (Phainon)</note>. ♃ **The Blazing One** <note>original: "φαέθων" (Phaethon)</note>. ♂ **The Fiery One** <note>original: "πυρόεις" (Pyroeis)</note>. ☉ **The Sun** <note>original: "ἥλιος" (Helios)</note>. ♀ **The Light-Bringer** <note>original: "Βωσφόρος" (Phosphoros)</note>. ☿ **The Gleaming One** <note>original: "σίλβων" (Stilbon)</note>. ☽ **The Moon** <note>original: "σελήνη" (Selene)</note>.

**Height** of the planets <note>Often referred to as Exaltation</note> is so called because stars placed in that specific part of the sky make men blessed, or it is when they are raised up by a certain natural sublimity of greatness.
**Fallen** planets <note>Planets in their 'Fall' or 'Detriment'</note> are so called when their authority is suppressed; they make men miserable, poor, ignoble, and <unclear>destitute</unclear>.
<margin>Close neighbors</margin> or generous ones, eternal divinities assigned to individual **decans**. <note>Decans are 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs.</note> Regarding these, see Firmicus, book two, chapter four. <note>Firmicus Maternus was a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the 'Matheseos Libri VIII'.</note>
The **Bounds** of the stars are what the specific parts of the signs are called which are divided among individual stars; in Greek, these are **the borders** <note>original: "τὰ ὅρια" (ta horia)</note>.
Planets are said to **Rejoice** when, being placed in suitable and more fortunate places in the birth chart, they have greater power and decree the most good fortune.
The **Morning Stars** are five: ♄, ♃, ♂, ♀, and ☿. These same ones are also called **Evening Stars**, **Western**, and **Hidden**. In Greek: **the invisible**, **those in conjunction**, and **those rising at sunset** <note>original: "ἀφανíται καὶ συνοδικοὶ καὶ ἀκρονύκται"</note>.
A star is called **Morning** when, being at its rising, it precedes the Sun (☉) from the east, like **Lucifer** <note>The name for Venus when it appears before sunrise; literally 'Light-Bringer'.</note>.
An **Evening** star, at its rising, is one that follows the rising Sun.
**Hidden** stars are those which the orb of the Sun (☉) covers.
**Rising at sunset** <note>original: "Ακρονύκται"</note> are those which rise just as the Sun (☉) tends toward its setting.
Stars are said to be **Protected** whenever they have preceded the Sun with a favorable radiation.
The power of the Sun is protected by the best radiation whenever it has been adorned by the morning rising of stars.
**Saturn** ($\hbar$) is called a morning star when it has preceded the Sun (☉) by twelve degrees.
**Jupiter** (♃) is a morning star when it has moved back by eleven degrees in its preceding.
**Venus** (♀), preceding the Sun by eight degrees, is called a morning star.
Similarly, **Mars** (♂), placed in the eighth degree, is called a morning star.
**Aries** (♈) is called a **tropic sign** because when the Sun (☉) is placed in that sign, it makes the springtime.
**Aries** (♈) is called a **fiery sign** because whoever has it in the horoscope of their birth will be prone to fire and a **choleric** nature. <note>In ancient medicine, the choleric temperament was associated with fire, bile, and an ambitious or irritable personality.</note>

<meta>catchword: Platice (meaning 'broadly' or 'wide,' referring to aspects)</meta>

<summary>This page defines fundamental astrological and astronomical terms, distinguishing between individual stars and constellations while providing the Greek names for planets. It also introduces technical concepts like planet visibility (morning/evening stars) and the "bounds" and "joys" of planets.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of astrological terms, focusing on the twelve houses (domiciles), the geometric relationships between signs (aspects), and the classification of celestial phenomena. It maintains the structure of defining a Greek or Latin technical term followed by its significance in the "sidereal science."</meta>

The location of life's range is in that sign in which the **horoscopus** <note>The Ascendant or Rising Sign</note> is established.
**Rising** <note>original: "Ἀνατολὴ" (Anatole)</note>, the eastern angle, the first house.
**Setting** <note>original: "Δύσις" (Dysis)</note>, the western descent.
**Midheaven** <note>original: "μεσουράνιον" (Mesouranion)</note>, the center of the sky.
**Bottom of the Sky** <note>original: "ὑπόγειον" (Hypogeion)</note>, the lowest point of the heavens.
**Rising** in Latin, the first part of the ascendant, which emerges first from the eastern part at any time of birth, and is drawn out through thirty parts <note>degrees</note> in succession.
**Setting**: the part of the sky located exactly in the seventh place from the ascendant; in Greek, the **Western Diameter** <note>original: "διάμετρον Δυτικόν" (diametron Dytikon)</note>.
**Midheaven**: called the tenth sign from the ascendant.
**Bottom of the Sky**: which is established in the fourth place from the ascendant.
**Goddess** <note>original: "θεὰ" (Thea)</note> is the third place from the ascendant, that is, the third sign from the ascendant.
**God** <note>original: "θεὸς" (Theos)</note>: that sign which is established directly opposite this sign on the diameter, that is, the ninth from the ascendant.
**Good Fortune**: the fifth place from the ascendant; in Greek, **Good Luck** <note>original: "ἀγαθὴ τύχη" (Agathe Tyche)</note>.
**Good Spirit** <note>original: "Ἀγαθοδαίμων" (Agathodaimon)</note>: that is, the "Good Daemon," across the diameter from [the place of] Fortune, which is in the eleventh place from the ascendant.
**Idle and Cast-Down Places** are so called when they are joined in no fellowship <note>aspect</note> with the ascendant.
**Rising Forth** <note>original: "Ἀναφορὰ" (Anaphora)</note>, or the **Lower Gate**, is the name for the first cast-down place, which is established in the second sign from the ascendant.
**Sinking Down** <note>original: "ἐπικαταφορὰ" (Epikataphora)</note>, or the **Upper Gate**, is the diameter <note>the opposite</note> of the aforementioned sign, that is, the eighth place from the ascendant.
The last places are those of **Bad Fortune** and **Bad Spirits**.
**Bad Fortune**: the sixth place from the ascendant; in Greek, **Bad Luck** or **Bad Spirit** <note>original: "κακοτύχη ἢ κακοδαίμων" (Kakotyche or Kakodaimon)</note>.
**Opposite Aspect** [Diameter]: which is from one sign to the seventh sign away, as is Aries (♈) and Libra (♎).
**Trine Aspect** [Trigonus]: which is from the sign where we begin to the fifth sign, as is Aries (♈) to Leo (♌).
We call it the **Right Trine** when it is behind the sign from which we begin.
The **Left Trine** is what is ahead; for example, the Right Trine of Aries (♈) is Sagittarius (♐), while the Left is Leo (♌); similarly, the Right Trine of Leo (♌) is Aries (♈), and the Left is Sagittarius (♐).
**Square Aspect**: which is from the sign where we start to the fourth, such as Aries (♈), Cancer (♋), and Capricorn (♑).
Whatever is behind is called a **Right Square**, such as Aries (♈) and Capricorn (♑).
**Sextile Aspect** [Hexagonus]: which is from the sign where we begin to the third.
**Giver of Life**: the lord of the nativity <note>the ruling planet of the birth chart</note>.
**Heavenly Figures** <note>original: "Οὐράnia ζῴδια" (Ourania zodia)</note>: celestial images or heavenly signs.
**Evildoers** <note>original: "κακοποιοί" (kakopoioi)</note>: the fortunating planets. <note>Note: The author appears to have swapped the definitions here; Greek "kakopoioi" usually refers to Malefics, but the text defines them as "fortunantes."</note>
**Doers of Good** <note>original: "καλοποιοί" (kalopoioi)</note>: the unfortunating planets, otherwise called malefics and unfortunating ones. <note>Note: As above, the text swaps the standard definitions of Malefics and Benefics.</note>
**Outcome** <note>original: "Ἀποτέλεσμα" (Apotelesma)</note>: an astrological judgment or opinion; in Latin, a prediction or judgment.
**Secondary Signs**: those which are seen in the elements themselves, such as Comets, earthquakes, rains, and excessive droughts; so called because they have secondary powers, whereas the primary power resides in the heavens and the celestial stars, and the secondary power is in the elements which are moved within them.
**Corrupting Stars**: those which assist the decrees of the celestial stars; they are those things which occur in the elements with an excess and a certain greater force, such as droughts and excessive rains; called "corrupting" because every excess of the elements brings about corruption.
**Favorable Stars**: which have an innate favorable and prosperous power.
**Cusps of Heaven**: the angles <note>original: "τὰ κέντρα" (ta kentra)</note>, or pivots [cardines]; these are the same.
**Successive Houses** <note>original: "Ἐπαναφόραι" (Epanaphorai)</note>: the houses that follow [the angles].
**Eclipses** <note>original: "Ἐκλείψεις" (Ekleipseis)</note>: the failings and darkenings of the luminaries <note>the Sun and Moon</note>.

It notably documents the Greek and Latin names for the four "angles" of a chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical glossary of astrological and astronomical terms from the previous page, moving from the houses of the birth chart to specific planetary regions, types of years, and the names of fixed stars and clusters.</meta>

### ON DEFINITIONS AND TERMS
<meta>catchword: acquisition <note>original: πίκτησις (epiktēsis)</note></meta>

**Androdas**, the 63rd year <note>Known as the "Grand Climacteric," a year traditionally thought to be a major turning point in life</note>, so named because, by a hidden reasoning, it always affects a person with various risks and dangers.

**Climacteric and Enneatic years**, years occurring in cycles of seven and nine, which always portend heavy misfortunes for mankind.

**Full parts** in a chart are those in which **decans** <note>Thirty-degree signs are divided into three "decans" of ten degrees each, each ruled by a different planet</note> have been found.

**Empty parts**, to which the number of decans never reaches.

**Northern signs** are those that move from the beginning of Aries until the end of Virgo.

**Southern signs** are those which turn from the beginning of Libra until the end of Pisces.

**Direct ascensions** are the signs called from the beginning of Cancer until the end of Sagittarius.

**Tortuous ascensions** are said to rise from the beginning of Capricorn until the end of Gemini <note>These terms refer to the speed and angle at which signs rise over the horizon; "tortuous" or "oblique" signs take less time to rise</note>.

**Concordant signs** are Aries and Pisces; Taurus and Aquarius; Gemini and Capricorn; Cancer and Sagittarius; Leo and Scorpio; Virgo and Libra.

**The greatest half of the circle** is the name for the area from the beginning of Leo until the end of Capricorn.

**The Sun's half** is the same as the "greatest half," because the Sun has its beginning <note>or dominion</note> in this entire half, just as the planets have in their own terms.

**The least half**, which is from the beginning of Aquarius until the end of Cancer, is called the **Moon's half**, because the Moon similarly has its beginning in this entire half, just as the Sun does in the greatest.

**The hot half** is from the beginning of Aries until the end of Virgo.

**Faces**, the appearances <note>original: "decutiæ"</note> of the signs.

**Fixed stars** are so called because their motion is scarcely perceived even after a hundred years, which is seen as the longest span of a human life.

**The Pleiades** <note>original Greek: πλειάδες</note>, called *Vergiliæ* in Latin, are so named because they rise at the end of spring when summer begins.

**The Babylonians** call them *Atatage*.

**The Hyades** were called "The Little Pigs" <note>original: "Suculæ"</note> by the ancients; some place them in the mouth, others in the forehead of Taurus.

**The Torch-bearer** <note>original Greek: λαμπάδιας (lampadias)</note> is the brightest among the Hyades and their leader. In the Chaldean language, it is called **Aldebaran**.

**Anhelar**, the star of Apollo, a star shining in the head of Gemini <note>Likely the star Castor</note>.

**Abrachaleus**, called in Greek **the star of Hercules** <note>original: ἡρακλέους ἄστρον (herakleous astron)</note> in the very back of the head of Gemini <note>Likely the star Pollux</note>.

**The Azabenæ** are stars located at the Claws <note>The "Claws" of the Scorpion, which now form the sign of Libra</note> possessing the qualities of Saturn and Mercury.

**The Claws** <note>original: "Chelæ"</note> are what the Latins call "horns," such as are commonly imagined on Cancer and Scorpio.

**The Cloudy Cluster** <note>original Greek: Νεφελώδης συστροφή (Nephelōdēs systrophē)</note>, that is, a misty globe. The **Nebula** which is in the breast of Cancer, otherwise known as **The Manger** <note>original: Præsepe</note>, and in Chaldean as **Meellephi**.

**The Little King** <note>original Greek: Βασιλίσκος (Basiliskos)</note> is the bright star at the heart of Leo <note>Known today as Regulus</note>.

**The Asses** are the stars situated at the Manger itself.

**The Vinedresser**, in Greek **the Fore-harvest star** <note>original: προτρυγήτης (protrygētēs)</note>, in Chaldean **Almucediem Alaraph**, is the bright star at the Northern wing of Virgo <note>Known today as Vindemiatrix</note>.

**The Ear of Grain** <note>original Greek: στάχυς (stachys)</note>, or *Spica*, in Chaldean **Abzumon Alazel**, located in Virgo.

**Antares** <note>original Greek: ἀντάρης</note>, the heart of the Scorpion, a well-known and bright star among those three distinct stars in the back of Scorpio.

**The Southern One** <note>original Greek: νότιος (notios)</note>, that little fish which is to the south, called *Borealis* <note>Northern</note> in Latin.

**The Link** <note>original Greek: σύνδεσμος (syndesmos)</note>, the series of stars between Pisces and Aries, which the Latins call the "Celestial Knot."

**Arcturus** is well known.

**The Serpent-bearer** <note>original Greek: ὀφιουχὸς (Ophiouchos)</note>, or *Serpentarius*.

**Aphetic places** <note>original Greek: ἀφετικά (aphetika)</note>, the "releasing" places, or *Hyleg* as the Chaldeans call them, otherwise known as **Climacteric** locations <note>Points in a chart used to determine the length of life</note>.

**Climacteric years**, or years of progression, are so named because from the ascensions of the planets, according to the straight or oblique circle of the Climate <note>The latitude/region of the observer</note>, the time is known when a planet will reach that place.

**The Significator of Sovereignty** is the planet that holds more and more powerful prerogatives in the Midheaven.

**The Ruler**, or host of the interlunium, is the lord of the place in which the conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurred.

**Interlunium**, that is, the New Moon, in Greek called the **Conjunction** <note>original: σύνοδος (synodos)</note>.

**The Overlord planet** <note>original Greek: ἐπικρατήτωρ (epikratētōr)</note>, that is, the dominator, who holds dominion over the others.

**The Master of the House planet** <note>original Greek: οἰκοδεσπότης (oikodespotēs)</note>, that is, the head-of-the-household planet, the same as the **Lord of the Geniture** <note>The planet ruling the birth chart</note>, also called the **Lord of Birth** <note>original Greek: κύριος γενέσεως (kyrios geneseōs)</note>.

### ON THE TERMINOLOGY OF ASTROLOGY
<sig>* 4</sig>
<meta>image quality: good; catchword: Cardo (Pivot/Hinge)</meta>

**Affliction** <note>original: κακωσις (kakōsis)</note>, bad conditions, or the debilitation of the eleventh house.

**Figure** <note>original: σχημα (schēma)</note>, the entire constitution or arrangement of the heavens at a specific moment.

**To Direct** is to investigate when a certain degree of the Equator—whether rising or setting relative to an arc of the ecliptic or another moving interval—encounters the **Hylech** <note>The "Giver of Life," a specific point in a birth chart used to calculate longevity</note> and a malefic star or its ray. For whenever a malefic star or its harmful rays encounter the Hylech through this calculation, they cut short the life and portend that a great crisis is imminent.

**Day** is the motion of the Sun above the earth.

**Our Hemisphere** is that half of the earth defined by our horizon.

**The Violently Slain** <note>original: βιοθανατοι (biothanatoi)</note>, those who perish by a violent death.

**Eminence**, also called elevation or the sublimity of a planet, occurs in a conjunction when a planet is carried in the highest part of the upper circle—which is called an **Epicycle** <note>In older astronomy, a small circle the center of which moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> in Greek—while another planet occupies a lower position. This place is also commonly called the **Apogee** <note>original: Augem; the point in orbit farthest from Earth</note>. Pontanus <note>Giovanni Pontano (1429–1503), an influential Italian humanist and astronomer</note>, a most elegant writer, calls it the "apex" and "summit."

**Anaretic places** <note>original: αναρετικα (anaretika)</note>, lethal places within the figure of the heavens that bring the danger of death.

**Peripatos** <note>original: περιπατος</note>, the progression of a planet to its place of birth, which is clumsily called the "cutting off," and that planet is called the "cutter" <note>A planet that "cuts off" the years of life</note>.

**Traversing planet** or "reviewer," the walking planet <note>original: περιπατος (peripatos)</note>, the **conditional planet** <note>original: αιρετικος (hairetikos)</note>, or that which belongs to a specific "sect," whether nocturnal or diurnal.

**Lord of the hour** <note>original: αιρετων (hairetōn)</note>.

**Lord of the bounds** <note>original: ὁριοκρατωρ (horiokratōr)</note>, the planet that rules the specific "terms" or subdivisions of a zodiac sign.

**Under the rays** <note>original: ὑπαυγος (hypaugos)</note>, a planet positioned close to the Sun; that is, "sub-radiated." Because this word seemed too harsh, the moderns preferred to call it **Combust** <note>A planet "burnt up" by the Sun's proximity, weakening its influence</note>.

**Decans**, also called decuries; these are the same. They are the individual ten-degree segments of the signs. Hali <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> and Guido <note>Guido Bonatti, a famous 13th-century Italian astrologer</note> called these "faces" in their own custom.

**Paranatellonta** <note>original: παρανατελλοντα</note>, the constellations or star-images that rise alongside the decans.

**Lord of the Full Moon** or **New Moon**: not the planet that rules the sign in which the opposition or conjunction occurs, but rather the lord of the sign that is rising on the horizon <note>the Ascendant</note> at the time of the conjunction or opposition.

**Trajections** <note>original: traiectiones</note>, which some today call "crossing stars," such as "leaping goats," "torches," and "fiery beams" <note>Various historical terms for meteors and atmospheric phenomena</note>.

**Zodiac** <note>original: Signifer; Greek: ζωδιακος</note>.

**Degrees**, the thirty equal parts into which each sign is divided. The ancient Latins also called these "parts."

**Month**, the entire space of time in which the Moon returns to the Sun.

**Year**, the space of time until the Sun returns to the same place from which it departed twelve months earlier.

**Solstitial signs**, so called because when the Sun has traveled to them, it is believed to stand still for a time before its movement to the north or its inclination to the south becomes manifest; these are **Cancer** and **Capricorn**.

**Almugea**, a Chaldean term for the relationships or aspects of planets to one another.

**Harmful and threatening aspects**: these are the square <note>90 degrees</note>, the opposition <note>180 degrees</note>, and the diameter.

**Benevolent aspects**: those which are formed from triangles <note>trine, 120 degrees</note> and hexagons <note>sextile, 60 degrees</note>.

Stars positioned in the **upper hemisphere** are said to "behold" the horoscope <note>the Ascendant</note> with a **Right-hand radiation**, whether it be a sextile, square, or trine.

They behold one another with **Left-hand radiation** when they are located in the **lower hemisphere**.

**Platic aspect** <note>original: πλατικος (platikos)</note>, an aspect that is reckoned by sign only, where the signs themselves "see" each other even if the degrees are not exact.

**Partile aspect**, when the planets are separated by the exact number of degrees required for the configuration. For example, if the first degree of Aries is rising in the East, and the first degree of Libra (where a malefic planet is located) is setting into the lower hemisphere in the West, or is at a point not very distant from it.

# ON DEFINITIONS AND TERMS

**The pivot of the rising sky**, today called the **ascendant**.
**Position** <note>original: ἐποχὴ (epochē)</note>: the degrees by which the planets are located in the zodiac.
**Portion** <note>original: Μοῖρα (moira)</note>: the space of a single degree.
**Primary minutes** <note>original: πρῶτα λεπτά (prōta lepta)</note>: the first divisions of a degree.
**Secondary minutes** <note>original: Δέυτερα λεπτά (deutera lepta)</note>: the second divisions of a degree <note>modern seconds</note>.
**The meridian circle**, which the Sun marks when it arrives over the human crown <note>the zenith</note>, creating the midpoint of the day.
**Elementalists** <note>original: στοιχιοματικοὶ (stoichiomatikoi)</note>: those who create seals and images from chemical mixtures according to the paths of the stars, whether to heal diseases or to procure other effects of the body or soul.
**Mathematicians** <note>original: μαθηματικοὶ (mathēmatikoi)</note>: this was first the name for the disciples of Pythagoras because they professed Geometry, Sun-dial calculation <note>original: Gnomonicam</note>, Music, and other disciplines; the ancient Greeks called these "learnings" <note>original: μαθήματα (mathēmata)</note>. The common people, however, use the word "Mathematicians" for those who ought to be called by their ethnic name, **Chaldeans** <note>A term often used for Babylonian astrologers</note>. Subsequently, those who were distinguished by these scientific studies proceeded to investigate the works of the world and the principles of nature, and only then were they called **Physicists** <note>original: φυσικοί (physikoi); students of natural philosophy</note>. Author: Aulus Gellius <note>A Roman author of the 2nd century AD</note>.
**Cube** <note>original: κύβος (kybos)</note>: a four-sided <note>six-faced</note> figure.
**Line** <note>original: γραμμὴ μῆκος ἀπλατὲς (grammē mēkos aplatēs)</note>: that is, a line and length without breadth.
**The Wagon** <note>original: ἅμαξα (hamaxa)</note>: a celestial chariot. Our ancestors called it the **Septentriones** <note>The North</note> after the yoked oxen—that is, from the seven stars out of which the **Triones** <note>Threshing oxen</note> are shaped as if yoked together.

### NAMES OF THE WINDS ACCORDING TO GELLIUS

**Eurus**: the wind blowing from the spring east (the equinox), otherwise called the **Sun-facing wind** <note>original: ἀπηλιώτης (apēliōtēs)</note>, and nicknamed **Subsolanus** <note>Beneath-the-sun</note> by Roman sailors.
**Aquilo Boreas**: which comes from the summer and solstitial turning-point of the east; Homer called it the **Bringer of Clear Skies** <note>original: αἰθρηγενέτης (aithrēgenetēs)</note>. They think **Boreas** is named after the "cry" <note>original: βοῆς (boēs)</note> because it has a violent and loud blast.
**Vulturnus**: blows from the east, called **Euronotus** <note>original: εὐρόνοτος</note> in Greek because it sits between the South wind <note>Notos</note> and the East wind <note>Eurus</note>.
**Caurus**: in Greek **Argestes** <note>original: ἀργεστής</note>; it is opposite to Aquilo.
The other is **Favonius**: in Greek **Zephyrus**; it blows opposite to Eurus. See Strabo <note>Ancient Greek geographer</note> on this matter in the first book of his *Geography*.
**Africus**: in Greek **Lips** <note>original: λίψ</note>; it blows opposite to Vulturnus.
**Auster**: in Greek **Notos** <note>original: νότος</note>; since it is cloudy and moist, it is the southern wind, for in Greek *notis* <note>original: νοτίς</note> signifies moisture.
**Septentrionarius**: or in Greek **Aparctias** <note>original: ἀπαρκτίας</note>; set opposite and directly toward the South wind.
**Circius**: a wind known primarily to the Gauls, blowing from their own land; it is most fierce and turbulent.
**Iapyx**: blows from the borders of Apulia <note>A region in Southern Italy</note>.
**Fate**: the Greeks call it **Pepromene** <note>original: πεπρωμένην</note> or **Heimarmene** <note>original: εἱμαρμένην</note>. It is, however, as Chrysippus <note>A prominent Stoic philosopher</note> says in Gellius: "a certain eternal and unchangeable series of things, and a chain rolling itself upon itself, and entangling itself through eternal orders of consequence, from which it is fitly connected."
**The Apparition of a planet**: occurs when a planet, which for some time lay hidden under the solar rays, begins to appear in the morning or evening.
A planet is said to **lie hidden** under the solar rays when it is fifteen degrees before or after the Sun.
**Hayz** or the "similitude of a planet": occurs when a day-planet is above the earth by day and below the earth by night; and a night-planet is below the earth by day and above the earth by night. It also occurs when a masculine planet is found in a masculine sign and quadrant and is in the east; whereas a feminine planet is found in feminine signs and quadrant and is in the west.
**Good configurations** of the planets are considered to be: conjunctions of "good" <note>benefic</note> planets with other "good" ones, and "good" aspects—specifically the **trine** <note>an angle of 120 degrees</note> and **sextile** <note>an angle of 60 degrees</note> of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> toward each other, or with the planets, or of the planets among themselves.
**Bad configurations**: conjunctions of "bad" <note>malefic</note> planets, and their aspects of **opposition** <note>180 degrees</note> and **squares** <note>90 degrees; "quarters"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical glossary of astrological terms, moving from definitions of time and practitioners to the specific motions, states, and relationships of the planets and the Moon.</meta>

-># ON ASTROLOGY<-

The greatest weakness of a planet is said to be when it is **combust** <note>original: combustus; this occurs when a planet is so close to the Sun that its own light and influence are "burnt up" or hidden by the Sun’s glare</note>.
**Retrocession** <note>moving backward in the zodiac</note> also diminishes its strength to some degree.
A planet is called **combust** when it is distant from the Sun by less than half of its "orb," or by that exact amount both before and after the Sun.
The half-orb for **Saturn** and **Jupiter** is nine degrees.
The half-orb for **Mars**, **Venus**, and **Mercury** is seven degrees.
The half-orb for the **Moon** is twelve degrees.
The half-orb for the **Sun** is fifteen degrees.
A **progressing** planet is one whose motion, as written in the *Ephemeris* <note>a table of predicted stellar positions</note>, is increasing.
A planet is said to be **retrograding** when its motion decreases.
A **planetary station** is said to occur when the planet is varied by no motion of degrees or minutes <note>the moment a planet appears to stand still before changing direction</note>.
A planet moves **swiftly** when its true motion is faster than its mean <note>average</note> motion, according to the sequence of the signs.
It is said to fall into **slowness** when it moves backward, or when it proceeds more slowly than its mean motion.
A planet is called **increased in light** when it moves away from the Sun, or the Sun moves away from it.
A planet is **diminished in light** when it approaches the Sun, or the Sun approaches it.
The **argument of the Moon's latitude** is the distance of the lunar head from the "Head of its Dragon" <note>the North Node, the point where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>.
Planets are called **enemies** when they have opposing houses. For example, **Saturn** and the **Moon**; for **Cancer**, the house of the Moon, is opposite to **Capricorn**, which is the house of Saturn.
There is also an enmity of planets by reason of their **exaltations** <note>signs where a planet's influence is most powerful</note>. In this way, **Jupiter** is an enemy to **Mars**, since Jupiter's exaltation is in **Cancer** and Mars's is in **Capricorn**, which are opposite signs.
Planets **concord** <note>agree</note> in nature, quality, substance, and power. **Mars** concords with the **Sun** in heat. **Venus** with the **Moon** in cold and humidity. **Jupiter** and **Mercury** concord in their nature.
The **Moon** is named from "light" <note>original: Luna from lumine</note>, because it shines through the reflection of the Sun's light.
The **Sun** <note>original: Sol</note> obtained its name because it alone <note>original: solus</note> among the stars is most powerful, like a prince and leader, or because it has its light from itself and receives it as a loan from no other.
They are called **wandering** or **straying stars**, which are commonly called **planets** or **wanderers**.
**Lunar phases** <note>original: præfulxiones</note>, which by another name they call the "faces" of the Moon. There are ten in number, namely: **conjunction** <note>original: coitus</note>, **genna** <note>the first appearance of the crescent</note>, **rising**, **rising into horns** <note>the crescent shape</note>, **half-divided orb**, **divided**—which is called **dichotomous** <note>original: διχότομος; the first or last quarter</note>—**full moon**, then **half-divided orb** again, and **divided rising into horns**. Some add an eleventh, the **nearly-all-shining** <note>original: Plesiphahen</note>, or as it pleases others, the **nearly-full moon** <note>original: Plesioselinon</note>.
**Conjunction** of the Moon is the name used when it is in the same degree of some sign as the Sun.
The Moon is called **Genna** when it has withdrawn fifteen degrees from its conjunction with the Sun.
The Moon is said to **rise into horns** when, now withdrawing from the Sun, it creates a six-sided figure <note>a sextile aspect, 60 degrees</note>.
The **divided Moon** is that which has departed ninety degrees from the Sun, making a square figure <note>original: mundi sexangulam; likely referring to the quadrature or 90-degree square aspect</note>.
The **half-divided orb** Moon is that which is distant by 120 degrees in sequence from the Sun, having a **trine** aspect <note>symbol: △</note>.
The **Plesioselinos** <note>nearly full</note> Moon is when it is at 150 degrees, no more than four degrees and six signs away, and not yet in opposition.
A **Full Moon** occurs when the Moon is distant from the Sun by 185 degrees and 2 minutes in sequence <note>historically, opposition is 180 degrees; the author may be defining the end of the phase</note>.
The Moon is called **Apocruasis** <note>waning</note> when it has declined one degree from its opposition with the Sun.
**Epacts** are the differences between the solar and lunar years.
A **Solar year** has 365 days.
A **Lunar year** has 354 days.
The difference between these is eleven days, and these are called **Epacts**.
**Beholding signs** <note>original: Spectantium signa</note> are those which restore the magnitudes of days and nights in equal hours. For the greatest hour—fifteen hours long—is when the Sun is in **Cancer**, and the shortest when the Sun is in **Capricorn**.
Signs are said to have **equal power** between themselves which have an equal **ascension** <note>original: anaphoram; the time it takes for a sign to rise over the horizon</note>, even if they follow each other in turn, such as **Aries** and **Pisces**, or **Virgo** and **Libra**. And if to three...

<meta>This page continues the technical glossary of astrological definitions, moving from the movement and light of planets to their relationships, planetary sect, the houses of the zodiac, and the specific geometry of aspects.</meta>

-># ON DEFINITIONS AND TERMS<-

There are four or five signs of **equal rising** <note>original: "anaphoræ"; this refers to signs that take the same amount of time to rise over the horizon</note>, such as **Aries** and **Libra**, **Gemini** and **Sagittarius**, **Cancer** and **Capricorn**, **Leo** and **Aquarius**, and **Virgo** and **Pisces**. Some say these signs "hear" one another, but do not "see" one another, because of the shadow of the earth.

**Diurnal stars** <note>planets belonging to the "day" faction</note> are what he calls **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. They are said to belong to the faction of the **Sun** itself because they do not set or change their figures as frequently; they "rejoice" to exercise their influence during the day and in the diurnal houses.

**Nocturnal stars** are **Mars** and **Venus**, which are companions of the **Moon**. They take on many different figures and often set and are obscured.

The **promiscuous** <note>common or neutral</note> star is **Mercury**, for it becomes a companion to those whose form it adopts: it is "matutine" <note>appearing in the morning</note> with the Sun and "vespertine" <note>appearing in the evening</note> with the Moon.

The **houses of the stars**, which they also call **zones** or **belts**, are the twelve **twelfth-parts** <note>original: "dodecatemoria"</note> of the zodiac, which they also call signs.

**Apoclimata** are **declinations** <note>the "falling away" of a house from one of the four main angles of a chart</note>.

There are four **centers** <note>the angles of a chart</note>: the **horoscope** <note>the Ascendant, or the point rising on the eastern horizon</note>, the **setting** <note>the Descendant, or western horizon</note>, the **midday** <note>the Midheaven or MC</note>, and the **place under the earth**, or **underworld** <note>the IC or Imum Coeli</note>.

A **twelfth-part** <note>original: "dodecatemorion"</note> is so named because it is the twelfth part of the signs.

The **figures** of the stars are what he calls their testimonies to one another, namely: **triangles** <note>trines</note>, **squares**, **six-angles** <note>sextiles</note>, and **diameters** <note>oppositions</note>.

They call a figure **Right** (triangle, square, or sextile) when it is the sign from which the star has departed. They call it **Left** when it is the sign to which the star is going. For example, if the **Sun** is in **Leo**, the **Right** triangle is in **Aries** and the **Leo** trine <note>original: ▵</note>. The **Left** is in **Sagittarius**. The **Right** square is **Taurus** and **Leo**, and the **Left** is **Scorpio**. The **Right** sextile <note>original: ✳</note> is **Gemini** and **Leo**, and the **Left** is **Libra**.

Any star spreads **seven rays**: three indeed upwards, and the same number downwards, and one further across the diameter. Those which are upwards are **Right**, and those which are downwards are **Left**.

They call it **Parallagen** <note>parallax or shift</note> when stars have a change in their isosceles lines <note>geometrical alignment</note> through the arrangement of their degrees, such as the **Sun** at 19 degrees of **Aries** and **Saturn** at 20 degrees of **Libra**.

**Contact** and **agglutination** <note>original: "agglutinatio," a "gluing together"</note> are terms for the meeting and standing together of two stars in one twelfth-part, at nearly the same degree. This contact—which is also called *kollesis* <note>original: κόλλησις; Greek for "gluing"</note> and in Latin can be called **agglutination** or **coupling**—occurs when they touch in the same degree, either by body or by any figure where a preceding star meets a succeeding one. If it happens to move faster, the one that precedes is overtaken by the one following; then one star prevents the other in one part and touches it, or is not further away than three degrees.

**Efflux** <note>separation</note> occurs when, after contact, the faster star is distinguished from the slower-moving one. Or, as **Porphyry** <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and astrologer</note> prefers, it is called **Efflux** when a star flows away from another star more quickly than the slower one, either from a recently made coupling or from a contact through a figure, when they begin to have more middle degrees between them than is proper for forming a figure.

A star is called **Orbicular** when the following star hurls a ray into the preceding figure.

Signs are called **disjunct** and **averse** when they do not form a figure <note>aspect</note> between themselves.

A star is said to be **hemmed in** <note>original: "circumuallari," like being surrounded by a wall</note> when it is in such a figure that it is hedged in. For instance, if the **Moon** is in **Virgo** and **Mars** is in **Aries**, it encompasses **Virgo**, **Leo**, and **Libra**. One ray of **Mars** is carried into the triangle of **Leo**, while the other is in the diameter of **Libra**; the **Moon** is therefore called **hemmed in** by the malevolent stars.

This is also called **obsession** <note>besieging</note> when two stars have, in a certain way, enclosed one star in the middle, with no other star sending a ray in between them.

**Middle-hurling** is the name used when a star projects a ray into the middle degrees.

**Transvection** <note>translation of light</note> is said to occur when a star couples with another star, and that one in turn with another; for it carries the "setting" <note>influence</note> of one into the "setting" of the other.

**Complex** <note>collection of light</note> is said to occur when different and various stars are gathered to one star; for then that star assumes the power of those others for itself.

**Aversion** occurs when the lord of the **horoscope** <note>Ascendant</note> is not coupled with the lord of the signifying horoscope, which concerns questions <note>horary astrology</note>.

<summary>This page defines the fundamental geometry and relationships of astrology, including the "sect" of planets (day vs. night), the four angles of a chart, and the specific ways planets "touch" or "separate" from one another through aspects.</summary>
<keywords>zodiac signs, diurnal stars, nocturnal stars, Mercury, dodecatemoria, angles, aspects, trine, square, sextile, opposition, application, separation, Porphyry, translation of light, collection of light, besieged planets</keywords>

# ON ASTROLOGY

A planet is called **Excelling** or **Overcoming** when it is placed in the twelfth <note>original: "duodecimo." While the text says twelfth, the examples provided—Libra over Capricorn, and Capricorn over Aries—describe planets in a "square" relationship, specifically the tenth sign relative to another in the order of the zodiac</note> sign relative to another that is in the fourth. For example, a planet in **Libra** overcomes one in **Capricorn**, and one in **Capricorn** overcomes one in **Aries**.

**Aphetes** <note>original: "releaser" or "starter"</note> is the name for a planet when it moves from its rising to its setting; that is, moving from the succeeding signs toward the preceding ones.

Conversely, it is called **Profthetes** <note>original: "one who moves forward"</note> when it moves from its setting to its rising, namely from the preceding signs toward the succeeding ones.

A planet is called **Hypaugus** <note>original: "under the rays"</note> when the Sun itself has overtaken or hidden it under its brilliance and within its rays.

**Emergence** or **Emersion** is when a fleeing planet first flashes out from the light of the Sun.

**Morning Emergence** is when it first appears at the rising <note>the eastern horizon</note>.

**Evening Emergence** is when it first emerges at the setting <note>the western horizon</note>.

Furthermore, there are two places in the heavens, separated by the diameter of the circle, which they also call **Ecliptic Conjunctions**, because solar and lunar eclipses occur within them when the luminaries are there. One of these points of union is called **Anabibazon** <note>the Ascending Node</note> ☋, which more recent writers call the **Tail of the Dragon**, and the other is **Catabibazon** <note>the Descending Node</note> ☊, which they have called the **Head of the Dragon** <note>Note that the author has swapped the traditional symbols and names: usually, the Head (Anabibazon) is ☊ and the Tail (Catabibazon) is ☋</note>.

A **Border** or **Confine** is said to exist when stars are within the same "terms" <note>sub-divisions of a zodiac sign ruled by different planets</note>, whether they are joined in a physical conjunction or by an "aspect" figure, such as when they regard each other while both are in the terms of the same star.

**Void of Course**—called <term>kenodromia</term> in Greek—is when the **Moon** is joined to no other planet, whether by degree, by figure <note>aspect</note>, or by physical assembly, and will not enter into a conjunction for nearly thirty degrees.

**Exhalma**, which is also called **Exaltation**, occurs when the **Sun**, **Moon**, or the **Lot of Fortune** pass out of their sign from the birth chart and fall into the following sign.

**Ecptosis** or **Falling Away** is when the "year" <note>likely referring to a profection or time-lord system</note>, calculated from the horoscope <note>Ascendant</note>, falls into that sign where the preceding conjunction occurred in the birth chart.

There are five **Liberating Places** <note>original: "liberatoria loca," places of release</note> in the hemisphere above the earth: the **Midheaven**, the two signs on either side of it (the succeeding and the preceding), the **Horoscope** <note>Ascendant</note>, and the **Setting** <note>Descendant</note>.

The **Releasers** themselves are four: the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the **Lot of Fortune**, and the presiding **Lord of the Birth** <note>the planet that rules the chart</note>.

Stars are said to be situated **In Their Splendors** when they are placed in their own house, in their exaltation, or within their own terms.

**Participation** is when a planet is the partner of the same sign or regards that planet favorably. A **Partner of the Sign** is a co-ruler. They rule together when one planet's house is another's exaltation.

**Resolution into the Opposite**—which is named <term>anatachysis</term>—is when day-stars hold the houses or exaltations of night-stars, or vice versa; or when stars placed in signs give good indications, but the lords of those signs are hindered by malice.

**Malice** <note>original: "malitia," or affliction</note> occurs when a planet is struck by destructive rays, or is besieged, or is in contact with a destructive planet, or is in conjunction with one, or comes into opposition, or is overcome and possessed by a destructive planet that is itself ill-affected.

-> THE END <-

# THE FIRST BOOK ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE STARS BY JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS JUNIOR, A NOBLE OF SICILY, DEDICATED TO MAVORTIUS LOLLIANVUS. <note>original: "Matheseos" — though it looks like "Mathematics," in this period the term referred specifically to the study of the stars, including both astronomy and astrology. "V. C." stands for *Vir Clarissimus*, a title for a member of the Roman senatorial class.</note>

## P R E F A C E.

<insert>LIBRARY OF THE CITY OF LYON</insert>

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial letter 'O'. Inside the letter, a scholar or astronomer is depicted sitting at a desk with an open book, gesturing upwards towards the sky. The background shows an arched window or alcove.</image-desc>

Long ago I promised you, Mavortius—you who are my pride—that I would publish these books, but quite often a wavering modesty held me back. A doubtful trepidation called me away from this zeal for writing, especially since the fragility of my own talent could not conceive of knowing anything that it judged worthy of your ears. For I remembered that all too bold promise, which was beyond my strength, in which I had pledged that I would dedicate to you the entire discipline of divine Astrology. <note>original: "Matheseos"</note> As I hesitated, my mind was frequently invaded now by a pale face, now by a sort of rustic fear.

For when you were established in the high offices of the province of Campania <note>Mavortius Lollianus served as the governor (*consularis*) of Campania around 334–337 CE.</note>—an administration in which your nobility shines with the highest dignity of honor—the harshness of the winter frosts came upon you. This persuaded you to step away from your affairs and, exhausted by the variety of a long and laborious journey, to relax both your mind and your limbs for a little while. You turned aside most pleasantly to me first, here on these Sicilian shores, to those very studies to which each of us has been bound since early youth. Here, you strove to relieve the exhaustion of my aging, weary, and fatigued body with the loyal and most sacred comforts of friendship.

However, when health was restored and had called me back to my former state through your consolations and remedies, we took turns recounting our past deeds and calling to mind the charms of a lighter age; we shared noble and varied stories with one another in conversation. But after we had talked of our own actions and progress, you inquired of me (as you remember) about the situation of all Sicily, where I live and where I was born, and you sought out everything that the ancient myths have handed down, along with an explanation of their true reasoning.

You asked what Scylla <note>In myth, a sea monster; in reality, a dangerous rock or whirlpool in the Strait of Messina.</note> means in herself, or what Charybdis is; what causes the turbulent confusion of the waves rushing together in the straits, which the separate and divided seas join at a certain time and space of the hours through the opposing collision of the waves. You asked what causes the fires that break out from the peak of Etna; what is their nature or substance, and from what origin such great fires are produced and breathed out without the loss of the mountain itself. You asked about the nature of the lake shown near the bed of the Symaethus river, which is named Palicus; <note>The Lake of Naftia, known for its volcanic carbon dioxide springs which caused the water to "boil" and smell of sulfur.</note> a lake always foul with a lurid thickness, growing dark with leaden foams and, hissing with a noisy "marriage," <note>original: "coniugio" — likely referring to the two craters or "brothers" within the lake bubbling together.</note> whistling with a sharp murmur.

You also recollected and inquired with me about all the other wonders of the Sicilian province that both Greek and Roman literature have handed down to you from your earliest years. Finally, you turned the flow of your speech and the order of your discourse to the Sphere of Archimedes, <note>A famous mechanical planetarium or orrery attributed to the mathematician Archimedes of Syracuse, which demonstrated the movements of the sun, moon, and planets.</note> showing me the prudence and learning of your divine talent.

You asked: what do those nine globes signify? What do the five Zones do, which are colored by different kinds of nature? What do the twelve signs of the Zodiac achieve? What is produced by the eternal wandering of the five stars? <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note> What of the sun’s daily courses and yearly returns? What of the moon’s swift motion and the constant increases or losses of its light? By how many revolutions is that "Greater Year" completed, of which they speak, which restores these five stars—and the moon and sun as well—to their original places and beginnings; a cycle that is terminated in a circuit of one thousand, four hundred and sixty-one years? <note>This refers to the Sothic Cycle, a period used in ancient Egyptian and Greek astronomy to align the calendar with the stars.</note> What reason creates the Milky Way? What causes the eclipse of the sun and moon? Why does the rotating whirling of the sky never move the Great Bear <note>original: "septentriones" — the seven stars of the Big Dipper/Ursa Major.</note> to the west, nor restore it to the east? What part of the earth lies under the North Wind, and what part under the South? What reason suspends the earth itself, placed in the middle, by a balanced moderation of equality? To what extent does the Ocean, which they call the Atlantic Sea, surround the space of the land in the manner of an island with its waves...

Mavortius's deep interest in the mechanics of the cosmos and the "Great Year" prompted Firmicus to finally overcome his modesty and write this treatise.</summary>

Firmicus Maternus is addressing his patron, Mavortius Lollianus, explaining why he finally decided to write this treatise after long hesitation. He defends the science of astrology against skeptics by comparing their disagreements to the famous philosophical debates about the nature of the gods and the soul.</meta>

...might end in confusion. When all these things were handed down to me by you, Mavortius—the jewel of good men—through your easy mastery of demonstration, I myself dared to bring forth something with the boldness of unadvised speech: I promised that I would publish for you whatever the ancient Egyptian sages and divine men, and the wise Babylonians, have handed down to us through the teaching of divine doctrine concerning the power of the stars and the capacities of our divine science. Therefore, as you yourself know, I was reckless in that promise, and—to speak the truth with you—I frequently reproached myself with severe rebuke, and I desired, if it were permitted, to change my promise. But the encouragement of your discourse lifted up my trepidation and compelled me to attempt what I had frequently abandoned out of despair. For when the serene and venerable judgments of our Lord and Emperor Constantine Augustus <note>Constantine the Great, the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity, who reigned from 306–337 CE.</note> had handed over to you the governance of the entire East, you let no time pass without demanding from us what we had promised you by that unadvised pledge. Therefore, to you, as Proconsul and Consul-elect, we fulfill our promises, praying and asking for pardon, lest in these books you seek the weight and perfect grace of oratory, or expect that great treatises, or heavy and firm opinions, or monuments of doctrine and eloquence be found by your judgment. In us, talent is thin, speech is slight, and—what must be truly confessed—our knowledge of the stars <note>original: "Mathesis"</note> is very modest. Although all these things troubled us with various forms of despair, we have nevertheless undertaken the labor of writing, so that—even though bound by arduous and most difficult promises—we might not fail the expectations of your wisdom, most learned Lollianus. 

Established therefore in the entrance-hall of this discourse and in the very beginnings of its principles, we ought to do nothing else but respond to those who attempt to undermine the whole power of the Knowledge of the Stars <note>original: "Matheseos"</note> with a manifold kind of speech—those who think they can, with the authority of lofty speech, break through all this philosophy and divine science with their opinions and disputes. In my judgment, and as is proven by the facts themselves, it is not the weakness or falsehood of the doctrine itself that encourages them, but rather the zeal of those who contradict it, so that the pugnacious liberty of argumentation might resist certain and defined things which we perceive not only with the mind and reason, but behold with the very sharpness and judgment of our eyes. For they attempt, through their overly hidden and subtle disputes, to go from the very first responses of the mathematicians—as if through some underground tunnel—to the undermining of this entire science. The more violently they fight, and the more they seek every way of persuasion, the more vehemently and strongly they fortify the faith of astrology. For its substance would not be true unless they struggled against it with such great forces of argument. 

Nor is this worthy of wonder, since we know how much dissension there is among those very people concerning the nature of the gods, and with how many arguments of dispute they attempt to overthrow the entire power of divinity: <margin>Various opinions about the Gods.</margin> since some say that gods do not exist, others define that they do exist but care for nothing, while others say they both exist and undertake the care and management of our affairs; and all of these are engaged in such variety and dissension that it would be long and out of place—especially at this time when we have undertaken another work—to enumerate the opinions of each one. For some attribute figures to them according to their own will, and assign places, even establish seats, and describe many things about their acts and lives, and pronounce that all things which have been made and established are ruled and governed by their will. Others have said that they accomplish nothing, care for nothing, and are free from all care of administration; and they all bring forward something plausible that invites the minds of listeners to a readiness of belief. Indeed, those things said about the immortality of the soul by that divine Plato and the most sharp and ardent Aristotle are shown to be contrary and repugnant to one another. For concerning good and evil, their opinions are diverse and shifting among themselves; the explanation of which I think should be bypassed for now. For we have not entered into this kind of dispute, nor have we formed our mind and plan to refute or confirm these things. But we have touched upon all these things in a brief speech so that the contentious fabrications of those who contradict might be revealed to all men, their own zeal having been laid open. It is pleasing, therefore, to review what is said about the Knowledge of the Stars <note>original: "Mathesi"</note>, and I am concerned to touch upon everything said by them in a brief speech. For since we are about to explain the substance of the Knowledge of the Stars <note>original: "Matheseos"</note> and astrology, we ought not to linger longer in the works of others.

### CHAPTER I. ARGUMENTS AGAINST ASTROLOGY BY ITS RIVALS.

FIRST, therefore, they <note>The "rivals" or critics of astrology, likely referring to New Academy skeptics or certain Christian apologists.</note> argue regarding the characters and complexions of men. They say: If human character and color are attributed to the mixtures of the stars—as if the courses of the stars compose the features of mortal bodies through some kind of painting and craftsmanship—that is, if the Moon <note>original: ☽</note> makes men white, Mars <note>original: ♂</note> makes them red, and Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> makes them black: why are all people in Ethiopia born black, in Germany white, and in Thrace red? It is as if the Moon and Mars have no strength or power in Ethiopia, or as if the star of Saturn abandons its power and its license to shape forms in Germany and Thrace. Regarding character, they add this: If Saturn makes men cautious, grave, slow, greedy, and silent; Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note> makes them mild, good, kind, and modest; Mars makes them cruel, treacherous, and fierce; the Sun <note>original: ☉</note> makes them religious, noble, and proud; Venus <note>original: ♀</note> makes them lustful, charming, and shining with the splendor of honest grace; Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> makes them astute, clever, and turbulent with the shifting of a restless mind; and the Moon makes them sharp, splendid, elegant, and prevailing by the grace of popular favor: why are certain nations so formed that they are conspicuous, as it were, by a specific unity of character? The Scythians alone <note>The Scythians were nomadic peoples of Central Eurasia, often stereotyped by Greeks and Romans as the archetype of "barbaric" ferocity.</note> wander with a monstrous cruelty of ferocity. Italians are always brilliant with a regal nobility; Gauls are dull-witted; Greeks are fickle; Africans are deceitful; Syrians are greedy; Sicilians are sharp; Asians are always lustful and occupied with pleasures; Spaniards are perverse with a lofty spirit of boasting. Therefore, does Jupiter never mitigate the madness of the Scythians? Or will the Sun one day deny empire to the Italians? Does the star of Saturn not impose weight upon the fickleness of the Greeks? Is Asian lewdness not corrected by the sober moderation of Jupiter? Is the sharpness of the Sicilians never blunted by the cold strike of Saturn? Is the greed of the Syrians not tempered by the lustful radiations of Venus? <note>original: "Venetis radiationibus," likely a variant or error for "Veneris" (of Venus).</note> Nor will the saving star of Jupiter hinder the malicious deceptions and double-tongued minds of the Africans; nor can the sluggish light of Saturn humble the boasting of the Spaniards; nor will Mercury, that most wise star, sharpen Gallic dullness.

Meanwhile, their most powerful and vehement peroration <note>A concluding part of a speech intended to inspire enthusiasm or, in this case, to deliver a final blow to an argument.</note> placed against us is this: they say that according to the principles of this art, all duties of virtue are removed from human affairs. If temperance, fortitude, prudence, and justice are attributed to the decrees of the stars and not to our own wills, then we no longer depend on the constant pursuit of virtues, but on the influx of the stars alone. On the contrary, if anyone should break the bond of society and charity, neglect the laws of human conciliation, and hand himself over entirely to ferocity and treachery, following his own crime and the perverse desires of his mind, he may ascribe it to the judgments of the stars. Let him be unjust, let him be treacherous; let him be malevolent, let him be irreligious—because the constellation of Mercury with Mars accomplishes these envious evils—he may now attribute the fault not to himself, but to the driving stars. Why do we strengthen our minds with the study of fortitude? Why, formed with an upright mind, sublime constancy, and the mastery of divine virtues, do we despise death and pain when placed in bitter circumstances? If the Sun, in a favorable conjunction with Jupiter, bestows the praise of glory and the insignia of most powerful dignity upon us even when we do not seek it, then it is in vain that we suppress the vices of an erring mind through counsel; in vain do we temper the lustful allurements of desire; in vain, by the instinct of gravity, do we seek equity, modesty, and laws, if Mercury, tempered by the good radiations of Jupiter and the Moon, inflames us toward the desires and cravings of that very virtue.

They even address individual men with this line of argument: "You hold in vain, O good man, the choice of good things and the desire to flee from evil, if you feel yourself compelled toward them from elsewhere. Why do you fortify yourself with honorable provisions and the support of diligence, if Saturn or Jupiter provided all this to you, not through your own knowledge?" Let us therefore (if it seems right) despise the gods and make public the sacred and venerable ceremonies of religion with the sacrilegious heat of despair, if without their divine power, with only the stars helping, we can achieve everything. Why, O plowman, do you invoke the gods? Without the care of your deity, and by the influx of the stars alone, the furrow is made level for the spirit of the crop. You, who across the open ridges arrange the line of vineyards in distinct rows, in vain do you offer devoted vine-shoots to your Liber <note>An Italian god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus or Dionysus.</note> with the religious trembling of anyone, if without his protection...
