of divinity, are either denied or granted by the course of the stars. You, who promulgate laws and sanction rights, take away the decrees, break the legal tablets, and free us from those most severe punishments. It was Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> (as the astrologers claim) who made that man sacrilegious; it was Venus <note>original: ♀</note> who made that one an adulterer; and it was the star of Mars <note>original: ♂</note> that armed that man for the slaughter of others. It is Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> who compels a man to forge documents or mix poisons; he is the one who, with wicked incantations, rouses the peaceful souls of the dead, even those already purified by the forgetfulness of the River Lethe <note>In mythology, the river in the underworld that caused souls to forget their past lives before reincarnation.</note>. Look there: that man is inflamed by incestuous passions, or you see another clinging to the embraces of boys—we attribute the cause of such great evil to Mars or Venus. And yet, that man is struck down by the hand of the executioner at your command, without cause; the sentence passed against him is a mistake if he was compelled to sin not by his own desire, but by the flawed radiation of the stars. You magistrates have no just basis for punishment, because you know we are always incited to these vices by the malignant fuel of the stars. 

These and other similar speeches they compose, asking whether we say the stars are animate or inanimate beings, hoping that by the conclusion of this question we will be confused and find it difficult to express the judgment and opinion of our minds. For whichever of these is said, they turn it to the contrary with the stings of their syllogisms, so that the speech of those responding is forced to agree with their own whim. In these matters and disputes, we certainly praise their cleverness, but we avoid their purpose and method, because astrology <note>original: *astrologia*</note> has proven its good faith to us through the divine and most manifest authorities of its responses and <term>results<gloss>original: *apotelesmatum*; the predicted outcomes or effects of planetary configurations</gloss></term>. 

Certain others add—so that they might seem to agree with us on one hand, while on the other, they disturb this entire science with a flattering consensus born of despairing doubt—that while this teaching has the greatest power, no mortal can reach it with total clarity. They cite the brevity of the minute parts of the zodiac, the extremely rapid course of the stars, and the steep, whirling fall of the heavens' rotation. They do this so that by their plausible-sounding definitions, the substance of the entire science might be undermined. We, however, though our talent is thin and our speech almost ineffective in its narrow oratory, ought to refute what they say using only the truth of the matter itself. We should confirm the precepts of this divine science through the consistency of its responses and results. Nevertheless, we shall respond, asking for your indulgence, Lollianus <note>Mavortius Lollianus, the Roman senator to whom this work is dedicated.</note>, our great honor, so that in all our refutations, the faithfulness of the truth—not the splendor and substance of the oratory—is what is sought.

### THE REFUTATION OF OBJECTIONS.
#### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'E' featuring ornate foliage and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
And first, I would wish that this vehement accuser of the <term>Mathematicians<gloss>original: *Mathematicorum*; in this era, this term specifically referred to practitioners of astrology rather than modern arithmetic</gloss></term>, who pursues this art with such lofty speech, would declare whether he has ever personally undertaken any experiment in this science. I wonder if no one ever gave him a true answer when he inquired, or if he instead refused to listen, fearing his ears would be defiled by such responses. Perhaps he is simply being severe and forceful, disturbing the laws of all divinity in a way, sharpening the stings of his arguments with the license of practiced speech. If he received true answers to his questions, and the certainty of truth confirms the opinion of the one who responded, why does he brand with infamy what he ought to have admired? Why does this treacherous accuser attack a divine science with the mind of a traitor? 

If, however, the one who professed to know <term>Astrology<gloss>original: *Mathesin*; the divine knowledge of the stars</gloss></term> was unable to fulfill what he said because of erratic responses, and his lies stained the promise of his words, then it is only that man's ignorance and rashness—not Astrology itself—that should be attacked. It is the deceptive promise that should be brought into infamy. Indeed, such a man is worthy of every misfortune for causing the study of so noble an art to be overshadowed by the false lies of his answers. 

But he who has refused to ask or hear anything, and has not lent the judgment of his ears to those who answer truly—fearing, no doubt, that the faith of the truth would shatter his rigid thoughts—acts unjustly. He is wrong to think he should criticize whatever he could not, or would not, perceive with the dull focus of his mind. For as we know, those judges are always unjust who pronounce judgment on things unknown to them. Those who are led to make a determination by the unskilled license of rashness possess no authority to judge, nor do they bring a sentence to its proper effect if they have not thoroughly examined the allegations of the [other] party...

<meta>The previous page concluded with a skeptical argument suggesting that if the stars control human actions, then laws and punishments are unjust because the "sinner" is merely following a celestial command. This page begins the transition into Firmicus Maternus’s defense of the science of astrology, shifting from the critics' words to his own philosophical justification of why the study is difficult yet divine.</meta>

...they are held. Hence, if someone who has heard, believed, and approved something from a most wise Mathematician <note>original: "Mathematico"; in this period, the term referred primarily to astrologers because the study was seen as a branch of applied mathematics.</note> then attacks it out of a malicious instinct of mind and a pugnacious zeal, he has conceived a notable desire for contradiction. If, however, an unskilled professor gave false answers to his questions, let the deceptive and reckless ignorance of the man be noted, not the Mathematical Science <note>original: "Mathesis"; the art of astrology.</note> itself. He who neither wished to listen nor to judge claims the role of pronouncing judgment in vain; for of that thing which he refused to experience, he is not a fit judge to note its substance.

As for the fact that some deter us from this study by citing the difficulty of its science, we willingly embrace this. For true
<margin>The soul polluted by vices.</margin>
matters are arduous and difficult, and a soul hindered by the earthly snares of filth—even though it was formed by the fiery immortality of divinity—cannot easily perceive them by a simple method of inquiry. Its divinity, which is sustained by eternal movement, suffers a kind of temporary loss of its godhood if it is enclosed in an earthly body, since its force and substance are dulled by the union and fellowship of the earthly body and the constant dissolution of its immortality. 

From this, it happens that all things pertaining to the investigation of the divine arts always present a difficult knowledge to you. Therefore, because we willingly and easily agree on this part, showing why divine things are perceived through difficult inquiry, you must also confess that the soul—which is immortal—if it is separated from the vices and lusts of the earthly body and retains the constancy of its origin and seed, acknowledging the power of its own majesty, may easily attain all things thought to be difficult and arduous through the investigation of the divine mind. 

Tell me, who sees the paths of the sea in the heavens? Who, by the rubbing of stones, strikes out the spark of hidden fire? Who has known the powers of herbs? To whom has the whole nature of divinity revealed and betrayed itself, if not to the soul, which, proceeding from celestial fire, was sent in to rule and
<margin>Power of the soul.</margin>
govern earthly fragility? It was the soul itself that handed down the logic of this science, it was the soul that delivered the calculations, it was the soul that showed the courses, regressions, stations, associations, increases, risings, and settings of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars which we call "wanderers" <note>original: "errantes"</note> but are called "planets" <note>original: "planetae"</note> by the Greeks. And though situated in the fragility of an earthly body, the soul, by a brief recollection of its own majesty, did not "learn" these things in order to pass them on, but "recognized" them.

Behold, it is recognized, and the soul finds in which sign the star of
<margin>The star Saturn.</margin>
Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> rejoices, and when its coldness grows warm by the fuel of another's heat. Behold, we gather its motions and courses through individual days and hours. We also predict when it will return to its former station in retrograde, when the neighboring divinity of the Sun may drive its sluggish courses with the royal authority of majesty, when the heat of the Sun departing from it gives quiet power to its slow agitation, and after how much time it returns with sluggish exertion to that same part of the sign from which it had once departed. 

These things are also seen in the star of Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note>
<margin>Jupiter</margin>
by the same and equal logic; for although it moves through the twelve signs in a shorter space of time, it strikes with a similar
<margin>Mars</margin>
agitation. Mars <note>original: ♂</note> also, whom you see blood-red with the fiery heat of lightnings and terrible with the menacing flash of light—behold, when he comes to the moist house of Saturn, he tempers his fires by the nature of the other's cold; and though the
<margin>Venus, Mercury</margin>
courses of this star are more rapid, they are nonetheless seen by the same logic. 

The daily services of Venus <note>original: ♀</note> and Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> have also been shown to us. For these stars, within a short intervening space, run around the Sun's orb together; they either follow it, or one star following allows the other the service of going before it. We know when they appear to us in the evening rising or the morning rising; when they lie hidden, obscured by the Sun's orb; and when, freed from the brilliance of its rays, they shine forth with their own clear luster. 

What do you think of the course of the Moon <note>original: ☽</note>? By which we
<margin>Moon</margin>
have learned when she announces the losses of her worn orb with solemn supplements, and when, impoverished of her lights, she acknowledges the loss of her own majesty. For she, whether waxing or waning, when near the Sun, lowers the rays of her light as if venerating the Sun, so that, adorned again by her brother's fires when she makes her course more distant, she may carry around the ornaments of her shining brilliance, reborn and renewed. 

Behold, we learn another even greater thing, which, whenever it occurs,
<margin>Eclipse.</margin>
always disturbs unskilled men with monstrous fear: when the Sun <note>original: ☉</note> in the middle of the day...

...hindered by the rays of the moon, as if by certain obstacles, [the sun] denies the shining light of its splendor to all mortals. This event, the wise focus of the Mathematicians <note>original: "Mathematicorum"; in the 4th century, this term referred to astrologers and astronomers who used complex calculations.</note> predicted would happen for all people during the consulship of Optatius and Paulinus <note>Flavius Optatus and Amnius Anicius Paulinus were consuls in the year 334 AD, providing a contemporary reference for the author’s audience.</note>. Likewise, we have frequently seen during the serenity of a clear night that the moon fails in a similar way when it is shadowed by the heights of the earthly regions <note>This refers to a lunar eclipse, where the Earth's shadow falls on the moon.</note>. The genius of the Mathematicians gathered all these observations and, through skillful calculation, thoroughly learned the secrets of divine discourse.

I would wish, therefore, for you—whoever you are—to answer my question: what do you think is more difficult? To discover the courses of the stars, which I have just explained have now been found? These stars are carried now through the heights, now through the breadths, now through the depths; they join themselves now to the regions and winds of the South, now to those of the North. Sometimes they withdraw, sometimes they hide; they move now in a direct course, now in a retrograde <note>term: "retrograde" refers to the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky as seen from Earth.</note> motion; sometimes they stand still in a stationary slowness and, by this very variety of their course, they confound the focus of those seeking them. Or is it more difficult, once the courses of the stars have been found, to determine what their mixture and radiation achieve across the entire circuit of the earth?

Since you are compelled by the very truth of reason to agree that we have found these courses of the stars through the persistent observation of calculation, you must necessarily agree that, once the stellar course is found, we may easily 
<margin>Every beginning is difficult.</margin>
judge their duties and powers afterward. For things are always difficult and arduous when we—as the unrefined and unlearned—approach them with the inconsistency of trepidation. Nor can we easily attain by reason anything which previous mastery has not handed down to us. Thus, we first learn the signs of letters with a certain harshness of dislike. Thus, when set upon an unknown journey, we almost fail at the very first steps. You see how those first learning arithmetic move their fingers with slow agitation; or that man you see swimming, who at first faints from the frequent fear of drowning, but a little later, strengthened by the constant movement of his arms, glides through the highest foam of the waves and supports himself with an easy, mobile lightness. 

Because we run through all these things—that is, letters, arithmetic, music, and the other things we learn—with easy reason only when a confirmed discipline of the mind has grasped the way of their first origin. Therefore, since it is established that it was more difficult to find the courses of the stars than to define what they do—for there is no doubt about the discovered course of the same stars, which we demonstrate to those wishing to learn first by calculation and then by the vision of the eyes themselves—why do you attack this science? By agreeing with its principles and parts, you strengthen its entire substance.

## THE CONFUSION OF ARGUMENTS

### CHAPTER III

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'S' depicting a seated human figure in a classical style within the letter's framework.</image-desc>
It follows that we should discuss complexions and characters, and that we should refute that entire area of spiteful questioning with the true strength of arguments. Once all things have been discussed and cleared away, we may come safely to the secrets of this venerable science itself. "Why," says the critic, "are all people in Ethiopia black, and in Germany white, if the courses of the stars bestow the shapes and colors of men through various mixtures of radiation?" 

Indeed, it would be appropriate for us to fight this part of the question with a copious speech, so that these cunning and spiteful inventions might be conquered by the strength of mature oratory. However, we have restricted our entire zeal for speaking to the strengths of truth alone, lest we transfer the ears of the judges—captured by the charms of a copious speech, the flow of words, and the license of argumentation—to the absurdities of false opinions. 

And first, I would wish for that man to answer my question: within this very people among whom we are now settled, is there one single and similar form for all men, even though there is one nature for all? I believe he will say that our citizens are all formed with a dissimilar variety of faces, and that the form of all is not the same or similar. And if he doubts it (which I do not think he does), let him look when a multitude of the entire populace has gathered in one place, such as in theaters...

Let fathers, children, and brothers come forward together; for although they are joined by the necessity of a single bloodline, they are nonetheless seen to be formed with different features. Nor can anyone be found so similar that his face does not differ in some part from the face of another. From this it is clear that the substance of our race, and the very form of the naked and solitary body, was shaped from a mixture of the **four elements** <note>Ancient science held that all physical things were composed of Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> by the craftsmanship of a provident divinity. Our colors, however, and our forms, even our morals and habits, are distributed to us from no other source than the eternal agitation of the stars' course. For the stars possess their own sense and divine prudence; indeed, by a pure concept of an animated divinity, they obey that highest and governing God—who composed all things by the arrangement of an eternal law—with untiring harmony, in order to preserve the order of perpetual procreation. For there is no

<margin>That there is no prudence on Earth.</margin>
man whom a despair of such sacrilegious recklessness could drive to say that on Earth—where he sees all things are mortal—there is prudence, but that in the heavens—where all things are adorned with the perpetuities of immortality—there is no prudence, no reason, or order of foresight; only a mind of obstinate animosity would define it so. Who doubts that through these stars, that divine mind is infused into earthly bodies by the necessity of a certain law? To this mind, a descent is granted through the orb of the **Sun**, while an ascent is prepared through the orb of the **Moon**. For that divine mind and

<margin>All things are governed by the divine mind.</margin>
celestial soul, situated throughout the entire body of the world in the manner of a circle, and placed now within and now without, governs and composes all things. Conceived by the generation of its own origin, it perpetuates itself in a fiery and everlasting agitation to procreate and preserve all things. Nor does it set aside this duty through any fatigue, sustaining itself, the world, and everything within the world by its own perpetual and untiring mobility. From this soul, these eternal fires of the stars—which are formed in the appearance of a globular roundness and complete their circles and orbits with swift haste—are animated by the majesty of that divine mind. They transfer a portion of the soul to earthly bodies and borrow spirit from those perpetual fuel-sources of the soul. By this reasoning, the immortal soul within us adorns the decaying fragility of the earthly body with the confidence of its own majesty, so that it may, in some part, correspond to its author and origin. This soul, diffused through all living beings born of earthly conception, causes them to flourish through the perpetual propagation of generation, animated by divine nourishment. Therefore, since we are now joined to the stars by a certain kinship, we ought not to deprive them of their own powers through sacrilegious disputes, for by their daily courses we are both formed and created.

When you claim that we could recall men from the worship of the gods and from the profane madness of religious rites by saying that all our acts are accomplished by the divine courses of the stars, you are mistaken. You think the opposite of the truth and dissent too far from true reason. For it is we who cause the gods to be feared and worshipped; we demonstrate their divinity and majesty when we say that all our acts are governed by their divine agitations. Let us therefore worship the gods, whose origin has joined itself to us through the eternal agitation of the stars, and let the human race always receive their majesty with suppliant veneration. Let us humbly invoke the gods and religiously fulfill the vows promised to the divine powers, so that our souls, strengthened by divinity, may in some part resist the **violent powers of the stars' decrees** <note>The author suggests that while stars influence fate, religious devotion and the "divine" part of the human soul can provide a measure of free will or resilience.</note>. A man of divine wisdom,

<margin>Socrates</margin>

"But all these things," he said, "have been overcome by me through prudence and the authority of the virtues; and whatever vice the body possessed from its base composition, the divinity of the soul, well-conscious of itself, has tempered." ...is what we suffer, and what goads us with certain inciting fires; however, it is the divinity of the soul that allows us to resist. For as pertains to the laws by which the sins of men are punished with severe correction, a most wise antiquity established them discreetly. For through these laws, antiquity brought aid to those laboring in spirit, so that through them, the power of the divine mind might purge the destructive vices of the body. But now, for the sake of the person who led us to this necessary inquiry, let us set aside for a moment the discussion regarding character and physical traits—the foundations of which have already been laid in part—and let us show that even the laws serve the power and necessity of the fates, and that they always do what the authority of the fates has decreed. To prove this, we must recount examples at greater length. 

<margin>He indicates the force and necessity of the fates through examples.</margin>
Behold that young man, sound in strength, wealthy, innocent, and modest: driven by no impulse of domestic crime, compelled by no trembling of fear, he hanged himself with a noose and perished. For another man already gasping for breath, an enemy cut the noose; and he who had given himself over to death by his own judgment due to the disgrace of his life, once the noose was loosened, was liberated by the sentence of a judge. Who else accomplished this but the force and necessity of fate? It ensured that the ministers of death, who had been destined to produce the accused, would instead liberate a man overwhelmed by his own evils and condemned by the judgment of his conscience from the midst of the imminent danger of death. 

Then again, consider that man to whom everyone bore witness of innocence: he fell upon a drawn sword as if compelled, and buried the threatening sharp edge of the blade in his innocent ribs. That upright man—sober and modest, whose life and conduct we always admired—behold, he threw his body over a precipice and scattered it in a mournful tearing of limbs. Meanwhile, that just man sustains his life through wretched begging. Yet another, whom the infamy of a notorious crime has stained, is raised up by lucky gains and is heaped with the greatest marks of honor. 

Behold the pirate: after infinite slaughters of the innocent, he receives happy sons into his bloodstained lap. Yet that innocent man, removed from all contagion of crimes, is separated from every gift of happiness by the envy of wicked men. To whom do you attribute these things? Who permits them to happen so? Who has been allowed such power over us? Give me your hand <note>original: "Da manus" - a Latin idiom meaning "yield" or "agree with me."</note>, and finally free us from these conflicts of contention, so that you may confirm, even by your own confession, that all these things which fragile and fleeting mortality is accustomed to bear are seen to be governed by the fortuitous courses of the stars. 

What shall we say of the honors given to the wicked, or the flight and exile of the good? 

<margin>Varying Fortune.</margin>
You see that man, infected with the stains of a slave <note>In the Roman context, this refers to someone of low social birth or "servile" character.</note>, protecting the filth and disgrace of his lineage with the nobility of the consular fasces <note>The *fasces* were a bundle of rods and an axe symbolizing the high judicial and executive power of a Roman Consul.</note>. Another man, carrying the ornaments of free-born blood, is deprived of the marks of honor due to him. One man, placed at the first stage of life and displaying no ornaments of virtue, continues through all honors with headlong speed. Another, already exhausted by the feebleness of declining age and adorned with the testimony of an excellent life, only now begins his first steps in seeking honors. What reason delayed that old man? Or what was it that promised the other man the ornaments of all honors as a merit of his life? 

<margin>The force of fate is accomplished by the movement of the stars.</margin>
What impulse of sudden happiness drove that young man to such a heap of honors, for which we could have hoped for nothing of the sort until now? None other than that power we call Fate, which is accomplished by the agitation of the stars; it worked to compel the one and delay the other. 

What shall I now say regarding the condemnations of the wicked, of sins, or of crimes? 

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
You were saying rightly a moment ago that we frequently see injustices of this kind, by the consenting judgment of all, inflicted upon the innocent. Burdened by a bitter denunciation, undefended and betrayed by envy, he succumbed to the severe power of those passing judgment. 

<margin>Alcibiades.</margin>

Alcibiades suffered these things—he who was instructed in the manner of commanding by the divine teachings of Socrates—and though he had led the army successfully always and everywhere, he nevertheless could not avoid the envy of Fortune raging against him...

<margin>Plato</margin> Fate sold Plato—even with those virtues of mind and that doctrine of wisdom—and handed over that discipline of a divine soul to the cruelties of a tyrant and the mocking power of Dionysius <note>Plato was famously sold into slavery by Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse, after a dispute.</note>. What kind of man he was is known to all: his virtue, wisdom, and prudence, as well as the inventions of his divine mind, were approved by the judgments of both men and gods. Behold, he learned all things to the highest degree, and so that nothing might be lacking to his divine genius, he was imbued even with foreign teachings and penetrated all the secrets of wisdom. To speak more truly, he was the first—or rather the only one—who, while placed in this earthly fragility, found the nature and origin of the provident deity and the divine majesty through the focus of a divine mind. For a saving and provident deity (as some would have it) spoke through him daily; by whose warnings and precepts, having purged the filth of the soul, he attained all the ornaments of virtue. Yet, the most severe decrees of his fellow citizens made him an outcast and an exile. Fleeing his own fatherland and all of Greece, he first passed over to foreign empires and lived as an exile in Sybaris and Croton. But even there, fortune did not hold him for long: for he wandered as a fugitive now through Locri, now through Tarentum, and through almost all the shores of Italy. Behold, in the end, he was surrounded by raging flames and, together with a crowd of miserable men, was consumed by the spreading fire <note>The Pythagorean school in Croton was burned by political rivals, leading to the death of many of his followers.</note>. 

What do you say? Do you even now disparage fate? Do you despise the power of the stars with such stubborn animosity? When you see the bad ends of good men, the prosperous acts of the wicked, and the security of the guilty: to whom do you attribute these things? By whose decrees do you think these things happen? We are unjust if, while all these things are decreed for us by the commands of the fates, we still resist with the animosity of rigid contradiction. In short, you must be answered that present examples exhort us to do this: the one who is guilty is saved by the compulsion of fate, and the one who is innocent is condemned and, driven by fatal necessity, suffers the sentence of severe punishment.

<margin>Plotinus</margin> We shall now come to you, Plotinus—that singular man—so that we may fortify our allegations with the patronage of recent examples. Which parts of philosophy did he not touch? For his doctrine followed the distinctions of his life, and what he taught was demonstrated not by the example of another's virtue, but by his own. From his mouth, as if from some inner sanctuary, divine sentences were brought forth. For that man was composed for all the ornaments of virtue and formed by every study of divine arrangements: just, brave, provident, and temperate, and one who believed he could overcome the impulses of fortune by the reason of providence. Therefore, he first chose for himself a place of quiet residence so that, separated from all the noise of human conversation, he might free himself from the envy of fortune, intending to devote himself only to the marks of divine instruction. Thus, he might arm himself against all the threats of fortune with the whole and incorruptible protection of virtue. 

Raised up by this confidence of mind, he even undertook the care and protection of his body. So that he might leave nothing empty or naked where the license of raging fortune could exert itself, he established himself in a healthy and pure part of the region. For it is told that he chose the pleasant soil of a Campanian city to place his home, where the quiet moderation of the air always sustains all inhabitants with healthy vigor. <margin>Praise of Campania.</margin> There, there is neither the violence of winter nor the approach of the scorching sun, but a composed temperance is moderated from both; there, for men laboring under some sickness, health is restored and nourished by the heat of great springs and the healing warmth of boiling waters. Having settled there, he first despised the emblems of honors, thinking those were true honors which the divine mastery of prudence had conferred upon him. No desires for riches had seized him; rather, he thought those were riches by which the soul, being adorned, could find the author of its own origin. 

Behold, in a certain part of his discourse (as it seems to me), he was improvident and incautious, and he attacked the power of fatal necessity. He chastised men who fear the decrees of fortune with the rebuke of a severe speech, attributing nothing to the power of the stars and reserving nothing for the necessities of the fates, but saying that everything is placed in our own power. It is a long task to enumerate what he said regarding individual matters...

Immediately, without any hesitation, he exercised every kind of cruelty, so that he might satiate the unbridled desires of his soul through the daily shedding of the blood of citizens. <margin>Marius is miserably tortured</margin>
his legs were first crushed, then his arms were cast down from his body's stature, wrenched loose as far as the shoulder; thirdly, his tongue was cut out, leaving his voice in his throat. Behold, in the lists of the proscriptions <note>Proscriptions were published lists of individuals declared outlaws; their property was confiscated, and anyone who killed them was rewarded.</note>, he even wrote the names of women and matrons, so that he might exercise the bloody power of the sword over all of humanity. Nor does he yet have a limit, since he is satisfied neither by bloody greed nor by the infinite slaughter of citizens. That Roman people, after all nations had been subdued, after the world had been traversed and even the furthest shore of the ocean possessed, was compelled to serve the wicked command of Sulla's power. But he, while the minds of all were possessed by a debilitating fear and the most wretched trembling of horror, placed even a third list of proscriptions amidst the Porcian and Sempronian laws <note>The Porcian and Semproian laws were historic Roman statutes intended to protect citizens from summary execution or corporal punishment without trial.</note>, to the groans of all citizens.
<margin>Lucretius.</margin>
Not content with this evil, lest he reserve any time of life free from crimes, he killed Lucretius even as a private citizen; even after laying down his royal power, the destructive cruelty of his mind persisted in him. Do you wish that I tell you something of the Servilian Lake,
<margin>The Servilian Lake.</margin>
since we are lingering on the times of Sulla? In that lake, the heads of many senators hung, with their necks severed, as a display of his most monstrous crime. Secure and arrogant, Sulla always looked upon the wounds of the Republic while standing among the very cushions of the gods and placed amid sacred ceremonies. What can be done more cruelly? He inflicted wretched bereavements upon children and wives under the title of a publicized calamity; nothing was permitted to piety, nothing to faith, nothing to fortitude, nothing to providence against Sulla. Where are they now, those who believe our sins can be punished by law, human and divine? Behold, Sulla feeds on wicked slaughters; behold, he rages with tyrannical command, and no power of divinity opposes his desires. What do you feel? What do you judge? Do you refute what we say? Show us the order of things. Where are the laws? Where are the judgments? We are destitute of human and divine judgment, because Sulla committed all these things we have mentioned with impunity. Therefore, while his crimes were fed by such great slaughters, no whips of the avenging goddesses <note>A reference to the Furies, the mythological deities of vengeance who punished crimes against the natural order.</note> chastised him, nor is there anyone to betray his pain with words and tears. Even the final funeral fire is snatched from those killed by him, and justice could not see this? You say the sins of men are punished day by day by avenging gods: all these things, as you see, were done with impunity, and Fortune did what she wished with them all, and whatever the fates decreed for each individual. These things were fulfilled by the punishment of Sulla's ferocity. And so that you may know we have spoken with true reason, a prosperous outcome followed him after these evils; he was heaped with the insignia of a perpetual Dictatorship, and he laid down his commands by his own will. By his order, the limbs of the mangled republic and the blood-stained money were gathered into the riches of ignoble men. After these evils, he enjoyed quiet security, and fattened by an abundance of crimes, he was honored by a decree of the most distinguished Senate and people with the title of "prosperous and perpetual happiness" <note>original: "nomine prosperae, et perpetuae felicitatis"; referring to Sulla's self-adopted title "Felix," meaning the Fortunate or Lucky.</note>. Where are they now who deny that our acts are governed by the chance courses of the stars? That cruel, treacherous man, whom we know raged through every kind of cruelty, securely attains all the ornaments of dignity. Marius, however—after his triumph over Jugurtha and the other nations he subdued, and after he freed the city of Rome from both foreign and domestic dangers—after the triumphal purple robes, after the embroidered and golden palm-leaf tunics <note>The "toga palmata" was a gold-embroidered robe worn by victorious generals during their triumphs.</note>, is bound in chains with iron shackles. Behold, the exile hides in the marshes of Minturnae; behold, he is weighed down by the squalor of a prison. Do you see how the fugitive approaches the ruins of Carthage? What god had made either Marius an exile or Sulla fortunate? Paulus the commander promised commands to Marius while he was a soldier; Sulla, as a legate, was deserting the Roman army; and yet, afterwards, by the judgment of Fortune, the former was made an exile, and the latter fortunate. In this overlong speech, we have lamented the force and necessity of fate, the power of the stars, and the cruel deeds of Sulla's domination. Scipio, after so many triumphs—

### I

...[Sci]pio, after the destruction of Carthage and the leveling of Numantia, after traveling through Greece, Asia, and Bithynia, and surveying Syria; after the irreproachable acts of his Dictatorship, he was crushed within his own private walls by the domestic plots of his household, by the bitter agony of death and the wicked hands of those who throttled him; he was consumed, in a manner of speaking, by a private execution. 
<margin>Regulus</margin>
How did loyalty benefit Regulus? The force of fate, after the wretched disgrace of his captivity, laid him low among the hands of his enemies through the wakeful atrocity of their cruelty. <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus was a Roman general famously tortured to death by the Carthaginians after he kept his word to return to them as a prisoner.</note> What other force, when the kings of the Persians were unloosed, handed over the captive Crassus along with the Roman fasces? 
<margin>Crassus</margin>
And yet he had been a vigorous man, and his virtues—which shone with their own brilliance—protected the Roman armies. 
<margin>Pompey</margin>
In the case of Pompey, after his fifth consulship, after so many and such distinguished triumphs, at the bank of the Nile river, a sword of a half-man <note>Referring to the eunuch Pothinus or the low-born assassins in Egypt who murdered Pompey the Great.</note> fell upon those unconquered and royal necks—necks which the triumphal purple had so often embraced—in a wicked kind of death. 
<margin>Cato</margin>
Who armed the hands of Cato for his own slaughter? Who, amidst the mournful and wretched weeping of all, handed over the venerable blood of Cicero to the impure and effeminate desires of Antony? 
<margin>Cicero</margin>
Caesar later armed those very men for the destruction of his own safety whom he, by his own indulgence, had freed from all fear. You see how fortune dominates everywhere and always; you see how varied and always changeable are the outcomes of men. The brave is overcome by the cowardly; the inferior has laid low the good; justice did not benefit the just; providence often deceived the chaste; and the immodest and dissolute man was preferred in the seeking of honors over the modest and sober. The vigorous lie low, the wicked are praised, and whatever benefited one man deceived another through reckless imitation. All these things are attributed by us to the courses of the stars; fortune wears us down with these varieties. Driven and shaped by so many examples and so many reasons, let us prove the law of fatal necessity—not by the license of arguments or a flood of words, but by the probable and right judgment of truth.

But now, even those who used to contradict us agree in some part with our allegation, saying: there is indeed a certain force of fortune and fate, which they call 
<margin>Fate</margin>
<term>Fate</term> <note>original: εἱμαρμένη (Heimarmene)</note>. But to this necessity, by the license of their own disputation, their law and the necessity of the fates grants some things and denies others, so that fate seems both unable to do anything and yet able. For they want this 
<term>Fate</term> <note>original: εἱμαρμένη</note> to be joined to the nature of humans and other living creatures in a certain fellowship; they believe that because we were so made and procreated that, living for a certain time and completing the course of life, we are returned to that divine spirit which sustains us once the fragility of the body is dissolved, we are subjected to fate and lot equally to fulfill that end. Thus, one and the same fatal conclusion of dissolution would finish us and all living creatures by the law of a fatal decree. However, they claim that everything pertaining to the course of life is placed in our will and power, so that how we live is our own, but only that we die seems to belong to fate and lot. 

I do not know what this inconsistency of conclusion achieves; I do not know who could be persuaded by what is said. If anyone confesses that there is fate, and says the end of all things is subject to fatal necessities, let him stand by his own arguments—yet here he somehow prejudices his own confession. He diminishes the power of fate in smaller matters but increases it in larger ones, granting many and more powerful things to it, yet saying our acts are placed in our own power, while recalling the end of living to the license of fatal lot. In such an inept disputation, he extols himself by the license of his argument, so that while he grants fate the license to observe us and concedes the empire of total power, he nevertheless denies it the lesser thing: namely, the power of ruling a human being. For if fate leads us forth into the light after we are procreated and opens the doors of life to men coming into earthly dealings—and if it is fate's doing (as they themselves confess) whatever is extracted from us by the necessity of death once the course of life is complete—then if the necessity of fatal law establishes for us both the beginning and the end of living, what else is there that is not placed in its power? Since both the beginnings of life are conferred by fate upon those being born, and the day of death and the end of living are terminated by its decrees and judgments. 

Look at that child: before the forming of the body is even complete, he dies prematurely within his mother's womb. Another, with the forming of the body complete and even freed from the narrowness of the mother's womb, is not nourished by the breath of the vital spirit. In another, established in the first cradles of life, amidst the beginnings of wailing infancy, life deserts the fleeing soul. That boyish fragility...

->### I<-

...deceived, he falls. Another, already of ripening age and trained through perfect instruction for all those acts of life which you recently said were placed in our own power, is snatched away by the sudden occurrence of death. Yet another, through a great length of days, lacking nearly all his senses and enfeebled by the pleasure of a declining age and a vice-ridden senility, unwillingly sustains the wearying burden of the light <note>original: "lucis sustinet sarcinam," a poetic way of describing the burden of staying alive</note>. Who is it that delivers to death the one not yet born, or the one on his first birthday, or the one shortly after, or the youth, or the old man? Let him, I pray, find something for us to follow; let him find something that can instruct us and show the reason of truth to us who are struggling.

He will say on every side that it is Fate, and the necessity of human death, which distributes the time of living by its own judicial disposition to all living things born of earthly gathering, so that it denies a longer substance of life to some and grants it to others. It is absurd, while confessing the necessity of fate, to later detract from fate; and <margin>Various deaths</margin> it is quite unjust for a man to avoid in the following parts of his speech that which had been strengthened by his preceding profession of confession. For what shall we say of the various outcomes of deaths? This man, by the compulsion of fate, is hung by a noose; but that one is struck by the sword; another is submerged in the sea and rivers; another, handed over to raging flames and fire, is turned into ash and embers; another is cast down precipices; another is crushed by the ruin of falling roofs; the breath of another was shut out by the pestilential virus of poison. One is gradually consumed by the slow heat of fevers; another, glowing with the swift deflagration of burning veins, seethes with the violence of sudden heat; the thoughtless madness of raging wild beasts tears another to pieces; one suffers his end unharmed; the bite of a venomous serpent constricts all the veins of another unto death.

From this, the Fates describe to us the variety of deaths. These are those decrees of the stars which we put forward a moment ago. From this come those wretched ends of illustrious men, and the happy ends of the wicked and the guilty; from this, the life of men is passed in a varied course, with Fortune always deciding; from this, it is established that the beginning and end of life—and even our entire acts, studies, desires, and whatever else pertains to the conduct of human reason—are contained within the inevitable sentence of fatal necessity. Therefore, let us yield, <margin>All must be granted to fate.</margin> overwhelmed by the faith of truth, and let us confess, following the judgments of true reason, that nothing is placed in our power, but everything is in the power of fate, so that whatever we either do or suffer, all of this is conferred upon us by the judgment of Fortune.

#### CHAPTER IV

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical figure, possibly a scholar or deity, seated amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

<margin>Five Zones.</margin> Having explained and treated all these things, which have shown the force of fate and the laws of the deciding stars through the discussion of true reason, let us return to that question which we left in the first part of this oration: namely, concerning the colors and character of men. Thus, with that question cleared away in every respect, and we ourselves being secured and strengthened by the confidence of constancy, we may explain to you, Lollianus, everything we promised regarding this study.

To the person who asks: "Why in certain regions do the bodies of men always become soiled with a black color, while elsewhere they shine with a pure splendor of whiteness?"—to him who seeks these causes, I will respond with a brief speech of discussion, especially since the learned opinions of many wise men may be brought forward on this part. In the entire sky—which is of a round formation and embraces the lands, seas, and all other things within itself by a surrounding of fiery spirit—there is not one single, uniform substance of the <term>Five Zones</term> <note>The "Five Zones" was a classical geographical theory dividing the Earth into a Torrid zone, two Temperate zones, and two Frigid zones.</note> themselves. For some of them are uniform and have no foreign admixture, while others are composed of a mixed temperament of moderation.

The one of these which is in the middle, set on fire by the lights of the glittering sun and parched by the scorching of eternal heat, is stained with a fiery color of perpetual redness. But the two which contain the extreme parts of the world, clinging to the right and left sides, are marked with a leaden-blue <note>original: "caeruleo"</note> color, always flooded by dark clouds, and besieged by congealed ice, eternal frosts, and snows hardened by cold. Between these two cold zones and that fiery one which is drawn through the middle part of the world, the two remaining zones are established, which a mixed temperament of cold and heat has formed with mild moderation. These <margin>Temperate Zones.</margin> are the two zones which generate every kind of living thing within the borders of the earth out of that tranquil moderation of mixing; through these zones, for the births and...

In which the sun and moon, and also the five wandering stars, which are called <term>planets<note>From the Greek 'planētai', meaning 'wanderers'.</note></term> by the Greeks, run their courses with a certain and always defined motion, so that according to the course of these stars, every kind of living creature might succeed itself by a perpetual propagation of its kind. The power and nature of these five <term>Zones<note>Ancient geography divided the world into five latitudinal bands: two frigid, two temperate, and one torrid.</note></term> produces men of certain nations with a uniform color; yet, even within that appearance of uniformity, the bodies of men are varied by whatever radiation of the stars may occur. Therefore, whatever nation of men lies adjacent to that <margin>The Torrid Zone</margin> Zone which is scorched by fires in everlasting burning—even if it be located under the parts of that Zone which is formed with a composed moderation—it nevertheless borrows for itself fire from the connections of its neighboring association to fashion the colors of men, so that a form of black color always darkens the men in imitation of scorched things. But those parts which lie adjacent to the <margin>The Frigid Zones</margin> icy Zones, which, being widowed and deserted by the heat of the sun, are oppressed by perpetual frost and snows—all those nations of men which the neighboring Zone produces, they cause to be adorned with the brilliance of a splendid whiteness. 

But both in those regions which procreate white men, and in those again which procreate black men, the power of the stars works greatly to vary the forms of men; and to each individual, although the substance of his color be one, it assigns a different appearance of shape. For how else would individuals recognize themselves by the specific lineaments of the body? How would they know their sons, brothers, and kinsmen? How would they distinguish citizens, foreigners, neighbors, friends, or guests, if the power of the stars did not ascribe various and diverse countenances to each? Let us therefore consider the bonding of the human race, and by reflecting we shall find how wicked and how impious the crimes that could be committed there, if a single face for everyone confounded those peoples with an equal formation of similarity: A brother, deceived by the likeness, might enter unto his sister as if he were her husband; another might take the wife of someone else through an imprudence contracted by the error; others might struggle in the conflict of a wandering dispute over a son; others would not know who those people were who had served them only a moment before. Another born of noble birth might be dragged away like a slave due to the confused similarity and the error of a stubborn leader, unless the greatest dissimilarity of countenances varied that uniform likeness of colors—all of which things are tempered by the composed mixtures and reasons of the stars. Behold, the whiteness of one man may grow dusky in some part with a thin shadowing of black color; the black face of another is illuminated by the brilliance of a modest whiteness. What shall I say now of the hair of the head, into which various colors secretly creep? What of the sharpness of the eyes, which are always colored with diverse lights? Behold the bodies themselves, even in those nations and <margin>The power of the Zones and stars</margin> all others, are sometimes tall, sometimes small, sometimes slender with a thin frailty, sometimes broader with a fat thickness. From which it is proved by manifest reasons that it belongs to the Zones that men are black or white, but it belongs to the stars that within that variety of color, they are embodied with variations of dissimilar forms.

Regarding the <margin>Diverse customs of nations</margin> character of nations, however, a dispute is superfluous; for we see very many Asians, indeed almost all, displaying the signs of sobriety; and the levity of the Greeks frequently takes on the weight of modest gravity; and the unbridled rage of the Scythians is sometimes mitigated by the mercy of humanity; and in the borders of the Gauls, the people grow strong in the wisdom of prudence; and the deceitful minds of the Africans are graced with the ornaments of honest faith; and the vices of boasting are deserted by many Spaniards; and a sudden profusion has changed the greed of the Syrians; nor is it difficult to find fools among those sharp Sicilians; and the commands of empire have frequently been transferred from the Italians. 

Nor shall we bring forth examples of this matter from afar, or only from ancient books: our <margin>The Divine Constantine</margin> Lord and Augustus, and Emperor of the whole world, a pious, fortunate, and provident prince—namely, Constantine the Great, son of the Divine Constantius, a prince of August and venerable memory—who was chosen by the favor of propitious majesty to liberate the world from tyrannical immoderations and to suppress domestic evils, so that through him, the filth of slavery having been wiped away, the gifts of secure liberty might be restored to us, and so that we might lay down the yokes of captivity from our already exhausted and oppressed necks. Though the most uncertain fortune of war among human chances sometimes deceived him while he was fighting for our liberty, he was born at Tarsus <note>This detail identifies the author as Firmicus Maternus, though modern historians usually place Constantine's birth in Naissus.</note>, and from the first stage of his age he held the rudders of the empire, which he had obtained under prosperous auspices, for the increase of the eternal happiness of the Roman world...

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' depicting a figure amidst scrolled foliage.</image-desc>
When about to write books on <term>Mathesis<note>The Greek term for "learning" or "science," which in this period referred specifically to astrology.</note></term>, we must first instruct those who wish to learn these things, so that, shaped by correct beginnings, they may more easily attain the knowledge of making prognostications. For no one can attain true knowledge of it unless they have been educated in the first principles. Our Fronto, following the <term>antiscia<note>A technique involving "shadow" points or reflections of planets across the solstice axis (Cancer/Capricorn).</note></term> of Hipparchus, set forth the meanings of the <term>apotelesmata<note>The "outcomes" or judicial predictions derived from an astrological chart.</note></term> as if he were speaking with those who were already perfected and skilled, prescribing nothing regarding the instruction or the mastery of the craft. But almost no one among the Latins has written books of instruction on this art, except for a few verses by Julius Caesar, <margin>Julius Caesar</margin> and even those he borrowed from another's work. Indeed, Marcus Tullius [Cicero], the prince and glory of Roman eloquence, <margin>Cicero</margin> lest he leave anything unattempted that his divine genius might attain, also replied briefly regarding instruction in heroic verses. 

Whence we have translated into a teachable system of discourse all that the Egyptians and Babylonians have said, so that those who are formed to explain the fates of men, having been imbued step-by-step, may attain the whole knowledge of divinity. But because we made mention of the <term>antiscia</term>, we ought not to pass over this place with pretense. Fronto followed the <term>antiscia</term> of Hipparchus, <margin>The antiscia of Hipparchus.</margin> which have no power and no substance; and while there are indeed in Fronto's work meaningful opinions on prognostications and outcomes, yet the study of the <term>antiscia</term> which he followed is ineffective because he had not attained the true theory. For those <term>antiscia</term> are true which our Nauigius <margin>Nauigius</margin> also proves, and which the later Ptolemy showed by a true investigation of definition. We shall show of what sort these are in the later parts of this book, demonstrating which part sends its rays into which other part; for Fronto wrote most truly regarding the outcomes, which are contained most abundantly in the books and monuments of the Greeks. Therefore, having set aside this discussion for the time being, let us return to the beginnings of our instruction.

### THE DIVISION OF THE ZODIAC SIGNS AND THE CONDITION OF THEIR NATURE CHAPTER I.

<margin>The Zodiac.</margin>
The Zodiac is the circle in which the twelve signs are fixed, through which the planets—as well as the Sun ☉ and Moon ☽—direct their courses; it is always turned with an oblique motion. The twelve signs themselves are called by these names: Aries ♈︎, Taurus ♉︎, Gemini ♊︎, Cancer ♋︎, Leo ♌︎, Virgo ♍︎, Libra ♎︎, Scorpio ♏︎, Sagittarius ♐︎, Capricorn ♑︎, Aquarius ♒︎, and Pisces ♓︎. There are different types among these signs, for some are masculine and others feminine. The masculine signs are Aries ♈︎, Gemini ♊︎, Leo ♌︎, Libra ♎︎, Sagittarius ♐︎, and Aquarius ♒︎. The feminine signs, however, are Taurus ♉︎, Cancer ♋︎, Virgo ♍︎, Scorpio ♏︎, Capricorn ♑︎, and Pisces ♓︎.

#### THE SIGNS OF THE ZODIAC.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of the zodiac, divided into twelve segments. Each segment contains a zodiac symbol on the outer rim and a handwritten cursive label in the inner section designating it as either "Mas." (Masculine) or "Fem." (Feminine). The signs are arranged around the wheel. Starting from the top and moving clockwise, they are: Aries (Mas.), Pisces (Fem.), Aquarius (Mas.), Capricorn (Fem.), Sagittarius (Mas.), Scorpio (Fem.), Libra (Mas.), Virgo (Fem.), Leo (Mas.), Cancer (Fem.), Gemini (Mas.), and Taurus (Fem.).</image-desc>

### THE DOMICILES, NAMES, AND POWERS OF THE STARS IN THE SIGNS CHAPTER II.

<margin>Various names of the planets.</margin>
Out of these twelve signs, the Sun ☉ and the Moon ☽ have each been allotted a single sign, while the other five planets—that is, Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Venus ♀, and Mercury ☿—have been given two each. Within these, each planet holds its own command and established domicile <term>domicile: the specific zodiac sign where a planet is said to "reside" and exert its strongest, most natural influence</term>. But the Egyptians do not name these stars by the same names that we do, or as they are called in Greek. For the one we call Saturn is called "the Shining One" <note>original: φαίνων (*phainon*)</note> by the Egyptians; the one we call Jupiter, the Egyptians call "the Radiant One" <note>original: φαέθοντα (*phaethonta*)</note>; the one we call Mars is called "the Fiery One" <note>original: πυρόεις (*pyroeis*)</note> by them; the one we call Venus is called "the Light-bringer" <note>original: φωσφόρος (*phosphoros*)</note> by them; and the one we call Mercury, they call "the Gleaming One" <note>original: σίλβοντα (*stilbonta*)</note>.
<margin>The domiciles of the planets.</margin>
The Sun’s domicile is Leo ♌︎, and in this sign he holds his home and power; the Moon's is Cancer ♋︎. You see how aptly and how secretly this was arranged: the Sun, a masculine planet, is the lord of a masculine sign, while the Moon, a feminine planet, is lord of a feminine sign. In this way, each sex claimed a domicile similar to its own nature, according to the quality of its gender. The other five planets, as we said above, have two signs each in which they exercise the power of their command. Of the two signs that each possesses, one is masculine and the other is feminine. So that this can be understood more clearly, let us explain them all specifically. Saturn ♄ has his domicile in Aquarius ♒︎ and Capricorn ♑︎, of which Aquarius is masculine and Capricorn is feminine. Jupiter ♃ has his domicile in Sagittarius ♐︎ and Pisces ♓︎, but of these, Sagittarius is masculine and Pisces is feminine. Mars ♂ placed his domicile in Aries ♈︎ and Scorpio ♏︎, of which Aries is masculine and Scorpio is feminine. The houses of Venus ♀ are Taurus ♉︎ and Libra ♎︎, of which Libra is a masculine sign and Taurus is feminine. Mercury ☿ has his domicile in Gemini ♊︎ and Virgo ♍︎, of which Gemini is a masculine sign and Virgo is feminine.

## THE HEIGHT AND DEJECTION OF THE STARS, AND THEIR CONDITION. CHAPTER III.

<margin>The height <note>Latin: *altitudo*; in astrology, this refers to a planet's "exaltation," a position where its influence is most powerful.</note> of the stars.</margin>
<margin>The dejection <note>Latin: *deiectio*; in astrology, this refers to a planet's "fall" or "depression," where its power is weakened.</note> of the stars.</margin>
We must also know what the heights of each individual star are, in which they are raised up by a certain natural loftiness of greatness, and what their dejections are, in which they are placed when the power of their authority is oppressed and diminished. Therefore, when established and rejoicing in their heights, they decree signs of the greatest happiness, whenever in the births of men the majority of the stars possess the signs of their heights <term>partiliter</term> <note>Latin: *partiliter* means "by specific degree," rather than just being anywhere in the sign.</note>. But men are truly oppressed by the misfortunes of unhappiness whenever the majority of the stars are positioned in those parts where, in humble dejection, they lose much of their power. These are called "heights" because when the stars are in that specific part in which they are exalted—provided they are in favorable places in the birth chart—they make men blessed. Their dejections, however, make men wretched, poor, ignoble, and helpless, and those upon whom misfortune falls in constant succession. For this reason, the Babylonians <note>The author attributes many foundational astrological concepts to the Babylonians, who were renowned as the master astronomers of antiquity.</note> wished those signs in which the stars are exalted to be their domiciles. We, however, having been trained in this instruction, should know that all stars decree better results when in their heights than when in their [standard] domiciles.

The **Sun** ☉ is exalted in the 19th degree of **Aries** ♈, but is dejected in the 19th degree of **Libra** ♎.
The **Moon** ☽ is exalted in the 3rd degree of **Taurus** ♉, and is dejected in the 3rd degree of **Scorpio** ♏.
**Saturn** ♄ is exalted in the 20th degree of **Libra** ♎, and is dejected again in the 19th degree of **Aries** ♈.
**Jupiter** ♃ is exalted in the 15th degree of **Cancer** ♋, but is dejected in the 15th degree of **Capricorn** ♑.
**Mars** ♂ is exalted in the 28th degree of **Capricorn** ♑, but is dejected in the 28th degree of **Cancer** ♋.
**Venus** ♀ is exalted in the 27th degree of **Pisces** ♓, but is dejected in the 27th degree of **Virgo** ♍.
**Mercury** ☿ is exalted in the 15th degree of **Virgo** ♍, but is dejected in the 15th degree of **Pisces** ♓.

For this reason, since the individual planets are exalted through these signs, the Babylonians also wished their houses to be arranged this way, saying indeed that the domicile of **Saturn** ♄ is in **Aquarius** ♒, **Jupiter** ♃ in **Cancer** ♋, **Mars** ♂ in **Capricorn** ♑, the **Sun** ☉ in **Leo** ♌, **Venus** ♀ in **Pisces** ♓, **Mercury** ☿ in **Virgo** ♍, and the **Moon** ☽ in **Taurus** ♉.

## THE DECANS OF THE SIGNS, AND THEIR LORDS. CHAPTER IV.

Each individual sign is divided into three parts; furthermore, each part has an individual <term>decan</term> <note>From the Greek *dekannos*, meaning "ten." Each 30-degree zodiac sign is divided into three 10-degree segments, each ruled by a specific planet.</note>, so that there are three decans in each sign. Each of these possesses ten degrees out of the thirty, and they extend their lordship and power over those ten parts. They are of infinite power and freedom, and they designate the fates of men by the authority of their power. Moreover, these decans themselves are assigned to individual stars; and when a star is within its own decan, even if it is in someone else's domicile, it is to be regarded as if it were established in its own domicile. For when placed in its own decan, it performs the same things that it decrees when established in its own sign, as follows.

<margin>The Munificent Ones.</margin>
Certain authors, however, wishing to explain this topic more subtly, assign three deities to each individual decan, whom they wished to be called *Munificent Ones* <note>Latin: *munifices*, meaning those who perform a duty or bestow gifts.</note>, which is to say *helpers* <note>Greek: *synergos*</note>. Thus, within each individual sign, nine "Munificent Ones" can be found, so that each decan is presided over by three of these helpers. Furthermore, these nine helpers—whom they claim are established in each sign—they divide into infinite powers of deities. For they say that sudden accidents, pains, illnesses, chills, and fevers are decreed by them, as well as whatever else usually happens to those who neither expect nor know of it. Through these helpers they also claim that monstrous births are brought forth from humans. However, we must necessarily bypass this part in this book of instruction; for even the Greeks, who attempted to touch upon the secrets of this debate, left this entire treatise behind with a certain disdainful avoidance at the very first steps of the constitution. But now, let the order of our instruction return to where it had withdrawn.

### CHAPTER V. THE DIVISION OF THE SIGNS INTO THIRTY PARTS.

Each sign has 30 parts <note>Latin: *partes*; in modern astrology, these are called degrees.</note>. A "part" in a sign is a space as large as the orb of the Sun or Moon encompasses in its circuit; but one part is divided into sixty minutes, and so on thereafter.

The outer ring is divided into numerical segments of 10, 20, and 30 for each sign, representing the degrees of the ecliptic.</image-desc>

### CHAPTER VI. THE BOUNDS OF THE STARS IN EACH SIGN OF THE ZODIAC.

<margin>Bounds <note>Greek: *horia*</note>.</margin>
Although the sign itself may belong to the power of another and may have the domicile of a specific planet as its own, its parts are nevertheless divided among individual stars as if they were their own property. These parts are called the "bounds" of the stars; the Greeks call these *horia* <note>Greek: *ὅρια*, referring to the 'terms' or 'bounds,' which are specific degrees within a sign ruled by a planet other than the sign's main ruler.</note>. But we must gather these through subtle inquiry, for when...

If a star is found within its own **bounds** <term>Latin: *fines*; specific segments of a zodiac sign where a planet other than the sign's main ruler holds influence</term>, it is just as if it were established in its own home. To make this more clearly understood, we must explain it in detail, so that through these bounds, the secrets of **birth charts** <term>Latin: *geniturarum*; the study of a person's fate based on their birth moment</term> may be known.

### THE DIURNAL OR NOCTURNAL JOYS OF THE STARS. CHAPTER VII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' featuring a grotesque mask or face within ornate scrollwork.</image-desc>

HAVING set forth and demonstrated the boundaries <note>the "Bounds" or "Terms" detailed on the previous page</note> of the stars, we must now explain which stars rejoice by day and whose condition they follow, and which indeed rejoice by night and whose condition they imitate in like manner. By day, therefore, the Sun ($\odot$), Jupiter ($♃$), and Saturn ($♄$) rejoice; thus, Jupiter and Saturn follow the condition of the Sun. For this reason, in diurnal nativities <note>birth charts for people born during the day</note>, when placed in favorable locations, they possess greater power and, for the most part, decree good fortune and happiness. By night, however, the Moon ($\mathbb{C}$), Mars ($\male$), and Venus ($\female$) rejoice; thus, Mars and Venus follow the condition of the Moon. As for Mercury ($\text{\mercury}$), since he adapts himself to either nature, he is sometimes diurnal and sometimes nocturnal; however, when he is Oriental <note>rising before the Sun</note> he is diurnal, but when Occidental <note>setting after the Sun</note> he is nocturnal; he is stronger in the former case, yet Mercury yields between both when the stars are mixed. But the superior stars <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, according to their various mutual radiations <note>aspects or angles between planets</note>, sometimes decree happy fortune and sometimes unhappy or evil fortune. For if Venus ($\female$) or Mars ($\male$) should receive the waning Moon ($\mathbb{C}$) in a nocturnal nativity, then they decree all things to be prosperous and happy. If, however, Venus or Mars joins the Moon by some radiation while she is full of light or waxing, it causes the greatest calamities and the greatest misfortunes to be stirred up. But for this reason, Venus is contrary to the waxing Moon, because by a certain natural clash of envy they disagree. Let it suffice for us to have said these things summarily in this introductory book, for we shall explain all things most fully, regarding both the Moon and the other stars, specifically in the following books.

<margin>
Invisible and in conjunction, or rising at sunset.
Proximity to the Sun harms all stars.
</margin>

### THE RISING AND SETTING OF THE STARS, AND THEIR CONDITION. CHAPTER VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' depicting a human figure in robes wrestling with or being entwined by a large serpent or dragon.</image-desc>

NOW, the five stars—namely Saturn ($♄$), Jupiter ($♃$), Mars ($\male$), Venus ($\female$), and Mercury ($\text{\mercury}$)—become morning stars, or evening stars, or Western stars, or hidden stars, which by the Greeks are called *aphanitai* and *synodikoi* <note>original: "ἀφανίται καὶ συνοδικοὶ"; referring to stars made invisible by being in conjunction with the Sun</note>, or *akronyktal* <note>original: "ἀκρονύκται"; stars that rise exactly as the Sun sets</note>. By what method they become such, or for what reason they receive these names, let us now explain. They are morning stars at their rising when, preceding the Sun, they rise before the Sun’s disk. They are evening stars at their rising when they follow the rising Sun. They are hidden, however, when the Sun’s disk covers them; and they are *akronyktal* <note>original: "ἀκρονύκται"</note> when they rise at the same time the Sun sets. When these configurations of the stars are beneficial and when they are harmful, we shall explain in later books, for this has not been said by us without reason. In summary, however, it seems necessary to say that the proximity of the Sun harms all stars <note>this refers to "combustion," where a planet's power is scorched by being too close to the Sun</note>. Some indeed claim that Mars ($\male$) turns out prosperously when he has been oppressed by the rays of the Sun, for, showing respect to the Sun, he loses his natural malice. It also behooves us to know with what conditions the morning stars rejoice, and with what the evening stars. For they are protected whenever they have preceded the Sun with a favorable radiation. For the other stars, when established in a morning rising, rejoice, and then the divine power of the Sun is protected by the best radiation whenever it has been adorned by the morning rising of the stars. But the stars become ineffective whenever they have followed the Sun’s disk in an evening rising. In the light of the Moon, however, they are placed and greatly protected by her radiations, or when they have preceded her disk by some radiation. Moreover, what the mixture of stars produces in nativities <note>birth charts</note> when the stars are made morning or evening stars, we must also show; that is, how many parts <note>degrees</note> the stars must recede from the Sun to be made morning stars.

### THE DEGREES OF THE MORNING AND EVENING STARS. CHAPTER IX.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' showing a seated figure, possibly a child or a scholar, holding a small object, framed by architectural elements.</image-desc>

WE HAVE explained sufficiently and more than enough by what method stars become evening or morning stars. Now it must be known that the star Saturn ($♄$), when it has receded 12 parts <note>degrees</note> from the Sun—that is, when it has risen preceding the Sun—it will be a morning star. In a similar way also, Jupiter ($♃$), receding by 11 parts, makes himself a morning star by preceding the Sun. Venus ($\female$), however, becomes so at 8 parts. Mars ($\male$) also, preceding and established in the 8th part, is made a morning star. Mercury ($\text{\mercury}$) also, preceding and established in the 8th part, is a morning star. They are indeed evening stars when, established in that same number of parts, they have followed the Sun,

### THE GOVERNANCE OF ALL THE WANDERING STARS <note>erraticarum; referring to the planets</note>. CHAPTER X.

**W**e shall now explain the governance of the stars to you, Mavortius <note>original: "Mauorti"; referring to Lollianus Mavortius, a 4th-century Roman senator and the author's patron</note>, our great honor, so that nothing pertaining to this divine discipline of Astrology <note>original: "Matheseos"; in this period, the word encompasses both mathematics and astrology</note> may seem to have been overlooked by us. Beginning from here, we will attempt to reveal in a brief exposition what each of the planets has decreed by its own fate.

<margin>The nature and significance of Saturn.</margin>
**Saturn** (♄) is by nature cold and dry, but occasionally moist by accident; he is dark, harsh, heavy, foul-smelling, greedy, and tenacious, possessing much capacity for thought and a deep memory. His significance covers the cultivation of lands, dwelling upon the waters, the measurement and weight of things, and whatever pertains to rustic affairs. Likewise, it includes whatever crafts are performed by hand, such as masonry, digging, carpentry, and the like. Furthermore, he signifies extreme poverty, a long and difficult life, exile, dangers, deceits, wickedness, betrayals, and solitude—yet in deliberation, he grants a most keen intellect, reliable speech, stable friendship, long foresight, and royal counsel. He also represents violence, captivity, damnation, stubbornness, treachery, anger, and all hatred of what is good; likewise fear, anguish, pain, repentance, funerals, mourning, and bereavement. He also signifies ancient inheritances, as well as wicked or old men, but also slaves, bondservants, mercenaries, eunuchs, and men who are either lowly or infamous, such as sorcerers, thieves, pallbearers, and embalmers <note>original: "pollinctores"; those who prepared the body for the funeral pyre</note>. He further signifies the magic art, long-held thoughts in a man, rare speech, but a high understanding and a profound knowledge of things. Regarding the parts of the body, he governs the right ear, the spleen, and melancholy <note>original: "melancholiam"; referring to the "black bile," the humor associated with Saturn</note>.

<margin>Which limbs he possesses.</margin>
**Jupiter** (♃) is by nature hot and moist, but so temperate that his inherent power is adapted by the stable decree of the Fates for nourishing the bodies of mortals and propagating offspring through many generations. His significance includes dignity of form, nobility of soul, sound wisdom and intellect, and the interpretation of dreams. Furthermore, he governs rights, laws, and established religion, as well as piety, modesty, grace, faith, and whatever the fair mind of a well-instructed man can conceive. Truly, by accident at times—perhaps due to excessive self-confidence—he signifies an ill-advised approach to things and sometimes a difficult outcome of works for such a reason. He also signifies a patient soul, yet one eager for vengeance, and for the most part, a victor in every contention. He also signifies high priests <note>original: "pontifices"</note>, petty kings, leaders, tribunes, and the authors of every most distinguished magistracy. Then he signifies hope, joy, self-control, generosity, the reconciliation of men, the public good, mature counsel, and speech that is grave, pleasant, festive, and always suited to public benefit. Regarding the parts of the body, he governs the left ear and the liver.

<margin>Limbs.</margin>
**Mars** (♂) is by nature hot and dry, irascible, vehement, and often headlong with stirred-up anger. His significance is betrayal, battle, slaughter, audacity, rashness, pride, sedition, controversy, plunder, snares, and banditry. Furthermore, he signifies wounds, captivities, fear, flight, and difficulty. Then treachery, obscenity, reckless love, being easily offended, wandering thoughts, and a lack of counsel. He also signifies violent princes—fierce, inhuman, lusting after the wives of others <note>original: "alienæ femicædis," likely a corruption of "alienæ feminæ" or "killing of women," but usually interpreted as adultery in this context</note>, perjurers, deceitful, inconstant, slanderous, disorderly, contaminating all...

Limbs.

**The Sun** (☉) is indeed fiery by nature, hot and dry, but tempered in a wonderful way, and therefore inhabiting the middle of the habitable zone <note>referring to the central celestial path that keeps the earth temperate enough for life</note>. Its significance is the most honorable gathering of men, ambitious reputation, the desire for gold and honors, the long-awaited vengeance against enemies, strength of mind, beauty of body, magnificence, victory, clear cleanliness, an incredible expectation among all, and whatever seems to pertain to the royal pinnacle. It also signifies kings and princes who are not cruel, not difficult, and not unjust, but righteous, affable, approachable, mild, and honored with every kind of virtue—though sometimes inflated by a tiny spirit of pride. It also signifies grave eloquence, mature counsel, severe judgment, and a splendid and thoroughly magnificent action in every matter, as well as all brilliance, clarity, and royal apparatus. Of the body parts, it governs the head of the universal living being, the spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; the vital breath or life force</note>, and the right eye.

Venus (♀)
Arts.
Limbs.
