[[meta: This page continues from the previous chapter, which established the possibility of astrological prediction. Here, Ptolemy shifts from the theoretical "can we know the future?" to the practical "why should we want to know it?" focusing on the psychological and physical benefits of foreknowledge.]]

# ->CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY’S QUADRIPARTITUM<-

### ->The Utility of the Work. Chapter III.<-

**Q**ualitatively, how the prognostications [[notes: "Prognostications" here refers to astrological predictions or forecasts.]] of the stars are understood has been generally proven—specifically, that those events which occur in the sphere of the air surrounding the earth, and those which happen to humans because of these conditions, can be known. We have shown that these human events pertain to the body and soul, their respective faculties, and the works they perform from their first years to their last. We also considered those external events which naturally and inevitably cling to the aforementioned things, such as the bonds of affection between the body and its material substance [[notes: Ptolemy is likely referring to physical health and possessions or status]], as well as the connections between the soul and its offspring or its authority, and however much of these things might occur at any given time. Now, however, we shall describe the remainder of our promises: to briefly investigate the **utility** [[notes: Latin: *utilitas*, meaning the practical use or benefit]] of this work. But first, we propose to clarify the method and intention of knowing the extent of this science and its fruits. For we say that if we wish to consider the degree of utility this offers the soul, we will find nothing else from which the spirit's vigor and joy can take such great improvement. Universally, we say there is nothing in which the soul profits so much as in the forecasting of this science. For through it, we arrive at the knowledge of things divine and human. Likewise, there is utility for the body, since we cannot attain those things which suit each person's **complexion** [[notes: In ancient medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's health and personality.]] except through the knowledge of this work. Regarding wealth, honors, and similar matters, we may say the same as we do for all of philosophy. For it is not the nature of philosophy itself to lead anyone toward the profit of these things, yet it is not right for men to blame it for that. Similarly, this science should not be blamed on that account, nor should its great benefits be set aside. Generally, it will be clear to those who pay attention that the arguments of those who blame this science—saying it is of no use—are not truthfully uttered. For their foolish deliberation was more inclined to say that prognostications of things that happen inevitably are superfluous and useless. To these people, their own words are incoherent, lacking subtle insight and proper knowledge. First, we ought to know that when necessarily occurring things happen, unless they are feared in advance, they will perhaps harm a person greatly—to the point that they take away sense and memory, or bring such a degree of joy or sorrow that the same result occurs [[notes: Ptolemy argues that unexpected shock, whether good or bad, can overwhelm the mind]]. Forecast, however, prepares and draws the soul toward the frequent memory of things still far off, so that it holds them as if they were constant and present, and it smoothly and gently adapts the soul to receive whatever future event may come.

Furthermore, it must not be thought that the heavens proceed toward what they signify in an "inevitable" way, like those things which occur by divine decree and can in no way be avoided, nor like those things which proceed truly and out of absolute necessity. Rather, we must know that while the powers of the celestial bodies act by divine disposition—and cannot be prevented from truly happening—the variation of terrestrial things follows a natural path. These things vary and receive the primary influences of the higher bodies "accidentally." [[notes: An "accident" in this philosophical context is a property or event that is not part of the essential nature of a thing; it is a circumstance that happens to occur.]] We must also know that certain events occur to humans through general harm, not from the specific nature of any one person—as when a change in the air occurs, from which we can scarcely protect ourselves, resulting in the deaths of many people through atmospheric excess, or pestilence, or flooding. These things happen because a great and powerful cause always overcomes a small and weak cause. Furthermore, certain accidents occur according to the natural and specific **complexions** of each individual, through any change contrary to them. Since these things are of such a nature, it is proven in both general and individual matters that those accidents whose primary cause is stronger and greater than all opposing causes will necessarily happen. It must also be known that those things which are not so fixed will change easily when they receive an equally strong contrary influence; those that do not find such a contrary influence will follow their primary natures. This occurs due to laziness or ignorance of those forces that are not strictly necessary. We see this same thing happen in all things whose beginnings are natural, such as in the nature of certain stones and plants, and even in wounds, abscesses, and illnesses, which necessarily produce some effect—though some are such that they produce that effect only if they are not countered by something opposite. Likewise, it is fitting for all who dwell in this science to consider the accidents that happen to men, and within them 

[[margin: naturally]]

[[summary: This page discusses the "utility" of astrology, arguing that it benefits the soul by providing divine knowledge and prepares the mind for future shocks. Ptolemy clarifies that while celestial forces are powerful, they are not always strictly "inevitable" because local circumstances or human intervention (like medicine) can sometimes counter their effects.]]

-> **BOOK I.** <-

To predict by natural means, and so that they do not cling to false opinions—since some things cannot be avoided because the occasions from which they proceed are many and great, while others are the opposite and undergo alteration. Just as physicians, to whom human infirmities become known, predict which of them are curable and which are not at all. In those matters also in which alteration can exist, we ought to pay attention to the methods of judgment that I shall subjoin. For when an astrologer [[notes: *Aſtrologus* here refers to a practitioner of scientific astronomy and astrology, which were not yet distinct fields]] says in anyone's nativity [[notes: A birth chart or horoscope]] that since his complexion [[notes: *Complexio* refers to the "temperament" or balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined health and personality]] is of a certain kind, and if the change of the air is such, then the tempered complexion will be altered, and according to the increase or decrease [of these factors], such an infirmity will follow. Just as a physician might sometimes say that this infirmity or these ulcers will increase and putrefy. And similarly, if someone who knows the natures of metallic things says that a magnet attracts iron, each of these things will necessarily happen—unless through the ignorance of the craftsman a contrary is not applied to it—and it will proceed according to the powers of its own nature. Yet, the ulcers will not increase nor putrefy when medicine is used to oppose them. Nor likewise will the magnet-stone attract iron [[margin: *Nature of the magnet.*]] if it is smeared with other things [[notes: Ancient and medieval writers often claimed that garlic or onion juice could negate a magnet's power; this was a common example of "antipathy" in nature]]. These things which are predicted are not prohibited except by those things which are naturally contrary to them; and according to what has already been indicated, it will happen similarly in those matters: that when things happen to men, they will be ignorant of the accidents, or when they are known but no contraries are opposed to them, the primary order of nature will necessarily follow. But if they are foreknown, and someone is found who knows how to heal them, they will either happen not at all by the natural way previously indicated, or if they do happen, they will happen only to a small degree. And since the same power exists in general matters and in individuals, [[margin: *General prognostications.*]] it is a wonder why it is conceded by men that a prognostication of general things can be had and can be guarded against by them. For there are very many who concede the prognostications of the seasons of the year and the clouds and configurations of the fixed stars, and are much occupied with them; and they even guard themselves against those things which are to come through them, and they reserve what is cold in the summer, and in the winter truly what is warm. Generally, also, they strive to entice their temperaments to be more temperate. Likewise, when they wish to guard themselves against misfortunes and accidents that happen at sea, they pay attention to the clouds of the fixed stars. Also, in the conceptions of beasts and the planting of plants, they observe the phases of the Moon, which are formed according to the quantity of its light, and what they should do. We have seen no one who ever denied this, or who said it could neither be useful nor exist. Truly, there are some who judge that no one can arrive at prognostications of individuals [[margin: *Individuals*]] in their own complexion—as in the increase or decrease of heat or cold—and similarly in the proper complexion of each thing. They even think there are many things from which no one can guard himself. But if it is clear that when we cool our bodies before the arrival of general heat, less heat falls upon us, we can do the same in individual matters which increase heat, so that we may convert them to a more temperate state. This is only because the occasion of this deception is the difficult prognostication of individual things, and because very few have it in use, so much so that it is almost the reason that other things are by no means believed. For things having powers of contrariety are not easily found without those things through whose powers we prognosticate, and therefore for the most part they are not found perfectly. For which reason, since primary natures are always winning out when there is no prohibitor, they thought that they themselves did whatever happens inevitably, and in such a way that it cannot be prohibited. And as it seems to me, they thought the same in that very same prognostication. But although it might happen that in the greater part the prognostication might fail, it is fitting that we investigate it subtly, because there is something of truth in it; just as in the art of medicine, which demonstrates how to preserve health, although it is not the cause of health for all men, yet it is for some; which, although it be modest, is yet to be sought and cherished, and we ought to consider this to be of great profit. It is also clear that the Egyptians [[notes: Refers to the ancient tradition that astrology and medicine (iatromathematics) originated with Egyptian priest-scholars]] showed the greatest powers of this work, since in all medical books they joined the science of the stars to prognostications. Because of this, they knew these things would be so, nor would they at the same hour join those things together in order to make incantations and medicines to wipe out present or future impediments—whether general or particular accidents occurring through the surrounding body—unless they thought that what was to come from there could be changed or converted. For this reason, that which is of this nature, and the things which follow it, having the power of contradiction, they placed in the second order, in virtue and power. And you see the utility of its work joined with the powers of prognostication in the books which show the [remedies] of medicine...

->## CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY: QUADRIPARTITUM<-

[[notes: The *Quadripartitum*, or *Tetrabiblos* ("Four Books"), is Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century treatise on the philosophy and practice of astrology.]]

...they are so named so that he might understand the qualities of existing temperaments through the stars, as well as the events which are to occur through the surrounding atmosphere [[notes: *Corpus circundans* literally means "the surrounding body," a term used by Ptolemy to describe the air or environment that mediates celestial influence]], and their causes. This knowledge ensures that people might be skilled in this science of things, and in the doctrine of healing those things which are largely curable. This is necessary because it is impossible for all bodies and illnesses to be of the same quality of imbalance [[notes: *Intemperie* refers to a lack of balance in the "humors," the bodily fluids thought to control health]]. Thus, through medicine and through things suitable (or unsuitable) to each specific body, they might heal without any deficiency or deception, and by this means reach the highest perfection attainable. This, then, had to be stated as a general introduction. Now, proceeding in an introductory manner, we shall follow with the discourse. We will first demonstrate those works by which the alterations of celestial things specifically occur. We shall follow the observations of the ancients arranged in their natural order, and from these, God willing, we will first treat the works of the wandering stars and the luminaries.

->### On the powers of the luminaries and the wandering stars. Chapter IV.<-

[[notes: In ancient astronomy, "luminaries" refers to the Sun and Moon, while "wandering stars" (*erraticae stellae*) is the literal translation of the Greek *planētēs*, from which we get the word "planets."]]

# **I**t is indeed manifest that the nature of the Sun is to heat and, to a small degree, to dry. This effect is more easily perceived than that of the other bodies, and knowledge of it is more readily gained because of the Sun's great size and the obvious changes of the seasons. For the closer the Sun comes to the zenith point above our heads, the more it heats us.

->#### On the power of the Moon.<-

The greater power of the Moon, however, is to moisten; for she is closer to the Earth, from which moist vapors rise up toward her. For this reason, she changes bodies with an obvious transformation. For as she acts upon their parts within the body, she matures and decomposes them. Likewise, like the Sun, she possesses a small degree of heating power, since she receives light from him.

->#### On the power of Saturn.<-

The star of Saturn, for the greater part of its influence, cools; and by its extreme cold, it dries slightly. This seems to occur because of its great distance from the heat of the Sun and from the moist vapors which are near the Earth. The knowledge of the effects of this star and the others proceeds from observations of their configurations, which are found in their relationship with the Sun and Moon. For in the cycles of change, which differ according to increase and decrease, we see certain qualities of the air varied in one way, and others in another.

->#### On the power of Jupiter.<-

The active power of the star of Jupiter is of a temperate nature. For the place of its motion is midway between the cold of Saturn and the heat of Mars. Therefore, it simultaneously heats and moistens; and because its heating power is greater, and it moves above the other spheres, it is the author of the winds that cause things to grow.

->#### On the power of Mars.<-

The star of Mars specifically dries, and the force of its nature burns; for its heat is likened to the heat of fire, and it holds a place near the Sun, whose sphere sits just below it.

->#### On the power of Venus.<-

The star of Venus, because of the temperateness of its nature, imitates Jupiter in its effects, except that in Venus the order of Jupiter is reversed: it heats slightly because it is near the Sun, but it moistens as much as the Moon because of the great quantity of its light, and therefore it attracts to itself the vapors that rise from the moisture surrounding the Earth.

->#### On the power of Mercury.<-

The work of the star of Mercury is, for the most part, to dry and equally to moisten. For in certain hours it dries humors because it is never far removed from the heat of the Sun; yet in others it moistens, because its place is just above the lunar sphere, which is closer to the Earth. In both of these, its alteration is swift. It is also an author of winds, because its motion around the Sun is considered rapid.

[[margin: On fortune]]

-># BOOK I.<-

->### On Fortunes and Misfortunes. Chapter V.<-

[[margin: † Or, "with those which they aspect"]]
**S**ince there are the aforementioned configurations, as we have said, and since there are four natures—namely, heat and moisture, which are procreative and active, for nothing increases except through these; and two others, namely coldness and dryness, which are destructive, for through them things diminish and cease to be—the men of ancient authority have said that two of the wandering stars [[notes: The "wandering stars" or *stellae erraticae* are the planets, as opposed to the "fixed" stars.]], namely **Jupiter** and **Venus**, and also the **Moon**, are "fortunes" [[notes: In astrology, these are the "benefics," planets thought to have a positive, life-giving influence.]]. This is because their temperament is balanced, and because they contain much heat and moisture. They testified that the works of **Saturn** and **Mars** are naturally contrary to the works of the aforementioned stars, because one of them works through intense cold and the other through intense dryness [[notes: These are the "malefics," associated with destruction or hardship.]]. However, they added that the **Sun** and **Mercury** possess dryness in their nature, because they provide the effects of both; according to the changes of the other stars with which they have *ictisal* [[notes: Likely a Latinization of the Arabic astrological term *itisāl*, meaning "application" or the approach of one planet to a conjunction with another.]], they compel things to change more than any of the other stars.

->### On Masculine and Feminine Signs. Chapter VI.<-

**S**ince there are likewise two primary types of natural parts, namely the masculine and the feminine, and since among the aforementioned powers the feminine power specifically arises from a moist substance (as this quality is generally found in females, and the remaining quality is always properly found in males), it was aptly said by the ancients that the **Moon** and **Venus**, in which there is much moisture, are feminine. The **Sun**, **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** are masculine. **Mercury**, however, because it works equally with dryness and moisture, was said to have a share in both genders. They also say that the planets, so to speak, "masculinize" and "feminize" according to the configurations they form in relation to the Sun. For when they precede the Sun and are in the east, they are called masculine; but when they follow the Sun and are in the west, they are called feminine. The same is proven by the configurations they form on the horizon. For when they are in the places from the east to the mid-heaven, or from the west to the opposite mid-heaven [[notes: Referring to the quadrants of the astrological chart above and below the horizon.]], they are masculine under the earth, because being oriental (in the east), they dwell in the part from which the wind called **Assabe** [[notes: A transliteration of the Arabic *as-sabā*, referring to the East Wind.]] proceeds. In the two remaining quarters they are feminine, because they occupy that part from which **Adabor** [[notes: From the Arabic *ad-dabūr*, the West Wind.]] proceeds.

[[margin: † Otherwise, the East Wind. † Otherwise, the West Wind.]]

->### On Diurnal and Nocturnal Planets. Chapter VII.<-

**S**ince there are likewise two spaces from which time is made—one of which is day, which is properly masculine because of its heat and its active and moving power; the other of which is night, which is feminine because of its moisture and rest—they said that the **Moon** and **Venus** are nocturnal, while the **Sun** and **Jupiter** are diurnal. **Mercury**, as we said before, they made a companion to both, reporting it to be diurnal in the east and nocturnal in the west. Regarding the "fortunes" [[notes: The benefics/malefics]], they divided them into two modes beyond this, not by nature, but by the principle of opposites. For when similar things are mixed with things of a suitable temperament, their health improves. But when dissimilar things are mixed with destructive things, their harm is diminished. Therefore, they assigned **Saturn** (which cools) to the heat of the day, and **Mars** (because it dries) to the moisture of the night. Thus, because each of these is tempered by its opposite, the resulting mix will be like a balanced temperament.

->### On the Powers of the Configurations Formed According to the Position of the Sun. Chapter VIII.<-

**T**he **Moon** and the three wandering stars positioned above the Sun [[notes: The "superior" planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.]] take on a decrease or increase in their own powers based on the configurations they form in relation to the Sun. For the **Moon**, from its first "horning" [[notes: The waxing crescent.]] until its first dichotomy [[notes: The first quarter moon.]], provides moisture; from there until the full moon, it provides heat; from there until the second dichotomy [[notes: The last quarter moon.]], it dries; and from then until it is hidden and sits in line with the Sun, it cools. The "morning stars," from the time they appear from under the Sun's rays until their first station [[notes: When a planet appears to stop moving before turning retrograde.]], provide more moisture; from their first station until their evening rising, they provide more heat; from there until the second station, they dry more; and from that point until they are hidden, they cool more. It is clear that when these are mixed with one another, they produce different qualities in the air in many ways...

-> ## On the natures of the fixed stars. Chapter IX. <-

**C**oncerning the natures of the fixed stars, as the aforementioned treatise follows on the properties they assume according to their effects, let us begin these in sequence and record their variations as discovered through experience. From these, we shall indicate their similarities with the wandering stars [[notes: The "wandering stars" (planets) include Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, alongside the Sun and Moon.]]. And first, let us set down the record of those located within the figures of the zodiacal circle itself.

[[margin: *Aries*]] The stars existing in the head of Aries are assimilated to the combined powers of Saturn and Mars. However, the powers of those in the mouth are said to be similar to the powers of Mercury, and also slightly resemble those of Saturn. The effect of those in the hind foot does not differ from the works of Mars, and those located in the tail follow the powers of Venus.

[[margin: *Taurus*]] Regarding the stars in Taurus, the temperament of the star on the shoulder does not differ from the temperament of Venus, and is also somewhat assimilated to Saturn. From the chest, the temperament is proven to be similar to the combined temperament of Mars and the Moon. But of the stars in the head of Taurus, the brighter one which bears a resemblance to a clear redness and is called **Aldebaran** [[notes: A prominent red giant star, the "Eye of the Bull."]], I say that its temperament is not far from that of Mars. The temperament of the other stars there is equal to Saturn's and bears the likeness of Mars for a short time. Those placed on the tips of the horns work the same as Mars.

[[margin: *Gemini*]] Likewise, of the stars situated in the sign of Gemini, those placed in the feet do not depart from the Mercurial quality, though they are somewhat associated with the quality of Venus. The brighter stars positioned in their hips are equal to the temperament of Saturn. Two large stars are also marked upon their two heads, the first of which is assimilated to Mercury in its effects and is called **Auellar** [[notes: Identified historically as Castor.]]; the other imitates the temperament of Mars and is called **Abrucaleus** [[notes: Identified historically as Pollux.]].

[[margin: *Cancer*]] In Cancer, the effect of the two stars in the foot is one and the same, and they are assimilated to Mercurial works and slightly to Martial ones. The temperament of those in the *azubene* [[notes: From the Arabic for "claws," referring here to the limbs of the Crab.]] is not contrary to the temperament of Saturn and Mercury. The effect of the star in the breast, which bears the likeness of a cloud and is called **Meelef** [[notes: Known today as the Praesepe or "Beehive" star cluster.]], equals the works of the Moon and Mars. The powers of the two stars on either side of Meelef, called the two **Asini** [[notes: The "Donkeys" (Asellus Borealis and Australis).]], do not depart from the powers of Mars and the Sun, and it is manifest that this temperament is piercing and destructive.

[[margin: *Leo*]] Of the two stars in the head of Leo, the work is assimilated to Saturnian works and slightly to Martial ones. Of the three in the neck, the works are equal to Saturnian works and somewhat resemble Martial ones. The bright star placed in the heart of the Lion, which they call the **Regia** [[notes: Regulus, the "Royal Star."]], works just as Jupiter and Mars. The star on the back and the bright star in the tail are equal to the powers of Venus and Saturn, and somewhat imitate Mercury in their effects. The two on the hips...

[[margin: *Virgo*]] In Virgo, those in the head, the eye, and the tip of the southern wing are not removed from Mercurial effects and are somewhat assimilated to Mars. Other bright stars in the Northern wing and back do not differ from Mercury and bear a likeness to Mars. The bright star on the Northern wing, called **Almucedeme alacaf** [[notes: Likely Vindemiatrix (Epsilon Virginis).]], works as Mercury and Saturn. But the work of the star called **Azimech alaazel** [[notes: Spica (Alpha Virginis), the "Ear of Grain."]] does not depart from the powers of Venus and is somewhat assimilated to Mercurial ones. Those at the tips of the feet and the hem of the garment are equal to the powers of Mercury and Mars. Those appearing at the tips of the two "Azubene" [[notes: Here referring to the "Claws" which became the constellation Libra.]] of the Scorpion imitate Saturn and Mercury, and those in the middle resemble Saturn and follow the temperament of Mars.

[[margin: *Scorpio*]] In Scorpio, the powers of the bright stars in the forehead do not depart from Mars. Of the three in the mouth, the middle one is the brightest, has a slight redness, and is called the **Heart of the Scorpion** [[notes: Antares (Alpha Scorpii).]]; it is not separated from the works of Mars, and although...

[[margin: The Dragon.]] Truly, the qualities of those in the *ficaris* [[notes: Likely a corruption of *figuris*, meaning "the figures"]] do not disagree with the qualities of **Jupiter** and **Saturn**. Those which express the form of the Hen [[notes: The constellation **Cygnus**, the Swan]], [[margin: The Hen.]] are likened to these aforementioned stars. But those which possess the figure in which the Seat [[notes: The constellation **Cassiopeia**]] is, are equaled by **Saturn** and **Venus**. Truly, the stars of that which is called the head of the chained one [[notes: **Andromeda**]], do not reject the works of **Saturn** and **Venus**; and those which hold the likeness of the "cloudy" part contained in the handle of the knife [[notes: Referring to the hilt of the sword held by **Perseus**]], imitate **Martial** and **Mercurial** temperaments. Also, the bright stars of that figure in which the hours are formed [[notes: Likely referring to **Auriga**, the Charioteer, though the Latin *hora* is ambiguous here]], do not depart from the powers of **Mars** and **Mercury**. Likewise, the works of the stars which represent the image of the man holding the serpent [[margin: Ophiuchus.]] are likened to **Saturnian** works and a little to **Venus**; indeed, those fixed in the serpent's body itself do not differ in their works from **Saturn** and **Mars**. Truly, those located in the Arrow [[notes: The constellation **Sagitta**]] retain the likeness of **Mars** and a little of **Venus**. Those figured in the Flying Vulture [[notes: The constellation **Aquila**, the Eagle]] follow the temperament of **Mars** and **Jupiter**. And those which indicate the form of the Dolphin act as **Saturn** and **Mars**. [[margin: Dolphin.]] Truly, the clear stars situated in the Horse [[notes: **Pegasus**]] do not refuse to act just as **Mars** and **Jupiter**. Indeed, the stars of Andromeda have **Venusian** powers. [[margin: Andromeda.]]

->### CL. PTOLEMY'S QUADRIPARTITUM<-

[[margin: The Triangle]] **The stars of the Triangle** are well-attested. Indeed, the stars of the Triangle are considered [[notes: literally "do not disdain"]] to have the temperaments of Mercury. Likewise,

It is clear that the bright star formed in the mouth of the southern fish [[notes: This is the star Fomalhaut]] is similar in power to Venus and Mercury, and those located in the body of the same fish are equal to Saturn in their effects. Moreover, the powers of the stars in the figure of the Mighty One [[notes: Referring to the constellation Orion]], namely those in each of his shoulders, do not differ from the powers of Mars and Mercury. Also, the last of the stars of the River [[notes: The constellation Eridanus]], which is the brightest, imitates Jupiter, while the others

But the bright star formed in its mouth—which is called **ascehere** [[notes: A Latinized version of the Arabic 'al-Shi’ra,' known today as Sirius]]—is not inferior to the works of Jupiter, and is even slightly associated with the works of Mars. [[margin: The Centaur]] In the Centaur, those which possess its human form bear the likeness of Venus and Mars. But the bright ones situated in its equine figure work just as Jupiter and Venus do.

->#### *Of the Strengths of the Four Seasons. Chap. X.*<-

[[insert: Large decorative initial S]] **The qualities** of the stars' strengths within themselves, as discovered by the ancients, are these. It is said that there are four seasons of the year: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. In the time of **Spring**, moisture is stronger; for, once the cold of winter has passed, heat begins to move toward a disturbance of the humors [[notes: The "Four Humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament]] which were frozen because of the winter's cold. But in the **Summer** season, because of the Sun's approach to the zenith above our heads, heat prevails. In the **Autumn** season, dryness conquers, for the heat of the past summer has dried out the moisture. But in the **Winter** season, because of the Sun's removal from the zenith above our heads, cold overcomes. For this reason, since the circle of the signs lacks a natural beginning (as does any circle), they established the sign of the **Vernal Equinox**, which is Aries, as its beginning. They took the start from that point at which the moist temperament begins to grow—just as in living creatures, the first part of the years of life is the time in which their temperament is most moist—and they arranged the other seasons in that same order. For in the temperament of all living things, moisture prevails in the first years, just as in Spring, for in those years the creature is soft and tender. In the second years, up until the full standing-point of heat, heat conquers as if in Summer. In the third years, in which the creature is near its decline and around the beginning of its diminishing, dryness is stronger, as if in Autumn; and in the final years, in which it reaches destruction, cold overcomes as if in Winter.

->#### *Of the Strengths of the Four Angles, and the Four Parts of the Horizon. Chap XI.*<-

For in the part called the **East**, dryness is stronger; because when the sun moves through that part, it does not stop drying whatever the night has moistened, and because the winds which emit their blasts from that direction—generally called Oriental—are deprived of all moisture and cause drying. But the **Southern** part is the hottest,
[[margin: The South]] because the heat of the sun is great when it lingers in the middle of heaven, and because this part, as far as our [clime]...

-># THE QUADRIPARTITE<- [[page number: 14]]

[[notes: The *Quadripartitum*, or *Tetrabiblos*, is Claudius Ptolemy's foundational 2nd-century work on astrology. This edition uses the fourfold division of the world's qualities—Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry—to explain planetary influence.]]

situated to the right of our region, the winds that proceed from that part are generally called "meridional" [[notes: "Meridional" refers to the South or the midday sun.]], which are hot and burning. But the Western part is humid, because [[margin: *West*]] when the sun lingers in that part, those things which the day has dried out soon begin to be moistened; and the winds that proceed from there, which we generally call "Western" [[notes: Often referred to as Zephyrs.]], are softening and moistening. However, the Northern part [[margin: *North*]] is the coldest, because the causes of heat which fall upon us due to the sun’s presence in the middle of the sky are greatly distanced from us according to our location. And since it is placed in opposition to the sun occupying the middle of the sky, the winds proceeding from this part are very cold and constricting. Therefore, the knowledge of these things is useful and contributes to the understanding of the "complexions" [[notes: In this context, a "complexion" is the specific blend of elemental qualities—hot, cold, wet, dry—inherent in a person, place, or time.]] of all parts in every region. This is clearly because the effective power of the stars changes according to the qualities of the seasons of the year and the "angles" [[notes: The "angles" refer to the four most powerful points in a horoscope: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.]]. For when all things are made like unto them, their qualities will be pure and without the admixture of any other. Wherefore their works will be stronger—for example, stars that are naturally heating are stronger in hot modes, and similarly, stars that moisten are stronger in humid modes. But their powers are not pure in the presence of contrary modes, but being mixed with other things, they are weak; just as happens with the powers of heating stars in cold modes, or the strength of moistening stars in drying modes. We should not doubt that the same occurs in all other modes, according to the mixture of qualities.

->### *On fixed, movable, and common signs*  Cap. XII.<-

**H**aving premised these things, it follows that we should add the specific changes of the parts of the circle of signs [[notes: The Zodiac]] as they have come down to us. These are the general temperaments of the seasons which are likened to them. We shall also mention certain of their properties, which are likened to the sun, moon, and the rest of the stars, following the aforementioned powers of the signs in themselves without the mixture of any other, which we assign to them only from the comparison of one to another. Truly, the first difference among the signs is that some of them are called **tropical**, some **equinoctial**, some **fixed**, and some **common**. For the tropical signs are two: specifically the 30 degrees which follow the point of the summer solstice without interval, which are the degrees of **Cancer**; and the other 30 degrees arranged following the point of the winter solstice, which are the degrees of **Capricorn**. These are designated by these names for the reason that it is manifest that this occurs in them: for when the sun reaches the beginnings of these [[margin: *Tropical signs.*]] two signs, it then turns its motion back toward a latitude contrary to the motion it previously held [[notes: The word "Tropical" comes from the Greek *trepein*, meaning "to turn." Here, the sun reaches its highest or lowest point and begins its return toward the equator.]]. When it is in Cancer, it makes summer, and in Capricorn, it makes winter. There are also two equinoctial signs: namely, the sign immediately following the point of the vernal equinox, which are the degrees of **Aries**, and the sign following in order the point of the autumnal equinox, which is the sign of **Libra**. [[margin: *Equinoctial.*]] They obtain this name because it undoubtedly happens in them that when the sun enters their beginnings, the days are made equal to the nights everywhere. Of the remaining eight signs, which are located between the tropical and equinoctial signs, four are called **fixed** and four are named **common**. The fixed signs are those which follow the two solstitial and two equinoctial signs, which are **Taurus**, **Leo**, **Scorpio**, and **Aquarius**. This is because the changes of the four seasons, which follow the sun's entry into the solstitial and equinoctial signs, take their beginning there—whether the air is changed toward humidity, heat, cold, or dryness. They are "fixed" and become more apparent whenever the sun lingers in these fixed signs. The quality of the air then naturally exists in its pure state, for on account of the long durability of these qualities, it receives their powers most openly. Truly, the common signs are those which appear soon after the fixed signs, which are **Gemini**, **Virgo**, [[margin: *Common.*]] **Sagittarius**, and **Pisces**. They are so called because they are located between the movable and fixed signs, and in their beginnings and endings, they are assimilated to a nearly natural change, sharing in the two qualities of the movable and the fixed signs.

# CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY

->Division of signs into masculine and feminine. Chapter XIII.<-

**T**hey have judged six signs to be of a masculine and diurnal [[notes: 'Diurnal' refers to the day; in ancient astrology, masculine signs were linked to the active, bright nature of the sun.]] nature, while the remaining six they related to a feminine and nocturnal nature. These were arranged one after the other, for the reason that day adheres to night and always exists alongside it, and because the masculine sexes are close to the feminine and are frequently joined to them. They took the starting point of this arrangement from Aries, for the reasons previously mentioned, and because males are dominant and active, it is more fitting that they be preceding and held in higher honor than those who are passive [[notes: This reflects the social and biological theories of the 2nd century, where 'activity' was categorized as a masculine trait and 'passivity' as feminine.]]. For this reason, therefore, they made the beginning with a masculine sign. The signs of Aries and Libra are masculine and diurnal because the equinoctial circle [[notes: The Celestial Equator, where the sun crosses during the spring and autumn equinoxes.]] is stretched over them; from this, the first and strong movement—which is called the motion of the firmament—takes its origin.

The order of the signs following these two is, as we have said, a feminine following a masculine, and a masculine after a feminine. Some, however, began the order of the sexes of the signs from the Ascendant [[notes: The 'Ascendant' is the sign of the zodiac that was rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, such as a birth.]], naming one masculine and the other feminine. They began from the Ascendant just as some placed the beginnings of the "movable signs" [[notes: Also known as 'Cardinal' signs (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn).]] starting from the sign of the Moon, because she receives variation more quickly than any of the other stars. In a similar way, they began the starting points of the sexes of the signs from the Ascendant because it exists closer to the east, and they followed the subsequent order as previously described. 

Some also partitioned all the signs into four parts, saying that the signs called morning-oriented and masculine are those established from the Ascendant to the Midheaven [[notes: The highest point of the sun's path.]], and those opposite to them, from the West to the "Angle of the Earth" [[notes: The *Imum Coeli*, or the lowest point of the sky, directly opposite the Midheaven.]]. The remaining two quarters they called feminine and evening-oriented. They also bestowed many other names upon the signs according to the figures that are in them [[notes: Referring to the constellations' shapes.]]. For instance, some of them are "four-footed" and some are "wild." Some they named "of many offspring" [[notes: Signs considered fertile, like Pisces or Cancer.]] and things similar to these. But since the reason for these names is manifest, and because such things as are named through these figures can be discussed in that place where they will contribute to our science and utility, we have decided to remain silent on them in this section.

->On the affinity of signs and their figures. Chapter XIIII.<-

**T**he first affinity of the parts of the circle of signs among themselves is that which is held in their figures [[notes: This refers to 'Aspects,' the geometric angles formed between signs.]]. Just as there are parts between which there is the length of one diameter, which are subtended by two right angles [[notes: This describes an 'Opposition'—an angle of 180 degrees.]], and there are six signs and one hundred and eighty degrees; and also parts between which is a "trine" length, containing one right angle and a third of another [[notes: This describes a 'Trine'—an angle of 120 degrees.]], and there are four si—

# -> BOOK I. <-

...signs and one hundred and twenty degrees [[notes: This refers to the **Trine** aspect]]. There are also parts between which there is a **tetragonal** distance [[notes: The **Square** aspect, 90 degrees]] which contain one right angle, consisting of three signs and ninety degrees. Furthermore, there are parts between which there is a **hexagonal** distance [[notes: The **Sextile** aspect, 60 degrees]] which twice over encompass one right angle, consisting of two signs and sixty degrees. We shall learn from what follows the reasons why we ought to observe these distances alone and no others. For the reasons for observing the distance of a single diameter [[notes: The **Opposition**, 180 degrees]] are manifest in themselves, because they are elongated in a straight line opposite one another; and when we consider the two larger portions in which there is a harmony of the quantity of the part, and the quantity of the whole and the part, these remaining figures are established. 

By the harmony of the part, it is thus: when we assign to the distance of two right angles [[notes: 180 degrees]] the proportion which is the length of the diameter from its half and its third, its half will be the tetragonal distance, and its third will be the hexagonal distance. From this hexagonal distance, when doubled, the **trine** distance is established. 

By the harmony of the whole and the part, however, it happens thus: when we make a proportion from the tetragonal distance to the two other distances between which it is established, the proportion of one is **sesquialter** [[notes: A ratio of 3:2, or 1.5]] and the other is **sesquitertian** [[notes: A ratio of 4:3, or 1.33]]. When we assign the proportion from it to that which is less than it, and whose proportion to it is sesquialter, the hexagonal distance is made therefrom; and when we assign that proportion to the greater, whose proportion to it is sesquitertian, we establish the trine distance. 

Therefore, they have called the trine and hexagonal of these affinities "agreeable," because they are composed of signs that agree in their nature—for they are all either masculine or feminine [[notes: In traditional astrology, signs alternate gender; trines and sextiles always connect signs of the same gender]]. However, those formed from the diameter or the tetragonal figure they named "disagreeable," because they are always found to be in disagreement regarding the nature of the signs [[notes: Squares and oppositions connect masculine signs with feminine signs, creating "tension"]].

## -> *On the high and low signs which are called "commanding" and "obeying." Chapter XV.* <-

**P**arts of the zodiac whose distance from any one and the same point of the equinoctial points [[notes: The points where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator, i.e., the first points of Aries and Libra]] is the same, are called "high" and "low." These are the parts whose ascensions and descents happen in equal times, because they are carried in equal circumferences of parallel circles to the equinoctial circle. Of these parts, those formed in the middle of the summer circle [[notes: Signs near the Summer Solstice, like Gemini and Cancer]] are called "high," and those in the middle of the winter circle [[notes: Signs near the Winter Solstice, like Sagittarius and Capricorn]] are named "low." This is because when the Sun proceeds through the middle of the summer circle, it makes the days longer than the nights; but when it illuminates the middle of the winter circle, it shows the days to be shorter than the nights.

## -> *On signs "beholding" one another, and those equal to themselves in power. Chapter XVI.* <-

**T**hey say likewise that there are certain parts which are equal to other parts in "power" [[notes: *Fortitudo*, referring here to the strength of daylight]] when their distance from any one of the two tropic points [[notes: The Solstices]] is one and the same. This is because when the Sun has traveled through either of these two points, day will be equal to day and night to night, and the length of the hours will be the same. They also say that these parts "behold" one another because of the aforesaid reasons, and that each of them rises from the same parts of the horizon in the east and sets in the same parts in the west.

## -> *On signs contradicting each other, between which there is no link. Chapter XVII.* <-

**I**ndeed, those parts which are called "contradicting" and "estranged" are those between which no affinity is contained from the aforementioned types of relationship. That is, they are neither among the commanding nor the obeying signs, nor among those beholding each other (which are equal to one another in power), nor are they among those which have an affinity to one another through any of the four established figures—that is, through the figure of the diameter, the trine, the tetragonal, or the hexagonal. The parts which we find to be associated in no way through these modes **B** are...

->On the houses of the five wandering stars, and of the Sun and Moon. Chapter XVIII.<-

[[meta: Woodcut initial P featuring a figure, possibly an astronomer or deity, within an architectural frame.]]

# P
arts of the circle of signs—which are named houses, triplicities, exaltations, and terms—are assigned to the seven planets because of a kinship in which they have some similarity or dignity. The nature of the houses is as I shall subjoin. Since, therefore, out of the twelve signs, two are northernmost—namely those which are closest to the zenith [[notes: The point directly overhead.]] of our heads and for that reason generate heat, which are Cancer and Leo—they were attributed to the two greatest and most dignified lights as houses. They designated the sign of Leo, which is masculine, as the house of the Sun, and established the sign of Cancer, which is feminine, as the house of the Moon. Therefore, they called the half of the circle from Leo to Capricorn the Solar half; the other half, from Aquarius to Cancer, they called the Lunar half, so that in each of the two halves of the circle (the solar and the lunar), each of the planets might have a house suitable to itself according to the order of their spheres and natures. 

[[margin: The complexion of Saturn.]] For this reason, because Saturn is naturally cold and contrary to heat, and its heaven is highest and most remote from the lights, they assigned to it the two signs of Capricorn and Aquarius, which are in opposition to Cancer and Leo; this is because these two, Capricorn and Aquarius, are cold and wintry, and again because the affinity of the figures, which arises from opposition, is not favorable for good fortune. 

[[margin: Of Jupiter.]] But because Jupiter is of a temperate complexion and is carried beneath the sphere of Saturn, the two signs following Capricorn and Aquarius—which are Sagittarius and Pisces—were attributed to it, because they produce winds and compel things to arise; they are at a trine distance [[notes: A "trine" is an aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious and lucky in traditional astrology.]] from the houses of the lights, which is suitable and fortunate. 

[[margin: Of Mars.]] After these, because Mars naturally dries and its sphere revolves beneath the sphere of Jupiter, they gave to it the two signs located after the lodgings of Jupiter, which are Aries and Scorpio, whose distance from the houses of the lights is a quartile [[notes: A "quartile" or square is an aspect of 90 degrees, traditionally considered challenging or destructive.]], as is fitting for a destructive and contradictory heat, which is likened to the nature of Mars. 

[[margin: Of Venus.]] Furthermore, because the star of Venus is of a temperate complexion and revolves beneath the sphere of Mars, the two signs following the habitations of Mars were attributed to it, because they cause things to arise, and these are Taurus and Libra; their distance from the houses of the lights is a sextile [[notes: A "sextile" is an aspect of 60 degrees, considered a distance of "similarity and containment."]], which is a distance of similarity and containment. And because Venus is found in two parts, it is never elongated from the Sun by more than two signs. 

[[margin: Of Mercury.]] Likewise, since Mercury remained from the wandering stars—who, in neither of the two parts, is ever elongated from the Sun by more than the space of one sign, and is carried beneath the other stars—the two remaining signs were given to it, which are located after the places of the lights: Gemini and Virgo.

->On the triplicities and their lords. Chapter XIX.<-

[[meta: Woodcut initial T featuring astronomical/mathematical instruments.]]

# T
he affinities of the triplicities with the planets are these. Since the figure of an equilateral triangle is equal and harmonious in itself, and because there are three circles that terminate the zodiac circle—namely the equinoctial circle and the two solstitial circles—they divided the twelve parts of the zodiac circle into four equilateral triangles. The first triplicity, therefore, consists of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, which are masculine signs and are the domiciles of the Sun, Jupiter, and Mars. Therefore, they gave this triplicity to the Sun and Jupiter, rejecting Mars because Mars is of a *haiz* [[notes: *Haiz* is a technical term referring to "sect"—whether a planet is in its preferred day/night condition. Mars is a nocturnal planet and does not "fit" in this diurnal/daytime group.]] contrary to the *haiz* of the Sun. Of this triplicity, the first lord by day is the Sun, and by night Jupiter. The sign of Aries also follows the equinoctial circle, Leo is nearer to the summer circle, and Sagittarius stands closer to the winter circle. This triplicity is also Northern, because Jupiter has dominion there; also, the sign of Aries follows the equinoctial circle, they compel things to arise, and it brings forth Northern winds. Besides this, because the house of Mars is in it, who is said to have a partnership there with the Northern wind, somewhat from the Western...

is mixed. For this reason, a wind is gathered from a mixture of the north and west; for Mars brings such winds, and the western part is also feminine [[notes: In traditional astrology, the compass points were assigned genders; West was often considered feminine]]. But the second triplicity, which is gathered from the three feminine signs—namely **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**—is assigned to the **Moon** and **Venus**, because it belongs to the *haiz* [[notes: *Haiz* is a technical term from Arabic astrology referring to a planet being in a favorable "sect"—for example, a feminine planet in a feminine sign below the horizon at night]] of the Moon. The ruler of this triplicity by day is the Moon, and by night it is Venus. Taurus is closer to the summer circle, Virgo to the equinoctial circle, and Capricorn to the winter circle [[notes: These "circles" refer to the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn and the Equator]]. This triplicity is more suited to the south because of Venus's dominion in it, for this star brings such winds, as her power produces them through heat and moisture. Moreover, because of the house of **Saturn**, which is Capricorn, and because of his association within it, the winds born through this triplicity will be joined from the south and east—the opposite way of the first triplicity—because Saturn brings eastern winds, as he is of the *haiz* of the Sun.

The third triplicity, which is gathered from the three masculine signs—namely **Gemini**, **Libra**, and **Aquarius**—is attributed to **Saturn** and **Mercury**, because their houses are contained within it. Its diurnal [[notes: daytime]] ruler is Saturn, since he is of the *haiz* of the day, while the nocturnal [[notes: nighttime]] ruler is Mercury. The sign of Gemini stands closer to the summer circle, and Libra follows the equinoctial circle. Aquarius is considered nearer to the winter circle. This triplicity is better suited to the eastern wind because of Saturn’s dominion; and since **Jupiter** is assimilated to Saturn in *haiz* (for he is diurnal), the winds that arise by occasion of this triplicity will be between the north and the east.

The fourth triplicity is made up of **Cancer**, **Scorpio**, and **Pisces**. It remains, therefore, that **Mars** should dominate it and exercise his rule therein, because Scorpio is his domicile [[notes: The "home" sign of a planet]]. The Moon and Venus are associated with him in dominion because of *haiz* and because these signs are feminine—the **Moon** by night and **Venus** by day. Likewise, Cancer is closer to the summer circle, Scorpio to the winter, and Pisces to the equinoctial circle. This triplicity produces western winds because of the dominion of Mars and the Moon within it; and because Venus is associated with it, the wind will be gathered from the west and the south.

### *On the Exaltations.* -> Cap. XX. <-

[[insert: Large decorative woodcut initial S showing a figure in a landscape.]] Surely the modes of the signs, which are called the **exaltations** [[notes: An "exaltation" is a specific sign where a planet’s influence is most harmoniously amplified, second only to its home sign]] of the lights and the wandering stars [[notes: "Wandering stars" (stellarum erraticarum) is the literal translation of the Greek *planētēs*, referring to the planets]], are as I shall subjoin. For when the **Sun** is in the sign of **Aries**, it is moved toward the higher northern half of the circle; and when it enters the sign of **Libra**, it directs its own journey toward the lower southern half of the circle. For this reason, they placed the Sun's exaltation in the sign of Aries, in which the length of the days and the increase of their natural heat begins; but they said that Libra would be its "fall" [[notes: The "fall" or *casus* is the sign opposite the exaltation, where the planet's power is weakened or "tripped up"]] because of the opposition of the aforementioned conditions. 

Now for **Saturn**, his distance from the Sun should be one of opposition, just as it is in their houses [[notes: Saturn rules Capricorn/Aquarius, opposite the Sun's Leo]]; because where heat increases, cold is sent away, and where cold is intensified, heat is sent away. Thus, Saturn received the sign of Libra for its exaltation, and Aries for its fall. Likewise, when the **Moon** was in the sign of Aries with the Sun, which is the Sun's exaltation—since after this it will first appear in **Taurus**, in which the increase of its light will be, as it were, at its beginning—its exaltation was placed in Taurus, which is the first sign of its own triplicity. But in the sign of **Scorpio**, which is formed in opposition to that, its fall is designated. 

And because **Jupiter** is the author of northern winds, which cause things to grow, and since his own power appears most when he is in the greatest northern declination (which is in **Cancer**) and produces northern winds, they assigned the sign of Cancer to him as an exaltation, and **Capricorn** as his fall. **Mars**, however, since he is naturally "combusting" [[notes: burning/fiery]], and especially when he is in Capricorn (because his declination then is in the southern part), is uplifted in Capricorn, contrary to the exaltation of Jupiter, but falls in Cancer. Again, because **Venus** naturally moistens, especially in the sign of **Pisces**—in which moisture appears in the winds and her natural power begins to grow—she is exalted in Pisces and falls in **Virgo**. But **Mercury**, since he dries out, in contrast to Venus, is exalted in the sign of Virgo,

...in which autumn, which is dry, begins to appear, as its own proper power increases again in opposition to spring; and its "fall" [[notes: In astrology, the "fall" is the sign where a planet or quality is at its weakest; here, he refers to the seasonal shift.]] is in the sign of Pisces.

->### On the Terms. Chapter XXI.<-

[[notes: "Terms" (or *boundaries*) are subdivisions of the 30 degrees of a zodiac sign. Each segment is ruled by a specific planet, which influences how that planet acts when positioned there.]]

[[insert: Large decorative woodcut initial T featuring figures in a landscape or room]] **T**here are indeed two ways of determining the Terms: one is called the Egyptian, the other the Chaldean. [[notes: The "Chaldeans" refers to the ancient Babylonian astronomers/astrologers.]] The so-called Egyptian method is based primarily on the **lords of the houses**, while the Chaldean is taken from the **lords of the triplicities**. [[notes: A "House" is the sign a planet rules (e.g., Venus rules Libra); a "Triplicity" is a group of three signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).]] However, the Egyptian method does not truly hold to a consistent rule, neither in the order of the planets nor in the specific quantities assigned to each, which is the very foundation of the system. 

For in the order of the houses, they sometimes assign the first term to the lords of the houses, sometimes to the lords of the triplicities, and sometimes even to the lords of the exaltations. [[notes: "Exaltation" is the specific sign where a planet is considered to be at its maximum strength.]] For example, in **Libra**, they do not begin with **Venus** [its ruler], but with **Saturn**. In **Aries**, they begin not with **Mars**, but with **Jupiter**. If they were following the lords of the triplicities and no others, why in **Capricorn** did they start with **Mercury** and not **Venus**? Likewise, if they followed the lords of exaltations and no others, why in **Cancer** do they begin with **Mars** and not **Jupiter**? 

Again, if they followed only those planets which have the most "fortitudes" [[notes: "Fortitudes" are various types of accidental or essential strengths a planet possesses in a specific location]] in the aforementioned signs, why in **Aquarius** did they make the beginning with **Mercury**, who has only his triplicity there, and not with **Saturn**, who possesses both his house and his triplicity there? In **Capricorn** as well, they began with **Mercury**, who has no authority there at all. The order of the remaining terms is found to be of this same inconsistent manner. 

Furthermore, regarding the quantities of the terms, they seem to observe no order. For in the total number of all these terms assigned to each planet—which they claim corresponds to the number of years in the planet’s own period—there is no logical reason provided to prove that the length of a life is determined by this. [[notes: Ancient astrologers used these degree totals to predict the "length of life" for a person born under these influences. Ptolemy is skeptical of the math here.]] 

Even if we were to grant that the total number affirmed by the Egyptians is correct, the same total could perhaps be reached even if the quantities of the terms were varied in many different ways. Some, however, who seem to affirm this point because it appears to satisfy "physical reason," claim that when the "times of ascension" [[notes: "Times of ascension" refers to the time it takes for a sign of the zodiac to rise above the horizon at a specific latitude.]] of the terms for each planet are added up, one and the same total will arise in all climates. This is clearly false. Indeed, they have followed what is found in the "book of the foolish" [[notes: Ptolemy is likely disparaging a specific popular but inaccurate astrological text of his day]], and have used equal additions instead of true ascensions. No one can doubt that this is contrary to the truth. 

For it is found in that book that the ascensions of **Virgo** and **Libra**—on the equatorial line parallel to the line passing through lower Egypt—are 37 and a third "times" for each of the two signs, and that the ascensions for **Leo** and **Scorpio** are 35 times. However, it is proven by geometric logic that **Leo** and **Scorpio** take more than 35 times to ascend, while **Virgo** and **Libra** take less than the aforementioned times. 

Furthermore, those who brought forward this reasoning did not even follow the quantities of terms that most people agree upon. In many places, their calculations are necessarily found to be lies. Yet, so that their opinion might appear more solid, they divided the degrees into minutes; however, we affirm that they are not truthful because of this, but rather most deceptive, as we have already shown. Their terms, which we here criticize for the reasons stated above, are as they stated below. The total of the degrees assigned to each of these planets from the aforementioned calculations is this: **Saturn** 57, **Jupiter** 79, **Mars** 66, **Venus** 82, and **Mercury** 76; the collection of all of these is 360 degrees.

He specifically refutes the idea that these calculations align with the astronomical "times of ascension" or provide a reliable basis for predicting the length of a life.]]

Regarding the other method, which they have called **Chaldean**, they reason by means of the lords of the triplicities; [[notes: "Triplicities" are groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water. The "lords" are the planets that rule these elements.]] however, their reasons are found to be both more obvious and more consistent. Nevertheless, they do not always follow the planets that rule the triplicities in either the order or the quantities [of the degrees]. The opinion of these [Chaldeans], however, can be committed to memory briefly and without a book. For the first triplicity, which consists of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, the division of the terms among them is one and the same in each of its signs. Indeed, they give the first term to the lord of the triplicity, which is **Jupiter**; the second to the lord of the following triplicity, which is **Venus**; the third and fourth to the two lords of the triplicity of Gemini [[notes: The Air triplicity]], which are **Saturn** and **Mercury**; and the fifth to the lord of the remaining triplicity, which is **Mars**. 

For the second triplicity, which gathers together Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn, each of the signs undergoes one and the same division: they assign the first term to **Venus** because of her lordship over it; the second and third to the two lords of the triplicity of Gemini, which are **Saturn** and **Mercury**; after these, they assigned the fourth to **Mars**, and the remainder to **Jupiter**. They followed this order most closely in the two remaining triplicities, except that for the third triplicity, which is said to have two lords, namely **Saturn** and **Mercury**, **Saturn** takes the first part by day, but **Mercury** by night. 

The method for the quantity of the terms found in each sign, which observes the aforementioned order, is indeed singular and manifest, nor do their quantities differ except by an equal decrease. For each of the terms is reduced by the quantity of one degree from the one preceding it. Indeed, they placed the first term of any sign at 8 degrees, the second at seven, the third at six, the fourth at five, and the fifth at four, which marks the end of the thirty degrees. From all of these, there are collected for **Saturn** 78 degrees by day, but 66 by night; for **Jupiter** 72; for **Mars** 60; for **Venus** 75; but for **Mercury** 66 by day and 78 by night. 

Yet of these two [systems], that which was stated by the **Egyptians** is more in accord with the truth, for the reason that the authors of the Egyptian books collected them from what they found recorded in actual nativities [[notes: *Nativities* refers to birth charts or horoscopes used for personal predictions.]], and wrote them in their books as an exemplary path of degrees.

[[notes: "Terms" (Latin: *termini*) are unequal subdivisions of the thirty degrees of a zodiac sign, each ruled by one of the five planets (excluding the Sun and Moon). The table for Aquarius contains a likely error: Venus is listed twice, once for 7 degrees and again for 4 degrees, replacing Mercury.]]

...had arranged the terms in those places where they had need of them. And since those who composed these books did not write down the order of the terms, nor did they account for them in any of their own volumes, doubts and deceptions are necessarily found within them. However, we ourselves found the terms in a certain exceedingly ancient book [[notes: Ptolemy is likely referring to a legendary old manuscript he claims to have found to justify his corrections to the astrological system]], the greater part of which had been consumed by its great age and was full of holes. In this book, that which was contained regarding the order and quantity of the terms had been arranged naturally and reasonably. Likewise, we found in it the degrees of the aforementioned births [[notes: referring to the "nativity" or birth charts used as examples]], and how many degrees each of the planets possessed; it agreed with that which is found in the books of the ancients. There was also a very long discourse in it, in which these same terms were proven by many necessary arguments, but because of its excessive age and the frequent holes in the pages, we were unable to transcribe it, and its reasoning seemed difficult and obscure to us. Nevertheless, the sections concerning the degrees of the terms—which helped us greatly in understanding these matters—remained at the end of the book, intact and without damage; whatever we found there regarding the terms is added in this place.

For in the ordering of them, consideration was given within each of the signs to the lord of the exaltation, the triplicity, and the house [[notes: These are "essential dignities." A planet is "strong" if it is in the sign it rules (house), the sign where it is "exalted," or the sign belonging to its "triplicity" (a group of three signs linked to an element like Fire or Water)]]. Whoever among them held two such powers in a sign, and if it were a "fortune" [[notes: The "fortunes" or benefics are Jupiter and Venus]], it was placed first in the order. But if it were of the manner of the "infortunes" [[notes: The "infortunes" or malefics are Saturn and Mars]], it was arranged instead at the end of the sign. Furthermore, the lords of the exaltation preceded, followed by the lords of the triplicities, and then the lords of the houses followed according to the order of the signs. Whoever indeed held two powers in a sign was placed ahead of the one holding only one power. An exception was made in Leo and Cancer, which are the domiciles of the Sun and Moon, to which terms are not assigned; they attributed the first term of each of these signs to one of the infortunes. For they gave the first term of Cancer to Mars, and the first of Leo to Saturn. The order of these two planets was maintained in these two signs because in all other signs they were placed last.

The method for the quantity of the degrees of the terms is thus: when two powers of any planet were not found either in the same sign or in the following signs up to the fourth sign, then if it were one of the two fortunes (which are Jupiter and Venus), they assigned seven degrees to it. But if it were an infortune [[unclear: *alata*, perhaps intended as *allata* or a specific technical term]], such as Saturn and Mars, they gave five degrees to it.

-> **BOOK I.** <-

To Mercury, however, because he is of a mixed nature [[notes: Astrologers considered Mercury "mixed" because he could be masculine or feminine, productive or destructive, depending on his planetary neighbors]], they assigned six degrees, which are the end of the 30 degrees. 
And because some of them possess two powers—as Venus does in Taurus, where she has her domicile and her triplicity [[notes: A 'domicile' is the sign a planet 'rules,' while 'triplicity' refers to a group of three signs of the same element; having both increased a planet's 'dignity' or strength]]—her power is increased in that sign. For this reason, since the Moon has no degrees in the boundaries, one of her degrees is added to those planets so situated, whether in the same sign or in the following ones up to the fourth; this is what they held. We also find in the aforementioned book a single point marked above each of these. Therefore, that degree which is added to the boundary of a planet possessing two powers was taken away from the remaining planetary boundaries of those having only a single power there; it was stolen first from Saturn, then from Jupiter, because their motion is slow. These boundaries are ordered thus. When these are brought together into one sum, 57 are assigned to Saturn, 67 to Mars, 82 to Venus, 76 to Mercury, and 79 to Jupiter, which, when collected together, make 360 degrees.

-> ## *On Twelfth-parts. Chap. XXII.* <-

[[notes: The following paragraph begins with a large decorative woodcut initial 'S'.]]

**F**or there are indeed some who divided the signs into parts even shorter than those mentioned before, calling them "places" and "degrees." Specifically, they called a "place" the twelfth part of a sign, which is two and a half degrees [[notes: These are known as *dodecatemoria*, a micro-zodiac where each 30-degree sign is divided into twelve 2.5-degree segments]], and they assigned their lords according to the succession of the signs. Some, however, divided them by other parts—namely by ten signs [[notes: Likely a reference to 'decans,' which are 10-degree divisions]]—and followed an order that the Chaldeans used in the arrangement of boundaries. But because their method is inconsistent, we believe it should be set aside; instead, we shall follow another method that we ought to imitate because it is consistent. Regarding these twelfth-parts and boundaries, we shall therefore begin from the two equinoctial points and the two solsticial points, just as the authors of the books have explained. Since the forces of nature and their similarities are properly understood only starting from the two equinoctial and two solsticial points, they began there, as we said, and had no reason to begin from anywhere else. For if any other beginning besides these were found, it would necessarily follow that either no progress could be made in understanding their nature within this science, or that it must be granted and observed to be useful in some way. If anyone admits otherwise, he will be deceived, because he has not observed the parts of the circle of signs through which these powers manifest.

> *Concerning the "almugea"—that is, in a vision of one another face to face—and concerning the "alchinara"—that is, splendor—and things similar to these. Chapter XXIII.*

[[notes: *Almugea* and *Alchinara* are Latinized forms of Arabic astrological terms (*al-muwajaha* and *al-inara*). They refer to specific geometric relationships between the planets and the luminaries (the Sun and Moon).]]

[[margin: [[insert: Decorative woodcut drop cap E]]]] **T**he similarities of the wandering stars [[notes: "Erraticatum stellarum" refers to the planets, which were called "wandering stars" to distinguish them from the "fixed stars" of the constellations.]] to the signs are indeed as we have stated before. Likewise, he shows that the planets properly possess *almugea* in a similar way when each of them has some association in the figure [[notes: The "figure" is the astrological chart or horoscope.]] with the Sun or the Moon, in the manner called *almugea*. This means that the longitudinal distance between each planet and the Sun or Moon is equal to the distance between the planet's own home [[notes: Its "domicile" or the sign it rules.]] and the home of the Sun or the Moon. For example, if Venus were in a sextile aspect [[notes: A 60-degree angle.]] with either luminary, such that she was western to the Sun or eastern to the Moon, she would then be in *almugea*. This, then, is the mode of *almugea* for each of the planets with the luminaries. Following this is the *alchinara*, which occurs when a planet is in its own *haiz* [[notes: A condition of "dignity" where a planet is in a sign/sector that matches its own nature (e.g., a day planet in a day sign).]] and in its like, from places suitable to it.

And when any of them has two or more authorities in its place, it is said to be in its "joy" and "honor," and their powers are then increased because they are assimilated to the signs in which they reside, which assist their powers. They are also said to "rejoice" when they are not assimilated to the signs in the aforementioned way, but the planets that are in their *haiz* are assimilated to those places; although this similarity is very remote, it is nonetheless something. When they are found in foreign places—namely, in a contrary *haiz*—their own powers greatly decrease, and then their temperaments are contrary to the temperament of the signs in which they reside. Therefore, the result of this will be a work gathered from two natures.
