[[page number: 124]]

->**ON NATIVITIES**<-
[[notes: "Nativities" is the traditional term for the study of birth charts or personal horoscopes, used to predict a person's character and destiny based on the sky at the moment of their first breath.]]

->*How great effects in the lower realms are judged.*<-
[[notes: "The lower realms" (*inferioribus*) refers to the Earth and all material things, which in the medieval worldview were thought to be governed by the "superior" celestial spheres.]]

**S**ix are the principles by which great effects in the lower realms are judged. First, through the chart of the revolution of the conjunction [[notes: The "revolution of the conjunction" refers to the specific moment planets align, recalculated for the current year]], especially with the chart of the revolution of that year. The second principle is through the chart of the revolution of the conjunction of **♄** (Saturn) & **♂** (Mars) when it changes triplicity [[notes: A "triplicity" is a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element—Fire, Earth, Air, or Water. A "great mutation" occurred when these planets met in a new element for the first time in centuries]], along with the positions of the planets in the revolution of the year in which such a conjunction occurs. The third principle is through the chart of the revolution of the conjunction of **♄** (Saturn) & **♂** (Mars) at the beginning of **☿** (Mercury) [[notes: Likely referring to the start of a cycle or a specific degree associated with Mercury]] with the chart of the revolution of the year in which such a conjunction occurs. The fourth principle is through the chart of the revolution of the conjunction of **♄** (Saturn) & **♀** (Venus) which occurs every 20 years. The fifth principle is through the chart of the conjunction or opposition of the **☉** (Sun) & **☽** (Moon) [[notes: A New Moon or Full Moon]] preceding the entry of the **☉** (Sun) into the "heads" of the movable signs [[notes: The "movable" or cardinal signs—Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn—which mark the start of the four seasons]]. The sixth principle is through the chart of the conjunction or opposition of the **☉** (Sun) & **☽** (Moon) before the entry of the **☉** (Sun) into the head of any of the 12 signs, and the chart of the entry of the **☉** (Sun) into any sign.

->*On finding the ascendant of the birth.*<-
[[notes: The "ascendant" is the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth. Because clocks were unreliable in the 16th century, astrologers used complex mathematical "rectification" to find the exact minute of birth.]]

**F**irst, let the estimated time of the birth be taken, namely the hours after noon; and from these let the "equation of days" be subtracted [[notes: The "equation of days" is a correction for the fact that solar days vary slightly in length throughout the year]], and there will remain the estimated time, un-equated. At this time, seek the true position of the sun and the true position of the moon, and with the first equated time, seek the ascendant. Then, see the distance of the moon from the western angle [[notes: The descendant]], if it was above the earth, or from the ascendant, if it was below the earth. Double that distance, and however many degrees there are, there will be that many hours. Once these hours are converted into days—if there are more than 24—add them to 258 days if the moon was above the earth, or add them to 273 days if it was below the earth. This will provide the estimated "delay of the birth" (gestation) in the mother’s womb [[notes: This is the "Trutine of Hermes," a traditional method based on the belief that the Moon's place at birth was the Ascendant at conception]]. Subtract this from the time of birth, taking care for leap years, so that you have the estimated time of conception in un-equated days. At this time, find the position of the sun, whose right ascensions you must subtract from the oblique ascensions of the moon at the hour of the estimated birth. Convert the remainder into hours, and place these hours and minutes with the days of the estimated conception in place of the hours that were previously there. You will then have the first examined time of conception in equated days. Seek the equation of days by the degrees of the sun at conception, subtract it from this time, and you will have the first examined time of conception in un-equated days. At this time, find the true position of the sun and moon; if the true position of the moon then agrees with the ascendant of the birth, the work is done, because then the estimated birth was true. If it does not agree, find the oblique ascensions of the position of the moon at the first equated conception, and subtract from them the right ascensions of the sun’s position at birth. From the residue, after taking away the equation of days found in the true position of the sun at birth, convert what remains into hours and minutes. Place these hours and minutes in the place of the hours and minutes with the days in the estimated birth, and it will result in the first examined time of birth in un-equated days. For this, let the true position of the sun be found, and the true position of the moon, and the right ascensions of the sun’s position, and the oblique ascensions of the moon’s position. Then subtract the right ascensions of the sun’s position at the first examined time of conception from the oblique ascensions of the moon at the estimated time of birth. Convert the last found remainder into hours and minutes, and place them in the place of the hours and minutes that were with the days in the first examined conception. You will then have the second examined time of conception in equated days, from which you subtract the equation of days of the degree of the sun at conception, and you will have that time in un-equated days. For this time, seek the position of the moon, and you may without fear set the ascendant at conception as the ascendant at birth, and vice versa.

->*On finding the Hyleg according to John of Saxony.*<-
[[notes: "John of Saxony" was a prominent 14th-century astronomer. The "Hyleg" (or *Hylech*) is the "Life-Giver"—a specific planet or point in a birth chart used to determine the health and lifespan of the person.]]

**T**o find the Hyleg, the significator of life in nativities, one must begin from the sun if the birth was by day: and if it was within five degrees before the degree of the ascendant—namely, above the eastern horizon—or if it was in the 10th or 11th house, we take it as the Hyleg, whether it be in masculine or feminine signs. If, however, it was not in these places, we must see if it was in the 7th, 8th, or 4th house in masculine signs; there it can still be the Hyleg. For if it were in the aforementioned places in feminine signs, it would not be a fit Hyleg. If, therefore, the sun is not a fit Hyleg, let the moon be looked upon; if it was in the 4th, 2nd, or 3rd house, or in the seventh or eighth house, she herself shall be the Hyleg, whether she was in a masculine sign or femi-

[[meta: This page continues a technical discussion by John of Saxony, a 14th-century astronomer and commentator on the work of Alchabitius. ### ->JOHN OF SAXONY<-

...or in a feminine sign. If the Sun is not in these places, but is within five degrees before the degree of the ascending sign [[notes: The Ascendant]], or in the tenth house, or in the fourth, or in the fifth in a [[notes: likely a feminine]] sign, it shall still be the **Hylech** [[notes: From the Persian *haylāj*, the "Giver of Life," this is the planet or point in a birth chart that carries the person's life force]]. However, if it is in these places but in masculine signs, it cannot be the **Hylech**. If the birth is nocturnal [[notes: a night-time birth]], we must begin our search with the **Moon**. If the Moon is within five degrees before the degree of the West [[notes: The Descendant or 7th house cusp]]—that is, within those five degrees that are below the earth on the western side—or in any of the other aforementioned places according to the stated method, it shall be the **Hylech**. 

If the Moon is not fit for this role, we shall look to the **Sun**. If the Sun is within five degrees before the degree of the seventh house, or below it (that is, beneath the earth), or in the fourth or fifth house, it will be a fit **Hylech**, whether the signs are masculine or feminine. If it is in the Ascendant or in the second house in a masculine sign, it will be a fit **Hylech**; but if it is in a feminine sign, it will not. 

If the **Luminaries** [[notes: The Sun and the Moon]] are not fit to be the **Hylech**, we must observe whether a **Conjunction** [[notes: a New Moon]] or an **Opposition** [[notes: a Full Moon]] preceded the birth. If a Conjunction preceded it, we examine the degree of that Conjunction; if we find that degree in any of the four **Angles** [[notes: The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses, the most powerful areas of a chart]] or their **Succedent** houses [[notes: The 2nd, 5th, 8th, or 11th houses]], we take it as the **Hylech**. If we do not find it in any of the Angles or Succedents, we must look to the degree of the **Part of Fortune** [[notes: A mathematical point calculated from the positions of the Sun, Moon, and Ascendant, representing prosperity and health]]. If it is in any of the Angles or Succedents, we must take it as the **Hylech**. If it is in none of these places, we must finally take the **Ascending degree** of the birth. 

However, if an **Opposition** preceded the birth, we must examine the degree of that Opposition just as was said regarding the Conjunction, then look to the **Part of Fortune**, and finally to the **Ascending degree** of the birth. It is not necessary to check whether the signs are masculine or feminine for the degree of Conjunction, Opposition, or the Part of Fortune. Thus, it is clear that the **Sun** can be the **Hylech** by day or by night, above or below the earth, in eleven places, and the **Moon** similarly. 

But if the **Moon** is **combust** [[notes: So close to the Sun—usually within 8.5 degrees—that its power is said to be "burnt up" and weakened]] in any of the aforesaid places under the rays of the Sun, it will not be a fit **Hylech**. Furthermore, the aforementioned places or planets cannot be the **Hylech** unless some planet having **dignity** [[notes: Essential dignity refers to a planet's strength based on its position in specific signs, such as being in its own Home, Exaltation, Triplicity, Term, or Face]] in those places aspects that location by any aspect whatsoever, and holds at least one of the **five dignities**. 

The brief summary of this chapter is as follows: there are five places from which the **Hylech** (that is, the significator of life or the place of life) is taken. These are: the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the degree of the preceding **Conjunction** or **Opposition**, the **Part of Fortune**, and the **Ascending degree** of the birth. If the birth is by day, one must begin with the **Sun**; if it is not in a fit place, the **Moon** is taken; if that is not fit, the degree of the **Conjunction** or **Opposition** is taken; if that is not fit, the **Part of Fortune** is taken; and if that is not fit, the **Ascending degree** of the birth must be taken.

# ->MARCUS MANILIUS’<-
## ->ASTRONOMICON TO CAESAR AUGUSTUS,<-
### ->BOOK ONE.<-

[[insert: Historiated initial C depicting a seated figure, likely a child or cherub, holding what appears to be a celestial instrument or globe.]] **O**f divine arts and the stars conscious of fate, which vary the diverse lots of human lives—the work of celestial reason—I begin to bring down to the world. I am the first to stir the springs of Helicon [[notes: Mount Helicon was the mythical home of the Muses; Manilius is claiming to be the first to write a technical poem on astrology in Latin hexameters]] with these new songs, bringing to its green-topped forests a guest-theme never recounted by those who came before. 

Now you, Caesar [[notes: Most scholars identify this as Augustus, the first Roman Emperor, though some argue for his successor, Tiberius]], prince and father of your country, give me the spirit and the strength to sing of such great things. You rule a world obedient to Augustan laws—a world granted to your father [[notes: A reference to the deified Julius Caesar]]—and you yourself deserve the status of a god. Now the universe favors those who study it more closely, and it urges me to reveal ethereal meanings through my verses. Only in times of peace is there such leisure; it is a joy to travel through the air itself, to live while wandering the immense sky, and to learn the signs and the opposing paths of the stars. 

Merely knowing these things is not enough; it is more deeply rewarding to know the very heart of the great universe: to see what power rules and creates living beings according to their signs, and to record these things in rhythm as Phoebus [[notes: Apollo, the god of music and prophecy]] plays his tune. Two altars shine for me with set flames; I pray at two temples, caught in a double tide of both poetry and science. As I sing with a fixed law, the universe resounds around the poet within its immense orb. My words, though barely released from their forms, are sent forth.

Who was first permitted to know the gifts of the heavenly beings on this lower earth? For who could have stolen the world by stealth while the gods were hiding it—that world by which all things are ruled? Who would have dared so much in a human heart as to wish to appear a god themselves against the will of the gods? You, Cyllenius [[notes: An epithet for Mercury (Hermes), the messenger god and patron of secret knowledge, born on Mt. Cyllene]], were the first author of this great sacred mystery. Through you, heaven is now found on earth and the stars are known. You opened the sublime paths, showing how the stars in the void obey their own boundaries under a single sky. You revealed their names, their courses, and the powers of the signs, so that the face of the universe might be made greater—not just a sight to be revered, but the very power of nature itself. 

The nations now feel how great the god is who arranged his works through time so they might be known by all, including the face of the universe and the heavens above. Nature gave her strength and disclosed herself, first deigning to move the minds of kings who reached the highest summits of human affairs, closest to heaven. These were the ones who tamed wild nations in the East: those lands through which the Euphrates flows and where the Nile floods, where the world turns back and flies over the cities of the Black people [[notes: Referring to the inhabitants of Aethiopia/sub-Saharan Africa as known to the Romans]]. Then came those who tended the temples with sacred rites through every age,

[[meta: This page continues the introduction to Book I of Manilius's *Astronomica*. In the previous section, the poet likely established his intent to sing of the heavens. -> # BOOK I <-

And chosen priests, through public vows, linked the gods to their sacred duties. The very presence of the powerful Divinity kindled their pure minds; God himself led them toward the Divine and revealed himself to his servants. These men were the first to know such glory. Through their skill, they were the first to see the fates hanging from the wandering stars [[notes: The "wandering stars" refers to the planets, which appear to move independently against the fixed background of the constellations]]. They recorded each moment and its specific outcome, grasping long centuries through tireless devotion: the day of birth for each person, what their life would be, under what laws of fortune they fell, which hour held power, and how the smallest celestial movements could create vast differences in human life.

Once the entire appearance of the sky was understood as the stars returned to their proper places, and the power of each constellation was assigned to a fixed order of fate, experience created the art [[notes: The Latin word *ars* refers to a systematic branch of knowledge or science]] through varied practice, with precedent leading the way. Through long observation, experience detected the stars ruling by silent laws, saw that the entire universe is moved by a balanced logic, and learned to distinguish the cycles of fate by certain signs.

Before these sages, human life was raw and lacked discernment; people looked at the world but lacked the logic to understand its workings. They were struck dumb with awe by the world's new light. They mourned the "loss" of stars as they set and rejoiced at their "rebirth" when they rose. They could not yet distinguish the causes of changing day-lengths, the uncertain hours of the night, the shifting shadows, or the sun's return. Ingenuity had not yet crafted the learned sciences. The vast earth lay untilled under unskilled farmers. Gold remained hidden in lonely mountains, and the unknown sea concealed undiscovered lands. Men dared not trust their lives to the ocean or their prayers to the winds; each thought it enough merely to know himself.

But as the long passage of time sharpened mortal wits, and necessity [[notes: literally 'labor' or 'toil']] granted genius to the suffering, and as fortune forced each man to look out for himself by the pressure of want, their minds branched out into various pursuits. Whatever wisdom experience discovered through trial, they joyfully shared for the common good. Then, even "barbarous" tongues received the structure of laws. Wild fields were tamed to produce various crops. The wandering sailor ventured out onto the now-charted sea, and trade routes were established through unknown lands. Then, the ancients devised the arts of war and peace; for one discovery always sows the seeds for the next.

I will not sing of common superstitions: interpreting the cries of birds [[notes: Augury, a Roman practice of seeking omens in the behavior of birds]], consulting entrails [[notes: Haruspicy, the inspection of animal livers to predict the future]], or killing snakes with incantations. I will not speak of summoning ghosts or stirring the depths of Acheron [[notes: A river in the underworld, here representing the realm of the dead]], nor of turning day into night and night into day. Teachable ingenuity has conquered all through effort; nor did it set a limit or boundary to its reach,

[[meta: This translation is from the opening of Book I of Marcus Manilius's *Astronomicon*, a 1st-century CE didactic poem about astronomy and astrology. The text follows a tradition of scientific poetry (like Lucretius) where the author explains the physical universe through verse.]]

# ->B O O K   I<-

How far reason has climbed into the sky! It began its search into the deep causes of nature and saw everything that exists. It saw why clouds were shaken, struck by such great crashes; why winter snow was softer than summer hail. It saw why the lands burned and the solid world trembled. It saw why rains rushed down, and what cause moved the winds; it saw through all and released the "miracles" of things from our minds [[notes: Manilius is arguing that scientific understanding (ratio) removes the superstitious "miracle" or "wonder" from natural events]]. It snatched the lightning bolt from Jupiter and the powers from the Thunderer [[notes: "The Thunderer" is a common epithet for Jupiter (Zeus). The poet suggests that human reason has demystified the lightning once thought to be a divine weapon]]; it assigned the sound to the winds and the fire to the clouds. 

After reason traced each of these things back to its own proper cause, it turned to know the nearby mass of the universe from on high, intending to grasp the whole sky in the mind. It assigned their own shapes and names to the signs [[notes: "The signs" refers to the constellations of the Zodiac]], and noted what turns they took under a fixed law. It saw that everything is moved by the divine power and face of the world, with varying stars changing events in a fixed order. 

Now this work of mine rises, hallowed by no poems before [[notes: Manilius claims to be the first to write a technical poem on astrology/astronomy in Latin]]. May fortune favor this great labor. May a long life and gentle old age be granted, so that I may bring to light these great masses of facts and run through great things and small with equal care.

->*On the origin of the world and the shape of the earth.*<-
->Chapter I<-

# **A**ND since this song descends from the high heaven, and the established order of the fates comes down to the lands, first the very form of nature must be sung by me, and the whole world must be placed beneath its own image. 

Whether we seek the seeds of the world from no prior things, and it pleases us that it lacked a birth and has always been—and will always be, equal to its beginning and lacking a fate [[notes: This refers to the Aristotelian view of an eternal, uncreated universe]]. 

Or whether Chaos once sorted the mixed beginnings of things through birth, and having labored to bring forth the shining world, the darkness was driven away and fled into the infernal gloom. 

Or whether nature remains after a thousand ages, dissolved into indivisible principles [[notes: "Individuis principiis" refers to atoms, the concept that matter is made of tiny, "uncuttable" parts, a view held by the Epicurean philosophers]] only to return to the same state—and the highest things came almost from nothing and will be nothing again, while blind matter perfected the sky and the orb of the earth. 

Or whether fire fashioned the work, and flickering flames, which made the eyes of the world [[notes: A poetic reference to the Sun and the Moon]] and dwell throughout the whole body, shaping the vibrating lightning in the sky. 

Or whether moisture gave birth to this, without which the dry matter of things grows stiff, and which calls upon the very fire by which it is dissolved. 

Or maybe neither earth, nor flame, nor air, nor water knows its own father, but they create a god through their four limbs [[notes: The "four limbs" are the four classical elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water]]. They built the globe of the world and forbid us from seeking anything beyond themselves, since all things are created through them. Thus cold things do not lack heat, nor moist things lack dry, nor spirit lack solids; and so let there be this "harmonious discord" [[notes: *Discordia concors* is a central Stoic concept—the idea that the universe is held together by the productive tension of opposing forces]], which a skillful bond and a procreative work fashions, as the elements make themselves capable of every birth.

[[meta: This page continues Book 1 of Manilius's *Astronomica*. The previous section discussed the origins of the universe and the various philosophical theories regarding its substance. Here, the poet describes the physical ordering of the four elements and the central, stable position of the Earth within the cosmos.]]

# ->BOOK ONE.<-

There will always be a kind of struggle [[notes: Manilius refers to the ongoing debate among ancient philosophers—like the Stoics and Epicureans—about how the world began]], and it will remain a matter of doubt, for the truth is hidden and lies far beyond the reach of both men and gods. But whatever the appearance of things was at the origin of the world, they came together, and the body of the universe was arranged in a certain fixed order.

Fire, being swift, lifted itself up into the ethereal breezes. Embracing the highest peaks of the starry sky, it created the very walls of nature with a rampart of flames [[notes: In the ancient geocentric model, the outermost sphere was composed of "pyrene" or elemental fire]]. Next, the spirit [[notes: The Latin *spiritus* here refers to the element of Air]] descended into the thin breezes and spread the atmosphere through the middle voids of the world. This breath of air feeds the fire, being placed just below the neighboring stars.

A third lot spread out the waters, and the floating breath drenched the surfaces emerging across the whole deep. This was so the thin liquid might exhale and breathe out breezes, nourishing the air that draws its "seeds" from the water itself.

Last of all, the earth settled down with its massed weight. The slime, mixed with wandering sands, came together gradually at the bottom as the thin liquid fled toward the top. The more the crumbling moisture withdrew into waves, and the more the dried surfaces constricted the lands, the more the water lay adjacent in the hollow valleys of the rivers. Mountains emerged from the depths, and the dry land leaped up through the waves—yet it remained enclosed on all sides by the vast ocean. It holds the lowest and central seat of all things.

For this reason, the Earth remains stable: because the entire universe flees from it at an equal distance from every side. By "falling" toward the center from every direction, the world has ensured that the Earth itself cannot fall; it is both the center and the bottom-most point of the whole. These elemental bodies consist within these narrow regions, and by pressing against one another, they prevent any further movement [[notes: This is an early intuition of gravitational equilibrium: the Earth stays in the center because it is being pushed or pulled equally from all directions]].

If the Earth did not hang there with its weight perfectly balanced, Phoebus [[notes: A poetic name for the Sun]] would not be able to drive his course toward the sunset while the stars rise beneath him, and he would never return to his starting point in the east. Nor could the Moon guide her submerged path through the voids. Nor would Lucifer [[notes: The "Light-Bringer," the name for the planet Venus when it appears as the Morning Star]] shine in the morning hours, nor Hesperus [[notes: Venus when it appears as the Evening Star]], who gives light to the heavens once they are immersed in darkness.

Now, because the Earth is not cast down into some bottomless pit but remains suspended in the middle, all paths are passable. Where a star sets, it may go beneath the heavens and rise once again. For I cannot believe that the rising stars are mere accidents, nor that the world is "born" anew so many times, nor that there are constant new births and daily creations of the sun [[notes: Manilius is arguing against the Epicurean view that the sun was a new fire ignited every morning and extinguished every night]]. I believe this because the same face of the zodiac signs remains constant through the ages.

The same Phoebus travels from the same parts of heaven. From there, he curves his bends through the legs and feet of the Centaur [[notes: The constellation Centaurus]], and then begins to ascend the sky again, passing the Argive ship [[notes: The constellation Argo Navis, representing the ship of Jason and the Argonauts]] by the highest ornaments of its stern. The Moon, too, changes through the same number of phases and circles, and Nature keeps the paths she herself first made. Nor does she make mistakes through inexperience, but is carried around with eternal light, marking the passage of time. Now to these regions, now to those, the same world—

<meta>This page continues Book 1 of Manilius's Astronomica. Following the description of the four elements (Fire, Air, Water, Earth) and how they settled into their respective places, the poet now turns his focus to the specific shape of the Earth and its position within the spherical cosmos. He employs the Stoic argument that the Earth must be a sphere because the heavens themselves are spherical and because celestial phenomena, like eclipses and the visibility of stars, vary by geography.</meta>

# ->BOOK ONE<-

Forever, and for those traveling further from sunrise to sunrise, or from sunrise to sunset, let the heavens and the sun endure.
->## On the form of the world and the roundness of the earth.<-
->### Chapter II<-

**N**or indeed should the nature of the hanging earth seem a cause for wonder to you, since the world itself hangs and places its footsteps on no foundation. This is clear from its very motion and the path of its flight, as Phoebus <note>The sun-god, often used poetically for the Sun itself.</note> travels suspended and turns his course back and forth, keeping his swift markers in the ether. As the moon and stars fly through the empty spaces of the world, the earth too, having followed the laws of the air, has remained suspended. Therefore, the earth has been allotted the middle hollow of the air and is lifted up equally by the whole depth; it is not stretched out into wide flat expanses, but established into a globe rising equally and falling equally on all sides. This is the face of nature; thus the world itself, flying into convex curves, makes the shapes of the stars smooth. We see the orb of the sun and the roundness of the moon as it seeks light with its swelling body, because a whole globe does not receive slanting fires all at once. This form remains eternal and most like the gods, which has no beginning anywhere nor end within itself, but remains similar in its whole and is equal through all its parts. Thus the stars remain clustered and give shape to the world. For this reason, we do not see all the signs <note>The constellations of the Zodiac.</note> from all lands; you will never find Canopus <note>A bright star in the southern constellation Carina, invisible from northern latitudes like Rome.</note> shining until you have come through the Sea to the shores of the Nile. But those over whom that star rises will look for Helice <note>The constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear), which is always visible in the northern sky but disappears as one travels south.</note>; for the central swellings of the earth take away the sky from those who inhabit the lateral regions, and their views are obstructed. The moon gives you witness of its own spherical orb; when she fails <term>fails: an eclipse</term> during the night, submerged in black shadows, she does not disturb all nations equally with her light, but the eastern peoples miss her light first. Afterward, she reaches whatever lands are cultivated under the middle of the sky; finally, she flies with stained wings to the Westerners. Late is the bronze struck among the furthest peoples <note>original: "Sera'q; in extremis quatiuntur gentibus æra." This refers to the ancient custom of clashing bronze pots and making noise during a lunar eclipse to "help" the moon and drive away the shadow.</note>. For if the earth were flat, this pitiable eclipse would occur for everyone at the same time across the whole world. But because the earth is drawn out in a smooth swelling, Delia <note>A name for the Moon-goddess, Diana, born on the island of Delos.</note> appears now to these lands and later to those, rising and setting at the same time; because she is carried around the curve of the earth's belly, she joins the rising and falling slopes equally, and she passes over some circuits while leaving others behind. From this, it is concluded that the form of the lands is round. Around this globe dwell various nations of men and wild beasts, and the birds of the air. Part of it stands out toward the North, and part is habitable in the Southern regions. It lies beneath our feet and is seen above...

The Earth itself, with its surface deceiving the eye, has long slopes,
Rising and falling in equal measure along the way.

-> *On the twelve signs of the zodiac.* <-
-> ### Chapter III <-

**N**ow I shall tell you of the flames of the signs shining on all sides

Which gird the slanted world in a middle row <note>This refers to the ecliptic, the apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>
And carry the Sun by turns through the seasons,
And those other stars struggling against the turning world,
All of which you can discern in a serene sky.
From these, the entire calculation of the fates is drawn,

-> *On Aries and the other following signs.* <-
-> ### Chapter IV <-

**A**ries, the leader, shining in his golden fleece <note>Aries represents the ram of the Golden Fleece from the myth of Jason and the Argonauts.</note>,
Looks back in wonder at the Bull <note>Taurus</note> rising opposite him
With a lowered face, and the Twins <note>Gemini</note> calling him with their brow;
The Crab <note>Cancer</note> follows them, the Lion <note>Leo</note> the Crab, the Virgin <note>Virgo</note> the Lion.
Then the Scales <note>Libra</note>, when the day is made equal with the time of night,
Draws the Scorpion, shining with its burning star,
At whose tail the one joined with a horse <note>Sagittarius, the Centaur</note> directs his strained bow,
Already about to let fly his swift arrow.
Then comes Capricorn, bent in its narrow sign.
After him, Aquarius pours out his tilted urn
Into the waters greedily approached by the habitual Fish <note>Pisces</note>,
Whom Aries touches as they close the final signs.
But the stars rise toward the shining Bears <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor</note> in the sky,
All of which look down upon the stars from the highest heaven.
They know no setting, and being situated in only one pole
They turn the heaven and the stars in a different position;
Through the icy air, the slender Axis is drawn,
And it rules the balanced world from its opposing poles.
The starry orb revolves around the middle of this axis,
And rotates its heavenly courses unmoved; but the axis itself,
Through the empty spaces of the great world toward the two Bears,
And through the very globe of the earth, is directed straight.
Nor indeed does it stand consisting of solid strength of body,

# -> BOOK <-

It carries no heavy weight to bear the burden of the high heavens, but since the entire air is forever whirled in a circle, and once it has begun, it flies entirely from all sides into itself. Whatever lies in the center, around which all things move, is so thin that it cannot be turned into itself, nor can it now be tilted or rotate. Men have called this the **axis**, because it possesses no movement of its own. It watches all things as they fly and move around it. The highest points of this axis hold signs very well known to weary sailors, leading the eager across the immense sea. 

Helice <note>original: "Helice"; the Greek name for the Great Bear or Ursa Major.</note> marks out a larger circle around the pole. Seven stars, competing in brightness, mark it; with Helice as their guide through the waves, Greek ships set their sails. Small Cynosura <note>original: "Cynosura"; the Greek name for the Little Bear or Ursa Minor.</note> is whirled in a narrow circle, smaller in both size and light, but by a judge’s verdict, it surpasses the larger one. For the Phoenicians <note>original: "Tyrio Poenis"; referring to the famous sailors of Tyre and Carthage.</note>, this is a more certain guide for those seeking the pole that is not apparent on the open sea. 

The two Bears are not placed with their faces matching, but the tail of one points toward the snout of the other, and one follows the other as it follows in turn. Flowing between them and embracing both, a Snake <term>Draco: The "Dragon" constellation, which winds its way between the Great and Little Bears.</term> divides them and surrounds them with burning stars, so that they may never come together or ever leave their assigned places. 

Between this and the middle circle, where seven stars <note>Likely referring to the planets or the sun and moon.</note> fly through the twelve opposing signs <note>The Zodiac.</note>, stars rise up mixed from diverse powers—here neighboring the pole, and there closest to the fires of heaven. Because the air, where these stars struggle, is of a different nature, it tempers them and renders the fruitful world below to mortals. 

Near the freezing Bears and the stiffening north wind, a figure comes leaning on its knees, conscious of the reason for its pose <note>This is the "Kneeler" (Engonasin), an ancient constellation later identified as Hercules.</note>. Behind its back shines the Bear-Watcher <note>original: "Arctophylax".</note>, also known as Boötes, who stands like a driver over yoked oxen and carries the star Arcturus <note>A bright star whose name literally means "Bear-guard".</note> with him under the middle of his breast. 

But from another part, the Crown <note>Corona Borealis.</note> flies in a bright circle, gleaming with varied light; for one star in the middle of the radiant circle surpasses the rest. This star, being closest to the front and white, distinguishes the lights with a burning flame: these are the Gnosian monuments of the abandoned girl <note>Ariadne, the princess of Knossos (Gnosia) in Crete. After she was abandoned by Theseus, Bacchus turned her crown into this constellation.</note> which shine in the sky. 

And the Lyre <note>Lyra.</note> is seen among the stars with its horns extended through the sky; with this instrument, Orpheus once moved everything he touched with song. He even journeyed through the spirits of the dead themselves and conquered the laws of the underworld with his melody. It holds heavenly honor and a similar power of cause: once drawing forests and stones to it, it now leads the stars and carries along the immense sphere of the revolving world. 

Ophiuchus <term>The Serpent-Bearer: Represented as a man holding a large snake.</term> divides the Serpent with great signs and displays a body merging into another body, so that he looks back upon the coils and arched backs through the spheres; yet he, with his neck bent back softly, has offered his palms to the loosely flowing coils.

There will always be a war between equals, because they balance each other with equal forces. Next is the lot of the **Swan** <note>original: "Cygni"; the constellation Cygnus.</note>, whom Jupiter himself placed in the sky as a reward for the form he took to seize his lover, when the god descended transformed into a snow-white swan and placed his feathery back beneath the trusting **Leda**. Even now, he flies among the stars with outstretched wings. From here, stars shine in imitation of the flight and shape of an **Arrow** <note>original: "sagittæ"; the constellation Sagitta.</note>; then the bird of great Jupiter <note>The Eagle, or Aquila.</note> is carried into the heights, flying as he is accustomed, whether he carries the thunderbolts of the world worthy of Jove and heaven, which he equips with sacred arms. 

Then also the **Dolphin** rises from the sea to the stars of the Ocean, the glory of the sky, made sacred through both realms. The **Horse** <note>Pegasus.</note>, shining in his breast with a radiant star, hastens to catch him in a rapid course. And the sequence ends in **Andromeda**, whom **Perseus** rescues with his arms and joins to himself. Following her, divided by an unequal space, is a constellation seen with three lights, unequal yet with equal sides, named **Deltoton** <term>Deltoton: A constellation named for its resemblance to the Greek letter Delta (Δ), known today as Triangulum.</term>, so called from its likeness; then **Cepheus** and **Cassiopeia**. Nor does the shining orb of the sun desert the void. Thus he moves the world in both directions and returns things to their opposites.

Those who watch **Taurus** <note>The Bull.</note> as he rises, when he is first returned at dawn from the high peak of a mountain, speak of the various outcomes of crops and the seasons: what health may come, how much concord brings about wars, or brings back peace, returning in various ways. Thus he moves as he has seen the world and governs its vastness. His color is a great proof of this power, and his paths, flashing with rays, are scarcely less than the sun, except that, clinging far off, he hurls cold lights from a dark blue face. 

Other stars are surpassed in beauty; no brighter star is dipped in the ocean or revisits the sky from the waves. Then comes **Procyon** <note>meaning "Before the Dog," referring to its rising before Sirius.</note>, and the swift **Hare**, then the noble **Argo** <note>The first ship, which carried Jason and the Argonauts.</note>, drawn up into the sky; because she first ran upon the sea, having served her time through great storms, she now holds the world, made a goddess for saving the gods. Next to her, the **Snake** <note>The constellation Hydra.</note> imitates scaly lights with its arranged flames. There is also the **Bird** sacred to Phoebus <note>The Crow, or Corvus.</note>, and the **Bowl** <note>The constellation Crater.</note> pleasing to great Iacchus <note>another name for Bacchus or Dionysus.</note>, and the **Centaur** shines with a double image, a man’s part joined to a horse’s back. 

From here is the temple of the world itself, and the victorious **Altar** shines with the sacred rites released, from the time when the Earth, raging, brought the vast **Giants** into heaven. Then the arrogant ones sought the great gods, and Jupiter himself hesitated, fearing that he might not be able to do what he could, when he saw the Earth rising and believed all nature was being overturned—with mountains and other mountains piled up to grow, and the hills, bringing arms, so close to the fleeing stars, born from their ruptured mother, discordant in face and with bodies of mixed parts.

The gods did not yet know anyone hostile to them. 
If any powers were greater than his own, then Jupiter established 
the stars, which even now shine with the greatest light. 
For this reason, the **Whale** <note>original: "Cetus"; the sea monster sent by Poseidon.</note>, coiling its scaly back, 
rises with twisted loops and heaves with its belly, 
threatening with a bite as if just about to seize its prey— 
just as it was when it came from the waves to the doom of the 
exposed daughter of **Cepheus** <note>Andromeda.</note>, driving the sea far beyond its shores. 
Then the **Southern Fish** <note>original: "Notius piscis"; Piscis Austrinus.</note>, named after the south wind, 
rises from the direction of the South, toward which all things are 
carried, bent through the vast swirling rivers of the stars. 
**Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer.</note> joins the waters of the **River** <note>The constellation Eridanus.</note> to his own head, 
and they flow together into the middle, mixing their stars, 
marked for their own punishments, and near the abandoned 
**Andromeda**. Fearing the vast, gaping jaws of the fish, she 
weeps while exposed to the sea and bound to the rocks, 
lest **Perseus** should also preserve his old love in the sky, 
and help her with his aid, and hold up the face of the 
**Gorgon** <note>Medusa.</note> which must be shunned—a trophy for himself, 
and a witness to the one who sees it. 
Then, bringing his nearby footsteps to the bent **Bull** <note>Taurus.</note>, 
comes the **Charioteer** <term>Eniochus: The Greek name for the constellation Auriga.</term>, who gained both his place in the world and his name through his devotion. 
Jupiter first saw him flying in his high chariot 
with a team of four horses, and hallowed him in the heavens. 
Then follow the **Kids** <note>original: "Haedi"; stars in the constellation Auriga.</note>, closing off the sea with their constellation 
amidst the clouds, and the **Goat** <note>original: "Capella".</note> who nursed the king of the world; 
from her udders, that great god ascended high Olympus, 
growing strong upon wild milk for the thunderbolts and the power of thundering. 
Therefore, Jupiter deservedly hallowed her among the eternal stars, 
and repaid heaven to the sky as a reward. <margin>But the head</margin>
The **Pleiades** and the wild **Hyades**, both parts of the Bull, 
climb toward the North; these are the northern signs. 
Look now below the rising courses of the sun, 
at the stars which glide above the scorched lands, 
and those lights that turn within the frozen constellation of **Capricorn** 
and the axis supported at the very bottom of the world. 
The other part of the globe lies beneath the waters, inaccessible to us, 
where unknown races of men and kingdoms never visited 
draw their shared light from a single sun; 
they watch different shadows, and stars falling to the left 
and rising to the right in a reversed sky. 
Their world is no smaller than ours, nor is its light worse, 
nor are the stars born in that circle any fewer; 
the rest do not yield, but they are surpassed by one star: 
**Augustus** <note>A reference to the Roman Emperor as a celestial body.</note>, a constellation that fell to our world— 
Caesar, now the greatest guiding authority on earth, and later in heaven. 
One may also see **Orion** near the **Twins** <note>Gemini.</note>, 
stretching his arms into a great portion of the sky. 
Nor does he shine with a lesser stride toward the stars; 
individual lights mark his glowing shoulders, 
and his sword is drawn down with three slanted stars.

-># BOOK I<-

But the head of **Orion** <note>original: "Orion"; a prominent constellation representing a giant hunter.</note> is marked by three stars on his upturned face, immeasurable in the high heavens. It is not that they are less bright, but that they recede further into the heights. Nor do the stars run harshly through the whole world. The **Little Dog** <term>Canicula: The "Dog Star," known today as Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.</term> follows in a rapid course; no star comes to the lands more violently than this, nor leaves more heavily, nor rises shivering with cold <note>The rising of Sirius in summer was associated with the "Dog Days" of intense heat and disease.</note>. Between these paths of the sun and the hidden North, where the sky's axis groans as it turns under the weight of the world, the heavens are painted with stars in a foreign circuit. These the ancient bards called the **Southern** <note>original: "Notia"</note> stars, which always revolve at the very bottom of the world. The shining temples of heaven remain woven into these, never returning to our sight as the pole turns; they reflect the sublime appearance of the world and similar figures of stars, and show the **Bears** <note>original: "arctos"; referring to Ursa Major and Ursa Minor.</note> with their fronts turned, distinguished in the middle and enclosed by the **Dragon** <note>original: "Draco"; the constellation winding between the two Bears.</note>. We believe by this example—even though the stars now shining as the heavens turn see the world supported by a similar pole—that the sky paints the same patterns at its summit. Therefore, these signs hold seats divided in the great ether, drawn through the whole circuit of the world. Do not look for figures exactly like human bodies, nor for all limbs to shine with equal color. Let nothing be lacking, so that no vacuum exists where light ceases; yet the world would not be able to endure such great fires if all stars burned with full limbs. Whatever nature withdrew from the flames, she spared so the world could bear the weight, content only to separate the forms. Thus, a line designates the appearance of the constellations with specific stars, and fires respond to fires: the middle to the extremes, and the last to the highest. It is enough if they do not all hide themselves. Especially when the **Moon** is full in its orbit, only certain stars shine in the world; when the moon is hidden, the whole crowd of stars—the nameless signs—flee. Then more stars can be seen in the empty sky. They do not fail in number, nor are they carried along mixed as small things. Indeed, you can recognize the signs more clearly then. They do not know varied settings or varied returns, but certain stars rise with their own lights; they keep their births and their settings in order. Nor is anything more wonderful in such a massive structure than its Reason, and the fact that all things are subject to certain laws. Nowhere does the crowd of stars cause harm, and nothing in those parts wanders. Is anything carried wider or lighter by a changed order? What is so confused in appearance, yet so certain in its cycles?

And that the world itself is a god, and did not happen to come together by chance as a guide—
As he [[notes: A reference to Epicurus or Lucretius, who argued that the world was formed by the random collision of atoms]] wished it to be believed, who first built the walls of the world
From the smallest seeds, and dissolved them into
Equal parts: the seas, the lands, the stars of heaven,
And the ether, fashioning immense orbs within their boundaries;
And who believed that some things dissolve while all return
Into their own principles, and that the shapes of things change.
Who could believe that such great masses of works, without divine power,
Were created from the smallest things, and a world born of a blind pact?
If chance gave this to us, let chance herself govern it.
But why do we see the signs rise in arranged turns,
And, as if by command, return to their prescribed courses,
And none are left behind while others hasten?
Why do the same stars always adorn the summer nights,
And the same the winter ones, and why does each day
Restore a certain figure to the world, and leave it certain?
Even then, when the Greek nations overthrew Pergama [[notes: Another name for the city of Troy]],
The Bear [[notes: Arctos, the constellation Ursa Major]] and Orion went with opposing fronts.
The Bear content to bend her circles at the summit [of the pole],
The other [Orion] rising opposite from a different direction
To meet her, and always running through the whole world.
Already they were able to catch each moment of the dark night
By the signs, and the sky had distinguished its own hours.
How many kingdoms have been uprooted since the fall of Troy?
How many peoples captured? How often has fortune brought
Slavery and empire throughout the world? And how variously has it
Restored the Trojan ashes, and how much has it cherished, though forgotten?
Greece is now pressed down by the fates of Asia’s empire [[notes: Likely referring to the rise of the Roman Empire, which Manilius sees as a restoration of the Trojan/Eastern lineage]].
It is wearisome to count the ages, and how often the fiery sun,
Returning in its varying orb, has surveyed the world.
All things created by mortal law are changed.
The lands do not recognize themselves as the years turn,
Nor do the nations, stripped of their various faces through the ages.
But the world remains unharmed and preserves all its own things,
Which neither a long day increases, nor old age diminishes.
Its motion does not run out in a moment, nor does its course tire it.
It will always be the same, since it has always been the same.
Our fathers saw no different world, nor will our grandsons
Behold another. It is a god, who is not changed in time.
Never does the sun run down toward the transverse Bears,
Nor change its ways, nor turn its course toward the rising,
Nor show the dawning Aurora [[notes: The goddess of the dawn]] to new lands.
Nor does the moon exceed the certain orbs of her light,
But keeps the measure by which she grows or recedes.
Nor do the stars, hanging from heaven, fall into the earth.

Since in a sixth part, in which the whole world revolves,
They draw the accompanying threads of the high heaven,
Always keeping their intervals by an equal boundary,

-># BOOK ONE<-

Where once the sky has pressed down, it turns and rises again.
->### *On the magnitude and latitude of the world, and the distance of the signs. Chap. VII*<-

**I**t is reason itself that teaches us how much space the world occupies within the vaulted heavens <term>Olympus|A poetic term for the sky or the celestial sphere</term>, and within what vast boundaries the twelve stars <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> are carried. To reason, nothing stays closed; no immense mass can resist it, and even the furthest reaches of space yield to its touch. All things succumb to it, for even the sky itself can be penetrated by the mind. For as far as the constellations are removed from the lands and the sea, so far do two signs extend in width; and as much as the world-sphere is cut through the middle, it creates a third part of the Great Circle <term>Gyrus|The circular path or orbit of the heavens</term>, dividing the solid sum of the whole by a small difference. Therefore, the highest heaven rises four measures <note>original: "bis bina"; literally 'twice two', referring here to the width of four zodiac signs</note> from the bottom, so that this portion constitutes a third part of the twelve signs.

But because the Earth hangs suspended in the middle of the deep, it sits two signs away from the top and the bottom. Thus, whatever you look up at above yourself, wherever your eyes travel through the void or where they fail to reach, it is equal to four signs; two-sixths <note>original: "sextante"; a sixth part of a circle, which in a 12-part zodiac equals two signs</note> of the round zone make up the orb through which the twelve signs are carried, weaving through the sky in equal space. Nor do the stars send forth wandering births by chance. Our fate is mixed with a great distinction of character, since each individual sign holds so much power and is carried for so much time, with six constellations rising in the full light of day.

It remains for me to try to describe the celestial boundaries for you, and the threads that accompany the sky in their arranged turns, through which the flaming order of the signs is directed. One circle <note>The North-South line or 'Colure'</note> permeates the world, starting from its very peak, seeking the Bear-Watcher <term>Arctophylax|The constellation Boötes</term> through the back of the Dragon <term>Draco|The serpent constellation between the two Bears</term>; it cuts the end of the Water-Snake <term>Hydra</term> and the middle of the Centaur beneath the stars, then runs back again toward the axis, returning to the Whale <term>Cetus</term> and its scaly back. It marks the boundaries of the Wool-Bearer <term>Laniger|The constellation Aries, the Ram</term>, the bright Triangle, the lowest folds of Andromeda’s robes, and the head of her Mother <note>The constellation Cassiopeia</note>. Finally, it closes its own beginning, having returned to the pole.

Another circle <note>The second 'Colure'</note> lies across the middle of this one and rests upon the highest axis. It passes through the front feet and the neck of the Great Bear <term>Ursa</term>—the first constellation to appear when the sun is gone, offering its lights to the black night. It separates the Crab <term>Cancer</term> from the Twins <term>Gemini</term>, and brushes against the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note> as it blazes from its mouth, and the steering-oar of the Ship <term>Ratis|The constellation Argo Navis</term> which once conquered the sea. From there, it touches the hidden axis through the signs of the previous circle, crossing over from another boundary to find you, Capricorn! From your stars, it marks out the Eagle <term>Aquila</term>. Running through the inverted Lyre and the coils of the Dragon, it treads upon the stars of the hind feet of the Lesser Bear <term>Cinosura|The 'Dog's Tail', an ancient name for Ursa Minor</term>, cutting across the tail at the nearby pole. Here it joins back with itself, remembering where it first began.

<meta>This page continues Manilius’s explanation of the celestial sphere. Having previously described the mathematical proportions of the universe and the distance between the zodiac signs, he now moves to the specific great circles that define the sky: the Meridian and the Horizon.</meta>

-># **BOOK ONE**<-

->### **On the Meridian and the Horizon. Chap. VIII**<-

# **A**nd these seasons have fixed their eternal seat in unchanging ways throughout the signs in a perpetual station. Nature made two of these circles fleeting; for one, rising from Helice <note>The constellation of the Great Bear, marking the North Pole</note> itself, cuts through the middle of the sky <term>Olympus|The celestial sphere</term>, distinguishes the day, and weighs out the sixth hour <note>Midday or noon</note>, seeing the sunset and sunrise at equal distances. This circle changes its position through the signs; whether one seeks the Dawn-lands <note>The East</note> or the Hesperian lands <note>The West</note>, it circles the sphere above the traveler, standing over the crown of the head <term>Vertex|The zenith, the point directly above the observer</term>, cutting the middle of the sky and marking the world with divided light. Since one person’s middle-point is different from another’s, the hour flies across the globe. As a man changes his place on earth, he changes the sky and the times. Where the Sun <term>Phoebus|The god of the Sun, Apollo</term> first lifts himself from the waves, the sixth hour already remains for those whom the golden orb then presses from above. Again, it is the sixth hour for the Westerners when he yields to the shadows; we count both the first and the highest sixth, and feel the cold light from the furthest fire.

If you wish to know the circuits of the other boundary, turn your easy eyes and face around the orb. Whatever shall be the first part of the sky and the last of the earth, where the world meets itself with no distinction and returns or receives the shining stars from the sea—this girds the transverse world with a thin boundary. This line, too, will fly through the whole sky <note>original: "coelum"; ink bleed or printer artifacts appear here in the source</note>, turning only toward the middle and suddenly becoming the middle of the orb; now moved toward the seven stars <note>The Big Dipper, indicating the North</note>, now beneath the stars of the south. But wherever your wandering feet carry your steps, whether to these shores of the earth or those, there will always be a new arc, and the curve will change with the lands. Indeed, showing one sky and leaving another, it rules and brings back a half-sphere; it marks the world with a varying boundary, moving its threads along with your sight. This shall be called the terrestrial circle, because it embraces the earth and has girded the world with a flat boundary. Drawing its title from this, it is called the Horizon <term>Orizon|From the Greek word for 'boundary'</term>.

->### **On the Zodiac, the Milky Way, and Comets. Chap. IX**<-

# **H**ere they add other circles drawing different threads among themselves, one of which holds the shining signs <note>The Zodiac</note> through which the Sun <term>Phoebus|Apollo</term> governs his reins. The wandering Moon <term>Delia|Diana, goddess of the moon, named for her birth on Delos</term> follows the sun in her own chariot, and five stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> struggling against the turning world perform their various dances by the law of nature. Cancer holds the top of this circle and Capricorn the bottom. Twice it receives the light that equals the shadows <note>The Equinoxes</note>, cutting its threads at the sign of the Wool-bearer <term>Laniger|The Ram, or Aries</term> and the Balance <term>Libra</term>. Thus the orb is led in a curve through three circuits, and with its sloping incline, it deceives the path of a straight line. Nor does it escape our vision or sharp sight; it can be marked by the mind just as the previous circles are seen by the mind.

->**O But**<-

<summary>Manilius describes the Meridian and Horizon as circles that change based on the observer's location, and introduces the Zodiac as the inclined path of the sun, moon, and planets.</summary>

--- Page 421 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the great circles of the heavens. Having previously defined the Horizon and the Meridian—circles which are relative to the observer's position—Manilius now turns to the most visible and permanent "belt" in the night sky: the Milky Way.</meta>

-># BOOK ONE<-

**B**ut the starry Belt <note>original: *Baltheus*; here referring to the Milky Way</note> shines in a vast circle and distinguishes the world with its engraved light. It extends three hundred and sixty degrees in length, while the band spans twelve degrees in width, encompassing the stars that glide in their varied courses. This circle passes toward the Bears <note>The constellations Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, marking the North</note> positioned opposite, and draws its threads back slightly from the North Wind’s <term>Boreas|The North Wind</term> circuit. It passes through the stars of Cassiopeia, who is turned upside down. From there, descending crosswise, it touches the Swan <note>original: *Olor*; the constellation Cygnus</note> and cuts the summer boundaries and the outstretched Eagle. It crosses the circle that equalizes the times <note>The Celestial Equator, where day and night are equal</note> and the zone that carries the Sun’s horses <note>The Zodiac or Ecliptic</note>, passing within the tail where the Scorpion burns and the furthest left hand and arrow of the Archer.

From there, it winds its curves through the legs and feet of the second Centaur <note>Probably referring to the constellation Centaurus, distinct from Sagittarius</note> and begins to ascend the sky again, cutting through the highest steering-oars <term>Aplustria|The carved stern-post of an ancient ship</term> of the ship Argo, through the middle circuit of the universe, and through the Twins <note>Gemini</note> at their lowest point. It approaches the Charioteer <note>original: *Heniochus*; the constellation Auriga</note>, and seeking you, Cassiopeia, from whom it first set out, it passes over Perseus himself. It concludes the circle in her, having begun it from her. It cuts the three middle circles and the Zodiac in two places whenever it crosses them.

One does not need to search for it; it meets the eyes of its own accord, reveals itself, and compels itself to be noticed. For in the blue world, a white-hot track shines as if it were about to suddenly bring forth the day, laying open the heavens. Just as a path divides green fields—a track worn by constant use as the wheels renew the journey—this path lies between equal divisions of the sky. As the seas grow white when a ship’s keel draws a furrow, and the waves receive a path in the foaming water moved by the twisting vortex of the turned depths, so does this white boundary shine in the black heavens <term>Olympus|A poetic term for the sky or the dwelling of the gods</term>, cleaving the blue world with immense light.

Just as the Rainbow <term>Iris|The goddess of the rainbow and messenger of the gods</term> circles her arches through the clouds, so does this white boundary lean over from the marked summit. It causes mortals to turn their faces upward in awe while these strange lights vibrate through the dark night, and they inquire with human hearts into the sacred causes: whether the vast mass of the universe is attempting to dissolve itself as its elemental seeds are drawn away, and whether the hull of the world will slip away from its entire frame, admitting a new light through a loosened breast. What then? Is it not as if they fear, when they behold the wounds of the great sky, that the injury of the world might strike their eyes? Or perhaps the world is coming together, and the ends of the double cavern meet, touching the shores of heaven and the stars? And perhaps a visible scar joins them through these very connections, making a fissure in the world, where the crowded orb, turned into an aerial cloud within this bright structure, forces the foundations of the high heaven into wedges.

->**Or better yet**<-

<summary>Manilius describes the physical path of the Milky Way through the constellations and reflects on the awe and dread it inspires in humanity, who wonder if it represents a "scar" or "fissure" in the fabric of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Milky Way, constellations, Cassiopeia, Cygnus, Sagittarius, Argo, Gemini, celestial mechanics, ancient cosmology, omens</keywords>

--- Page 422 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Milky Way. Having previously described its physical path across the constellations (Cassiopeia, Cygnus, and the Archer), Manilius now shifts to the various mythological and philosophical theories regarding its origin—ranging from the scorched path of Phaethon to the milk of Juno and the gathered souls of ancient heroes.</meta>

-> # BOOK ONE <-

Or does that belief hold more truth through the ancient ages: that the horses of the Sun once traveled there with different chariots, treading another path? And that through a long span of time, these scorched regions and stars—cooked by flames—changed their deep-blue appearance as their color turned, pouring ash upon the place and leaving the universe buried. A legend has also descended to us from years of old: that Phaethon <note>The son of the sun-god Helios who attempted to drive his father's chariot</note> flew through the signs of the Zodiac in his father’s chariot. While he marveled at the new spectacles of the world from too close a distance—a boy playing in the heavens—he reveled in his pride. Desiring things greater than his father's world, he abandoned the shown paths; he attempted to impose a new ruler of the orb upon the pole, but could not master the unaccustomed signs. At the whim of a wanderer, the flames and the chariot were loosed, deflected from their usual course. Because of those curved four-horse teams, we lament that flames raged throughout the whole world, and that all the cities of the earth burned as a funeral pyre. When the wandering lights of the scattered chariot flickered and the sky was scorched, the world itself paid the price for the fire, and new stars blazed from the neighboring flames.

Even now, traces remain that preserve the appearance of that disaster. Nor must I hide the well-known ancient story: that a liquor of milk, softer than snow, flowed from the snowy breast of the Queen of the Gods <note>Juno (Hera); according to legend, she was startled while nursing the infant Hercules, and her spilled milk became the Milky Way</note> and stained the heavens with its color. For this reason, it is called the Milky Circle <note>original: *Lacteus orbis*</note>, and the name descends from the cause itself.

Or is it a greater crowd of stars in a dense Crown <note>A poetic description of the Galaxy as a gathered assembly of stars</note> that weaves these flames, shining with a thick light, the circle appearing brighter because of their combined radiance? Or do brave souls and names worthy of heaven—once released from their bodies and sent back from the earth—migrate here from the world below? Inhabiting their own sky, they live through ethereal years and enjoy the universe. Here we venerate the descendants of Aeacus <note>original: *Aeacidas*; the family of Achilles and Ajax</note>, and here the sons of Atreus <note>original: *Atridas*; Agamemnon and Menelaus</note>. We see fierce Diomedes <note>original: *Tydidem*</note>, and the man of Ithaca <note>Odysseus</note>, victor over nature through his triumphs on land and sea. We see the man of Pylos <note>Nestor</note>, distinguished by his triple old age <note>Nestor was said to have lived through three generations</note>, and the kings of the Greeks at the gates of Troy <note>original: *Pergama*</note>—the camp of leaders and the Troy that was finally conquered under Hector. Here too is the dark offspring of the Dawn <note>Memnon, the Ethiopian king</note>, and the ruler of Lycia <note>Sarpedon</note>, son of the Thunderer <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. Nor shall I pass you by, Maiden of Mars <note>Penthesilea, the Amazon Queen</note>, or the other kings sent by Greece and the nations of Asia, all great in that massive war.

There too are the men who possessed strength of spirit and prudent minds through the weight of their intellect, whose entire wealth lay within themselves: the just Solon, the brave Lycurgus, and ethereal Plato. There too is he who had fashioned Plato <note>Socrates</note>, who, though condemned, better condemned his own Athens. There is the victor over the Persians who paved the sea with his fleets <note>Themistocles, victor at the Battle of Salamis</note>. And there are the Roman men, who now form the greatest crowd: those who faced the Tarquin kings with threats, and the offspring of Horatius.

<meta>This page continues Manilius's exploration of the Milky Way, specifically the theory that it serves as the celestial abode for the souls of Rome’s greatest heroes and statesmen. The poet transitions from these "earthly gods" to the structure of the planetary spheres and the nature of comets.</meta>

-> # BOOK ONE <-

The whole battle-line of the bridge <note>Referencing Horatius Cocles, who defended the Sublician Bridge against the Etruscans</note>, and Scaevola, made more noble by his stump <note>Mucius Scaevola, who proved his Roman resolve by burning off his own right hand in a fire</note>, greater than any man; the maiden Cloelia, and Cocles protecting the Roman walls he carried. There too is Corvinus, who gained both spoils and a name with the help of a bird <note>A raven (corvus) famously helped him in a duel by distracting his opponent</note>, and who carries the god Apollo in that winged creature. There is Camillus, who earned heaven through Jupiter and restored Rome by saving it; and Brutus, the founder of the city reclaimed from kings; and Papirius, the avenger during the wars of Pyrrhus. Fabricius and Curius, equals in virtue, and Marcellus, the third to win the palm; and Cossus, who was first to slay a king. The Decii, striving together, alike in their sacred vows and their triumphs. Fabius, undefeated through his delays <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus, "The Delayer," who defeated Hannibal by avoiding direct battle</note>, and Livius, the victor over the slain Hasdrubal, with Nero as his ally through the wars. The Scipios, those leaders who were the singular doom of Carthage. Pompey, the subduer of the world through three triumphs, a prince even before he was a god; and Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note>, who earned heaven through the richness of his speech; and the great lineage of the Claudian house. The noble leaders of the house of Aemilius, and the famous Metelli. And Cato, the victor over fortune; and Agrippa, a soldier under the arms of his mother <note>Likely referring to the "Mother of Rome" or the State; Agrippa was Augustus's right-hand general</note>; and the Julian offspring, descending from the origin of Venus, has come down from heaven and filled heaven again. This line, ruling over the Augustan heirs, sees its leaders among the gathering of the gods, alongside the great Quirinus <note>The deified name of Romulus, Rome's founder</note>, with the Thunderer <note>Jupiter</note> as their ally.

Higher up, where the circle of the ethereal world glows white, is the seat of the gods; this path <note>The Milky Way</note> is closest to those divine ones who, by their own virtue, follow in their footsteps. There are other stars that fight against the rotation of the world, which hang suspended, flitting between the heaven and the earth: the stars of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and the Sun; and beneath these, Mercury is situated between Venus and the Moon. Here I shall begin, before I assign powers to the stars or sing the fatal laws and songs of the Zodiac signs. The face of the universe must be filled in, and throughout the entire body of the sky, whatever shines everywhere and flourishes must be noted. There are also stars of a rare birth-fate that go forth immediately, and suddenly glowing flames flash through the clear air; rare ages have seen comets perish after being drawn through massive movements. This happens either because the vapor produced by the breathing earth—the moist breath—is overcome by the dry air when the clouds cease, driven away by a long period of clear weather, and the scorched air dries out under the sun's rays. Then, the fire, once released, seizes the fuel it has driven toward itself, and the flame finds material capable of sustaining it. And because the body of a comet is not solid, but is made of scattered, thin elements of air—most similar to flying smoke—it lives for only a brief task; the fires, once begun, stop at their end and fall just as the comet was shining. For if they did not lead their rising so close to their setting, and if the time for the kindled flames were not so short—

[[margin: Dark <note>original: "Atra"</note>]]

<meta>This page transitions from the catalog of Roman heroes residing in the Milky Way to a detailed physical and metaphysical discussion of comets and celestial fires. It continues the first book of Manilius's "Astronomica," shifting from the fixed stars to the unpredictable phenomena of the upper atmosphere.</meta>

-># BOOK ONE<-

Night would become a second day, and the immense heaven would return and find the whole world in sleep. Then, because not every drier vapor is dispersed in a single form, and the earth’s vapor is caught by fire, lights are carried in diverse appearances, born of sudden darkness. For sometimes, as if long hair flows from a head, the flame flies mimicking tresses, and it unfolds fires spread with burning rays like thin hair. Now this first appearance comes forth with scattered hair; then a globe of fire follows in the likeness of a burning beard. Sometimes, drawn with an equal joining of sides, it forms a square beam <note>The "trabs" was a contemporary classification for a long, rectangular meteor</note> or a rounded column. Indeed, it even matches the shape of storage jars <note>original: "dolia"</note> with swollen flames, distended with a tall belly; or it feigns small hairs, or is gathered into orbs with small signs, shaggy, representing the appearance of harvests under a flickering light, or it pours forth lamps and torches split into branching fires. Falling stars are seen flying everywhere when wandering lights sparkle through the clear world, and thin fires are tossed with long hair. They burn far off, mimicking swift arrows, when a dry path is thinned out with a slender thread. 

But fires are mixed in all parts, which inhabit the heavy clouds that manufacture thunderbolts. They even penetrate the earth, mimicking the fires of Mount Etna <note>The famous Sicilian volcano</note> in the heights of Olympus <note>Used here to mean the heavens</note>. They make the waters warm in the very springs, and they find a seat in hard flint and in green bark, as when a forest is burned by colliding with itself. All nature is so abundant with fire that it sends sudden torches bursting from heaven, and the ignited air shines with flashing flames, having embraced the dry seeds of the breathing earth. These the swift fire follows as it feeds upon them, and then flees, just as you see lightnings vibrating a flickering light in the midst of rains, and the sky broken by a thunderbolt. 

Whether, therefore, the nature of the earth providing these "seeds" can generate these swift fires we call Comets, or whether nature created those torches beneath all the stars, shining through the heaven with thin flames—it is the Sun <note>original: "Titanius," referring to the Titan sun-god</note> who draws them to himself with his rapid heat, and involves his own Comets in burning fire. At times he sends them away just like the orbit of Mercury <note>original: "Cyllenius," referring to the god born on Mt. Cyllene</note>, or like Venus when she leads the creeping night with the ignited evening star; they deceive our eyes, then revisit us again. Or perhaps God, pitying the world for its approaching fate, sends signs through these movements and the fires of heaven. Never has the sky glowed with useless fires. When they appear, the cheated farmers mourn their squalid fields, and the exhausted plowman laments among the sterile furrows...
