<meta>This page concludes Book I of the *Astronomica*. It transitions from the physical description of comets and meteors to their traditional role as omens of disaster—specifically plague, the defeat of Varus in Germany, and the Roman Civil Wars—before ending with a prayer for the peace established by Augustus.</meta>

-># **B O O K   O N E**<-

<margin>**MARCUS**</margin> It <note>The comet or celestial fire mentioned previously</note> forces the bullocks to the yokes in vain while they grieve for their masters. Or it seizes bodies with heavy diseases and a slow decay, a lethal flame burning through the very marrow. It snatches away failing peoples, and throughout entire cities, the final rites of the public are performed over tombs already set ablaze. Such was the plague that once devastated the settlers of Erichthonius <note>original: "Erichthonios"; a reference to the mythical king of Athens, here meaning the Athenians during the Great Plague of 430 BCE</note>, carrying off ancient Athens through funerals even in a time of peace, when one person, falling, looked upon the death of another. There was no place for the medical arts, nor did any vows to the gods prevail. Duty gave way to disease; there were no funerals for the dead and no tears left to shed, for the very fire of the pyres had grown weary and failed. Bodies burned with their limbs all heaped together. And from such a great population, an heir to a legacy was scarcely to be found.

Such things are often signified by the shining Comets; funerals come along with these torches, and they threaten the lands with burning pyres without end, when the world and nature itself falls ill, having drawn a new tomb as its lot. Nay, these fires even sing of wars and sudden tumults, and of arms rising from secret treachery. Such were the weapons recently proceeding to the furthest borders when the treaty was broken, and wild Germany snatched away the leader Varus <note>Publius Quinctilius Varus, the Roman general who lost three legions in the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE</note>, staining the fields with the blood of three legions. These threatening lights, seen everywhere throughout the whole world, claim such disasters; nature herself waged war through these fires, opposed her own forces, and threatened the end. 

Nor did she cease to send heavy ruins upon both things and men. Often the fault lies at home, yet we do not know how to trust the sky. These fires also signify civil commotions and wars between kin; nor did the world ever endure more fires than when arms, sworn to bloody leaders, filled the fields of Philippi <note>The site of the decisive battle in 42 BCE where Octavian and Mark Antony defeated the assassins of Julius Caesar</note> with their ranks. Even in the dry sand <note>original: "hatena," a variant of "arena"</note>, the Roman soldier could scarcely look upon the bones of men and limbs torn while the victims were still surviving. The Empire clashed with its own strength, and Augustus, the Father, conquered by following the footsteps of his father <note>Julius Caesar</note>. 

Nor yet was there an end; the wars of Actium <note>The naval battle in 31 BCE where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra</note> remained, fought with a fleet that was part of a dowry, and battles were repeated again upon the sea as the ruler of heaven <note>Augustus</note> was sought. Having drawn a woman's yoke as its lot, the triumph finally repaid the struggle, and even the thunderbolts of Rome contended with the Egyptian rattle <note>term: "sistro" (sistrum); a percussion instrument used in the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis</note>. There remained also the wars against the fugitive soldier <note>Sextus Pompey, who led a naval resistance against the Triumvirs</note>, when the son, Pompey, imitating his father's enemies with arms, occupied the seas that were protected by the open expanse. 

But let this be enough for the fates; now the wars are at rest. May Discord, conquered by adamantine chains and shut up in her prison, be held by eternal bits. Let the Father of the Country <note>Augustus</note> remain unconquered, and let Rome be under his rule. And when he has at last given a god to heaven <note>A reference to Augustus eventually joining Julius Caesar in deification</note>, let him not have to seek another god on earth.

<meta>This page begins the second book of Manilius’s *Astronomica*. While Book I focused on the physical structure of the universe and the appearance of comets as omens, Book II moves toward the technical rules of astrology—the "reason" or "logic" behind the stars. Manilius begins with a poetic survey of his literary predecessors (Homer, Hesiod, and the mythological poets) to distinguish his own scientific and philosophical project from theirs.</meta>

-># **MARCUS MANILIUS, MATHEMATICAL ASTRONOMER: BOOK II**<-
### ->*On the cause of all reason, and on the sex and appearance of the signs. Chapter I*<-

**M**AXIMUS <note>original: "Maximus... uates"; referring to Homer, the "greatest poet"</note>, the supreme poet, sang with a sacred mouth of the contests of the Trojan race, of fifty kings, of the "king of kings" <note>Agamemnon</note> and the "father" <note>Priam</note>; he sang of the Hectorean torch <note>The fires Hector brought to the Greek ships</note> and of Troy, safe while Hector stood; he sang of the wandering of the leader <note>Odysseus/Ulysses</note> during as many years as the war itself had lasted, as he struggled against the sea and the double waters of the deep; and he sang of the final battle in his homeland for his captured household gods. This poet, while giving laws and a homeland to those who sought them, also took them away <note>A poetic way of saying Homer's fame surpassed his subjects' reality</note>. From his overflowing mouth, all posterity has drawn the waters for their own poems, daring to lead that great river into thin streams, made fertile by the riches of a single man. 

But next to him, Hesiod tells of the gods and the parents of the gods: how Chaos brought forth the lands, of the world as an infant beneath it, and how the stars were the first bodies to stumble into being. He tells how the Titans assisted the cradle of the great Ancient One <note>Saturn/Cronus</note>, and of the name of the Father <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> who lived under a brother’s rule and then without a brother. He sings also of Bacchus being born a second time from his father’s body <note>Bacchus was famously sewn into Jupiter's thigh</note>, and of all the divine powers flitting through the immense world. Furthermore, he asked after the cultivation and laws of the countryside, the "military service" of the soil—how Bacchus loved the hills and fertile Ceres the plains, and how Bacchus loved both; how orchards were made "adulterous" by grafted fruits <note>original: "adultera pomis"; referring to the mixing of different fruit species through grafting</note>, and he set the gods of the woods and the sacred powers of the nymphs to the great uses of nature, a work of peace.

Certain others have described the various shapes of the stars. They told of the signs gliding here and there through the sprawling sky, and assigned to each their own nature and origins: the punishments of Perseus and Andromeda, the grieving mother <note>Cassiopeia</note> and the father <note>Cepheus</note> who freed her; the daughter snatched from Lycaon <note>Callisto, turned into the Great Bear</note>; and, by the service of Jove, Cynosura <note>The Little Bear</note> and the goat with its milk <note>Amalthea</note>; and the Swan <note>Cygnus</note> born of a trick, and Erigone <note>Virgo</note> led to the stars by her piety; Scorpio <note>original: "Nepa"</note> by its sting, the Lion by its hide, the Crab by its bite, and the Fishes <note>Pisces</note> from the transformed daughter of Cythera <note>Venus/Aphrodite, who turned into a fish to escape Typhon</note>. They told of the Wool-bearer <note>Aries, the Ram</note> leading the constellations across the conquered sea, and the other stars hanging from various fates, which they wished to see fixed and revolving through the high ether. In their songs, the heaven is nothing but a fable; it was the Earth that composed the Heavens, which in truth hang from it.

Furthermore, he who was born on Sicilian soil <note>Theocritus, the father of pastoral poetry</note> recounts the rituals of the flocks and Pan sounding his reeds. He does not sing of the woods in a "woody" way, but strikes a rhythm through the rough countryside and leads the Muse into the sweet breezes. Look, another sings of painted birds and the wars of wild beasts. One tells of venomous snakes; another of the fates born from herbs, and those things that carry life in their own roots. They even call the immense Tartarus <note>The Underworld</note> out from the darkness of night into the light, and they unroll a world turned inward, the laws of nature having been broken. The learned sisters <note>The Muses</note> have sung of every kind of thing.

---
| | O 4 | Omnis |

<summary>In this opening to Book II, Manilius surveys the history of epic, didactic, and mythological poetry—citing Homer, Hesiod, and others—to establish the literary tradition before pivoting to his own unique subject: the scientific and logical laws of astrology.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Hesiod, Trojan War, Greek Mythology, Catasterism, Perseus, Andromeda, Bacchus, Constellations, History of Poetry</keywords>

--- Page 427 ---
<meta>This page continues Manilius’s introduction to Book II. Having just discussed his epic and didactic predecessors like Homer and Hesiod, he now asserts his own originality. He moves from literary history into the core philosophical argument of his work: that the universe is a living, rational organism governed by a divine spirit (the Stoic "World Soul"), which allows the stars to influence earthly life.</meta>

->**BOOK II**<-

Every path to the approach of **Helicon** <note>The mountain home of the Muses, symbolizing poetic inspiration</note> is now well-worn. And already, confused rivers flow from those springs. They no longer provide a fresh draft of water for the crowd rushing to the sacred rites. Let us seek untouched meadows where the grass rolls in the wind, and a stream that meditates its murmur in hidden caves—water that birds have not yet tasted with hardened beaks, nor **Phoebus** <note>The Sun god</note> himself has sipped with his celestial fire. I shall speak of my own things; I shall owe my beginnings to no other bard. This will not be a theft, but a new work; I fly into the sky in my own chariot, and I drive the waves in my own boat.

For I shall sing of a God who is powerful through the silent mind of nature, a spirit infused into the sky, the earth, and the sea, governing this massive weight with an equal covenant. I sing that the whole world lives by a mutual consent and is driven by the motion of **Reason** <note>original: "ratio"; the Stoic concept of a rational governing principle</note>, since one spirit dwells through all its parts and waters the globe, flying through all things and shaping the universe as a living body. Unless this **Machine** <note>original: "Machina"; the structural framework of the cosmos</note> remained woven together by related members, and lay entirely open to the Master <note>The divine intellect</note> placed over it—and unless a great Prudence ruled the senses of the world—the earth would have no stable station, and the stars would have no orbit. The wandering world would stick fast and grow stiff by standing still. The stars would not keep their arranged courses. Alternating night would flee the day, but then fail to put it to flight in turn. Rains would not nourish the lands, nor winds the upper air. The sea would not feed the heavy clouds, nor would the rivers feed the sea. The deep would not sustain the springs, nor would the sum of all things remain always equal through every part, arranged by an impartial Parent <note>The Creator/Nature</note>, so that neither the waves nor the stars would ever fail us. Nor would the sky rotate any more or less than is just.

Motion nourishes the work, it does not change it; thus all things remain distributed throughout the whole world and follow their Master. This, therefore, is the God and the Reason which governs all things. It leads earthly animals by the influence of the celestial signs. Although the God drives these signs from a far-removed distance, He allows them to be felt so that they may administer life and fates to the nations, and grant specific characters to individual bodies.

Nor is proof of this far to seek: thus the sky tempers the fields; thus it yields and snatches away various fruits. Thus it moves the sea, and sends it onto the lands, and takes it away again. This rebellion of the deep <note>The tides</note> is held now by the moved stars of the **Moon**, now stimulated by her various retreats, and now following **Phoebus** as he flies through the space of a year. Thus even the creatures submerged in the straits and closed in the prison of shells <note>Shellfish, which ancients believed grew and shrank with the moon</note> vary their bodies according to the motion of the moon. And when your losses, **Delia** <note>A name for the Moon/Diana, born on the island of Delos</note>, imitate your powers, you also return your face to your brother's horns <note>The Sun's rays</note>, and again you seek light from them; as much as he leaves or gives, she brings back, and star depends upon star. Finally, thus the cattle and the mute animals on the lands...

->**With**<-

<summary>Manilius declares his poetic independence and outlines the Stoic doctrine of the World Soul, arguing that a rational divine spirit binds the universe together and allows the stars to influence earthly life and the tides.</summary>
<keywords>Stoicism, World Soul, Helicon, Moon, Tides, Reason, Machine of the World, Phoebus, Delia, Divine Providence</keywords>

--- Page 428 ---
<meta>This page continues Manilius’s introduction to Book II. Having just discussed his epic and didactic predecessors like Homer and Hesiod, he now asserts his own originality. He moves from literary history into the core philosophical argument of his work: that the universe is a living, rational organism governed by a divine spirit (the Stoic "World Soul"), which allows the stars to influence earthly life.</meta>

# ->B O O K   T W O<-

Though they [the animals] remain untaught, bound by their own law through the ages, yet as Nature calls them back toward the parent world, they lift their spirits and watch the heavens and the stars. They purify their bodies at the horns of the rising moon <note>A reference to animals observing lunar cycles or performing instinctive rituals at night</note>. They foresee the coming winters and the return of fair weather. Who, after this, would doubt to join man to heaven? Nature gave him an exceptional tongue and a capable mind, a swift spirit into which, finally, God descends and dwells, seeking himself. I pass over other arts, which are left to our will. 

I pass over the fact that nothing is granted under an equal law [of nature] <note>Meaning that humans possess unique faculties not shared by other creatures</note>, which reveals that authors exist for the human body. I pass over what is certain and inevitable fate: it is given to matter to be driven, but it is given to the world to drive. Who could grasp the heavens, unless he had received the gift of the heavens? And who could find God, unless he himself were a part of the gods? Who could perceive this vast structure of our eternal Parent, the dances of the constellations, and the flaming vaults of the world? The eternal war of the planets <note>original: "stellis"; literally "stars," but here referring to the wandering planets</note> against the stars <note>The "fixed" stars of the constellations</note>, the lands and the sea beneath the sky—who could behold all this and enclose it within the narrow confines of the breast, had Nature not given such great eyes to our souls? Had she not turned a mind kindred to her own toward herself? Had she not enriched such a masterpiece and come from the heavens? For we are called into the heavens for a sacred commerce of things.

And those primary laws which the stars give to the newborn—who would deny it is a sin to attempt to grasp the universe against its will, and to bring it down into the world as if captured by itself? But let not these obvious truths be proved by a long circuit. The very truth shall give weight and credibility to the work. For **Reason** <note>original: "ratio"; the Stoic concept of a rational, governing principle of the universe</note> is never deceived, nor does it ever deceive. The path is duly favorable and entrusted to true causes. The outcome is granted just as it is predicted beforehand. Who would dare call it false, that Fortune creates Fate? Or to overcome the votes of so great a destiny?

Inspired by a divine breath, I desire to carry these themes to the stars. I shall not compose my poems for the crowd, nor hide them within the crowd. Instead, like one carried alone through an empty sphere, with no other chariots clashing against mine, nor companions performing common deeds alongside me, I shall sing of things to be learned by heaven, while the stars look on in wonder and the world rejoices in the poems of its own poet. 

I sing for those to whom the stars have not begrudged their sacred paths or the knowledge of themselves. This is the smallest of crowds throughout the world—not that which loves riches, gold, empires and the **rods of office** <note>original: "fasces"; the bundles of rods symbolizing Roman magisterial power</note>, or soft luxury in idleness, or a sweet affection through the ears with flattering sounds. So that the fates may be known with modest labor—this too is a part of fate: to learn the law of fate.

->But first<-

<summary>Manilius argues that humans possess a divine "Reason" that allows them to understand the heavens, unlike animals who only follow instinct. He asserts his role as a divinely inspired poet revealing the laws of Fate to a select, enlightened audience.</summary>
<keywords>Stoicism, Fate, Reason, Astrology, Human Nature, Divine Spark, Manilius, Cosmos</keywords>

--- Page 429 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical transition in Book 2. Having established the philosophical underpinnings of astrology—that the universe is a rational, divine organism—Manilius now begins the "didactic" portion of his poem. He moves from abstract theory to the specific classification of the Zodiac signs, starting with their gender and their physical forms (single vs. double-bodied).</meta>

# ->B O O K   T W O<-

But first, the varied nature of the stars must be noted in my verses through each of their classes. For there are six masculine signs, and just as many of a different gender <note>In ancient astrology, the twelve signs were divided into "masculine" and "feminine" categories, which generally alternated around the wheel</note>. Under the leadership of the Bull <note>original: "Tauro"</note>, you see how he rises in an arc, returning backward. They alternate their gender and vary in turns around the circle. You will also see human forms among some of them. Nor do the parts of cattle and wild beasts differ in their lethal nature. Their character will be created by those signs which must now be marked by a keen mind—each one being driven by its own particular lot.

-> ### Concerning common and double-formed signs <-
-> #### Chapter II <-

**N**ow focus on the pairs; these doubled signs will grant powerful effects through a partner, for a companion adds and takes away much. They are influential in ambiguous ways, whatever alliances are formed by the fates. For merit and for harm, look to the two Fishes <note>original: "Pisces"</note> among the stars, and just as many Twins <note>original: "Geminos"</note> with their limbs bared. Their arms remain joined to each other in an alternating embrace. Their path is dissimilar, as they are turned in opposite directions. The number is the same, but a different nature must be noted. And these signs, rejoicing in their pairs throughout the whole sky, remain complete; they marvel at nothing external to themselves, nor do they grieve for anything lost. This is unlike certain others which have parts cut away, their limbs joined from a different kind of body.

Take, for instance, Capricorn, or the one who aims the stretched bow <note>The Archer, Sagittarius</note>. Joined to a horse, a part of this sign is human, but no part of the former. This distinction must also be observed in the deep art of astrology. For there is a difference between whether there are two separate things, or a single figure that is double. Indeed, even Erigone <note>A poetic name for the constellation Virgo</note> is counted among the doubled stars. Logic will not make her nature twofold, for the summer ends and autumn begins in the middle of the Virgin; she belongs to both. For that reason, two stars precede all the Tropical signs <note>The "turning points" of the seasons: the Solstices and Equinoxes</note>: the Lyre <note>original: "Chelys"; here referring to Libra</note> precedes the Wool-bearer <note>original: "Lanigero"; Aries</note>, as do the Crab <note>Cancer</note> and the Goat <note>Capricorn</note>. They possess doubled powers because they connect two times. Just as the Crab follows the Brother stars <note>Gemini</note>, one of the Twins provides for the flowering times of spring, while the other brings forth the parched summer. Yet both are naked, because both feel the heat: the one is part of the fading spring, and the other is the first part of the coming summer, the final lot assigned to a father.

So too is the Archer <note>original: "Arcitenens"</note>, who promises you, O Capricorn, beneath himself; he is said to be formed of a double image. The gentler autumn claims his soft limbs for itself, while he bears a rigid frame on his back <note>Referring to the Centaur's half-human, half-horse anatomy</note>. They receive the winter and send the sign into those times. And the two Fishes, which the Ram <note>Aries</note> sends before himself, bring two seasons: one closes the winter, the other begins the spring. When the sun, flying back from the stars of the sea, runs its course, the winter rains meet the strength of spring, because the final signs have floating forms in their upper parts.

<meta>This page continues Manilius's systematic classification of the zodiac signs. Having previously discussed their genders and physical pairings, he now moves into their specific astronomical orientations during rising, their association with day and night, and their reproductive qualities (fertility vs. sterility).</meta>

->S E C V N D V S 9<-

### Concerning signs that rise backwards. Chapter III

**N**ote how three signs are opposed to the other nine, and how a sort of rebellion holds the heavens. Observe the Bull <note>original: "Taurum"</note> rising by its hindquarters, the Twins <note>original: "Geminos"</note> by their feet, and the Crab <note>original: "Cancrum"</note> by its shell, whereas the other signs rise with their limbs upright. Do not wonder at the delay when the sun, moving through these awkward stars, raises the summer year in the slow months <note>Manilius explains the "slow" arrival of summer by the fact that these signs appear to emerge "backwards" or "sideways" on the horizon, taking longer to fully rise</note>.

### Concerning day and night signs. Chapter IV

**D**o not overlook the signs of the day and night. You must discern them and derive them by their own law—not that they perform their duties only in darkness or light <note>The classification of "diurnal" or "nocturnal" is an inherent quality of the sign, regardless of whether it is currently visible in the sky</note>. For a common name nourishes all things without distinction that shine in turns throughout the seasons; sometimes they follow the days, and sometimes the nights. But for those signs to which nature, the sacred parent of the world, has attributed a permanent station in a specific part of time: for the sign of the Archer <note>original: "Sagittarii"</note>, the swift Lion <note>original: "Leonis"</note>, and the Ram <note>original: "Aries"</note> looking back at its own back with its golden fleece; then the Fish <note>original: "Pisces"</note>, the Crab <note>original: "Cancer"</note>, and the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpion"</note> following the Crab's sting—all these, whether neighboring in location or divided by equal parts, are said to be under a similar lot as day-signs.

The others are carried differently, neither sharing the same number, nor alternating position, nor placed with as many signs between them. Indeed, some have said that the six continuous turns of Castor <note>The Twins, Gemini</note> are diurnal—those which start from the leading sign of the Fleece-bearer <note>Aries</note>—and the six starting from the Scales <note>Libra</note> are seen as nocturnal. There are those who prefer that the signs which rise as masculine are diurnal, and the feminine ones rejoice in the safe shadows of night—a fact that some signs speak for themselves without anyone showing them. The rocky Crab <note>original: "Cancer"</note> in the waves and the Fish <note>original: "Pisces"</note> rejoicing in the poured-out sea owe their lineage to Neptune <note>The god of the sea</note>. Just as those stars which are reckoned by an earthly lot: the Bull <note>original: "Taurus"</note> as leader of the herd, the Ram <note>original: "Aries"</note> proud in its kingdom of the fleecy flock, and the Lion <note>original: "Leo"</note> the predator placed between the two, and the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpius"</note> in the brambly fields. There are also signs of a "middle law" <term>middle law: signs that share both terrestrial and aquatic natures, often called "amphibious" signs</term>. Capricorn <note>original: "Capricornus"</note> belongs to the ambiguous lands, and the Water-bearer <note>original: "Aquarius"</note> to the waves. And the shining marine part of the ever-pouring Water-bearer is moist, yet mixed with earthly things so that he may live among them.

### Concerning fertile signs. Chapter V

**O**ne must not turn the mind away from even the smallest causes; nothing is without reason or created in vain. The nature of the Crab <note>original: "Cancri"</note> is properly fertile, as is the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpius"</note> sharp with its sting, and the Fish <note>original: "Pisces"</note> filling the seas with their offspring <note>Water signs were traditionally associated with fertility due to the life-giving nature of water</note>. But the Virgin <note>original: "Virgo"</note> is sterile, joined with the similar Lion <note>original: "Leoni"</note>. Nor does the Water-bearer <note>original: "Aquarius"</note> conceive or pour out the seeds it has received. Between both remains the Goat <note>original: "Capricornus"</note> with its mixed body, and the Centaur <note>the Archer/Sagittarius</note> who shines with his taut bow. The Ram <note>original: "Aries"</note> is common <note>neutral or average fertility</note>, and counts the Scales <note>original: "Libram"</note> which equalizes time, the Twins <note>original: "Geminos"</note>, and the Bull <note>original: "Taurum"</note> as subject to the same lot.

-> B O O K [[unclear: S E C O N D]] [[page number: 12]] <-

## Concerning running and upright signs, and the aspect of the planets. Chapter VI

# **A**nd do not think that Nature, in her work, has called upon any empty fancies in the fact that some signs are "running," such as the Lion <note>original: "Leo"</note>, the Archer <note>original: "Arcitenens," an epithet for Sagittarius</note>, and the Ram <note>original: "Aries"</note> with his twisted horns; or those which are balanced upright, standing on their own limbs, such as the Virgin <note>original: "Virgo"</note>, the Twins <note>original: "Gemini"</note>, and the Water-bearer <note>original: "Aquarius"</note> pouring out his floods. Or those which sit weary, reflecting sluggish minds: the Bull <note>original: "Taurus"</note>, falling asleep once the plows are set aside from his neck; the Scales <note>original: "Libra"</note>, ascending as the circle of labors is completed <note>referring to the end of the agricultural season or the "retirement" of the scales after the harvest</note>; and you, Capricorn <note>original: "Capricorne"</note>, shriveled by your own frost among the stars. Opposite these lies the Crab <note>original: "Cancer"</note>, stretched out upon his wide belly; the Scorpion <note>original: "Scorpius"</note>, pressing down with his flat body upon the ground; and the Fish <note>original: "Pisces"</note>, always lying upon their sides.

But if you look around at everything with skillful care, you will find constellations cheated of missing limbs. The Scorpion consumes his own arms in the Scales <note>In ancient astronomy, the claws of Scorpio originally formed the constellation we now call Libra</note>; the Bull falls lame on a curved foot; the eyes of the Crab are missing; for the Centaur <note>original: "Centauro," referring to Sagittarius</note> there is a surplus, and yet one limb is still sought. In this way, the universe consoles our own misfortunes among the stars and teaches us by example to endure losses patiently, since the entire order of fortune depends upon heaven, and the stars themselves are formed with weakened limbs.

The signs are also powerful in their own proper seasons: Summer rises from the Twins, Autumn from the Virgin; Winter begins with the Archer, and Spring with the Fish <note>Manilius identifies the start of seasons with these signs, though in modern Western astrology, seasons are usually marked by the "cardinal" signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn</note>. The constellations are assigned to four parts of the earth; the summer signs are opposed to the winter ones, and the spring signs to the autumn ones.

Nor is it enough to know the specific forms of the signs; they also move the fates by their <term>consensus</term> <note>agreement or harmony between signs</note> and rejoice in their alliance. One sign follows another by lot and by position. Just as the circle of signs is enclosed in a right-hand orbit, a line runs through it in three equal lengths, joining itself at its far ends. Whatever signs are called <term>trigonal</term> <note>triangular; signs of the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water) are 120 degrees apart, forming a triangle</note> are divided into threes, because the angle falls upon every third star. The signs that remain divided by distances on the earth—the Fleece-bearer <note>original: "Laniger," meaning Aries</note> and, at equal spaces, the two signs of the Lion and the Archer—behold one another from different risings. The star of the Virgin and the Bull harmonizes with Capricorn. The remaining signs are triangular by a similar logic.

Through just as many intervals, others are missing which were established in the world. But there will be a distinction between those on the right and those on the left. Those that follow are said to be on the right, and those that precede are on the left. To the Bull, Capricorn will be on the right, and the Virgin on the left. This example is sufficient for those signs which are established in four different parts with an equal length of sides <note>referring to the "square" aspect or <term>quadrature</term></note>. A perpendicular line designates their seats: those on the right support the Scales, and Capricorn looks toward them. The Ram beholds Capricorn, and the Crab beholds the Ram with equal parts, as do the stars of the Scales that follow on the left.

-> **Always** <-

He concludes by introducing the geometric relationships of triangles and squares that connect the signs across the heavens.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the second book of Manilius's Astronomica. Following the previous page's discussion on the physical postures of the signs (running, standing, or lying), the poet now transitions into the mathematical and geometric relationships between the signs—specifically the "aspects" of the triangle and the square.</meta>

-># BOOK SECOND<-

For the signs on the right are always reckoned as prior.
Namely, to divide all things into as many parts,
And to fashion four-sided shapes from twelve signs in groups of three,
By which means, in the proposed order, their powers <note>original: "uites," likely a typographical variant of "vires" (powers/strengths), common in early modern printing</note> are rendered.

->### On triangular and quadrangular signs. Chapter VII<-

**B**ut if anyone will be content to have merely numbered the squares,
He might think the world divided by groups of four signs,
Or that a triangle adorns three signs at five-sign intervals <note>The "trine" aspect, where signs are 120 degrees apart, or every fifth sign counting inclusively</note>.
So that he might demand shared strengths and friendly risings,
And find the kindred alliances of the world through the stars.
He will be mistaken; for although there are five signs on every side,
Nevertheless, hear about those stars born of the triangles
Which are cut at every fifth position.
They cannot hold their strength, even if they keep that name.
They have lost their gifts by their position and they clash with the numbers.
For since there are three hundred and sixty parts <note>original: "trecentæ et ter uicenæ" (300 and three-times-twenty degrees)</note> of the circle through the signs,
Which the heat of the Sun <note>original: "Phœbi" (Phoebus), a common poetic name for the Sun god</note> circles,
A third part of that number makes one side
Of a triangle extended into three parts through the signs.
However, a simple line does not return this sum of the number
If sign is noted from sign, and not degree from degree <note>original: "pars à parte," referring to the individual degrees within a sign</note>.
Because although these stars are separated by two signs,
If however you wish to compare the very end of the former
Or the first part of the previous one to each other and note the number,
They will fulfill one hundred and fifty parts in order.
The number will exceed the form, and the drawing will consume
The following borders; therefore, although they are called
Triangular signs, they do not preserve triangular proportions.
This same appearance deceives regarding the square signs,
Because while ninety parts <note>original: "ter triginta" (three times thirty)</note> return a square through the stars
Of the whole number which constructs the circle,
It happens that from the first part of a prior sign,
If a rod <note>meaning a geometric line</note> is drawn to the highest part of the following sign,
The sum of the prior will make one hundred and twenty <note>original: "bis sexagenas"</note>.
And if the first part is compared to those joined in the middle
Of the two signs, it both exceeds and falls short of the number:
It doubles thirty parts, but the third part will be missing,
And although one counts the fourth star from the fourth,
The degrees of one will suffer shipwreck in them.
Therefore it is not enough to have numbered triangles by signs,
Or the reliability of the square heaven through every four signs.
If by chance you wish to fashion the shape of a square,
Either you will make the members with three-part triangles,
Where the hundredth sum demands a fourth part <note>A mathematical explanation that 1/4 of 400 is 100, but 1/4 of 360 is 90</note>.
There it loses a tenth; thus the order agrees.
And whichever angle favors all four throughout,
And whatever places the line marks in a triple drawing,
When it leaves the marked paths of the straight way,
Nature gave to these a law by a common treaty,
And in turn, affections and mutual rights of favor.

<margin>P</margin>                                          **Whereby**

<summary>Manilius explains that astrological "aspects" (triangles and squares) must be calculated by precise degrees (360 in a circle) rather than simply counting signs, as counting by signs alone leads to mathematical errors. He emphasizes that the geometric harmony of the heavens governs the "treaties" and "affections" between different constellations.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, geometry, zodiac, aspects, trine, quadrate, degrees, Phoebus, Manilius, celestial harmony</keywords>

--- Page 433 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of astrological "aspects"—the geometric angles formed between signs of the zodiac. Having previously introduced the triangle (trine) and the square (quadrate), Manilius now explains why the exact degree-count matters more than just the number of signs, before moving on to describe the hexagon (sextile) and the lack of relationship between adjacent signs.</meta>

-> # BOOK SECOND <-

Therefore, not every birth-chart possesses triangles. Even if lines are drawn and signs are called "triangular" by their general section, they do not maintain the harmony of true triangular signs; nor, should they happen to be squares, do they continuously maintain an exchange of influence between themselves. For it makes a great difference whether the line covers the exact number of degrees and follows the precise measure of the number which the circle encompasses. Sometimes logic will lead the lines to form three sides, sometimes four on every side, which may proceed through more signs than are sometimes recorded by the simple count around the circuit.

But the power through the signs of the <term>triangle (trine)<gloss>an aspect of 120 degrees, considered the most harmonious in astrology</gloss></term> is far greater than those which bear the title of <term>square (quadrate)<gloss>an aspect of 90 degrees, often considered a point of tension or friction</gloss></term> at every fourth sign. The line of the triangles is "higher," as it passes through a deeper part of the celestial space <note>Manilius uses a geometric argument here: a chord forming a triangle stays deeper within the sphere than a chord forming a square, which is closer to the surface</note>. The line of the square travels closer to the surface and recedes from the deep heaven; its vision comes closer to the earth and sends its influence down into our air.

-> ## On hexagonal signs. Chapter VIII <-

**D**eviating relationships are granted to alternate signs. They do not keep their mutual pacts with great harmony because the line is bent reluctantly in a narrow circuit <note>The hexagon or "sextile" (60 degrees) was considered a weaker aspect than the trine or square in ancient astrology</note>. For when the individual stars are formed through slanting paths, and the line is curved into a circle through six windings, it goes from Taurus into Cancer; then, having touched Virgo, it enters Scorpio, where it finds you, stiff Capricorn, and from you the Fish <note>original: "Piscis" (Pisces)</note> find Gemini; and, touching the signs opposite Taurus, it ends where it began the circle.

There is a place for another drawing through the signs that were passed over <note>This refers to the second set of six signs starting with Aries</note>. Let me pass over that power, as I have spoken of the details. A similar circle is made for them with just as many bends. Therefore, the signs that follow one another escape these transverse gazes because they slant too much; they lie hidden from their neighbor, for a strike is surer when delivered from a straight line. These third signs are hidden in a backward retreat. And the line that follows is connected to the heaven in a single circuit, which passes only through alternate stars. Its power is far off and wanders in high heaven, and it sends thin strengths from afar into the world. 

But yet <term>Phoebus<gloss>a poetic name for the Sun</gloss></term> is near them under the law, because their gender is not different: masculine signs respond to masculine ones, and those of the feminine sex join the relationships of the world. Thus, the nature of one lies open to the shapes of the other, and kindred stars lie under fixed laws.

-> ## On conjoined signs. Chapter IX <-

**I**ndeed, no grace is given to signs that "cling" together <note>Adjacent signs, such as Aries and Taurus</note>, for they lack harmony because their sight of one another is taken away. They carry within themselves all the things which the mind can perceive <note>Being "blind" to each other, adjacent signs have no geometric relationship</note>. They are also of opposite genders connected throughout the circuit; masculine signs are always beset by feminine ones in turn.

-> **On dissimilar signs** <-

<summary>Manilius explains the geometric hierarchy of astrological aspects, noting that the trine (triangle) is more powerful than the quadrate (square) or the sextile (hexagon). He concludes by explaining that adjacent signs are "blind" to each other and incompatible due to their alternating genders.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Manilius’s exploration of the geometric relationships between the signs of the zodiac. Having previously discussed the "triangles" (trines) and "squares" (quadratures), he now concludes his thoughts on the "sixth" signs (sextiles) before moving into the significant influence of "opposition"—signs that face each other from across the sky.</meta>

-> BOOK SECOND <-

No harmony is granted to signs that are mismatched. The "sixth" signs <note>original: "Sexta"; these are signs separated by one other sign, forming a 60-degree angle or "sextile" aspect</note> are also counted as having no beneficial power. This is because a straight line is not drawn through the entire circle in an equal way; rather, it creates two figures <note>hexagons</note> removed from each other by four intervening signs, and a third line drawn after the circle is assumed is not sufficient to complete the strength.

-> ### On opposite and hostile signs. Chapter X <-

**A**nd so the stars shine from opposite sides of the sky, hanging with faces turned against one another through the middle of the universe. They remain divided across the whole heaven as adversaries. Although they are carried in the <term>seventh place<gloss>In astrology, counting a sign and its opposite—such as Aries to Libra—covers seven signs of the zodiac</gloss></term>, they nonetheless maintain their influence from across that long distance; they provide their powers for either war or peace as the seasons demand—now for the Sun <note>original: "Phoebo"</note>, now for the stars, and now for the distant paths.

If it pleases you to celebrate these opposite signs by their names and their seats, remember to oppose <term>Capricorn<gloss>the goat-horned sign of the winter solstice</gloss></term> to <term>Cancer<gloss>the crab-sign of the summer solstice</gloss></term>. Oppose the <term>Ram<gloss>Aries; the "wool-bearer" (Lanigerum)</gloss></term> to the <term>Balance<gloss>Libra</gloss></term>, for in both of these signs, the night is equal to the day. Oppose <term>Erigone<gloss>a poetic name for the constellation Virgo</gloss></term> to the Fishes, and the Lion to the Youth and his Urn <note>Aquarius</note>. When the Scorpion shines from the highest point, the Bull is at the lowest; and the <term>Bow-holder<gloss>Sagittarius (Arcitenens)</gloss></term> sets as the Twins rise in the circle. They observe their courses as opposites to one another.

But although they shine from opposite positions, they are sometimes carried along in a shared nature. A mutual harmony arises from their gender and their character: if a male sign responds to its equal, or if the signs are of the same kind. The Fishes and the star of the Virgin fly in opposition, yet they love common laws, and their nature overcomes their opposing positions. However, nature herself is sometimes defeated by the seasons: Cancer, you are at odds with Capricorn. Female sign fights female sign, because summer is at odds with winter. From the one comes rigor, ice, and fields white with snow; from the other, thirst, sweat, and the world bare upon the hills. Cold winter nights equal the long summer days. Thus nature wages war and disagrees throughout the year; do not wonder that the stars fight in that part of the sky.

Yet the sign of the Ram does not fight the Balance entirely, because the Spring differs from the time of Autumn. One fills the world with ripe fruits, the other with flowers. But they are of equal reckoning, for in both, the night is equal to the days. The seasons bring about harmony through a similar fabric, preserving both day and night at once during the transitional periods between winter and summer heat, so that the stars battle less fiercely in the sky. Such will be the logic applied to the different signs.

-> ### On the individual deities presiding over the signs. Chapter XI <-

**H**aving noticed these things, your next care is to learn of the guardians and the deities assigned to the signs, and which deity Nature dedicated to each thing. When she gave divine faces to these great virtues, she also established various characters under a sacred power.

...so that the weight of authority might be added to these matters by a personal guardian.
<term>Pallas<gloss>Minerva, goddess of wisdom and war</gloss></term> protects the <term>Wool-bearer<gloss>Aries, the Ram</gloss></term>; <term>Cytherea<gloss>Venus, goddess of love</gloss></term> looks after the Bull.
<term>Phoebus<gloss>Apollo, the sun god</gloss></term> guards the handsome Twins; the <term>Cyllenian<gloss>Mercury, the messenger god born on Mt. Cyllene</gloss></term> guards the Crab.
Jupiter himself, together with the <term>Mother of the Gods<gloss>Cybele, the Phrygian earth goddess</gloss></term>, rules the Lion.
The Virgin belongs to the <term>Wheat-bearer Ceres<gloss>Goddess of the harvest</gloss></term>; the Balance was forged by 
Vulcan; and the <term>warlike Scorpio<gloss>associated with the sting of battle</gloss></term> clings to <term>Mauors<gloss>Mars, the god of war</gloss></term>.
<term>Diana<gloss>Goddess of the hunt</gloss></term> favors the hunting man <note>original: "Venantem virum"; the Centaur or Sagittarius</note> who is partly horse;
while <term>Vesta<gloss>Goddess of the hearth and home</gloss></term> warms the narrow stars of Capricorn.
Opposite to Jupiter's sign <note>Sagittarius</note>, Aquarius is the star of Juno.
And Neptune recognizes his own in the sea-dwelling Pisces.
From these associations, too, great insights into your future will come.
When your reason leads you to care for the stars and constellations,
you will seek evidence from every part, and find the paths of this
Art, so that the power—divided by nature—may rise through your intellect.
Thus shall mortal hearts follow the constancy of the heavens.

-> ## Chapter XIII: On the parts of the body assigned to the signs. <-

**A**ccept now the parts of man divided among the stars,
and how each sign is obeyed within its own specific form.
Within these parts, the signs exercise the chief powers of the whole body:
Aries is the prince of all, being allotted the **head**; 
the Bull receives the most beautiful **neck** as his estate;
the Twins are written into an equal lot, with **arms**
connected to the **shoulders**; the **chest** is located
under the Crab; the Lion rules the **sides** and **shoulder blades**.
The **belly** <note>original: "ilia"; the loins or lower abdomen</note> falls into the Virgin’s own lot.
The Balance rules the **buttocks**, and Scorpio delights in the **groin**.
The **thighs** are added to the Centaur <note>Sagittarius</note>; Capricorn
commands both **knees**; the judgment of the **shins** belongs to
Aquarius, as he pours his water; and Pisces claims the rights over the **feet**.

-> ## Chapter XIIII: On the friendship or hatred of signs, and on the <term>twelfth-parts<gloss>the "duodecatemoria"—the subdivision of each zodiac sign into twelve smaller units</gloss></term>. <-

**I**ndeed, the stars also agree among themselves by their own laws,
maintaining a fixed exchange of influences.
By turns, they offer their sights to one another, or listen with their ears <note>This refers to "aspects"—signs that "see" each other (by trine or sextile) or "hear" each other (signs of equal power or rising time)</note>.
They either carry out a treaty or harbor hatred; and some, having turned back
into themselves, are led by their own specific fury.
Therefore, a grace sometimes exists between opposing signs,
while those that are allied may wage war; and in a foreign seat
they produce those joined through all time.
They fight and flee one another in turns, both the weak and the strong.
But when God founded the entire world according to these laws,
He also divided the feelings among the varying stars.
He brought together the eyes of some, and the ears of others.
He joined their friendships under a certain treaty,
so that they might be able to see one another, or hear certain things.
Some they would love; others they would move to harm and war.
There would even be an indulgence for their own lot,
so that they would always love themselves and be pleased with their own nature.
Just so, we see many of the temperaments of men,
who derive their character from the signs that formed their birth.

Aries is his own counsel, but <term>Taurus<gloss>the Bull</gloss></term> is worthy of a prince; he weaves a plot against the <term>Wool-bearer<gloss>Aries, the Ram</gloss></term>, and looks and hears across the stars toward the <term>Fish<gloss>Pisces</gloss></term>. The mind [of the Bull] is captured by the <term>Virgin<gloss>Virgo</gloss></term>, just as he once behaved when he carried <term>Europa<gloss>The Phoenician princess abducted by Zeus in the form of a bull</gloss></term> on his back, her left hand holding his horns. Clothed in the power of Jove, the Bull leads the ears of the <term>Twins<gloss>Gemini</gloss></term> toward the youth pouring eternal waters <note>original: "iuuenem aeternas fundentem... undas"; referring to Aquarius</note> for the Fish. <term>Cancer<gloss>the Crab</gloss></term> directs its mind toward the Fish themselves, and its eyes toward the <term>Lion<gloss>Leo</gloss></term>, while <term>Capricorn<gloss>the Horned Goat</gloss></term> is hidden in the opposite star.

<term>Aquarius<gloss>the Water-bearer</gloss></term> turns his eyes toward himself, stretches his hearing unchanged, and is caught by the star of the Crab. But the Lion joins his sight with the Twins, and his hearing with the <term>Centaur<gloss>Sagittarius</gloss></term>; the star of Capricorn loves the Twins. <term>Erigone<gloss>Virgo</gloss></term> looks at the Bull but hears the <term>Scorpion<gloss>Scorpio</gloss></term>, and she attempts to weave a plot against the <term>Archer<gloss>Sagittarius</gloss></term>. <term>Libra<gloss>the Balance</gloss></term> follows her own senses, seeing only the Wool-bearer and embracing the Scorpion below in her mind. He <note>the Scorpion</note> sees the Fish and hears the Balance through all things.

Likewise, the <term>Bow-bearer<gloss>Sagittarius</gloss></term> is accustomed to obeying the great Lion. With ears and eyes, he has grown used to watching the sign of the pouring Aquarius, and of all the stars, he loves Erigone alone. Conversely, Capricorn turns his sight toward her; for what greater thing could he admire than her, since he shone happily at the <term>August birth<gloss>The Emperor Augustus famously used Capricorn as his personal zodiacal sign</gloss></term>? With his ears, he catches the heights of topmost Cancer. Naked Aquarius aims his hearing at the Twins, honors the high Cancer, and watches the drawn-back arrows of the Archer. The Fish have directed their sight to the Scorpion and desire to pay attention to the Bull.

Nature granted these turns when she fixed the stars. Those born under these signs reflect similar senses toward each other, for they desire to hear some and see others. They are led now by hate for these, and now by love for those. They lay traps for some and are caught by others. Furthermore, opposing <term>trigones<gloss>Groups of three signs forming a triangle, or "trines"</gloss></term> can even conflict with other trigones. Another line leads to war along a different path; thus the order of truth harmonizes through the whole. For Aries, Leo, and the Bow-bearer, joined in a triangle, deny a pact with the <term>Claws<gloss>original: "Chelis"; the claws of the Scorpion which anciently formed the sign of Libra</gloss></term> and its whole triangle, which the Twins and the water-pouring Aquarius occupy.

A double reasoning forces us to admit this is true: first, that three signs shine in opposition to three other signs; and second, that eternal wars persist between humans and beasts. The face of the Balance is human, while the Lion’s is different. Therefore, the cattle yield; though their physical strength is ample, human wisdom is greater. The defeated Lion shines in the stars. The golden fleece granted stars to the Wool-bearer. The Centaur himself yields in his horse-like back. To such an extent is the beast conquered by the man, that one might marvel how they could be overcome by the triangle of the rising Balance.

Moreover, there is a shorter method to be followed through the signs. For whichever stars shine fashioned in human form, those of the beasts remain their enemies and are conquered by them. Yet each sign withdraws into its own thoughts and carries private weapons against secret enemies. Those born under the <term>Wool-bearer<gloss>Aries, the Ram</gloss></term> have war with those born of the <term>Virgin<gloss>Virgo, also called Erigone</gloss></term>. Both <term>Libra<gloss>the Balance</gloss></term> and the <term>Twins<gloss>Gemini</gloss></term>, as well as the <term>Fish<gloss>Pisces</gloss></term> whom the wave brought forth, are said to be enemies to the parts of <term>Taurus<gloss>the Bull</gloss></term>; so too are the breasts born under <term>Cancer<gloss>the Crab</gloss></term>, those in the <term>Claws<gloss>the scales of Libra, formerly seen as the Scorpion's pincers</gloss></term>, and those given by the sharp <term>Scorpion<gloss>Scorpio</gloss></term>. And the Fish and the stars of the Twins form these enmities as well. With these, the Wool-bearer is at war, along with those in his <term>trine<gloss>trigonum; a group of three signs spaced 120 degrees apart, sharing the same element</gloss></term>.

The seeds of <term>Capricorn<gloss>the Horned Goat</gloss></term> harm those born in Cancer, as do the offspring of Libra and those given by the star of the Virgin. And those who are counted under the star of the opposing Bull will be a common enemy to the Wool-bearer and the rabid <term>Lion<gloss>Leo</gloss></term>; but war is declared by just as many stars. Erigone fears the Bull, and the Twins fear the <term>Centaur<gloss>Sagittarius</gloss></term> under the Bow, and the Fish; and a great crowd attacks you, stiff Capricorn. Capricorn attacks Libra, and the Crab stands opposite him with its claws, because each relationship forms a <term>square<gloss>quadratum; an aspect where signs are 90 degrees apart, creating tension</gloss></term>.

And as for the signs counted in the Wool-bearer’s trine, the Scorpion is believed to be a fertile enemy to just as many. He himself, though he is to be feared, flees the <term>Youth of the Sea<gloss>Aquarius, the Water-bearer</gloss></term>, the Twins, the Bull, and the Lion. He also flees Erigone and Libra. Those offspring who come from the star of the <term>Archer<gloss>Sagittarius</gloss></term>, those born of the Twins, Libra, the Virgin, and the <term>Urn<gloss>the vessel of Aquarius</gloss></term> wish to weigh down; nature, commanding this law, says these same signs are enemies to yours, Capricorn.

And those whom Aquarius drenches with eternal waters he drives as he comes to battle, and the crowd of beasts is driven under the power of a single youth throughout the whole trine. Neighboring Aquarius presses upon the rising Fish, as do the twin brothers, those whom the star of the Virgin gives, and those offspring who depart from the star of the Archer.

Nor is this the only reasoning that gives weapons to those being born, and generates offspring into hatred and mutual desires. But for the most part, every third sign remains hostile by law, their gaze fixed across with a malignant expression. In whatever place signs remain contrary and bear opposing looks between themselves at the seventh position <note>This refers to "Opposition," where signs are 180 degrees apart</note>, every third sign is said to be a trine for both of them. Let it not be wondered at if <term>Phoebus<gloss>the Sun</gloss></term> is not given to the stars which are related to the opposing signs of the trine. Through so many types of signs, contrary bodies arise, and in as many ways as enemies are created. Therefore, nature has created nothing from its own heart greater than friendship, nor anything more rare. There will be but one <term>Pylades<gloss>the legendary friend of Orestes</gloss></term>, one <term>Orestes<gloss>who, with Pylades, became the classical archetype of devotion</gloss></term> who would prefer to die himself; there was but one pair through the ages for whom death was light because the one would seize the fate of the other, and the other would not yield.

->### B O O K  T W O<-

And there were two who were able to follow a path scarcely harmed by punishments, <note>A reference to the famous Pythagorean friendship of Damon and Pythias, where one offered his life as security for the other.</note> where the guarantor hoped the accused would not be able to return, and yet feared for the accused lest he should release the guarantor himself <note>by returning to face execution</note>. Through so many ages of men, so many eras and years, so many wars and varied labors even in times of peace, should Fortune search for loyalty, she hardly finds it anywhere. But how great is the mass of crimes throughout all centuries; how the burden of hatred is inexcusable upon the earth! Fathers are sold to their fates, and mothers to their graves. The <term>Sun-god<gloss>original: "Phoebus"</gloss></term> imposed night upon the world and abandoned the lands <note>A poetic allusion to the Sun turning away in horror from human atrocities, such as the mythical feast of Thyestes.</note>. Why should I speak of overturned cities and betrayed temples, the various calamities of peace and mixed poisons, the ambushes of the forum, the murders within the very walls, and the mob raging under the name of friendship? Crime is among the people, and all things overflow with madness. Right and wrong are mixed, and through the very laws themselves wickedness rages; guilt now surpasses its punishments. Certainly, among the many, discord prevails. Bodies are born, and parts are carried off across the world; the bond of loyalty is rare, as is the tribute of peace, and the earth itself hardly trusts the sky. The races of men are carried along by an enemy fate.

If, however, you also desire to know the kindred signs, which join spirits together and are carried along by a friendly lot, join the offspring of the <term>Wool-bearer<gloss>Aries, the Ram</gloss></term> with his whole <term>trine<gloss>trigonum; a triangular aspect where signs are 120 degrees apart, sharing an element—in this case, Fire</gloss></term>. He is exposed to his own harm, not knowing any deceits, and consists of a spirit no less soft than his body. In those other signs <note>Leo and Sagittarius</note> there is a wildness and a desire for prey, and a venal mind; he never compels loyalty to yield to convenience, nor is the gratitude for a deed long-lasting. But when the offspring of the Wool-bearer is under either trine, he does not bring forth war, but rarely wages it according to the season, because the ferocity of each is more compelled by the timing. Yet more strength is to be counted in the double sign where man is mixed <note>Sagittarius, who is half-man and half-horse</note> than in you, <term>Nemean one<gloss>Leo; referring to the Nemean Lion slain by Hercules</gloss></term>, who exists under a single form. Therefore there is peace among the signs, though with mixed complaints.

Furthermore, the star of the <term>Bull<gloss>Taurus</gloss></term> is joined to the <term>Horned Goat<gloss>Capricorn</gloss></term>. Nor do their minds come together any more closely for the making of treaties. Those who are created as the offspring of the <term>Virgin<gloss>Virgo</gloss></term> also desire to be embraced by the Bull, but they are often complained of. Those whom the <term>Claws<gloss>Chelae; the scales of Libra, which the ancients often depicted as being held by the Scorpion's pincers</gloss></term> give, and those births the <term>Water-bearer<gloss>Aquarius</gloss></term> provides, possess one heart and an immovable bond of loyalty. Great will be the love and a double harmony for the <term>Twins<gloss>Gemini</gloss></term>. Great success will also come to them in having many friends. The <term>Scorpion<gloss>Scorpio</gloss></term> and the <term>Crab<gloss>Cancer</gloss></term> lead those born from themselves into brotherly names; likewise, those born of the <term>Fish<gloss>Pisces</gloss></term> agree with them, for they often share a subtle way of acting.

->### B O O K   T W O<-

Scorpio scatters harm under the name of a friend. 
But for those to whom the Fish <note>The constellation Pisces.</note> are present at their coming into the light of birth, 
no single opinion ever remains in their heart. 
They change their minds, and sometimes even break their alliances. 
They seek again and let hidden plagues wander beneath their brow. <note>Manilius suggests that those born under Pisces are prone to fickleness or secret resentments.</note> 
In this way, you must take note of hatred and peace from the signs. 
Those born on earth are created under this law. 
Nor is it enough merely to dwell upon the signs alone. 
Observe the location of the sky and the seat of the wanderers. <term>Wanderers<gloss>original: "uagantum"</gloss></term> <note>The ancient term for the planets, which "wander" against the fixed background of the stars.</note> 
The lineage varies by their sector, and the geometric line changes their powers. 
For their own rights come to the <term>squares<gloss>original: "quadratis"</gloss></term>, and their own rights to the <term>triangles<gloss>original: "trigonis"</gloss></term>, <note>In astrology, a "square" aspect occurs between signs 90 degrees apart, while a "triangle" or "trine" occurs between signs 120 degrees apart.</note> 
as well as the line which runs through six divisions, <note>The "sextile" aspect (60 degrees).</note> 
and those lines which cut the middle of the sky with a transverse boundary. <note>The "opposition" aspect (180 degrees).</note> 
From here, the world now grants strength, and now the same world takes it away: 
those things which take up strength there, set it aside when moved here. 
For it makes a difference whether they are rising, or following, or falling. 
They produce powers whenever they occupy foreign realms 
and settle as guests in the furthest camps. 
These things shall be sung by me under a fixed portion of the stars. 
Hatred is more frequent between signs that are opposite; bodies are judged 
as kin in signs that form a square, and as friends in triangles. 
The reason is not obscure, for nature has placed every fourth sign 
of the same kind throughout the circle. 
Four signs mark the heavens with an equal division, 
in which God himself created the joints of the year. <note>The four "cardinal" signs that mark the beginning of the four seasons.</note> 
The Ram <note>Aries</note> brings Spring; the Crab <note>Cancer</note> serves <term>Ceres<gloss>original: "Cererem"</gloss></term>; <note>Ceres was the goddess of grain; this refers to the summer harvest.</note> 
the Balance <note>Libra</note> serves <term>Bacchus<gloss>original: "Bacchum"</gloss></term>; <note>Bacchus was the god of wine; this refers to the autumn vintage.</note> the Goat <note>Capricorn</note> brings midwinter, and the Fish <note>Pisces</note> are born for the cold. 
Furthermore, those signs connected by a double figure 
also occupy every fourth place: you can see the two Fish, 
and the youthful Twins <note>Gemini</note>, and the double form in the Virgin <note>Virgo</note>, 
and the two Centaurs <note>Sagittarius</note>, though woven into a single body. 
So too the square form stands for the "simple" signs. 
For the Bull <note>Taurus</note> has no companion, nor is the fearsome 
Lion <note>Leo</note> painted with anyone else, nor does Scorpio fear 
anyone without a body, and the Water-Bearer <note>Aquarius</note> is judged by a single star-figure. 
Thus, whatever signs remain established in the square temple 
reflect an equal lot in their numbers or their season. 
And they remain like kin under such a treaty. 
Therefore they mark relatives, and they approach heavy neighbors, 
and they hold those born under one image. 
A longer line is corrected into a greater space, 
which makes triangular stars from every third sign. 
These lead to friendships, imitating the laws and the degrees 
of blood-relation, and hearts clinging in spirit. 
And as the powers themselves meet though removed in a long retreat, 
so they join us across greater intervals. 
They consider these relationships better, which can join minds, 
than those which sometimes fail the treaty of blood. 
Every third sign subscribes to its neighboring guests; 
in this way the order of the stars will be preserved, 

however many...

<meta>This page continues the technical exposition of astrological geometry. Having previously discussed the major aspects (squares and triangles) that link different signs of the zodiac, Manilius now moves into a more granular level of detail: the "dodecatemories," or the twelve-fold subdivision of each individual sign.</meta>

-># BOOK TWO<-

However many signs are moved by the varying motion of their own <term>pivots<gloss>original: "cardinibus"</gloss></term> <note>The "cardines" or hinges of the sky: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Lower Midheaven.</note>. Although the stars have divided the world into four parts and form a square, they are not judged by the law of the square alone; the practical use of the pivot is less than its total number. For nothing serves itself entirely; all things are carried along in a mixture. They give boundaries to the stars themselves and receive them in turn, which will soon rise before me, arranged in a certain order.

Add now their own parts to the signs, and their own stars to the parts. Reason must be sought from all of these through the art of division, so that you can learn to recognize the signs even within their smaller sections. Behold now with keen vision a matter of great weight, which can only be designated by a Greek name: <term>Duodecatemoria<gloss>original: "duodecatemoria"</gloss></term> <note>From the Greek "dodekatemorion," meaning "twelfth-part." This refers to a system where each 30-degree zodiac sign is subdivided into twelve 2.5-degree segments, each associated with a different sign.</note>, marking the influences into specific titles. 

For since the signs consist of thirty parts <note>degrees</note> each, that whole number is again divided by twelve. Therefore, reason itself teaches that there are two and a half parts in these boundaries. A <term>twelfth-part<gloss>original: "duodecatemotium"</gloss></term> <note>Likely a printer's error for "duodecatemorion."</note> consists of this, and twelve of these make up the whole. In all the signs which that <term>founder of the world<gloss>original: "mundi conditor"</gloss></term> <note>The Divine Creator or Demiurge in Stoic philosophy.</note> assigned with as many shining stars, he did so so that the alternating stars might be joined by lot. 

Thus the world is similar to itself, and "all stars are in all stars," by whose mixtures harmony might rule the body and there would be mutual protection for a common cause. For that reason, although people are born under the same signs, they display diverse characters and hostile desires. And often nature wanders even into the beasts <note>Referring to the animal-shaped signs like Aries the Ram or Leo the Lion</note>, and the daughter follows the mother, and births are mixed by the stars, as individual stars vary by as many diverse parts in the twelfth-parts, changing their own powers.

Now, I shall sing of what this system is, to whom it belongs, and in what order they consist, lest you wander aimlessly through unknown parts of the signs. The signs themselves retain the first parts in their own "body." <note>The first 2.5 degrees of a sign like Aries belong to Aries itself.</note> Those segments that follow are assigned to their neighbors in order. The rest take their parts according to their sequence. The final calculation is granted to the last stars. Thus each sign retains <margin>Into two parts</margin> two and a half parts of its own, and the sum is filled by thirty completed lots in every sign.

Nor is there only one kind of this, nor is the revealed method simple. Nature has placed the reality of things in many modes; she has drawn out paths and willed that she be sought through all things. This method was also discovered under the same name: at whatever time of birth the Moon <note>original: "luna"</note> stands in its degrees, multiply this number by twelve, because just as many signs shine in the high world. Then assign the result to that sign in which the Moon shone. Remember to count the parts which are missing from there. The next calculation likewise leads to thirty; where this number fails, then the sum remaining...

Let a portion be added into two parts of a sign, 
and let a half-part be assigned to the remaining signs in order. 
In the sign where these stop, the Moon will regard you as accurate. 
After the rest, they shall lead by the signs of the <term>twelfth-parts<gloss>original: "Duodecatemoriis"</gloss></term>, 
each in its own order; thus the stars are established in their places. 
Lest this system also deceive you, observe it briefly. 
It is greater in effect than it is small in its divisions, 
for that which is called a <term>twelfth-part<gloss>original: "Duodecatemorium"</gloss></term> 
is marked by five parts <note>Manilius likely refers to the fact that two such parts equal five degrees, or he is transitioning to the influence of the five planets</note>, 
for just as many stars shine in the sky 
which are called "wandering" <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>; and they each command 
half-strengths and the care which they take up in these parts. 
In whichever sign, therefore, the five stars are located, 
it will be proper to look upon the twelfth-part; 
for in whichever star's territory they end, and into whichever sign 
they have fallen, it will give effects upon the minds of that person. 
The logic must be blended from all sides, through which all things consist. 
But I shall return all these things later in their own proper order. 
Now it is enough to have taught unknown things through their uses, 
so that when confidence stands firm upon the parts already learned, 
the whole body of knowledge may be noted by an easy logic, 
and the song may flow well regarding the whole after the individual parts. 
Just as letters are first shown to unrefined children 
by their appearance and their name, and then their use is practiced; 
then, joined in their own knots, a syllable is formed; 
from here comes the structure of words, and through words the practice of reading. 
Then again, the strengths and the use of the art are handed down, 
and through their own "feet" <note>A pun on poetic meter (feet) and the "steps" of learning.</note> the burgeoning poems arise. 
It is profitable to have learned each prior thing for the sake of the whole. 
Unless these stand firm, founded on their own elements, 
whatever precepts the masters have given quickly in verse, 
the disordered rank of things would flow away into a void. 
So it is for me, as I fly through the whole world in song, 
singing of fates unearthed from deep darkness, 
modulated even in the measures of the <term>Muses<gloss>original: "Pieridum"</gloss></term> <note>The Pierides or Muses, the goddesses of artistic inspiration.</note>, 
and recalling the divine power into the arts where God reigns; 
trust must be led through the parts, and the individual components 
must be handed down in their own steps; and when all things stand 
with certain knowledge, let them be recalled to their own uses. 
And just as cities rise up on bare mountains— 
the <term>Founder<gloss>original: "Conditor"</gloss></term> intends to surround the empty hills 
with walls before his hands attempt to cut the trenches. 
He turns to the work: behold, the forest falls, the ancient groves 
topple, and they see a new sun and new stars. 
Every race of birds and wild beasts is driven from the place, 
leaving behind their ancient homes and familiar dens. 
But the men search for flint for the walls and marble for the temple, 
and the hardness of iron is sought for the designated time; 
from here come the arts, from here every use assembles. 
Then at last the work rises up, when everything is available,

# -> SECOND BOOK <-

Lest a backward care break the middle of my course. 
In my handling of such a great mass, 
the material of things must first be delivered, 
the logic of the matter being set aside for now, 
lest that logic be in vain hereafter, or 
the arguments being born be numbed by new and unfamiliar matters.

## -> Of the Hinges of the World. Chapter XIV <-

### **S**o come now, apply a keen mind to learning
### the Hinges, which are four in total, distributed
throughout the world, and which always change the flying signs <note>Though the "hinges" (the Ascendant, Midheaven, etc.) stay fixed relative to the local horizon, the signs of the Zodiac pass through them as the Earth rotates.</note>.
One is from the rising of the sky as it is born into the world,
where it first perceives the lands with an equal boundary.
The other corresponds from the opposite shore of the ether,
from where the world flees, and tends headlong into the <term>underworld<gloss>original: "Tartara"</gloss></term>.
A third marks the tracks of the high sky,
where <term>Phoebus<gloss>The Sun</gloss></term>, weary with his horses' reins, halts,
and turns the day toward its decline, and examines the waters in the middle.
The fourth, noble in its established orb, holds the lowest point,
in which the beginning is raised up, and the end for the falling 
stars; it sees the settings and the risings equally.
These places report the principal lives and the greatest effects 
of the fates through the art, because the entire world 
leans upon them as if upon ethereal joints.
Unless these joints, by an alternating lot, catch the world 
flying in its perpetual courses, and bind it in double chains 
through the sides, and the bottom of the temple, and the highest peak, 
the machinery would flow apart, and the world would be dissolved.
But there is, however, a different power in each hinge,
and they vary according to the lot of their place, and differ in their order.
The first shall be the one which reigns at the peak of the highest sky,
and divides the middle world with a thin boundary.
Sublime glory occupies this through its high seat;
plainly, this guardianship befits the highest summits.
Whatever is eminent, it claims for itself, and every god 
contributes to it, and it reigns by granting various honors.
From here comes favor and appearance, and all the glory of the common people.
To render judgments, to settle the world by laws in the forum,
and to join foreign nations by their own treaties,
and to extol the name of each man according to his lot.
The next is the one located in the lowest station, though 
it sustains the world mixed with the roots of the other.
It is lesser in appearance of effect, but greater in its use.
It holds the foundations of things, and governs wealth.
How certain the prayers are that search for metals in trenches,
and how much you can obtain from that which is hidden.
And there is the third, lifting its shining part to those hinges,
which holds the rising, where the stars first surge.
A single day has given it, and it describes time in hours.
From here, among the Greek cities, the <term>horoscope<gloss>original: "horoscopus." In ancient astrology, this term refers specifically to the Ascendant, or the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</gloss></term> is proclaimed.
Nor does it take the last place by its own right, for it rejoices in its name.
This one holds the judgment of life, and here the rule is for motion.
