# -> BOOK <-

[The fourth hinge] will grant fortune to affairs and lead them through skills. It determines what first times receive the newborn, what care they receive, and in what seat they are created. The stars will endorse both [birth and upbringing] with their combined powers. The last hinge, which hides the stars when the world has been traversed <note>The Descendant or West, where stars "set" and disappear</note>, and holding the sunset, looks down upon the submerged world; it pertains to the summits of things and the end of labors. It joins together banquets, the final times of life, leisure, the assemblies of men, and the worship of the gods.

-> ### *On the divisions of the ages in the parts of heaven, and the significations of the twelve houses. Chapter XV* <-

**N**or will you be content with perceiving only the hinges. The intervals between them must also be noted with a mindful soul, for these spaces, measured over a greater distance, yield their own specific powers. 

Whatever part of the sky curves from the rising <note>The Ascendant</note> up to the highest point of the orb <note>The Midheaven</note> claims the years of the first age and the newborn. 

The part that is pressed down from the highest peak of the world until it comes to the setting <note>The Descendant</note> succeeds the years of childhood and governs youth, held beneath its seat. 

The part which descends between the setting and the lowest point of the orb <note>The Imum Coeli, or bottom of the sky</note> governs the times of mature life, exercised in its own sequence and varied course. 

But that part which is completed by the returning course from the bottom, ascending the upturned arc slowly with weary strength <note>The arc from the Imum Coeli back up to the Ascendant</note>, finally embraces the late years, the slipping days of life, and trembling old age. 

Indeed, every sign, under whatever figure it takes, is affected by these parts; the place in the world commands the stars. It grants gifts or harm; individual things turn in an orb, receive powers from their position, and return them to heaven. For nature overcomes the type <note>original: "Vincit enim natura genus"—meaning the astronomical "place" or House is more powerful than the inherent nature of the Zodiac sign itself</note> and administers laws within its own borders. It forces passing stars to adopt its own character—now rich with varied honor, now sterile—as the stars bear the punishment of the seat they occupy. 

The region which is above the rising, starting from the highest star of heaven <note>The 12th House, just above the Eastern horizon</note>, is an unhappy region, hostile to future affairs and too fertile in vice. Nor is it alone; for equal to it is that seat which shines with an opposing star, joined just below the setting <note>The 6th House</note>, lest it stand upon the hinge of the world. Both are said to be cast down by a past ruin; they are born of labor, where one must climb only to fall. Nor is it any better above the setting <note>The 9th House</note> or opposite, beneath the rising <note>The 3rd House</note>. 

The lot of the world is driven headlong; these high-hanging places either earned their end by being near a hinge or will fall, defrauded of power. These are deservedly held to be the horrendous seats of **Typhon** <note>Also known as Typhoeus, the monstrous giant of Greek myth who challenged the gods of Olympus</note>, whom the cruel Earth poured forth when she gave birth to war against heaven. Nor were her offspring smaller than their mother; but driven back by lightning into the heights, the mountains they threw fell back upon them. Even Typhoeus yielded to the tumult of war and of life.

## ->BOOK TWO<-

Mother Earth herself trembles beneath flaming Mount Etna <note>original: *Aetna*; Manilius uses the volcanic activity of Etna as a metaphor for the immense power and movement of the celestial spheres</note> and follows the peaks in the reflecting sky. So that she might not yield even to the one who performs the duty of the star <note>the "Hinge" or Cardinal point</note>, seeking the palm of victory and triumphing over her predecessors, she rises higher, added as a companion to the final summit. The courses then remain for the worse, and no prayers are left. Therefore, it is not at all surprising if the place next to the highest, yet below it, is called a venerable lot. 

Because its title is "Happy," if our Roman tongue adopts a name for the sake of virtue from the Greek language <note>Manilius refers to the 11th House, known in Greek as *Agathos Daimon* (Good Spirit) and in Latin as *Bonus Eventus* or *Felix* (Happy/Fortunate)</note>. Jupiter dwells here; he trusts this lot to the fortunate race. From here, the lowest lightning bolts of the submerged world, thrown down beneath the orb, touch the earth in a reversed impulse. 

On the opposite side, the military service shines, exhausted by its completed labors, and is again devoted to the new work of the Hinge, about to undergo the yoke and a powerful fate. It does not yet feel the toil of the world, but already it hopes for honor. The Greeks call this *Daemonium* <note>The 12th House, *Malus Daimon* (Evil Spirit), which precedes the Ascendant and was associated with hidden enemies and burdens</note> through Roman mouths; a title is sought beneath the wise, inverted heart. Conceal the place and the divinity of the all-powerful god, so that they may be called back later for great uses. From here, the turning points of our full health remain, and the wars of diseases fighting with foul weapons. Its power is ambiguous because of the Twins <note>possibly a reference to the sign Gemini or the dual nature of health and sickness</note> and the cause of the day, changing both lots now here, now there.

But after the stars of midday and the first curved peaks of the nodding world from the highest summit, Phoebus [the Sun] loves the upper air. Beneath him, our bodies also determine their vices and conceive their fortune from his strength. That place is called "God" <note>original: *deus*; referring to the 9th House, called *Theos* in Greek, which was the "Joy" of the Sun</note> under a Greek name. Opposite this, the part of the world that first rises from the lowest seats and leads back Olympus <note>the heavens</note> shines with a golden glow and governs the night. It recognizes Phoebe [the Moon] as its mistress, seeing her brother’s kingdoms shining through the opposite parts of the sky, and imitating the fates at the destructive borders of the world. To this part, the name will be "Goddess" <note>original: *dea*; referring to the 3rd House, *Thea* in Greek, the "Joy" of the Moon</note> through Roman mouths; Greece designates the same title with its own voice.

But in the citadel of heaven, where the highest slopes find an end and where the descents take their beginning—where the summits rise between the setting and the rising, and keep the world balanced in its own order—Cytherea <note>another name for Venus</note> claims this seat for herself among the stars. And as if she were the face of the world, she positions her own features. Through these, this specific power is added to her part of human affairs: she governs marriages, bridal chambers, and wedding torches. This guardianship suits Venus; her name for the place will be "Fortune" <note>The 5th House, known as *Bona Fortuna* (Good Fortune), associated with pleasure and children</note>. By this name, perceive the mind's intent, so that she may provide brief shortcuts in this long poem; and where the world sinks at the inverted hinge,

-> # BOOK TWO <-

Holding the foundations, he gazes up at the world from the opposite side. And Saturn, lying there in the middle of the night <note>original: *media sub nocte*; this refers to the *Imum Coeli* or the "Bottom of the Sky," the lowest point of the zodiacal circle</note>, exerts his power in that region—he who was himself once cast down from the command of the world and the throne of the gods. And as a father, he exercises his divine power over his own misfortunes and the fate of the elderly. This part of the sky, where the foundations are laid, is the primary fortune of two groups: those being born and their fathers. 

The time was harsh, to which Greece gave the title *Daemonium* <note>original: *Daemonium*; meaning "Spirit" or "Lesser Divinity." In this context, it refers to the 12th House, often associated with misfortune or hidden burdens</note>, marking its powers according to its name. 

Now, look upon the world rising from its first hinge <note>original: *primo de cardine*; the Ascendant or East, the point where stars first appear over the horizon</note>, where the birthing signs begin their firm return, and the moist sun <note>original: *Phoebus*; the sun god</note> swims out from the cold waves and is gradually Kindled with golden fire. Nor do the temples fail to carry you, Mercury, son of Maia born on Mount Cyllene <note>original: *Maia Cyllenie nate*; Manilius assigns Mercury to the First House</note>. O face marked with a sign! Nature has established in this place the names and arts by which one leads the way to heaven, and has stored here every fortune of those born; from this point, she suspends the prayers of parents. 

One place remains in the setting sun; that place casts the world headlong to the earth and drowns the stars. And the Earth gazes upon the face of the Sun which it had just seen. Do not be surprised if this is called the "Gate of Black Pluto" <note>original: *Ditis ianua*; Pluto/Dis was the god of the Underworld; the West is where the sun "dies" or enters the darkness</note>, and if it holds the end of life and is designated for death. From here, even the day itself dies, is stolen from the lands across the globe, and is shut away, captured in the prison of night. Furthermore, this place claims the guardianship of faith itself and the weight of the heart; such is the power in this seat which calls and hides the Sun, receives him and returns him, and consumes the day. 

Under such a law, you must note the powers of the Temples through which the entire series of stars flies; the law itself guides them and lends them its own rules. The stars, according to a fixed order as Nature defines it, traverse these places and produce various powers, whenever they take up foreign kingdoms and settle as guests in these furthest camps. 

These things will be sung by me under the specific portion of the stars. For now, it is enough to have noted the titles of the parts of heaven, the effects of each place in itself, and the gods who gave their names to the parts and established their citadels. This is the Eight-House system <note>original: *Octotopos*; a rare and early astrological system using eight divisions of the sky instead of the twelve that later became standard</note>, through which the stars fly in different directions; the movements they return will come in the proper order of things.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Three of Manilius's poem. # -> THE ASTRONOMICON OF MARCUS MANILIUS <-
## -> BOOK THREE <-

> *On Nature, the governess of all things; on the twelve parts of the houses upon which the fates of men depend; on the position of the cardinal points; and on the variation of days and nights and the inequality of the hours. Chapter I.*

**L**ead me, O Muses <note>original: *Pierides*; a common name for the Muses, the goddesses of inspiration, who were said to be the daughters of Pierus or to live in Pieria</note>, as I venture into a new theme rising greater than my own strength, and as I do not fear to travel through inaccessible groves. Look, I strive to expand your borders and to bring worthy songs into my verse. I shall not tell of wars rising for the destruction of heaven, of the thunderbolt and its flames, or of children buried within their mothers <note>These lines refer to the Gigantomachy (the war between the Giants and the Gods) and the myth of Saturn devouring his children</note>. I shall not tell of Hector being sold for his ashes, or of Priam bringing his ransom <note>Scenes from the end of the Trojan War</note>; nor shall I tell of the woman of Colchis <note>Medea</note> selling her father’s kingdom and her brother torn apart by her crime, nor of the harvest of armed men, the fierce flames of the bulls, and the watchful dragon <note>A summary of the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece</note>. Nor shall I speak of the years restored <note>the rejuvenation of Aeson</note>, nor of the fires caused by gold <note>the poisoned robe Medea gave to Creusa</note>, nor of children wrongly conceived and more wrongly slain. I shall not sing of the ancient wars of guilty Mycenae <note>Manilius uses the name *Messanæ*, likely a corruption of *Mycenae*</note>, nor of the Seven Leaders, nor the walls of Thebes snatched from the flames by a thunderbolt <note>the story of the Seven against Thebes and the death of Capaneus</note>, nor of the city that conquered the world it had once overcome. I shall not tell of a father’s brothers who were also a mother’s grandsons, or the banquets made of children, or the stars turned backward and the day snatched away <note>references to the gruesome feast of Thyestes, which caused the Sun to reverse its course in horror</note>. Nor shall I speak of the Persian wars declared upon the deep, of the sea lying hidden beneath a massive fleet, of the strait let loose upon the lands, and the path made for the waves through the earth <note>Xerxes the Great’s invasion of Greece, where he bridged the Hellespont and dug a canal through Mount Athos</note>.

I shall not sing of great kings; for the origins of the Roman race, so many leaders of the world, so many wars, and so many times of peace—and how the whole world yielded to the laws of a single people—would require a far greater space than if I spoke of the things I have touched upon. These things are deferred. It is easy to give one’s sails to favorable winds, to work a fertile soil through various arts, and to add luster to gold and ivory when the raw material itself shines. To build poems out of beautiful subjects is a common task and a simple composition. 

But I must struggle through numbers <note>mathematical calculations</note> and the unknown names of things, through times and various occurrences, and the moments of the world—the cycles of each and the parts within the parts themselves. To know these things is a great task; how great it is to speak of them in their own verse and to join them to fixed poetic feet! Come here, whoever you are, who can turn your ear and eyes to my undertakings, and perceive these true voices. Do not spend your mind on kings bound by oaths or the falling of Troy, nor seek sweet songs. The subject matter itself refuses to be decorated, content simply to be taught. And if any names are reported in a foreign tongue <note>original: *externa lingua*; Manilius refers to Greek technical terms which were standard in the astrology of his time</note>, this will be the fault of the work, not the poet; for not everything can be changed, and things are better noted under their own specific names. Now, come, perceive the core of the matter with subtle care—a matter which, once shown, will provide you with the most excellent uses and give certain paths in this art for seeing the fates.

-> # BOOK THREE <-

If these things have been well established by a watchful mind: 
Nature, the beginning of all things and the guardian of hidden mysteries, 
when she constructed such great masses within the walls of the world 
and enclosed the earth with surrounding stars 
hanging it from all sides in the middle, she joined diverse members 
into one body with certain orders. 
She commanded the air, the lands, the flames, and the flowing waves 
to provide mutual nourishment to one another, 
so that harmony might rule so many warring causes 
and the world might stand bound by a mutual pact, 
lest anything remain excluded from the highest reason, 
and so that what belonged to the world might be ruled by the world itself. 
She also suspended the fates and lives of men from the stars. 
These determine the primary parts of our labors, the honor of light, 
and fame; they fly on, never weary. 
These stars, which occupy what is like the mid-part of the world’s heart, 
surpass Phoebus <note>The Sun</note>, the Moon, and the wandering stars <note>The planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, 
yet they themselves are also surpassed. 
To these, Nature gave a kingdom and consecrated specific 
roles to each; she ordained that all things are brought together 
from every side, wherever the logic of fate is drawn into one. 
For whatever kind of matter, whatever labor, 
whatever works and arts, and whatever accidents 
could happen to human lot throughout life, 
Nature has encompassed in as many parts as the stars have named. 
She placed the realities, the fixed turns, and assigned names 
to each; she led the whole account of man’s life through the stars 
in a fixed order, so that one part would always stand 
neighbor to another in the nearby stars. 
She located the parts of these works <note>original: *partes*; referring to the "Lots" or mathematical points used in ancient astrology to predict specific outcomes</note> in individual signs, 
not so they would remain in a permanent station in the sky 
and be drawn equally for all human births 
reoccurring from the same places, but so they would receive 
their own seats according to the time of those being born, and migrate through the signs. 
Thus, a different lot would fall to a different star for different people, 
so that each birth might take a new form through the stars. 
Yet she did not confuse everything with uncertain motion; 
but when that part of the works which was established as the first part 
received its own seat at the time of birth, 
the rest follow and cling to the subsequent signs. 
The order follows the leader, until the circle comes back upon itself. 
Now, these "faces" of things located through the signs, 
in which all nature and the sum of things are established— 
just as when the seven stars <note>The five known planets plus the Sun and Moon</note> either harm or help, 
or when the divine power of the world moves through the cardinal points <note>original: *cardinibus*; the four pivotal points of the zodiac: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Lower Midheaven</note>, 
so a happy or sad fate comes through each individual thing. 
Such is the luck to be hoped for in that business. 
All these things must be sung by me in their solemn order, 
marked with their own titles and the figures of things, 
so that the position of the works, their name, and their kind may be clear.

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book Three of Manilius’s Astronomicon. After establishing that Nature governs the universe through a rational, mathematical order, the poet now describes the Twelve Lots (called Athla in Greek), which are specific points in the zodiac that govern different aspects of human experience, from wealth and war to marriage and health.</meta>

# ->BOOK THREE<-

The first lot has been given to **Fortune**; she is assessed by this title through our art <note>The "art" of astrology</note> because she contains within herself the immediate foundations of the home and everything clinging to that home. The lot determines the status of one’s slaves, the agreement found in the fields, and the power given to complete great masses of works, just as the wandering stars of the shining sky move in harmony.

After this comes the place of **military service**, where whatever occurs in the fields, or among those traversing foreign cities, is gathered under a single title.

The third station must be counted toward **urban labors**. This too is a kind of military service, but one composed of civil acts, and it holds the binding chains of loyalty. It forms friendships and reveals how many rewards may come from social duties and services that often seem to fall in vain, provided the world harmonizes with the stars positioned there.

Nature located the work of **legal judgments** in the fourth lot. Here is the fortune of the forum: the lawyer <note>original: "patronum"</note> pouring out words, the defendant hanging on his tongue, the speaker positioned on the rostrums <note>The "rostra" were the public speaking platforms in the Roman Forum</note> stripping bare the hidden laws for the people, and the man settling disputes by the sheer weight of his presence <note>original: "sua... fronte," literally "with his own brow," suggesting a stern or authoritative appearance</note>, when a judge summons nothing more than the man himself. Whatever eloquence achieves amidst the proposed laws, Nature has granted entirely to this one part. And however men conduct these affairs, the dominant stars flow through them.

The fifth step is dedicated through the signs to **marriage**; it holds partners and companions, and here hospitality is joined together, along with the covenant that unites like-minded friends.

In the sixth seat is counted **rich abundance** and the health of one’s affairs; one part of this lot advises how much wealth might be put to use, while the other advises how long it will last, just as the stars bend the vines and govern the temples.

The seventh is judged as fearsome for **cruel dangers**, if the stars located through the signs subscribe poorly to it.

**Nobility** holds the eighth, in which consists the condition of honor, the measure of fame, one's lineage, and grace under a beautiful pretext.

The ninth place occupies all the **doubtful lot of fates** and parental fears, and the entire mixed crowd of those entering life who require nurturing.

Neighboring this will be the lot of **life's conduct** <note>The tenth lot</note>, which contains the management of affairs, how the character of slaves is formed, how every house is shaped by examples, and in what certain order the slaves, arranged for their duties, depart to fulfill them.

A principal part is located in the eleventh lot, which always governs the **sum of our life** and our vitality. Here, health is determined—moving now free from diseases, now oppressed by them—as the stars move across the world. No other seat or time dictates the type of healing required, or at what time it may provide aid, or the healthy mixing of life-sustaining juices <note>Medicinal potions or humors</note>.

The last lot, concluding the entire sum in order...

# ->BOOK THREE<-

The effort required for attaining things involves all the results of our prayers, the pursuits that each person sets for himself and his kin, and the arts themselves, so that they may not be in vain. Whether one’s duty brings favor in every nod, or one attempts harsh quarrels in the forum through litigation, or seeks fortune on the deep sea following the winds; whether he ponders a full harvest <note>original: "Cererem," the goddess of grain, here representing the harvest</note> that overwhelms the granaries, or Bacchus <note>the god of wine</note> flowing through rich must: in this part of the zodiac, the days and these specific moments will be granted, provided the stars following through the signs agree. Later, I shall restore their powers—which are effective for both success and failure—under a fixed order when I begin to reveal the outcomes of things; for now, lest mixed details confuse the reader, it is enough to dwell upon the bare structure <note>literally "the naked limbs" of the system</note>.

And since we have worked out all the labors, names, and powers arranged across the whole circle, which the Greeks <note>original: "Graij"</note> call *Athla* <note>Greek: ἆθλα, meaning "contests," "labors," or "prizes." In astrology, these are the "Lots," mathematical points used to determine specific areas of life</note>, and which cohere as they are divided into twelve classes and parts: now I must sing of which signs they rise in and when. For they do not keep permanent seats, nor do they retain the same stars for everyone at birth; rather, they change their times, moving now here, now there through the circle according to the motion of the signs, yet in such a way that the established order remains unharmed.

Come then—lest a birth chart with a varying figure deceive you—if you wish to recall each labor to its proper sign, you must search for the **Place of Fortune** through all the stars. This is the part that was first mentioned under the numerous *Athla*. Once you have found this place by a certain calculation, you shall join the rest in the order previously described to the signs that follow, so that each may hold its own proper seat.

And lest by chance you begin to search for the seat of nature while wandering, grasp it in this twofold manner: When the chart of the birth has been established for you once the time of the birth is known, and the stars of heaven have been located in their signs, if the Sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> travels higher across the turning points <note>The "cardines" or angles of the chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note>—either the one that holds the sunrise or the one that sinks into the waves—you may affirm the child was born during the day. But if the Sun shines in the six lower stars <note>the signs below the horizon</note>, below the turning points that hold the world on the right and the left, then the child was born during the hours of night.

When these things are known to you by a certain distinction, then, if a nurturing day has received the newborn, you shall count the degrees of the signs in order from the Sun to the Moon; you shall then lead just as many degrees from the rising turning point <note>the Ascendant</note>, which they call the **Horoscope** <note>original: "horoscopon"</note> when the stars are properly divided. Into whatever sign that number reaches, give this to **Fortune**. You shall then join the rest of the *Athla* to their signs, all following in a fixed order.

But when night, covered with black wings, has hidden the world, if there is anyone who then emerges from the mother’s womb...

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of the "Twelve Lots" (Athla). Having established the significance of these twelve divisions of life, Manilius now transitions into the mathematical instructions for calculating the "Lot of Fortune"—the primary anchor for the system—and begins a technical critique of oversimplified methods for determining the Ascendant.</meta>

-># BOOK THREE<-

Turn your path, just as nature’s order turns. Then consult the Moon <note>original: "Phœben," the goddess of the moon</note>, who always imitates the light of her brother <note>the Sun</note> and reigns in her own time of night. However many degrees and signs the Sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> is distant from her, the shining Ascendant <note>original: "horoscopus," the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> commands you to count that same number starting from itself. Let Fortune hold this place as the stars come up in the order of nature, just as all things are situated.

Perhaps you might also ask, with a sharp mind, a matter worth noting: by what reasoning can you express the Ascendant rising from the immense circle at the moment of a person's birth? Unless this is grasped by reasoning under the stars, the foundations of the art fall, and the order does not harmonize. Because the world presents a false face when the pivots <note>original: "cardinibus," the four "hinge" points of a chart: the East, West, Zenith, and Nadir</note> that govern everything are incorrect, the origin is not consistent, and the stars of the celestial temple vary with every shifting moment.

But how full of labor is this task—to express the world flying through the signs in its eternal courses so that it surveys the whole circle in curved arcs—to establish its certain appearances and grasp the smallest point of such a great mass? Which part claims the sunrise, or which the heights of the world <note>the Midheaven</note>, which the sunset, or which sits at the bottom of the circle <note>the Imum Coeli</note>?

The order of the common method does not escape me, which grants two hours to each rising sign and distributes the stars equally in equal spaces. According to that method, the count would start from the degree where the Sun's orb begins, and apply the total to the stars until the time of birth itself is reached; and where it stops, that sign is said to rise.

But the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note> lies in an oblique path, and different stars rise with bent limbs <note>referring to the tilt of the Earth's axis/the ecliptic</note>. For those rising, the order is more upright as some star is nearer to us or farther away. Cancer <note>the sign of the summer solstice</note> scarcely ends the daylight; winter <note>original: "bruma," the winter solstice, associated with Capricorn</note> scarcely brings it back. As short as the latter lies, so long is the former's circle. Libra and Aries restore the night and day to equality. Thus the middle points struggle with the extremes, and the extremes with the highest.

Nighttime varies no less than the hours of light, yet the same order holds for opposite months. In such unequal spaces and varying patterns of days and shadows, who could believe that all the signs remain in the air under an equal law of the world? Add to this that the measurement of an hour is uncertain, nor does one part follow another; rather, as the sum of days turns, the parts rise and then recede. Since however many days are spent in any star, it has six signs above the earth and six signs beneath them; thus it happens that all signs cannot be born in two-hour increments, since there is not enough space for those hours in conflict—provided that twelve hours are maintained under every light.

-># BOOK III<-

->This is the number that reason demands, but common practice does not grasp.<-
->## *On the measurement of times and signs.* Chapter II<-

**N**or will the footprints of truth stand firm for you in any other way, unless you lay out the day and the night, measuring them into hours, showing how much they extend at various times under the known signs. Let a rule first be formed for exact hours, which may weigh the sluggish day, its positions, and its shadows. This will occur in Libra <note>The Scales</note>, when the nights begin to conquer the light, or when they yield in the middle of spring <note>the vernal equinox in Aries</note>. For only then do the times lie open in twelve equal hours, when Phoebus <note>original: "Phoebus," the sun god</note> runs through the middle of the sky. 

When the sun is moved away through the cold of winter in the star of the two-formed Capricorn <note>original: "Capricorni biformis," referring to the Sea-Goat's half-goat, half-fish body</note> and shines in its eighth degree, then the narrow spring-like <note>This likely refers to the "returning" light after the solstice</note> day turns into nine and a half hours; but the night, unmindful of the day, turns into twice seven plus one half <note>14.5 hours</note>, so that the number does not falter with that half-hour added, and thus each side results in twelve <note>i.e., the average or the total balance of the system</note>. And the sum total established by nature returns to the whole. 

From that point the nights fall, and the daylight rises into its times, until the stars have fought their way to burning Cancer <note>The Crab, the summer solstice</note>. And when the turns are reversed, they are changed into the winter hours; the days bring back the night, and the darkness brings back the winter light, and the alternating seasons conquer one another. Driven now here, now there, by certain steps through the stars—the reasoning of which has been gathered through manifest art—it shall come in its own text through these verses. And this is finally the measure through those hours, by which the Nile river <unclear>waters</uncall> with its parching summer steps and, breaking forth, imitates the stars of the world through its seven mouths and its faces that put the sea to flight.

->## *On the distances that the twelve signs occupy at their rising and setting.* Chapter III<-

**N**ow come, learn with a sagacious mind by how many *stadia* <term>stadium: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet; here used to measure the "space" a sign takes up as it crosses the horizon</term> and in how much time the stars rise, and in which they fall, lest great profits be lacking in these brief sayings. The noble sign of the Fleece-bearer <note>original: "lanigeri," referring to Aries the Ram</note>, which all things follow, takes up forty <margin>His</margin> doubled *stadia* <note>80 stadia</note> as it rises, and brings the same when it falls; and as it rises, it occupies an hour and a third of an hour, but doubling this when it sets. 

Meanwhile, the other signs increase by eight *stadia* as they rise into the circle, and admit as many as they stiffen into the cold shadows. The hour grows by a new quadrant <note>a quarter-hour</note> through each individual sign. And a third part [is added] in a fourth part if it is led through it. These are the increments for the rising stars up to the sign of Libra; the losses are drawn with equal momentum when they go under the circle. And again, returning to the stars of Libra, with the order changed, they return by equal moments through the reversed times. For by however many *stadia* or hours the star of the Fleece-bearer <note>Aries</note> had grown, by so much does Libra recede. And the space and time of rising that the setting Aries holds, the Claws <note>original: "Chelae," the "claws" of the Scorpion, an old name for the sign of Libra</note> maintain for as long as they persist in rising.

-># BOOK III<-

The following signs turn themselves toward this example. Once these rules have been stored in a watchful mind, it is now easy to recognize which star is acting as the Ascendant <note>original: "horoscopet," the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note> at any given time. Since one may trace the rising signs at fixed times and assign specific hours to their parts, the calculation is drawn from those signs in which Phoebus <note>original: "Phoebus," the sun god</note> resides, the sum of which I have already provided.

> *On the inclinations of the world, and in how many hours each sign rises and sets in any given region. Chapter IV*

# B
ut the measurement of days and shadows is not the same across all lands, nor do the seasons change with a similar course; the method varies while the underlying principle remains one. At the equator, where the fleece of the Phryxian sign <note>Aries, the Ram, associated with the golden fleece of Phryxus</note> and the faith of the Claws <note>original: "Chelarum," referring to the "Claws of the Scorpion," which were later redefined as the constellation Libra</note>, the scales of the balanced weight, are led, all signs rise over the course of two hours each. This is because the middle of the world is girded in a straight line, and the sky turns equally above a horizontal axis. There, dark nights are joined to days in perpetual peace, and time stands in an equal treaty. No clear deception of a false world is visible there. 

Night does not turn the same way across the whole globe. For all signs, Autumn and Spring are as one; a single line is traveled by an equal Sun <note>original: "coaequali... Phoebo"</note>. It does not matter then which star the Sun runs through—whether he scorches the shoreline Crab <note>Cancer</note> or is carried toward the opposite mid-point stars, or those four that lie between. Even though the circle of signs lies across three slanted arcs, the zones rise in a straight order and are carried above both head and land. They rise again in equal spaces through each circuit. The world lies hidden and revealed in a well-divided sphere. 

As soon as you depart from that part of the lands, whatever steps you take from the furthest pole across the convex tracks of the earth—which Nature has rounded into a swelling orb <note>original: "in tumidum," Manilius describes the Earth as a sphere</note> and suspended in the middle of the entire universe—you will see the change. Therefore, as you climb the rounded globe and move away, one part of the earth will vanish while another is restored; but as much as the earth curves, so too will the position of the flying heavens incline. Stars that had just been rising in a straight line are now drawn into the ether along a curved path. The belt of signs <note>the Zodiac</note>, which was once horizontal in space, will appear slanted in the sky, because while its own path is constant, our vantage points change. 

Thus, reason compels us to realize that time itself must move differently and bring varying lengths of days to such a region, since the slanted stars complete their difficult courses in a curved order. One sign may lie further back or closer than another. Because of this distance, a great delay is granted to those nearest to us...

<meta>This page continues Manilius's exploration of spherical astronomy. Having established how the signs of the zodiac rise at the equator, he now moves northward, explaining how the curvature of the Earth and the tilt of the celestial axis create longer periods of darkness and light, eventually culminating in the phenomenon of the six-month polar day and night.</meta>

-># BOOK<-

They rise up and are seen in the long circuits of the sky. Those signs that shine at the very edge are merged into blind shadows. And when one comes closer to the frozen North <note>original: "arctos," referring to the constellations of the Great and Little Bears which mark the celestial north</note>, the winter signs <note>the constellations the sun passes through during the winter months, like Capricorn</note> obstruct the eyes even more. Scarcely will there be a rising and a setting; if one proceeds further from there, individual signs will be hidden in all their parts, and they will drag out thirty nights in one continuous stretch of time. They will take away just as many days of light; thus a small delay of days is created, and the time is consumed by worn-away hours. Gradually, the space for the shining stars perishes, and more signs will be sought in the middle of the broken time, hidden by the swelling of the Earth's curve. They will bring Phoebus <note>original: "Phoebum," a common poetic name for the Sun god</note> with them and weave shadows together through the broken months until the year itself becomes feeble.

If indeed nature should allow a person to stand beneath the very zenith of the sky, which the frozen axis supports with its rigid joints—overcoming eternal snows—and if they were at the point touching the circle that gazes upon the downward-leaning limbs of the Lycaonian girl <note>original: "Lycaoniae... puellae," referring to Callisto, the daughter of the King of Lycaonia, who was transformed into the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear</note>, the appearance of the sky would seem to stand still. The paths of the sides run in a straight rotation like a spinning top. From there, only six signs will be open to your view in an oblique path, never escaping your sight in their circuit, but always accompanying the smooth world on its incline. Here, there will be a single day lasting for six months everywhere, dragging out half a year with continuous light. For in such a long time, Phoebus will never set while he traverses six stars <note>the six signs of the zodiac above the horizon</note> in his course, but flying around, he is turned in a level circle. 

But as soon as he descends headlong from the middle of that circle, seeking the lower stars in his downward course, and pours forth with loosened reins on the steep slope, one single night will join the darkness for just as many months. Beneath the zenith of the sky—for whoever watches from there—sees half the world from the entire round globe. The lower part lies hidden, for a straight line of sight cannot go around it, and it is divided as far as the middle of the belly <note>the celestial equator</note>. Therefore, it escapes the eyes of one watching from the top of the world while Phoebus is carried through the six submerged signs. He brings the light with him and leaves behind the shadows until, after as many months have passed as there are stars, he returns to where he had departed and ascends toward the twin Bears <note>Ursa Major and Ursa Minor</note>. This place divides the year into two: a single night and a single day, split between two halves of the Earth. 

And since it has been told with what great motion the seasons vary and for what causes, now receive the signs: how many rise in each place, and how many pass away through the hours, so that those rising can be grasped in certain parts, lest a false "horoscope" <note>original: "horoscopus," here meaning the Ascendant, or the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> wander with a doubtful calculation. And this must be followed as a certain law in its entirety: because individual signs cannot, through so many distant movements—

<meta>This page continues Manilius's explanation of the celestial sphere. Following the discussion of how latitudes affect the visibility of the stars, he now provides a mathematical method for calculating the "seasonal hours"—the variable lengths of day and night throughout the year—and how these relate to the rising times of the zodiac signs.</meta>

-> # BOOK THREE <-

Let the way to record exact times and their numbers begin with me; let each student follow the path set for them and proceed with their own steps. To me, they shall owe this art and the method by which it is prepared, and how each person may seek it across the lands. Let the student derive the proper hours for both night and day. The greatest day is found under the sign of **Cancer** <note>The Crab; the sign of the Summer Solstice in the Northern Hemisphere</note>, when the world is surrounded by the shortest shadows; whatever the sixth part of that total daylight duration is, let the student assign it to the neighboring sign of **Leo** <note>The Lion</note> after passing the temples of the Crab. 

But as for the measurement of the nightly shadows, it must be divided into as many parts by a similar calculation. Just as one part brings a certain amount of time to the rising of the stars, let that same amount be assigned to the stars rising in the opposite sign of **Taurus** <note>The Bull</note>. Between these signs, whatever time the **Nemean Lion** <note>original: "Nemaeus," a poetic reference to Leo, referring to the lion slain by Hercules</note> receives for its hours, you must divide that difference into three parts, so that a third part may be added to **Gemini** <note>The Twins</note>, which binds the times of the Bull and is similar to the times of the Crab and the Lion. In this way, the calculation will be led back to the previous total. 

This is how the Lion leads with its divided hours. From there, **Virgo** <note>The Maiden</note> proceeds with an equal flow of time, but always under a fixed law: she preserves the total of the previous stars unharmed and renews it while growing. For these signs, the portions of the hours are increased up to ten; then, through just as many parts, the stars of **Libra** <note>The Scales</note> will decrease. And by whatever measures they are raised to their rising in either direction toward a different lot, by those same measures shall they be submerged into the shadows. 

This is the system of hours to be calculated through the celestial circle, which shows the stars—which ones rise and which ones set. Since these consist of three hundred and twenty units <note>original: "tercentum... uicenaq" (320). In Manilius’s specific astronomical system, he uses a base of 320 to represent the units of time or degrees in a day-cycle at the solstice</note>, a full portion is subtracted from the sum, just as much as is taken from both [day and night] for all hours under the name of a "summer night," when **Phoebus** <note>The Sun</note> completes the solstice at the peak of **Olympus** <note>The highest point of the sky</note>. 

And whatever remains after these are taken away, divide that into six equal parts, and hand over a sixth to the fiery Lion. Again, whatever number stood under the name of night, that part must be assigned to the sign of the Bull. And what exceeds this part is surpassed by the other; it distinguishes the two sums by a middle difference. A third part of that number, added on top of the Bull’s number, is also given to the Twins; then the rest proceed with a similar gain, always protecting the previous numbers. They will increase the nine sums counted by name until they reach the times of the rightful Scales <note>Libra, the Autumnal Equinox, when day and night are equal</note>. 

From that point, they are shortened by just as many parts; the names are changed according to the law as they reach the borders of the **Wool-bearer** <note>original: "Laniger," a poetic term for Aries the Ram</note>, and as they recede, they lose equal portions of their lot. This path has shown how to set the totals of the distances <note>term: "stadium" (plural: stadia) — an ancient Greek unit of distance, here used to measure the "distance" a sign travels along the horizon</note> and how to count their risings through all the stars. When you have accepted this brief rule along with its proper hours, the **horoscopus** <note>term: "horoscopus" — the "Hour-Marker" or Ascendant; the specific point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a given moment</note> will never fail you in any region, since the individual signs, having been counted by fixed numbers...

From that part of the seasons which Phoebus <note>The Sun god</note> shall hold.
**Concerning the variety of seasons—namely of the year, month, day, and hours—**
**according to the risings of the signs. Chapter 5**

# N ow you must learn at what moments the winter months 
Begin to rise; for they do not proceed through all the stars 
With equal steps. While they reach the fleeces of the snowy sign <note>Aries the Ram, which marks the start of spring</note>, 
Compelling the light and the shadows to bear an equal 
Yoke <note>The Equinox, where day and night are of equal length</note>, there is a great system, which must be taught briefly. 
In the beginning, you must grasp the measurement of the day 
Which Capricorn <note>The Sea-Goat; the sign of the Winter Solstice</note> makes the shortest, and seek the hour 
Of the night which is the longest, and by how much it exceeds a fair hour. 
And if its daylight hours crackle <note>A poetic way of describing the sharp, short light of winter</note>, a third part 
Must always be handed to the middle sign; when that portion is held, 
Let it conquer the first by half, and let it be conquered itself 
By the last. In this way, direct the whole time into parts. 
By these means, also divide the three signs, but the sum of the previous 
Number is added, joined to the following stars. 
If it happens that the winter <note>original: "Brumali"</note> night is longer than the day 
By three hours, then let Capricorn raise the daylight 
By half an hour, and let Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer</note> 
Claim its own full hour, and add it to the previous sum; 
Let Pisces <note>The Fish</note> establish for itself as much time 
As it receives from the lot of the one before. 
And when the three hours are completed, let them hand over 
The night and day to the Wool-bearer <note>original: "Lanigero"; Aries the Ram</note> to be made equal in the time of spring. 
The time begins to proceed from the sixth part. 
The parched signs <note>The summer signs</note> triple the divided strengths, 
And the final signs double what they have received; thus the sum of the days 
Yields to the gliding seasons by a different law. 
For Aries leads away as many hours from the nights 
As Pisces had previously taken away under its own name. 
An hour is given to Taurus <note>The Bull</note>, and to pile up the previous losses, 
They add a half-hour to Gemini <note>The Twins</note>; thus the last is restored 
To the first, and the equalized nights are released from their debt. 
Again, they begin from their own lot for the days. 
They respond equally to those stars which shine closest, 
And the middle stars are judged with equalized strengths; 
They carry the principal motions for the seasons that must be varied. 
By this turn, the nights depart toward the stars of winter, 
The days are raised, and the circle of the year is inverted. 
When the solstice occurs under the sign of the slow-moving Cancer <note>The Crab; the Summer Solstice</note>, 
Then the night equals the day of midwinter; the long day 
Returns to the duration of the night, and returns by the same movement as it had grown. 
That path, as it is born, will also be able to lead to the South <note>original: "Austrum"</note>, 
Which at some time is returned to the world, having been sent out from the shallows. 
For you will see what portion of the light is required for the hour, 
And you will recall this number into itself, 
Multiplying it by ten and adding the same amount on top. 
Yet add five to the totals, because under any hour, 
Six signs take up fifteen parts of the world <note>Manilius is describing a mathematical formula to convert the length of a seasonal day into degrees of the celestial equator</note>.

-># THE THIRD BOOK<-

Once this total is fixed, combine it with those parts <note>degrees</note> that remain for Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> through the signs; remember to distribute from this total thirty parts through each of the constellations, beginning with the sign in which Phoebus shines, and from there to the others that follow the Sun in order. The sign in which the final remaining number lands, and the specific degree where it leaves its sum, this shall be the "rising sign" <note>the Ascendant</note>, both in its degree and its character among the stars. Should it contain thirty parts when it completes a single sum, you shall grant thirty to each individual sign until the number is exhausted; and in whatever part of the constellations that number falls, you must believe that it was born together with the human body and saw the world through the stars at that same moment. Thus you must seek for yourself the birth of the world <note>the "nativity" or birth chart</note> among the swift stars, and the Horoscope <term>Horoscope: In ancient astrology, this refers specifically to the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth, not a daily prediction.</term> with its certain rising. When the seat of the first pivot <note>original: "cardine"; the four main angles of an astrological chart</note> stands fixed by this method, it cannot fail to find the heights of the highest heaven. Nor will it be forgotten that the foundations remain at the very bottom <note>the Imum Coeli or bottom of the sky</note>. Let the true risings of the stars stand, and under those true risings, the ten <note>referring to the Lots or Sortes</note> withdraw into their own powers and fates.

->### *On the spans of life which are assigned to the Sun, the Moon, and the degree of the ascendant*<-
->### *for each year of a person's life. Chapter VI*<-

**N**ow the proper times will be restored to the signs according to their kind, which are also divided into their own years, months, their own days, and the hours of the days, through which each sign displays its particular power. The first year shall belong to the sign in which the Sun shines, because in traversing it, the Sun consumes the time of the world <note>the solar year</note>; the next year belongs to the sign immediately following it, and so on. The Moon shall grant the months, because the lunar cycles complete their course monthly. The Horoscope <note>the Ascendant</note> claims the first hours and days for its own protection, and thus hands them over to the following stars. In this way, nature willed that your years, your months, and your days, and even the hours themselves, be numbered through all the signs, so that all time would be divided among the stars. Through these, the alternating constellations vary their movements, so that each might take its turn as the cycle returns. Therefore, there is such great discord in the passage of time: good things are woven beneath evils, tears follow prayers, and Fortune does not maintain a steady course in all things. It flows along so utterly mixed, never remaining in one place, and has lost our trust by varying all things for everyone. Years do not always agree with years, nor months with months; a day leaves itself behind and becomes another, and an hour is produced that is unlike any other hour. These times consist of their own signs, divided through all the numbers of fleeting time. They bring about such months and threaten such causes as the stars whose turns we are under as we revolve; for there are hours which open the heavens to those being born,

After the previous page explained how to calculate the specific degree of the Ascendant (the Horoscope) using the Sun's position and the time of day, this page transitions into the application of that point: how it governs the division of time into years, months, and hours, and the specific "life-spans" assigned to each zodiac sign.</meta>

-> # BOOK THREE <-

The point in the stars which the founders of this art call the Horoscope <term>Horoscope: From the Greek "hōroskopos," meaning "watcher of the hour." In ancient astrology, this meant the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at birth.</term>. From that point, the hour of the day is also described. It governs every kind of calculation through time and stars; it draws from a single point the months, the years, and the days. It begins the hours and hands them off to the stars that follow. It determines everything that is born from a shared origin. Yet, these cycles vary, because some stars complete their circuit more slowly, and others more quickly. Every hour returns to its star, as does the day twice in a month, and a single month once in a year. Once twelve suns <note>original: "solibus"; meaning solar cycles or months</note> have passed, it is difficult for all these factors to coincide at the same moment—for the month and the year to belong to the same sign. A month may be harsher if it falls into a joyful star, yet the sign of the day is gloomy; or if fortune favors the day, but the hour is more difficult. For this reason, it is not right to trust entirely in one thing: not in the sign for the years, nor in the turning years for the months, nor the months for the days, nor the days for all the hours. Because now some things hasten too much, and now they delay; sometimes one thing is missing, sometimes it is present, receding in turns or returning, and time is changed at another time, interrupted by the lot of the varying days.

-> ## Chapter VII: On the years which each sign gives. <-

**A**ND since we are led through the individual periods of life, and must know what kind of time comes at what moment, which star governs which year, and which month, hour, and day, another calculation must now be rendered—one that contains the total sum of a lifetime: how many years each sign is said to grant. This is a calculation you must look to and mark with numbers when you seek the end of a life through the stars.
Aries <note>The Ram</note> will give twice five years <note>10</note> and one third <note>4 months</note> cheated from those added <note>likely referring to a subtraction from a base number</note>; you, Taurus <note>The Bull</note>, surpass this by two <note>12 years and 4 months</note>, but you are surpassed by the same amount by the star of Gemini <note>The Twins; back to 10 years and 4 months</note>. And you, Cancer <note>The Crab</note>, give twice eight <note>16</note> and two thirds <note>8 months</note>. You, Nemea <note>The Nemean Lion, or Leo</note>, shall give twice nine <note>18</note>, and beneath those, Erigone <note>Virgo</note> shall give twice ten <note>20</note> and a third <note>4 months</note>. Nor shall the years of Libra <note>The Scales</note> be more than those of the Virgin. Scorpio will equal the Lion who grants gifts <note>18</note>. The Centaur’s <note>Sagittarius</note> gifts shall be the same as those of Cancer <note>16 years and 8 months</note>. You would give three times five <note>15</note>, Capricorn, if four months were added. Aquarius triples the years <note>3 times 4 = 12</note> and extends life into eight months <note>12 years and 8 months</note>. And Pisces, clinging to Aries in both lot and boundary, will grant ten lustra <note>A "lustrum" is a five-year period; ten lustra equals 50 years</note> along with only eight months.

-> ## Chapter VIII: On the years which the Moon grants to the native. <-

**I**T is not enough to know the certain years of the signs. Lest the logic remain hidden from those seeking the end of a lifetime, the temples <note>The twelve "houses" or divisions of the sky</note> and the parts of heaven also know their own gifts. They grant their own sums with a fixed distinction, once the established order of the stars is well-arranged.

But now I will sing only of the laws of the temples <term>temples: Here referring to the "houses" or "places" (dodecatemoria) of the zodiacal circle, which govern specific areas of life and destiny.</term>.
Soon the whole mixture of yours will come with its powers.
When the material has stood well through the known nature of things,
it will not be disturbed on all sides by misplaced members.
If the Moon is well-positioned under the first pivot <term>pivot: Called a "cardine" in Latin; one of the four crucial points of the sky: the East (Ascendant), West (Descendant), Zenith (Midheaven), and Nadir (Imum Coeli).</term>,
which the world, returning to the lands and being born, held.
From its rising, it shall be led into eighty years,
if two are taken away <note>The calculation results in 78 years.</note>; but when at the highest summit
it stands, this number shall be cheated by three years <note>The calculation results in 77 years.</note>.
The setting was rich in eighty movements

And the first foundations <term>foundations: The "Imum Coeli," the lowest point of the sky directly beneath the earth.</term> are judged through twice thirty years
with twice six months added to the span of life,

this gives sixty, and doubles four.
That which is on the left, and follows the preferred signs,
doubles thirty years, and adds three more.
And that which is above the first sign born in this order
is the third form, and now closest to the highest heaven.
This doubles thrice twenty, and subtracts three years.
And that which comes below, divided by an equal space,
completes its duties for thrice fifty winters <note>original: "ter quinquagenas... brumas"; 150 years. This is a remarkably long span even for ancient astrology.</note>.
And the rising horoscope which overcomes the place, that one
calls back forty times the seasons of the turning sun,
and adds two cycles, and leaves the youth behind.
But that which falls before the hour of the rising pivot,
will give twenty-three years to those being born,
snatching away youth while it is barely tasted in its flower.
That which is attempted above the setting, returns ten
spaces of years, and applies a tenth to three increased <note>The calculation results in 13 years.</note>.
Further below, it will kill the boy, and once twice six are finished,
it will drag the immature bodies to a birthday death.

-> Concerning the tropical signs, and the four seasons of the year. **Chapter IX** <-

### **S**et, however, among the first things to be noted by a mindful memory,
are those signs which rise hidden in opposite parts,
and hold the divided sky with an equal distinction,
which they call tropical <term>tropical: From the Greek "tropikos," meaning "turning." These are the signs of the solstices and equinoxes where the sun "turns" back or the seasons change.</term>, because in those signs the four seasons

Then also bloody wars are handled by fierce Mars.

now flees with a dry earth, and the Nile swells into the fields <note>original: "aucas"; likely a transcription error for "arva" (fields).</note>.

<meta>This page concludes Book Three of Manilius’s Astronomica. Following the previous discussion on calculating the length of life based on the "houses" or "temples" of the sky, the poet now shifts to the four "tropical" or cardinal signs—Cancer, Capricorn, Aries, and Libra. These signs are presented as the pivotal points that govern the seasons and the shifting balance between light and darkness.</meta>

-> # BOOK THREE <-

-> ### THE TROPICAL SIGNS AND THE SEASONS ### <-

Here again is the position of Cancer, where Phoebus <note>A common poetic name for the Sun god, Apollo.</note> makes the summer solstice and turns at the highest point of heaven. From the opposite side, Capricorn compels the frozen midwinter, and through the shortest nights and the greatest spans of light <note>The poet describes the turning points: after the winter solstice, the days begin to lengthen ("producit diem"), and after the summer solstice, they begin to shorten.</note>, it draws out the day and dissolves the shadows. In turn, it now creates losses of light, and now refills the time. 

Then every field is stiff with frost, the sea is closed to ships, and the camps are hidden away. The jagged rocks cannot even endure the core of winter, and nature stands still in one place, resting for a little while.

Next in similar effect, they say that the signs that equate the light with the days bring back the movements. For Aries—restraining Phoebus as he seeks again the stars of Cancer—joins together the seasons in a harmonious division of the world, between the start of his return and the end. Aries turns the cycles of time; he commands the day, which had been conquered by the stars of midwinter, to now overcome, and he orders the nights to succumb, until they reach the summer stars of Cancer. 

Then, for the first time, the sea is smoothed with silent waves, and the earth dares to send forth various flowers. Then the race of cattle and birds rushes through the joyful pastures toward mating and birth; the whole grove speaks with a tuneful voice and grows green in every leaf. Nature is moved to such an extent by the strength of these signs.

Opposite to this, when Libra happens to shine with similar light, it leads the day and night in an equal treaty; except that from that point on, it commands the nights to conquer the days they had previously lost, even until the times of midwinter prevail. Then Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> descends, full, from the heavy elm tree, and the rich new wine foams from the pressed clusters of grapes. They also entrust Ceres <note>The goddess of grain and agriculture; here meaning the grain itself.</note> to the furrows, while the earth lies open, loosened by the warmth of autumn, and draws in the seeds. 

These four signs are powerful in the art <term>the art: Here referring to the "divine art" of astrology.</term>, and they turn the seasons, thus swaying the various outcomes of things and allowing nothing to remain in its original state. 

But the measurement is not equal through the entire figures, nor do all the stars turn at the completion of the signs. A single day under both times <note>The Spring and Autumn equinoxes.</note> matches the night to itself. For Libra and Aries give shape to Autumn and Spring; a single day is the longest in the whole sign of Cancer, to which an equal night is said to be brought in the sign of Capricorn. The other parts now press on in their turns, now yield in time. 

Therefore, one specific point must be observed in these tropical <term>tropical: From the Greek *tropikos*, meaning "turning." These are the signs where the Sun appears to "turn" its course.</term> figures, which moves the world and changes the seasons of things. It moves the decreed fates and turns them to other uses. They turn all things to their opposite and roll them back again. Some people place these powers in the eighth degree <note>The "eighth degree" was a common ancient convention (used by astronomers like Hipparchus) for the placement of the equinoxes and solstices within their respective signs.</note>. There are those who prefer them to be in the tenth; nor was an author lacking who would give these moments and the reins of the days to the very first degree.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Four. In the previous book, Manilius focused on the technical calculations of the "circles" of the sky and the determination of the length of a human life. Now, he pivots from technical instruction to a philosophical defense of Fate—the guiding force behind his entire astrological system—using examples from Roman history to prove that human effort is subordinate to destiny.</meta>

# ->M. MANILIUS’S THE ASTRONOMICON<-
## ->BOOK FOUR<-

### ->*On Fate, by which all things are governed, and what skills the twelve signs*<-
### ->*promise to those born under them. Chapter 1*<-

<insert>Large decorative drop cap 'Q'</insert> **WHY** do we consume our lives in years of such anxiety? 
We are tortured by fear and by a blind desire for things; 
As old men, we lose our time while seeking a lifetime in eternal cares, 
And we are never truly blessed, for there is no end to our prayers. 
We always act as if we are about to live, yet we never truly live. 
Each man is impoverished despite his goods, for he seeks more; 
He does not count what he has, but only longs for what he lacks. 
And though nature requires very little for its own use, 
We build up the material for a great ruin through our prayers. 
We buy luxury with our gains, and through luxury, we buy plunder. 
The ultimate price of a fortune is to squander that very fortune. 
Release your mortal minds, men, and relieve your cares, 
And cease to bewail your life with so many superfluous complaints. 
**Fate rules the world; all things stand fixed by a certain law.** <note>original: "Fata regunt orbem, certa stant omnia lege." This is one of the most famous expressions of Stoic philosophy, suggesting that the universe is governed by a rational, predetermined order.</note> 
Long ages are marked out by fixed courses. 
**As we are born, we die; our end hangs from our beginning.** <note>original: "Nascentes morimur." A classic Stoic paradox emphasizing that the moment of birth also marks the start of the journey toward death.</note> 
From Fate flow both wealth and kingdoms; from it, poverty more often arises, 
Skills are granted, and characters are shaped at birth, 
As are vices and disasters, the losses and the gains of life. 
No one lacks loss, nor can anyone possess what is denied to him, 
Nor can one force <term>Fortune</term><note>The personified goddess of chance and luck, though Manilius argues she is actually an agent of Fate.</note> to weigh his life according to his own prayers. 
We must bear our lot; even the attempt to flee imminent danger is part of our destiny. 
If Fate did not give the laws of life and death, 
Then the fires would have escaped Aeneas <note>The hero of the *Aeneid* who escaped the burning city of Troy.</note>, and Troy—
Not overturned by a single man—would have conquered amidst its own destinies. 
Or would the wolf of Mars have nursed the abandoned brothers <note>Romulus and Remus, the legendary founders of Rome, who were suckled by a she-wolf.</note>, 
And would Rome have been born in such a way, and would masters of cattle 
Have brought the lightning-bolts of power to the Capitoline Hill? 
Could Jupiter <note>The king of the Roman gods.</note> have been shut up and captured 
In his own citadel? Or would Rome be the head of the world? 
With his hand consumed by fire, Mucius <note>Mucius Scaevola, a Roman hero who proved his bravery to an enemy king by holding his right hand in a fire without flinching.</note> would not have returned to the city a victor. 
And Horatius <note>Horatius Cocles, who famously defended the Sublician Bridge alone against an invading army.</note> alone, with his arms ready, would not have closed 
The bridge and the city at once; nor would the Virgin <note>Cloelia, a Roman hostage who escaped her captors by swimming across the Tiber River.</note> have broken her treaties. 
Nor would three brothers have lain dead under the virtue of a single man. 
No battle-line conquered then; Rome was hanging 
On a single man, and she lay there having won the empire of the world. 
Why should I recall Cannae <note>A disastrous battle where the Carthaginians defeated the Romans.</note> and the weapons brought to our very walls, 
And the sluggish Varro, who was "great" only because he managed to survive? 
And after your lands, Lake Trasimene <note>The site of another major Roman defeat by Hannibal.</note>, why recall that 
Fabius <note>Fabius Maximus, known as "The Delayer," whose cautious tactics eventually wore down Hannibal's forces.</note> by waiting caused the conquered citadels of Carthage to take the yoke? 
Or that we saw Hannibal himself fall in our chains, 
And that his exile was followed by a secretive death in a toga? 
Add also the Italian strengths, and that Rome was 
Fighting against its own members; add also the civil wars. 
And see the Cimbrian defeated by Marius, and Marius himself in prison, 
He who was a consul so many times, and an exile, and from an exile, a consul again.

He lists numerous Roman heroes and historical turning points to illustrate that destiny, not mere chance or human effort, governs the world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the poet’s philosophical argument for the absolute power of Fate. Following the opening of Book Four, where Manilius argues that our lives are predetermined from birth, he now provides a series of historical examples—ranging from the rise and fall of Roman generals to the tragedies of legendary kings—to prove that human merit, wealth, and status are all secondary to the dictates of destiny.</meta>

# -> B O O K  IV <-

And he lay huddled among the ruins of Libya. <note>original: "Libycis... ruinis." This refers to Gaius Marius, a famous Roman general who, after being declared an enemy of the state, was famously depicted sitting as a fugitive among the ruins of Carthage before rising to power again.</note>
And yet, from the foundations of Carthage, he began to seize the world;
Unless the Fates had granted this, Fortune would never have brought it about.
Who would have believed, Magnus, that you would perish on the shores of the Nile, <note>original: "Magne." This refers to Pompey the Great. After a legendary career of military victories, he was murdered in Egypt upon escaping the Battle of Pharsalus.</note>
After the defeat of Mithridates’ wealth and the reclaiming of the sea,
And the three triumphs earned from a world you had traversed—
Even when you could still recognize another "Great" man— <note>original: "alium cognoscere Magnum." A reference to Julius Caesar, Pompey’s rival and equal in power.</note>
Who would believe that a shipwrecked man’s fire would bury your body,
And that the collected fragments of a boat would serve as your funeral pyre?
Who can change so much without the divine power of the Fates?
Even he, born of heaven and received by heaven, <note>original: "coelo genitus, coeloq; receptus." Referring to Julius Caesar, who claimed descent from Venus and was deified after death.</note>
When as a victor of civil arms he ruled the <term>laws of the toga</term>, <note>A phrase meaning he governed as a civilian statesman rather than a military dictator.</note>
He could not avoid the wounds predicted so many times;
While the entire Senate looked on, he held the evidence in his right hand <note>Caesar was famously handed a note warning him of the conspiracy on the way to the Senate, which he did not read.</note>
And wiped out his own name with his own blood,
So that the Fates might be victorious.
Why should I count overturned cities and the ruins of kings?
Croesus upon his pyre, and Priam a headless trunk on the shore,
For whom even Troy was not a pyre; what was greater than Xerxes,
Who suffered a shipwreck on the very Sea he once commanded? <note>Xerxes, the Persian King, famously "punished" the sea with chains, but was eventually defeated at the naval battle of Salamis.</note>
What of the kings captured in the ranks and put on display for the Romans,
And the sacred fires snatched from the fires,
When the flame yielded to the man who carried the temples? <note>Referring to Lucius Caecilius Metellus, who rescued the Palladium (the sacred image of Athena) from the burning Temple of Vesta in 241 BCE.</note>
How many sudden deaths come to the bodies of the strong?
And yet, others flee death and wander through the flames.
Certain men have even returned, carried out from their very graves.
To some, a double life was granted; to others, scarcely one.
Behold, a light illness kills, while a more serious one relents.
Medical arts succumb; the use of reason is defeated.
Anxious care causes harm, while doing nothing helps; delay often
Provides the causes of evils; foods injure, and poisons spare.
Sons degenerate from their fathers, and yet others surpass their parents;
They retain their own natural character, though they pass through the father’s line.
From Fate, Fortune comes; one man rages with love
And can swim across the sea or overturn a Troy; <note>References to Leander swimming the Hellespont and Paris causing the Trojan War.</note>
Another’s lot is suited for the writing of laws.
Behold, sons kill their father, and parents kill their sons.
Armed brothers come together to inflict mutual wounds.
This war is not our own; they are compelled to stir such things,
To be carried toward their own punishments and the tearing of their own limbs.
Not every age has produced the Decii, nor every age the Camilli, <note>The Decii were a Roman family famous for sacrificing their lives in battle for the state; the Camilli were exemplars of early Roman virtue.</note>
Or Cato, unconquered even as death was conquered. <note>Cato the Younger committed suicide to escape Caesar’s tyranny, an act Stoics viewed as a victory over death itself.</note>
The material for the deed is abundant, but it fights back against the law.
Poverty does not receive shorter years,
Nor are the Fates for sale to those with immense wealth.
But Fortune snatches the proud away to their funeral.
She dictates the pyre for the highest and establishes the tomb.
How great is this kingdom, which commands kings themselves?
Indeed, even virtue is often unhappy, while wickedness is lucky.
There is a reward for bad advice, while prudence fails.
Fortune does not approve of causes, nor does she follow those who deserve it,

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse of Book IV of Manilius’s Astronomica. While the previous page used historical examples of Roman figures like Marius and Pompey to demonstrate the inescapable power of Fate, this page addresses the ethical implications of determinism before transitioning into the technical descriptions of the zodiac signs and their influence on human character and professions.</meta>

But Fate wanders through all things, driven without distinction.
Truly, there is something else that both compels and rules us,
Something greater, which subjects mortals to its own laws,
And assigns their years to those being born from itself,
And the shifts of Fortune. It often mingles the bodies of beasts
With the limbs of men; <note>original: "permiscet saepe ferarum corpora cum membris hominum." Manilius suggests that biological "monsters" or birth defects are not accidents or the result of human sin, but the deliberate work of the stars.</note> that birth will not be female—
For what do we have in common with wild beasts?
Or what adulterer has sinned to cause the harm of such a portent?
The stars renew forms, and the heavens transform our faces.
Finally, if there is no Fate, why is the order of things passed down?
And why are all things that are to come sung at certain times?
Yet this reasoning does not go so far as to defend a crime,
Nor to rob Virtue of its gifts and rewards.
For no one hates deadly herbs any less
Because they do not grow by their own will, but from a fixed seed.
Nor is gratitude granted any more lightly to sweet foods
Because nature gave the crops, and not any human will.
So should the glory for the human mind be all the greater,
Because it comes while the Heavens rejoice; and again, the guilty
We shall hate more, created for blame and for punishment.
It matters not from where the crime falls; it must be confessed a crime.
This too is fated: to weigh the nature of Fate itself. <note>original: "Hoc quoque fatale est, sic ipsum expendere fatum." A famous stoic paradox: the very act of studying or analyzing destiny is itself a part of one's destiny.</note>
Since I have taught this, it now remains, in a certain order,
To build the celestial steps, which are able to lead the wise
Prophet to the stars by a winding path.
Now I shall return to you, in order, the characters of the signs, their highest color,
And the various arts of their pursuit.
Aries, rich with wool and fertile in its fleece,
Now stripped and then clothed again, will always have hope. <note>original: "Aries." The Ram is the first sign of the zodiac. Its association with wool leads Manilius to link it to the textile industry.</note>
And between sudden shipwreck and blessed wealth,
He will fall even as he grows, and be carried toward loss by his own prayers.
He will give fruits to the common people, and through a thousand arts,
His patient fleeces will provide diverse profits:
Now to gather the raw wool, now to loosen it again,
Now to thin it with a light thread, now to lead the looms,
Now to groan while selling various garments for profit—
Without which no nations could have ever survived.
Even without luxury, this work is so great that <term>Pallas</term> <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena, patron of weaving and wisdom.</note>
Claimed it for her own hands, and thought it worthy of herself,
And she considers her victory over Arachne to be a great triumph. <note>original: "Arachnaea... triumphum." Refers to the myth of Arachne, a mortal weaver who challenged Minerva/Pallas to a contest and was transformed into a spider.</note>
The Ram will assign these pursuits and similar arts to those being born,
And will fix a doubting heart within a trembling breast,
Always desiring to sell itself through its own praise.
Taurus has granted the countryside to simple farmers. <note>original: "Taurus." The Bull is the second sign, naturally associated with agriculture and plowing.</note>
Labor will come to the peaceful, and a patience for praise,
But he grants the offspring of the earth; he submits his neck
To the plows, and he himself demands the yoke for his shoulders.
He carries the orb of <term>Phoebus</term> <note>A title for the Sun god (Apollo). In Manilius’s time, the sun was perceived as passing through the constellation of the Bull.</note> upon his horns,
He declares military service to the lands and the sluggish fields;
He himself, the leader of labor, recalls them to ancient cultivation,
