<meta>This page continues the catalog of the zodiac signs' influences on human character and destiny from Book IV. While the previous page established the absolute power of Fate over human life and moral responsibility, this section provides the specific "horoscopic" details of how different constellations—Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, and Virgo—shape the professions and temperaments of those born under them.</meta>

-> # B O O K  F O U R <-

He <note>Referring to the native born under the sign of Taurus, the Bull, continued from the previous page.</note> does not lie idle in the furrows or tire his breast in the dust; he bore the <term>Serrani</term> and the <term>Curiuses</term> <note>historical: "Seranos Curiosq;". These were famous Roman archetypes of the "farmer-statesman," men like Atilius Regulus Serranus and Manius Curius Dentatus who lived simply on small farms but led Rome to great military victories.</note> who were easily led through the fields, and the **Dictator** <note>A reference to Cincinnatus, who famously returned to his plow after serving his term as emergency ruler of Rome.</note> came equally from his own plow. Love of praise, quiet minds, and bodies powerful with slow mass characterize them, and the boy Cupid dwells beneath their brow.

A gentler pursuit comes from the **Twins** <note>The constellation Gemini.</note>, and a milder age expressed through various songs and mouths modulated by voices, and slender pipes, and words woven into strings, and mighty sound; the labor itself is even a pleasure. They want arms far away, and trumpets, and gloomy old age. They spend their leisure and eternal youth in death. They find ways even to the stars, and through numbers and rhythms they exhaust the globe, even after the stars themselves leave them. Nature is less than genius, and serves it in all things. Into so many inventions are the fertile Twins carried.

**Cancer**, shining at the burning turning point <note>original: "ardenti fulgens in cardine." This refers to the summer solstice, the highest point of the sun's path and the "hinge" of the year.</note> which **Phoebus** <note>The Sun god, Apollo.</note>, recalled in his highest chariot, encircles, holds the joint of the world and reflects the light. He assigns a mind that is tenacious and poured into no useless habits, but rather various gains and the art of profit: to bring fortune through cities with foreign merchandise, and to speculate with a heavy, aged mind. To trust in wealth, and to be able to sell the goods of one world to another, and to join commerce through so many unknown lands, and to seek out new plunder under another sun, and to build sudden wealth from the price of things. He sails, and by hoping for barren years through lots, he sells even the seasons with sweet interest at a fair rate; a skillful genius, and fierce for his own advantage.

Who could doubt what the nature of the vast **Lion** <note>The constellation Leo.</note> might be, or what arts he dictates to those being born under his sign? He always prepares new battles, new wars of wild beasts and the spoiling of cattle, and lives on plunder. This is his habit, this his pursuit: to adorn proud gates with skins, and to fix captured prey to his house, and to provide fear for the woods, and to live by theft. There are those whose minds, similar to the lion, even walls do not restrain, but they prowl through the middle of the city for the limbs of cattle, and hang torn limbs at the front of shops, and prepare for luxury, and profit from slaughter and death. His genius is equal to sudden rages and easy retreats even as a boy, a simple sentiment in his breast.

But for those for whom **Erigone** <note>Another name for the constellation Virgo, often identified with the daughter of Icarius.</note> led their life at birth with a masterly mouth, the **Virgo**, restrained, leads their character toward study, and instructs their hearts in learned arts; she will grant them to seek out not so much the gains of wealth, but the causes and lives of things. She will make such a person the glory of the tongue and the kingdom of speaking, and provide the eyes of the mind, through which he may be able to discern all things, however much they are hidden by the secret causes of nature.

<meta>This page continues Manilius's astrological survey of the zodiac signs in Book 4. Having previously discussed the signs from Aries to Virgo, the text now transitions from the influence of Virgo into the sign of Libra (the Scales), then moves through Scorpio (the Scorpion), Sagittarius (the Centaur), and begins the section on Capricorn (the Sea-Goat).</meta>

-> # BOOK FOUR <-

This person will also be a lucky writer, for whom a single letter stands for a whole word. He will surpass the tongue with his shorthand signs <note>original: "notis". This refers to "Tironian notes," an ancient Roman system of stenography.</note> and outpace the speed of the speaker; he will capture long sentences through new abbreviations. In this sign, a virtuous modesty <note>original: "pudor"</note> hinders the tender years of youth and restrains great gifts of nature by holding them back. 

From here <note>The transition to Libra, the Scales.</note> will come a fertile birth—which is a wonder in the Virgin—when the **Claws** <note>original: "Chelæ". In ancient astronomy, the stars of Libra were often called the "Claws" of the Scorpion before being recognized as a separate sign of the Scales.</note> balance the night with the hours of light <note>The Autumn Equinox.</note>. Later, they will add the gifts of mature **Bacchus** <note>The god of wine; this refers to the grape harvest.</note> in their season, and will grant the use of measures and the weights of things. This sign also produces a birth that competes with the powers of **Palamedes** <note>mythological: A Greek hero during the Trojan War credited with inventing the alphabet, numbers, weights, and measures.</note>, who first assigned numbers to things, gave names to the highest honors, and established certain limits and proper shapes.

From this sign, too, one will know the tablets of the laws and established rights, and how words hang upon slight nuances. He will know what is permitted and what punishment follows what is forbidden. He will be a perpetual **Praetor** <note>A Roman judicial officer.</note> for the people even on his private doorstep. No other star would more likely have produced **Servius** <note>historical: "Seruius". Likely Servius Sulpicius Rufus, a famous Roman jurist and friend of Cicero known for his expertise in law.</note>, who established laws rather than merely unraveling legal rights. Finally, whatever has been placed in an ambiguous state and lacks a guide, the examinations of the **Scales** <note>Libra</note> will resolve.

**Scorpio**, with its violent sting in its armed tail, follows. When it leads the chariot of **Phoebus** <note>The Sun</note> through its own stars, it searches the earth and mixes seeds into the furrows. It creates minds burning for war and martial camps, and citizens who delight in much blood. They are driven not so much by plunder as by slaughter; and even when peace itself is conducted under arms, they take to the glades and wander through the forests. Now they wage the wars of men, now the violent wars of wild beasts. Now they sell their heads to death <note>A reference to gladiators who fought for hire or to satisfy debts.</note> and become the smoke of the arena. Each man prepares an enemy for himself even when wars are at rest. There are those whom even the images of battle and sport in arms please—so great is their love of fighting that they learn war during their leisure time. Indeed, whatever study is pursued with similar skill comes from this sign.

But to those for whom the lot of birth is granted in the double-shaped body of the **Centaur** <note>Sagittarius</note>, it is their pleasure to join chariots together, to lead fiery horses with gentle reins, and to follow herds grazing across all the fields. It is their task to tame every kind of quadruped after their masters have given up, to win over tigers by entreaty, and to take away the rage from the lion. They can speak with the elephant, and through speaking, adapt such a massive weight to human skills for various spectacles. Indeed, the body of a man is mixed with a beast among the stars, and so it remains; therefore, the sign reigns over those animals. Because the sign carries its arrows aimed from a curved bow, it grants strength to the limbs, sharpness to the heart, swift movements, and a breast that cannot be tired.

You, **Capricorn**, cherish hurried fires in your innermost chambers. From here you draw skill and passion: for whatever fire puts to use, and whatever requires new flames for its tasks, must be reckoned under your influence—the searching out of hidden metals...

Having previously discussed signs like Libra and Capricorn, the poet now moves into the final signs of the zodiac: Aquarius and Pisces. # -> BOOK IV <-

To dig up buried wealth and burn the veins of the earth, to double materials with a steady hand and certain skill—whatever is crafted from silver or from gold, and what iron or bronze the hot furnaces melt. The hearths will consume Ceres <note>original: "Cererem". The goddess of grain, here used metonymically for the bread or fuel consumed by the workers at their fires.</note>, and your gifts will rise. You also add an interest in clothing and fleeting merchandise, preserving a winter lot through the stars in the cold, where you draw back the nights that have been led to their highest peaks <note>The Winter Solstice, the longest night of the year.</note> and make the year born anew with recalled light.

Here also is the mobility of things, and the mind often shifts and swims; old age is found under the better-joined Fish <note>Pisces</note>. The earlier part of the sign also serves Venus with a mixed crime <note>original: "mixto cum crimine". This may refer to the mythological origins of the sign or complex romantic inclinations.</note>. 

He too, who pours forth a spring from a curved urn—youthful **Aquarius**—bestows kindred arts: to see what lies under the earth, to bring waters into the land, and to sprinkle the stars themselves with diverted waves. He grants the skill to play upon the sea with new shores for the sake of luxury, to build various lakes and artificial rivers, and to hang streams within traveling houses <note>This refers to the sophisticated Roman engineering of aqueducts and indoor plumbing/fountains in villas.</note>. A thousand arts dwell under this sign, which the wave tempers. Indeed, he will even move the face of the world and the starry seats, and turn the heaven into a new orb. These works come through the waters and follow through the gates. A gentle race, and sweet offspring flow toward the stars. Their hearts are not filthy; they are easily led to losses; wealth is neither lacking nor excessive—just as the urn flows <note>Meaning their finances are fluid; money goes out as easily as it comes in.</note>.

Those whom the final stars, the **Twin Fish** <note>Pisces</note>, produce, will have a passion for the sea and trust their lives to the deep. They will prepare ships, or arms for ships, and whatever the sea requires for its own uses. Countless arts come forth; names barely suffice for the things, so many are the parts even of a small keel. Add the study of piloting, which reaches to the stars and joins the sea to heaven. The pilot must know the globe, the rivers, the ports of the world, and the winds; it is necessary now to turn the helm this way and that in the darkness, to restrain the vessel and cut through the waves straight ahead, or to drive with oars and bend the flexible blades, to overturn the calm sea with drawn nets, and to bring "captured peoples" <note>A poetic way of referring to schools of fish caught in nets.</note> to their own shores; or to hide hooks with food, or fraud within a cage <note>A fish trap or lobster pot.</note>. They also assign naval battles and prudent wars, and the waves of the sea stained with blood.

This race is fertile in sailors, and has a love of pleasure, swift movements, and all things changed throughout the ages. These characters and these arts the twelve signs grant to those being born, each sign powerful in its own material. But nothing is wholly powerful in itself; all things associate their strengths with certain signs under equal parts, and join the commerce of the world as if by hospitality.

<meta>This page continues Manilius’s technical exposition of astrological influence. Following the description of the signs' characteristics, the poet now introduces the concept of "decanates"—the division of each thirty-degree zodiac sign into three ten-degree segments, each ruled by a different sign of the same triplicity or through specific complex relationships.</meta>

-> # BOOK FOUR <-

They grant their own portions to the stars that retain them. Foreign nations have called this tenth part <term>Decania</term> <note>These are "decans," 10-degree subdivisions of a zodiac sign. Each 30-degree sign contains three decans.</note>; the name is derived from the number <note>The Greek *deka*, meaning ten.</note>, because the stars are established in thirty individual parts under their own lot. And they assign ten degrees each to the stars that meet within them. In turn, the constellations are inhabited by three signs; thus Nature remains enclosed in deep darkness.

Truth in heaven is found through many windings of things. Experience is not brief, nor does the heaven love shortcuts. Indeed, one thing is set opposite to another, and the appearance deceives. It lies about its own powers and hides its names. You must dispel this deep darkness not with your eyes, but with your mind; the god <note>Here referring to the divine order of Nature or the Universe.</note> must be recognized from within, not by the outward face.

Now I shall explain which signs are joined, to whom, and in what order, lest other powers lie hidden through foreign stars. One lot yields to Taurus, and a third part to Gemini. Thus the sign is drawn out, divided among dense influences. It commands as many powers as it has received masters.

In **Taurus**, the calculation is different, and it is not assessed under its own portion; Nature, through the stars, grants the first part to **Cancer**, the middle to **Leo**, and the last to **Erigone** <note>original: "Erigonae". A poetic name for the constellation Virgo.</note>. Yet the sign remains, mixing its own powers through each individual part.

**Libra** takes up the first ten parts of **Gemini**. **Scorpio** takes the third part, joined by the **Centaur** <note>original: "Centauri". Referring here to Sagittarius.</note>. No sign is distinguished by its number alone, but by the order in which it is yielded.

**Cancer** directs its gaze toward the opposite sign, **Capricorn**. It deems ten parts worthy first at that point in time under which it is itself assessed—the point which makes the light equal to the winter shadows <note>This refers to the Tropic of Cancer and the relationship between the solstices.</note>—and it carries a kindred law at a different cardinal point. **Aquarius** pours forth the fires of the second part, and **Pisces** follows him at the final star of Cancer.

But **Leo** remembers the law of the shared <term>Trigon</term> <note>original: "trigoni". A "trine" or triangle, an aspect where signs are 120 degrees apart, belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water).</note>; it receives the **Wool-bearer** <note>original: "Lanigerum". A poetic title for Aries, the Ram.</note> as its leader, and **Taurus** is carried as a third part, joined to it in a <term>Square</term> <note>original: "quadrato". An aspect where signs are 90 degrees apart.</note> under Gemini.

**Erigone** <note>Virgo</note> grants special honor to **Cancer**. When she gives the first part, the neighbor is left behind. To you, **Nemean** <note>original: "Nemeæe". Referring to the Nemean Lion, the constellation Leo.</note>, one part of her belongs, which is granted to be held by a disdained right.

But **Libra** rejoices in the example, and follows the **Wool-bearer** <note>Aries</note> who rules the nights and days equally at a different time of year; she balances the yoke of the scales. Here, the bright sign arranges the autumnal hours. To no one does she grant the first part, but hands the neighboring part to the next sign; the third part belongs to the **Centaur** <note>Sagittarius</note>.

**Scorpio** placed **Capricorn** in the first part as the master of the second; the one whose name is taken from the waves <note>Aquarius, the Water-bearer.</note> she wished to be in the middle, and the final parts to be under **Pisces**.

The **Wool-bearer** <note>original: "Lanigero", referring to **Aries** the Ram.</note> hands over the first parts under the law of the **trigon** <term>Trigon: A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, or Water). And the middle parts to **Taurus**, and the final parts to **Gemini**.
Nor does **Capricorn** remain ungrateful with a shameful charge,
But returns the gift to **Cancer**, and having been received, is received in turn.
And it grants the beginning of its own; they say the realms
joined to **Leo** and the final parts belong to the **Virgin** <note>The constellation **Virgo**.</note>.
He who rejoices in eternal springs and the flowing **Urn** <note>The constellation **Aquarius**, the Water-bearer.</note>,
permits the first laws of his own to be ruled by **Libra**.

The **Centaur** <note>The constellation **Sagittarius**.</note> retains the final parts through the youthful star.

And you, **Taurus**, are received through the ten middle parts,
What remains they take for themselves, and are carried in the final
circle; thus the last part of the lot also yields.
This method reveals the strengths of the hidden world.
In more modes and repeated names, the heaven
divides, and better and more often associates the circle.
Lest your heart be deceived under the known titles,
The stars conceal themselves; they do not show themselves to mortals.
The edge of the sagacious mind must be sent deeper,
And it must be sought in another; one must follow with joined
strengths, and in whatever part of a sign someone is created <note>Born.</note>,
he possesses its character, and is born under that star.
Such a nature of the lot will be carried through the tens <note>The 10-degree decanates.</note>.
The varied offspring under the same sign will be witness to this.
And because in so many thousands of living things, under one
sign that they come, there are as many characters as there are bodies.
And they reflect a foreign nature through other stars.
The births of men and beasts flow together in confusion.
Clearly they are joined, established in many parts,
And they carry different laws under their own name.
Nor will **Aries** love only wool, nor **Taurus** the plows,
Nor **Gemini** the Muses, nor **Cancer** merchandise,
Nor **Leo** as a hunter, nor will **Virgo** come as a teacher,
Or **Libra** powerful in measures, or **Scorpio** in arms,
And the **Centaur** for wild beasts, **Capricorn** for fire, and for his own
waves the **Youth** <note>The constellation **Aquarius**.</note> himself, and the twin **Pisces** through the seas.
The stars are mixed, but associated into many powers.
"A great and delicate labor," you say, "you bid me to endure,
When one might see the light with an easy method."
What you seek is a god <note>The divine order of the cosmos.</note>, as you attempt to climb the heavens,
And being born under a fatal law, to know the fates,
And to transcend your own heart and possess the universe.
The labor is the price, nor are such great things free.
Do not wonder at the turns of the path or the chains of things.
It is enough to have been able to be admitted; let the rest be ours.
But unless the gold is dug from the mountains, it will escape you,
And again you submerge your mind in great darkness.
And the earth piled above will block its own riches.

<meta>While the previous page concluded a technical discussion of the decanates (the ten-degree subdivisions of the zodiac), this page marks the beginning of Book Four of the *Astronomica*. The author, Manilius, transitions from general celestial mechanics to a more philosophical reflection on the difficulty of his task before diving into the "harmful" degrees of specific signs.</meta>

-># BOOK FOUR<-

To find twin pearls, the whole world must be crossed. Nor will it feel regrettable to have braved the sea for the sake of precious stones. Anxious farmers expend their yearly prayers, and how great a price the deceptive fields will cost. We seek the profit of a ship and pursue death in search of plunder; one should be ashamed to desire fleeting goods so much. This also belongs to luxury; the belly stays awake amidst ruin, and heirs often sigh for their ancestors to perish. What shall we give to heaven? How great is that which comes to us entirely? Man must be expended so that the god within him can be realized. <note>A famous Stoic sentiment: Manilius suggests that by studying the heavens, the human mind—which is a spark of the divine—returns to its source.</note>

By this law, you must note the characters of those being born. It is not enough to learn the signs ruling within signs through groups of ten <note>A reference to the decanates discussed in the previous book.</note>, and what is innate to each. But remember to look at the specific degrees themselves. Either those stiff with ice, or those parched by fire, and yet sterile from both; those with abundant moisture, and those where the sap is already failing. For all stars arise with mixed forces and a varied texture. Nothing is uniform: look at the expanses of the land, and of the sea, and the rivers fleeing between known banks. Fault is frequent everywhere, and harm is joined to praise. 

Thus a sterile year intervenes upon fertile lands, and it breaks sudden offspring with a small distinction; and what was just now a harbor of the sea has now become a **Charybdis** <term>Charybdis: A mythical whirlpool in the Straits of Messina, used here to represent a sudden, dangerous change from safety to peril.</term>. The grace of the praised sea falls after a little while. And now the river glides through rocks, now through plains, either making its way, or seeking it, coming or returning. So also the parts of heaven vary among the stars. As one sign differs from another, so a sign differs from itself. In a moment, it denies healthy powers to both. And whatever is done through these degrees is created without fruit, or it falls, or it feels its blessings mixed with many complaints. 

These degrees must be marked by me in their own song. But who could report so many numbers so often under a law, repeat so many parts, learn so many sums? For various reasons, the appearance of my speech changes: I cut short words thus; it grieves me, but grace will be lacking. And labor yields to vanity when the ear despises it. But for me, as I bring the laws of fate through song, I must speak of the sacred movements of heaven as commanded. Nor is the figure given to be invented, but only to be shown. To have shown the god is too much; he gave weight to himself, nor is it right to suspend the world upon words. For the reality is greater, nor is the grace of our mouth small, if indeed it can sing these things with precision.

Receive now which degrees are to be condemned throughout the stars: 
Of the **Wool-bearer** <note>original: "Lanigeri", referring to the constellation **Aries**.</note>, the fourth part harms, nor is the sixth healthy. The seventh part is for him, and the tenth, and the twelfth. Also those which double two sums, both seven and nine <note>Meaning the 14th and 18th degrees.</note>. And one part added to twenty numbers <note>The 21st degree.</note> may be praised.

These parts lead a sterile air, either by frost or by fire, or by dryness, or by an excess of moisture. If swift Mars <note>original: "Mauors"</note> hurls his fires into that air, Saturn will take up the ice, and Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> the heat.

## *On the influence of the twelve signs.* Chapter 11

### **N**or should your care abandon you once the parts of the signs have been perceived; some things change according to time, and at their rising they receive their own particular powers, and of their own accord they let them go. For when Aries <note>The Ram</note> lifts itself from the highest waves, and proceeds neck-first with its curved horns, it will produce hearts not content with their own lot. It will give a spirit for plunder and will dissolve shame. It only delights in hearing the call to action, just as the Ram itself is carried upon its horns. It rushes forward, and though it moves, it remains the same in no fixed place. Soft leisure delights it through peaceful cares. But it always pleases it to traverse an unknown world, to search the new Sea, and to be a guest of the entire world; the Fleece-bearer <note>Aries</note> himself is your witness, who, cleaving the glassy sea with his golden fleece, carried Phryxus—bereft of his sister by the fates—back to the banks of the Phasis and the shores of Colchis <note>A reference to the myth of the Golden Fleece, where Phryxus escaped on a ram but his sister Helle fell into the sea</note>.

But those whom the first stars of the rising Taurus <note>The Bull</note> create, let them lie down effeminate; nor must the cause be sought far off, if only it is permitted to seek nature through causes. The Bull comes into the sky backward <note>In celestial mechanics, Taurus appears to rise "tail-first"</note>, and is rich in the girls of the Pleiades <note>A star cluster within Taurus</note>, bringing back that small, clustered constellation. Wealth will also come to them in turn, and the Bull adorns the fields turned by the plow with their own dowry.

But when the Twins <note>Gemini</note> are brought forth in an equal part as they join their bonds, they will give a love of study and lead the way to learned arts. Their nature is not gloomy, but creates hearts tinged with sweet charm; it equips them with a good voice and the sounding lyre <note>original: "cithara"</note>, and joins these gifts to a deep heart.

But when the black Cancer <note>The Crab</note> is carried with an obscure cloud—which, like the fires of Phoebus being extinguished, fails in its light and darkens the sign with much gloom—vision will fail the limbs of those born then, and the fates will give a double death to those created; but each both lives and carries out the dead <note>This likely refers to visual impairment or a "living death" through blindness</note>, if anyone greedily reaches out across the highest waves.

Should the Lion <note>Leo</note> show its face and climb the world with gaping jaws, that person will be a defendant to his father and his children; he will not bequeath the wealth he has gathered, but sinks it into his own estate. So great is the hunger, and such a dire desire seizes his mind, that he may consume himself and never be satisfied; he might even recall his own funeral for a feast, and spend the very price of his tomb.

Erigone <note>Virgo</note> rising, she who ruled the former ages with Justice and then fled the same as they fell into ruin, bestows high summits of power through supreme command; she will give a ruler of laws and of sacred right, a holy person cultivating modesty in the temples of the gods.

But when the autumnal Claws <note>original: "Chelæ"; the "Claws" of the Scorpion were the ancient name for the constellation Libra</note> begin to rise, he who is born under the equal weight of the Scales <note>original: "Libra"</note> will be a blessed judge of life and death. He will impose a yoke upon the lands and demand laws. Cities and kingdoms will tremble before him, and they shall be ruled by the nod of one man; after his time on earth, his laws will remain even in the heavens.
[[margin: *]] When Scorpio <note>The Scorpion</note> lifts the lights of the very end of its tail, if anyone is born while the stars are then favorable, he will expand the lands with cities; girded in his robe, he will mark out the walls with a curved plow pulled by joined oxen. Or, he will level established cities and return towns to the fields, bringing ripe stalks of grain where houses once stood. So great will be his virtue, and his power alongside that virtue.
Likewise, when the Archer <note>original: "Arcitenens," literally "the bow-holder"</note> rises with the first part of its garment, he will grant hearts famous in war, and will lead the victor, conspicuous for great triumphs, to the citadels of his fatherland. He will now establish high walls, and now overturn those already built. But fortune, being too indulgent in favorable circumstances, grows envious of his face and acts most harshly against his front. Such a victor—dreadful in the wars at Trebia, Cannae, and the Lake <note>These are the sites of Hannibal’s great victories over the Romans: the Trebia River, Cannae, and Lake Trasimene. Manilius suggests Hannibal’s horoscope shared these traits</note>—was weighing his fate in the ranks before his flight.
Last, Capricorn, at the highest point of its tail, dictates military service upon the sea and the tending of ships, hard labors and the risk of life in the waves <note>The original text "inettis" is likely a misprint for "in undis" (in the waves) or "in extis" (in the entrails/omens)</note>.
But if you wish for someone holy, chaste, and honest, such a man will be born to you when the first part of Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer</note> emerges.
Lest the mind should proceed to the first parts of Pisces <note>The Fish</note>, a hateful talkativeness is given, and the poison of the tongue: malicious words always whispering into new ears, carrying the crimes of the people through the people with a double-tongued mouth. No faith will be in those born then, but the highest lust. It is said that Venus <note>original: "Cytherea"</note> marked herself into the Fish when, submerged, she fled through the Babylonian waters from the snake-footed Typhon <note>A monster of Greek myth</note> who bore winged claws. She implanted her own fires into the scaly Fish. Nor was the birth under the Fish for the Twins <note>Gemini</note> alone; there was a sweet brother, or a sister, or the mother of the two.

<meta>This page continues Manilius’s astronomical and geographical survey in Book 4. Winds of a similar nature breathe forth, though their names are changed. The earth itself reveals this, surveyed by the crown of the Sea, which encircles the central world in its liquid embrace. The land receives the deep into its bays; admitted from the dark evening <note>The West/Atlantic</note> on the right, the sea washes the Numidians and burning Libya, and the citadels of once-great Carthage, drawing back the winding shores into the shallow Syrtis <note>A notoriously dangerous, shallow gulf off the coast of Libya</note>. Then, with its currents directed onward, it emerges at the Nile. On the left of the strait, the Spanish tribes yield to the water, and you, Gaul, clinging to the neighboring lands, and the cities of Italy as the sea curves into the right-hand waves, all the way to your dogs, Scylla, and the greedy Charybdis <note>The mythical monsters of the Strait of Messina</note>.

And as soon as the sea has poured itself out from that gate <note>The Straits of Gibraltar</note>, it swims in the Ionian Sea and wanders into the open waves. First, pouring out to the left, it circles all of Italy, accompanied by the name of the Adriatic Sea; it drinks the flows of the Eridanus <note>The Po River</note>, and cuts through the Illyrian waters with its surface. It washes Epirus and famous Corinth, and flies around the wide coasts of the Peloponnese. Again it flows back to the left, and in a vast retreat, it passes the borders of Thessaly and the fields of Achaia. Here is the youth’s strait and the drowned girl’s sea <note>The Hellespont, named after Helle who fell into it; the youth is Leander, who swam across it to see Hero</note>. It is said that the mouth of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note> is joined to the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> against its will, and to the waters of Maeotis <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, which remains joined at the back and supplies the sea.

From there, when the sailor is called back by the Hellespontic waves and comes out again into the narrow parts, he cuts the Icarian and Aegean seas. On the left, he admires the shining peoples of Asia <note>Asia Minor/Anatolia</note>, and as many trophies as there are places, and innumerable nations: the bow threatening the waves, the peoples of Cilicia, and scorched Syria, and the lands gleaming with the water in a huge bay. This continues until the shores return to Egypt, curving through the waves and striving toward the banks of the Nile. This line surrounds the central sea within the lands and binds the expanse of waves with these sands.

A thousand lands lie scattered through the middle of the seas. Sardinia is marked by the shape of a footprint <note>Ancient geographers often compared the shape of Sardinia to a human footprint</note> in the Libyan sea. Sicily <note>original: "Trinacria"</note>, severed from Italy, has pulled away just so far. Opposite Greece, the Euboean mountains gaze out. And Crete, the mother who claimed the Thunderer <note>Jupiter/Zeus, who was said to be born in Crete</note> as her citizen, lies there. Cyprus is beaten by the waves, entirely Egyptian in its currents. There are so many smaller lands rising nonetheless from the floor of the deep: the shores and the uniform Cyclades, Delos, and Rhodes, Aulis, and Tenedos, and Corsica neighboring the lands. There are the shores of Sardinia, and first as one enters the world’s Ocean <note>Coming from the Atlantic</note>, victorious Ibiza <note>original: "Ebusum"</note> and the Balearic realms. Countless rocks and mountains rise through the deep. Nor has the sea, by tearing away the straits, opened the world for itself from only one side; for many shores...

<meta>This page continues Manilius’s geographical survey in Book 4 of the *Astronomica*. The sea pushed in from the ocean instead, but was barred by high mountains from conquering the entire earth with its waters. For between the North wind and the sea shining in summer, the waves reach through in a long, narrow passage and finally spread out into wide fields. It creates the Caspian waters, which resemble a small sea. In another direction, beneath the midday sun, the ocean brought two "wars" <note>original: *bella*; the poet uses the word for 'war' or 'arms' metaphorically to describe the two great gulfs of the Indian Ocean</note> through the waves into the lands; for the waves hold the Persian fields, having stolen the name of the sea from those very places which it rules, and it pours into the wide world.

Not far away, the sea gently washes the twin shores of the soft Arabs, a land bearing delicacies and new scents from various roots. And that sea takes its name from the land <note>The Red Sea/Arabian Gulf</note>. There, in the middle, lies Carthage, which once held a kingdom under two wars <note>The Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage</note> with fire, when Hannibal crushed the Alban citadels <note>A poetic reference to Rome's early ancestors at Alba Longa</note>, and made the Trebia and Cannae <note>Two of Hannibal's greatest victories over Rome</note> into eternal tombs, and poured Libya into Italian cities.

Here, a nature hostile to future wars granted various plagues and diverse monsters of wild beasts: horrific snakes, limbs inhabited by poison, and offspring of death—the living crimes of the earth. It also holds vast elephants and savage lions; fertile for its own punishment, the land gives birth to horrific wars. And it plays at the monstrous births of the Cyclopes <note>Mythical one-eyed giants</note>. Worse than a barren land, it plagues the dry sands until it yields its rights to the farmers of Egypt.

Then come the peoples of Asia, a land rich in all things; rivers of gold flow, the sea shines with gems, and scented forests breathe out healing balms. India, greater than our knowledge, and the Parthians—almost another world—and the walls of the Taurus mountains rising into the sky. So many nations divided by name surround it, separated from Scythian cities <note>Central Asian nomadic tribes</note> only by the waves. There is the Maeotian Lake <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, the rough waters of the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, and the furthest Hellespont of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles</note>.

Here nature placed the boundary of mighty Asia. What remains, Europe holds—she who first received Jupiter as he swam through the waves, and released the Bull from his weight, having suffered under him; he gave the waves a girl’s name and consecrated monuments of love under this title <note>Refers to the myth of Europa, a Phoenician princess carried across the sea to Crete by Jupiter in the form of a bull</note>. A land greatest for the vine, and most fertile in learned cities: Athens, flourishing in the kingdom of eloquence; Sparta, famous for its hand <note>military strength</note>; and Thebes, divided even under a single king. Greece, that foremost house of the Trojan War; Thessaly, and powerful Epirus; Illyria neighboring the shores, and Thrace, which claimed Mars <note>the god of war</note> as its inhabitant. Germany stands amazed among her own offspring; Meadowed Gaul, and Italy, greatest in wars.

<meta>This page continues the geographic and astrological survey of Book 4. While the previous page focused on the seas and the rise of Carthage and its wars with Rome, this page shifts to the divine organization of the world, the "melothesia" (the mapping of the zodiac signs to the human body), and how these celestial influences dictate the physical traits and cultures of different nations.</meta>

Italy, at the summit where Great Rome—the greatest of all things—has placed it over the lands, is itself joined to the heavens. Here, the sea must be called to the boundaries of the world, which God divides into parts and individual stars. He has granted each its own protective kingdoms throughout the globe, and added its own nations and lofty cities, in which the stars might exert their outstanding powers. 

And just as the human figure is mapped out by the signs—and although a common protection <note>original: *tutella*; the overarching influence of the heavens</note> extends through the whole body, it flows out to the individual limbs as they are divided. For the Ram <note>original: *Aries*</note> clings to the head, the Bull <note>original: *Taurus*</note> to the neck, the arms are reckoned under the Twins <note>original: *Gemini*</note>, and the chest under the Crab <note>original: *Cancer*</note>. The shoulders call to you, O Nemean Lion <note>original: *Nemeæe*</note>, and the flanks to you, O Virgin <note>original: *Virgo*</note>. The Balance <note>original: *Libra*</note> dwells in the buttocks, and the Scorpion <note>original: *Scorpius*</note> reigns in the groin. The Archer <note>original: *Arcitenens*</note> loved the thigh, and Capricorn the knees; the Young Man <note>original: *Iuuenis*, referring to Aquarius the Water-bearer</note> defends the shins, and the Fish <note>original: *Pisces*</note> the feet. 

In this way, different stars claim different lands for themselves. Therefore, the human race is arranged under various laws and various forms; nations are shaped by their own color, and shared laws, through a private covenant, mark their members and their corresponding material. 

Blonde Germany rises through its massive offspring. Gaul is stained with too much neighboring redness. Rougher Spain contracts its solid limbs. The face of the Martial world <note>The world belonging to Mars, the god of war and father of Romulus</note> lies open to the Romans; mixing well with its own Gradivus <note>A surname for Mars</note>, it tempers the limbs well. Through its colored peoples, subtle Greece displays the gymnasium and strong wrestling schools in its expression. And the hair curled at the temples betrays the Syrians. 

The Ethiopians stain the world and give shape to their lands. India produces human races that are less scorched, creating a moderate middle temperament. Now closer, the Egyptian land, floating with the Nile, darkens bodies more gently in its irrigated plains. The Punic man, in the sandy lands of the Africans, dries out the peoples with dust; and Mauritania <note>The land of the Moors</note> has its name from its face, and carries its title in its own color <note>The name "Mauri" was thought to derive from the Greek word for dark or black</note>.

Add to this as many sounds of voices, insert as many languages, and customs—equal according to their lot—and the rites of various places. Add the specific types of crops from similar seeds: Grain <note>original: *Cererem*, referring to Ceres</note> returning with varying harvests across the world, with pods not yielding equal strength in all places. Nor do you, Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note>, gift the lands with an equal bounty, but pour different grapes on different hills. Cinnamon does not grow everywhere in all fields. There are diverse appearances of cattle, and specific ones for wild beasts, and elephants enclosed in the double prison of the earth <note>This likely refers to the elephants being native only to the extreme edges of the world, or perhaps a reference to their tusks</note>. As many parts of the world as there are, there are just as many worlds within those parts. The stars shine, mapped out by certain laws, and bathe the subject nations with their own influence.

<meta>This page continues the astrological geography of Book 4. While the previous page introduced the concept of the zodiac signs ruling different parts of the human body and established that Rome sits at the summit of the world, this page provides a detailed "chorography," mapping specific regions, seas, and nations to the twelve signs of the zodiac, emphasizing the divine order in the distribution of earthly kingdoms.</meta>

-># B O O K<-

The Wool-Bearer <note>original: *Laniger*; refers to Aries the Ram</note> receives his stars in the middle of the world. The axis is clothed through the seasons between chilly Cancer. It claims for its strength—and it had itself conquered its position—when the brother <note>Phrixus, who fled on the golden ram with his sister Helle</note> was carried to the shores after the Virgin <note>Helle, who fell into the sea, giving her name to the Hellespont</note> had slipped away. And the burden flowed down and was diminished, and his back was relieved. The nearby Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note> also honors and worships him, as do the Syrian people, and the Persian in his loose cloak, clinging to his own garments, and the swelling Nile, and the land of Egypt, which is commanded to swim into the sign of the Crab <note>original: *Cancrum*; the flooding of the Nile coincides with the sun entering Cancer</note>.

The Bull <note>original: *Taurus*</note> possesses the Scythian seas curved into bows. The Bull holds the mountains of Scythia <note>ancient region in Central Eurasia</note>, and powerful Asia, and the soft Arabs, the wealthy kingdoms of the forests. The Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note>, curved into Scythian bows, worships you, O Phoebus <note>the Sun-god</note>, under the Twins <note>original: *Geminis*</note>, the last sign after the arms of his brother; and the familiar Ganges and India worship the Crab. The Ethiopians burn under the Crab, in which there is the most fire. Their very color teaches this. The servant of the Idaean Mother <note>Cybele, the Phrygian goddess whose chariot was pulled by lions</note> has taken possession of Nemean Phrygia <note>referring to Leo, the Nemean Lion</note>, and of the fierce kingdom of the Cappadocians and the ridges of Armenia; wealthy Bithynia worships you, and the land of the Macedonians, which once conquered the world.

Under the chaste Virgin <note>original: *Virgine*; Virgo</note> is Rhodes, a land happy on both land and sea, the lodging-place of the prince who would rule the world <note>A reference to the future emperor Tiberius, who lived in self-imposed exile on the island of Rhodes</note>. And you, Rhodes, are truly the home of the Sun, to whom you are entirely consecrated, since you received the light of the great world under Caesar. Also included are the cities of Ionia, and the Doric countryside, the ancient Arcadians, and Caria, celebrated in fame.

What star would rather rule Italy, if it chose its own star, than that which rules all things, which knows the weights of matters, marks the highest points, and separates the unjust from the just? On which the seasons hang, and to which night and day yield; its own Balance <note>original: *Libra*</note> holds Hesperia <note>Italy</note>, in which Rome was founded; it retains the mastery of the world and the discernment of affairs, and with its scales it raises or presses down the nations placed within them. Here Remus, born with his brother, founded this city. And with its own nods, it bridles the hanging world.

Below this, the Scorpion <note>original: *Scorpius*</note>, radiating with tears, overthrows the citadels of conquered Carthage, and Libya, and the side of Egypt, and the gifted kingdoms of the Tyrrhenians <note>the Etruscans</note>; yet it looks back toward the waves of Italy. It also holds Sardinia, and the lands scattered through the seas. The Gnosian land <note>Crete</note>, surrounded by the sea, lies open to the Centaur <note>original: *Centauro*; Sagittarius</note>, as does the noble star of the son of Minos. He himself comes as a swift twin; from here Crete claims the arrows, and imitates the stretched bows of the constellation. The island of Sicily <note>original: *Trinacriae*</note>, having assisted its floating sister, follows Crete, established under the same sign; and the shore nearest to Italy, divided by a shallow depth, follows the laws of its father, and was not snatched away by the star. 

You, Capricorn <note>original: *Capricorne*</note>, rule whatever is exposed under the falling Sun, and what touches chilly Helice <note>the Great Bear constellation, indicating the North</note>; from there—

<meta>This page continues the "chorography" or astrological geography of Book 4. While the previous page assigned regions like Syria, Egypt, and India to Aries, Taurus, and Cancer, this page extends the mapping to Western Europe (Spain, Gaul, Germany) and the Near East (Parthia, Babylon). It then transitions into Chapter 4, which discusses "Ecliptic Signs"—the concept that the influence of the zodiac signs is not static but fluctuates over vast cycles of time, just as the Earth itself undergoes cataclysms of flood and fire.</meta>

# ->F O U R T H  B O O K<-

The Spanish peoples, or what wealthy Gaul produces, and Germany—a mother worthy only of wild offspring—claim a wavering star <note>original: *ambiguum sidus*; likely referring to a sign that sits on a boundary or exerts a dual influence</note>, which holds the land and the sea through constant tides of earth and ocean. But the softer youth shaped with a naked bow <note>The Archer, Sagittarius</note> withdraws to Egypt, to the city of Leptis, and the Tyrian citadels. The Cilician people and the fields neighboring Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer</note> also fall here. The Euphrates is given to the Fishes <note>Pisces</note>, where the plowing Fish <note>likely referring to a specific star or the "Southern Fish" associated with the myth</note> settled in the waves when Venus fled the monster Typhon. 

A great land lies surrounded by great shores: the Parthians, and the nations conquered by the Parthians through the ages; Bactra, and holy Babylon, and Susa, and the Persians <note>original: *Panos*; referring to the Eastern peoples often associated with the god Pan or simply the "Medes"</note>. Names barely to be embraced in uncounted forms. Also the Tigris and the radiant shores of the Red Sea <note>original: *rubri ponti*; in antiquity, this referred to the Erythraean Sea, including the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean</note>. Thus the earth remains divided through all the ages, from which laws must be drawn for their own parts. For these regions maintain the same relationships as the signs; just as the signs join together or resist in hatred, sometimes opposite in the sky, sometimes joined in a triangle <note>original: *trigono*; the "trine" aspect in astrology, where signs 120 degrees apart are considered harmonious</note>, and other causes governing various effects. Thus lands respond to lands, spheres to spheres, shores to shores, and kingdoms are opposed to kingdoms. Thus each person must flee or seek their station. Thus faith must be hoped for, and dangers feared, as the human race descends into the earth from high heaven.

### ->*On the Ecliptic Signs. Chapter 4*<-

**L**earn now also which signs are called "ecliptic" <note>original: *ecliptica*; from the Greek for "failing" or "fading"</note> by their Greek name; those which, as if exhausted through certain years, sometimes cease, lying dormant in barren motion. Surely, nothing remains equal throughout immense time; though things hold perpetual flowers and a single color, they change, and all things vary over the long cycle of the world. Even fertile fields stop producing their fruits, and, exhausted, deny continuous births in their creation. Conversely, lands that had been sterile for seeds later suffice with a harvest, with no one demanding tribute. The earth is shaken, clinging to various structures; it withdraws the ground from under our feet, and the world swims within itself. 

And the ocean comes upon the sea, and thirsting, dissolves it, nor does it contain itself; thus it once submerged cities, when Deucalion <note>the Greek "Noah" who survived a great flood</note> stood as the sole heir of the human race and possessed the world on a single rock. Likewise, when Phaethon <note>the son of the Sun-god who lost control of the solar chariot</note> attempted his father's reins, the nations burned, and heaven feared the fires; the glowing stars fled the new flames, and Nature feared she would be buried in a single tomb. To such a great extent do all things change over long periods, and then return again into themselves; thus at a fixed time, the signs also lose their strengths and take them back once regained. The cause is clear: because the Moon has failed in its own stars...

This page moves from physical geography to the celestial mechanics of eclipses and "ecliptic signs," eventually transitioning into a profound philosophical defense of the human mind's ability to comprehend the divine order of the stars.</meta>

-> # B O O K  F O U R <-

Bereft of her brother <note>original: *fratris*; referring to the Sun (Phoebus)</note>, and immersed in the shadows of night,
When the orb intercepts the middle rays of Phoebus,
Nor does she draw into the darkness that light by which Delia <note>A name for the Moon, who was born on the island of Delos</note> shines.
These signs also languish equally with their own star,
Bent low at the same time and deprived of their usual vigor,
And just as if mourning the bright Phoebe <note>The Moon</note> at her funeral.
The ecliptic signs themselves teach their titles and their causes.
The ancients said they labor equally in pairs,
Not neighboring in location, but those which shine opposite each other.
Just as the Moon only fails in her own orb
When she does not see Phoebus running with opposing stars.
Yet they do not all languish for an equal time.
For sometimes an entire year is drawn out, tainted by this state.
Now the stars remain weary for a shorter time, nor do they stay longer;
They exceed the solar times by their own falling away.
And when the space assigned to each is completed,
And their labors are fulfilled at their fixed station,
The two signs shining across the opposite heaven
Then waver as neighbors, clinging to those very signs
Which first come to the lands, and then leave the lands,
Not so that the star fights against the celestial orb,
But because the universe <note>original: *mundus*; the cosmic order or "world-system"</note> drives it, and it bows its own course.
It denies its lost strengths, and neither returns such great gifts,
Nor returns similar harms; the location turns all things.

-> *On the divinity of the mind, by which we perceive the logic of the fates and the heavens. Chapter V.* <-

# **B**ut what does it profit us to search out the world shining with such delicate logic <note>original: *ratione*; also meaning "reason" or "account"</note>, if each person's own mind fights against it?
Fear takes away hope, and bars us from the threshold of heaven.
For nature hides whatever she keeps in her vast retreat,
And she dulls mortal vision and our hearts.
Nor can it be useful that all things are ruled by fate,
When fate can be perceived by no logic.
Why does it please us to be carried into reproaches against ourselves,
And to cheat ourselves of the good things which not even God himself envies?
To cast down the eyes of the mind which nature gave us?
We perceive the heaven; why not also the gifts of heaven?
And why not allow the world to descend deep into our very senses,
And to compose such a great mass from its own seeds,
And to bear the prize of heaven through its own nourishment,
And to follow the final harbor, and to go beneath the stretches of the hanging earth,
And to live in the whole world?
How great a part remains to learn the logic of the night!
Now nature is hidden nowhere; we have seen her in her entirety,
And having captured the world, we possess it; and we see our parent
As a part of her; born from the stars, we approach them.
Is there any doubt that a god dwells within our breast?
That souls return to heaven, and come from heaven?
And just as the world is constructed from every substance—
Of ether and the highest fire, of earth, and of sea—

--- Page 478 ---
<meta>This page concludes Book 4 of Manilius’s Astronomica. While the previous page discussed the technicalities of eclipses and the "laboring" of the zodiac signs, this concluding passage shifts into a sublime philosophical defense of astrology. It argues that humans are capable of understanding the heavens because they are "microcosms"—miniature versions of the universe itself—possessing the same divine reason that moves the stars.</meta>

### ->B O O K  F O U R<-

The spirit, swift and pervasive, which governs all that is ordained <note>original: *iussa*; the laws of nature or divine commands</note>, 
Proves that just as there are bodies of earthly destiny within us, 
And souls of blood, so too is there a mind that governs all 
And directs the human being. What wonder is it then that men 
Can come to know the universe <note>original: *mundum*; the world-system or cosmos</note>, if they have that very universe within them? 
Each person is an example of God, a miniature image. 
Or is it right to believe that humans were born from anything 
But heaven? All other animals lie cast down 
Upon the earth, or are submerged in the depths, or hang in the air. 
For all of them, there is but one rest: the belly, and the senses through their limbs. 
And because they lack counsel, their tongues are stilled. 
Humanity alone has the contemplation of things, the power of speech, 
And a capable intellect; this offspring, who rules over all, 
Has withdrawn into the world's circle <note>Refers to the human capacity to internalize the cosmic order</note>. 
He has tamed the earth for crops and captured the wild beasts. 
He has imposed a path upon the sea; he alone stands tall 
Upon the citadel of his head. As a victor, he sends his 
Starry eyes to the stars, views <term>Olympus</term> <note>The home of the gods, often used by Manilius to mean the highest heavens</note> from closer by, 
And inquires after <term>Jove</term> <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods</note>. Nor is he content to remain 
Decorated only in his outward appearance; he scrutinizes heaven in his very marrow, 
And following his kindred body, he seeks himself among the stars. 
Hence we seek a path to truth in these great things—the same truth 
Which birds often receive <note>Referring to augury, or divination by the flight of birds</note>, and the trembling fibers <note>The entrails of sacrificed animals used in divination</note> beneath the breast. 
Is it less to derive reason from sacred signs 
Than to attend to the deaths of cattle or the songs of birds? 
And therefore, God himself does not envy the world the sight of heaven; 
He discloses his own face and his own body. 
By always revolving, he impresses and offers himself 
So that he may be well known, and teach us by being seen 
How he moves, and teach us to attend to his laws. 
The universe itself calls our souls to the stars, 
Nor does it allow its laws to lie hidden, for it does not conceal them. 
Who thinks it a sin to be born into what is lawful to behold? 
Do not despise your own strengths as if they were in a small body. 
That which has power is immense; just as small weights of gold 
Exceed in price numerous heaps of bronze. 
Thus the <term>diamond</term> <note>original: *adamas*; a stone of legendary hardness and value</note>, a mere point of stone, is more precious than gold. 
Thus the tiny pupil of the eye surveys the entire heaven. 
And what the eyes see is very small, even when they perceive the greatest things. 
Thus the seat of the mind, located within the slender heart, 
Reigns through the whole body from a narrow limit. 
Do not look for the measure of the matter, but behold its power, 
Which <term>Reason</term> <note>original: *ratio*; the guiding principle of the Stoic universe</note>, not weight, possesses; Reason conquers all things. 
Do not doubt that humans can be trusted with divine visions. 
Now he <note>Referring to the Emperor, likely Augustus or Tiberius</note> himself makes gods, and sends a greater 
Divinity to the stars; and heaven grows under a venerable prince.

# ->BOOK FIVE<-

He will not bring to the lands stars driven by blood upon the waves, nor will <term>Xerxes</term> <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE</note> both create and rule the sea.
Rome will not sink <term>Syracuse</term>, nor Salamis sink Athens.
The <term>Punic</term> <note>Carthaginian</note> prows will not float across the entire ocean,
nor will both halves of the world hang suspended between the <term>Actian gulfs</term> <note>Refers to the Battle of Actium (31 BCE), where Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra</note>,
and the fortune of the heavens swim upon the deep.
Under these guides, fleets are led through the blind sea.
The earth itself comes together, and through all the diverse uses
of things, the whole world is summoned by the winds.
But rising from the highest part of the left side
is greatest <term>Orion</term>, who embraces the great <term>Olympus</term> <note>Here, the word represents the entire vault of the heavens</note>.
While he shines above the lands and draws the sky along,
Night, having feigned the day, draws in her black wings.
He will fashion skillful spirits and swift bodies,
and a mind agile in duty, and hearts that, amidst all cares,
hurry to see the world with a relaxed heart.
He will be like a whole crowd in himself, and will dwell in the entire city,
flitting across thresholds, a common friend
carrying a single word of morning greeting through all places.
But when <term>Aries</term> <note>The Ram</note> has completed thrice-five degrees <note>15 degrees of the sign</note> 
and raises itself from the lands, first from the waves <term>Heniochus</term> <note>The Charioteer, also known as Auriga</note>
raises his yokes, and pulls his wheels from the bottom of the slope,
where the chilly <term>Boreas</term> <note>The North Wind</note> presses on with sharp Northern blasts.
He will grant his own particular passion: retaining in the sky
those arts which, as a driver, he had loved before on earth—
to stand in a light chariot, moderating four mouths
reined in with foaming bits, and to turn the
powerful strength of horses and guide them in a tight circle.
And when the barriers have been released from the loosened hinge,
to urge on the wild beasts, and to go before the flying ones as he leans forward.
Scarcely touching the top of the field with light wheels,
beating the winds with his feet, or holding the front of
the ranks, he performs malicious maneuvers on the slant,
and blocks the whole track by delaying the opponent.
Or in the middle of the crowd—now go through the right-hand circles—
trusting in the field, now to run past the sharp <term>turning post</term> <note>original: *meta*; the conical pillars marking the ends of the Roman race track</note>.
And to hang his wavering hope upon the final turn of fate.
Likewise, the <term>circus rider</term> <note>original: *desultor*; a performer who leaps between horses</note> from the alternating backs
of four-footed beasts, will be able to plant his feet steadily.
Across those horses he goes, he will play across the backs of the flying ones.
Or, carried on a single horse, now he will move his weapons.
Now he may receive rewards earned in the long circus.
Whatever is shaped from such a pursuit, he will possess.
From this star comes my <term>Salmoneus</term> <note>A mythological king who imitated Zeus's thunder by dragging bronze kettles; he was eventually struck by a real thunderbolt</note>, who imitates the sky in a circle
by the movements he imposes, and with four-horse chariots sent through the air,
he seemed to himself to have expressed the sound of the universe, and imagines
that he has displaced Jupiter himself from the lightning of the lands.
He felt the blow, and followed the immense fires above.
Through death, he learned of what rank the Jupiter who fathered him must be held.
You may believe <term>Bellerophon</term> <note>The hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus</note> was born of this star,
who laid a path for the world, flying through the signs of the sky.

When the degrees have been reclaimed from the sea, the monuments once belonging to **Ariadne’s Crown** <note>original: "Ariadneæ coronæ." In Greek myth, the god Dionysus gave Ariadne a jeweled crown, which was later placed in the stars as the constellation Corona Borealis.</note> will rise from the waves. They grant gentle skills; from here come the gifts of the girl, for the crown shines on one side, and the rising girl herself is on the other. This person cultivates a garden budding with bright flowers: pale violets, purple hyacinths, lilies, and poppies that mimic the glow of **Tyrian purple** <note>A famous and expensive dye made from sea snails in the city of Tyre, associated with royalty and luxury.</note>, and the flower of the spring rose with its blood-red bloom. He will add the blue-leafed hills and green grass to his care, painting the meadows with the true shapes of spring. Or he will weave various flowers together, placing them in garlands. He will fold them into his lap, pressing similar blooms together to blend them, and soften the scents of **Arabian forests** <note>Refers to exotic spices and resins like frankincense or myrrh.</note>. He will provide ointments that carry healing breaths, so that there is a greater charm in the mingling of juices; refinement and elegance are present here, along with the graceful arts, the allurements of life, and immediate pleasure. The flowers and the year of the Virgin demand this.

But when **Spica** <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo, representing an ear of grain held by the Virgin.</note> rises roughly through the tenth degree, the field will offer immediate ears of grain at their birth. It creates a passion for the fields and for cultivating the countryside, returning seeds to the furrowed earth for profit, following the interest of countless fruits received from a greater stake, and seeking granaries for the harvest. This alone taught mortals to know "metal" <note>This likely refers to the iron of the plow or the wealth produced by grain.</note>; otherwise, there would be no hunger, no fasting in the lands. The world’s wealth was rich once the nations were fed. And if by chance the labor of the countryside delayed the arts—without which **Ceres** <note>The goddess of agriculture and grain.</note> is nothing, and the use of seeds is naught—he will teach how to place grain in the furrows, and to draw hanging wheels <note>Likely referring to irrigation wheels or heavy plows.</note> over them, to sink the spelt, and to toast it at the hearths for human food, turning one kind of thing into many various shapes. And because the ear of grain is skillfully fitted with arranged seeds, a similar order is composed for the person trained by it. He provides cells and granaries for his seeds. He will make one who carves the paneled ceilings in holy temples, building a new heaven through the roofs of the **Thunderer** <note>A title for Jupiter, king of the gods.</note>. This skill was once granted only to the gods; now it is part of luxury, and dining rooms compete with temples; we now live under gold and "eat" gold <note>A metaphor for the excessive wealth and gilded architecture of the Roman elite.</note>.

But behold the **Arrow** <note>The constellation Sagitta.</note> rising at the eighth degree; it will grant the ability to throw the javelin with the arms, to launch the reed from the bowstring, and to hurl stones with slings. It allows one to catch the bird hanging in its own sky, or to pierce the unsuspecting fish with a triple-pronged spear. I would give all this to the lineage of **Teucer** <note>A famous archer in the Trojan War, brother of Ajax.</note> or to you, **Philoctetes** <note>The Greek hero who possessed the bow of Hercules, essential for the fall of Troy.</note>, to whose side I would prefer to trust it. Teucer fended off Hector’s torches with his bow and arrows, sending his own fires into a thousand ships. Philoctetes, however, carried the quiver and the war to **Troy**.

# ->BOOK FIVE<-

<note>This opening passage describes a man of great skill, specifically one who can navigate dangerous political or physical situations.</note>
A greater enemy, and an exile under a treaty of arms. Indeed, even that father could be born of such a star, who, when a serpent lay coiled upon the face of his unhappy son—drinking in both his sleep and his life-breath—endured the risk of aiming and striking the beast with a flung spear. It was an art to be a father; nature overcame the peril. At once, he delivered the youth from sleep and from death, restoring the son who had been snatched by fate through a dream.

But when the unwary **Kid** <note>original: "Haedus." A star in the constellation Auriga, the Charioteer, often associated with storms and restless energy.</note> among the hidden stars, appearing like a wanderer, seeks the tracks of its brothers and is led out at a long interval after the flock, it pours forth skillful minds and restless hearts. It creates a spirit that never tires, occupied with various cares. These talents are not tested merely at home; they are the servants of the people, carried through magistracies and public laws. Such men do not care for a spear that rests idle on any finger <note>This suggests they are active in the military or public defense rather than being lazy.</note>. The guilty plunderer shall be stripped of his goods and pay the penalty, and the debtor who has defrauded his fatherland shall be held to account. Such a man is an advocate in words, yet he also indulges in various wanton loves; he frequents the forum, and reeks of the marketplace <note>original: "madet atque lixo." This implies a life spent in the bustle of the city, sometimes associated with low-born street-traders or cooks.</note>. He is nimble in leaps and more delicate in the art of the stage.

Now, as the **Lyre** <note>original: "Lyra." The constellation representing the instrument of the mythical musician Orpheus.</note> rises, the shape of the shell <note>The lyre was traditionally made from a tortoise shell.</note> emerges from the waves of the sea, a form brought forth through the heir of the **Thunderer** <note>original: "tonantis," referring to Jupiter/Zeus.</note>. With this instrument, **Orpheus** <note>A legendary hero and musician whose music could move rocks and trees and charm the guardians of the Underworld.</note>, son of Oeagrus, once brought sound and ears to the cliffs and forests; he brought tears to the god of wealth <note>Pluto/Hades.</note> and finally a temporary end to death itself. From this influence shall come learned voices, sounding beautifully. It produces the talkative flute <note>term: "tibia" — an ancient wind instrument often made of two pipes.</note> with its various forms and melodies, and whatever speaks by the hand or is moved by the breath. This star will grant sweet songs during banquets; it will soothe **Bacchus** <note>The god of wine.</note> with its sound and hold the nights captive, modulating the voice in a secret, murmured song. Such a man will even sing to his own ears alone.

Further off from the Lyre, when the twenty-sixth degree of the **Claws** <note>original: "Chelarum." This refers to the constellation Libra, which the ancients often viewed as the "claws" of the neighboring Scorpion.</note> rises and leads its horns to the stars, the **Altar** <note>original: "Ara." This constellation represents the altar where the gods swore oaths before their war with the Titans.</note> appears in an equal region, though barely drawing eight degrees. It bears incense, with stars that mimic fire. On this altar, the devoted **Giants** <note>original: "gygantes." Mythological beings who rebelled against the Olympian gods.</note> once fell. Nor did **Jupiter** <note>The king of the gods.</note> arm his right hand with the violent lightning bolt until he himself stood as a priest before the gods. The rising of this star creates men who tend to temples rather than common things, and ministers sworn into sacred laws, venerating the divine voices of the gods. They are almost gods themselves, and those who are able to see things yet to come.

The **Centaur** <note>original: "Centaurus." The constellation representing Chiron, the wise half-man, half-horse tutor of heroes.</note> offers its stars when four degrees have been added, and from itself, it adds character to those being born. It will either drive them with goads or yoke all types of four-footed beasts in a mixed team; or such a man will go higher in a chariot. He will either load horses with armor or lead them into battle. He possesses the skills that bridge the gap to the limbs of wild beasts, and they learn to perform movements never heard of before.

<meta>This page continues the fifth book of Manilius’s *Astronomica*. The previous page concluded a section on the influence of stars on those who protect or heal others. This page transitions into the influence of the constellation Sagittarius (the Archer) and the rising of the Swan (Cygnus) and the Southern Fish, detailing how these celestial bodies govern professions related to bird-keeping, exotic imports, and the dangerous trade of pearl-diving.</meta>

-> # BOOK FIVE <-

This is the work of art: not to wait for the groaning sufferer, and not to believe the body is sick only when it has long been so. Now the **Archer** <note>original: "Arcitenens." Literally "the Bow-Bearer," referring to the constellation Sagittarius.</note> approaches, whose fifth part reveals the shining **Arcturus** <note>The brightest star in the constellation Boötes; its rising was often associated with storms or shifts in fortune.</note> to the sea. At this time, Fortune herself dares to commit her wealth to those born then, so that they may guard royal riches and the state treasuries. They remain rulers under a king, or ministers of the state.

When the Archer has fully emerged from the waves, with the stars forming the thirtieth degree of the wild beast, the feathery **Swan** <note>original: "Olor." Also referred to as Cygnus. In mythology, Jupiter took the form of a swan to seduce Leda.</note> flies into the sky on its bright wings. As it rises, drawing in the light and leaving its mother behind, it will call forth a people of the air—the race of winged creatures—as their study and their source of income. A thousand arts flow from this: either to declare war on the wild world, or to weigh the bird’s flight in mid-air, or to sit and call the bright birds with their own logic, or to lead the escaping lines of nets over the feeding birds. These men will act as guardians of the people, or, appointed to govern houses, they will confine their cares within a boundary belonging to another. 

And this trade will even extend further toward luxury for the belly; for now we feed on what comes from the shores of **Numidia** <note>A region in North Africa, famous for its exotic birds like the guinea fowl.</note>, and the market is summoned from **Phasis** <note>A river in Colchis (modern Georgia), legendary as the source of the pheasant and the location of the Golden Fleece.</note>, from where the golden fleece was once carried across a new sea. Furthermore, such a man will teach human languages and feelings to the birds of the air, creating a new kind of commerce; he will teach them words denied to them by the law of nature. The Swan itself honors the gods, and beneath that form, not being entirely a bird, it murmurs a voice within itself. 

Nor should those escape your notice who delight in feeding birds shut within the highest rooftop, or who breed the "blind" birds of **Venus** <note>Pigeons and doves were sacred to the goddess Venus.</note>. Or those who carry birds through the whole city in cages, ready for commands, whose entire wealth consists of feeding these small creatures. The Golden Swan, bestowing similar arts, will remain fixed there.

When the Archer, surrounded by the great circle of the **Dragon** <note>original: "Draconis." Referring to the constellation Draco.</note>, comes into the region of your figure, **Capricorn**, it does not make the limbs of serpents hostile to those born then. They will receive them into their laps and their flowing robes; they join kisses with the horrendous venom with impunity. 

But when the **Fish** <note>original: "Piscis." Likely referring to Piscis Austrinus (the Southern Fish), which rises near this time.</note> leads itself forth into its native sea, and enters into foreign borders as it rises into the sky, whoever is wise at such a time will spend their years around shores and marsh-pools. He will catch the fish hanging in the "blind" sea, and with their houses, he will drag forth the submerged shells hidden in the depths—nothing is left untouched by the daring. Profit is sought through shipwreck, and the body is sent into the deep just as the prey itself is sought. For the reward of such great labor is always small. Yet shells are equated to great fortunes, and the swift north winds are noted. Scarcely anyone is wealthy unless the earth is burdened by the riches of the deep.
