<meta>This page continues the fifth book of Manilius’s *Astronomica*. The previous section concluded with the rising of constellations governing those who catch or keep birds. This page transitions into the influence of stars on maritime trade, the judicial system, and the rising of the Dolphin (Delphinus) and Cepheus, which govern swimmers, divers, acrobats, and stern moralists.</meta>

-># BOOK FIVE<-

By such a fate, perhaps, he practices his arts along the shores. Either he buys foreign labors at a price, or as a **trader** <note>original: "institor." A retail merchant or peddler who sold goods on behalf of another.</note> of sea-borne goods, he exchanges them under various forms of merchandise. And when these stars succeed the faithful ones in the great world, there will come a **seeker of crimes** <note>original: "Quæsitor scelerum." A judicial investigator or prosecutor.</note> and a punisher of the guilty, who will scrutinize committed deeds with his own proofs. He will drag into the light what was hidden by silent fraud. From here also comes the pitiless torturer and the minister of punishment, and whoever favored the truth or utterly hated crime. A man is produced who can settle disputes from deep within his heart.

When the sea-blue **Dolphin** <note>original: "Delphinus." This constellation was associated by the ancients with the sea and agility.</note> raises itself from the deep toward the stars and emerges with its glittering scales, <margin>-</margin> it appears as a creature of ambiguous birth, born of the earth yet created for the sea. For just as the dolphin itself glides through the waters on swift fins, now cutting the surface of the sea, now diving into the deep, and takes its strength from the old ones <note>likely a reference to the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates being transformed into dolphins</note> and gives shape to the waves, so from this constellation comes anyone who will "fly" through the waves. Now he brings alternating arms into slow, long strokes, and the water will resound with his splashing; now he will pull down his palms submerged in the sea, acting as his own secret oar. Now he will enter the waters upright and swim here and there, making the surface of the deep seem like a solid field. Or, keeping his limbs and sides motionless, he will lie on his back, not burdening the waters, and recline upon the surface of the waves. He will hang over the entire sea without a rower. For such men, it is a joy to seek the sea within the sea; they submerge their bodies in the waves, striving to see **Nereus** <note>A sea god, often called the "Old Man of the Sea."</note> himself within his caves and to visit the sea-nymphs. They carry away the spoils of the ocean and shipwrecks snatched from the deep, greedily searching the bottommost sands.

Another group devotes itself to a different pursuit, and both are joined into one kind, united by a single seed. Linked to these numbers through art are those bodies which leap, shaken from a powerful **springboard** <note>original: "Petauto." An acrobatic apparatus, possibly a balanced beam or a type of springboard used in Roman spectacles.</note>, stirring alternating motions; one man is carried down and lies still, while the other is suspended by his comrade's fall. They are flung through flames and glowing hoops, lifted up, and then placed on the ground as if landing in liquid waves. They imitate the movements of dolphins, swimming through the empty air; stripped of wings, they fly and play in the breeze. But if these specific skills are lacking, a suitable nature will remain in them; nature will grant vigor, eager speed, and limbs that fly across the field.

But Cepheus, passing through the region of watery **Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer constellation.</note>, will not grant a character inclined toward play; he makes the face remain serious. He composes minds with the weight of the brow and the countenance. Such men will be nourished by cares and will always turn over the examples of the ancients. They will praise the words of old **Cato** <note>Cato the Elder, famous for his extreme austerity and traditional Roman morals.</note>, or the stern eyebrow of a tutor, or the rigor of an uncle. They will also be the ones to mold tender years, and as a master, they follow a master by the law of the **bordered toga** <note>original: "prætextæ." The *toga prætexta* was worn by Roman boys and high magistrates; here it refers to the authority of a teacher or guardian.</note>.

He casts down his strength; his glory is to yield to nothing.

such a man will be the minister of a king or a great leader through wars.

-> # THE BOOKS OF MANILIUS <-

And you, Cynosura <note>The constellation Ursa Minor, or the Little Bear, which contains the North Star.</note>, find a fatherly color beneath you, and the four fires which the Dolphin hurls forth, and the Triangle <note>original: "Deltoton," from the Greek letter Delta.</note> shining with its three torches, and the Eagle gleaming with a similar light, and the limbs bent across its slippery back. Then a fourth and fifth class are distinguished from the whole number, and the rank which is joined to the highest Snake <note>The constellation Draco.</note>; the greatest things are enclosed by the smallest in a single census <note>A reference to the Roman system of ranking citizens by wealth and status.</note>. These stars do not respond from the deep height of heaven through every night or at all times, but only when the bright Delia <note>A name for the Moon (Diana), born on the island of Delos.</note> turns away her course, and when she wanders and hides her light from the earth; and when golden Orion has submerged his glowing fires, and Phoebus <note>The Sun.</note>, having crossed the signs, changes through the seasons, the sky shines in the shadows and is lit up in the black night. Then, though the seeds of light be few, it is possible to perceive the crowded, gleaming temples of heaven, and the whole spirit of the sky shimmering with flickering lights. This is a harmonious discord: there is no space for the stars in the universe, nor do the highest things give way—just as flowers run across the fields or dry sands along the shore. But as many as the waves that are always being born from the sea, or as many as the thousands of leaves that fall in the forests, so many more are the fires that fly through the orb of heaven. 

Just as a population is described throughout a vast city, where the Fathers <note>The Senators, the highest social class in Rome.</note> retain the chief place, and the Equestrian order <note>The Knights, the second tier of the Roman social hierarchy.</note> occupies the next position, and you may see the common people follow the knights, and the idle crowd, and even a nameless throng. Thus nature, who established the sphere in the heavens, makes certain things correspond to the great universe. There are stars like the nobles; there are stars next to the first; there are ranks, and all are joined to what came before. The greatest is the population which is carried on the highest summit, to which nature gave strength in proportion to its number... <unclear>...</unclear> the ether itself could not endure its own flames, and the whole world would burn with a blazing Olympus.

-> ### END OF THE FIFTH AND FINAL BOOK. <-

MARCUS Manilius the Mathematician <term>Mathematicus: In the Roman world, this term specifically referred to an astrologer or one who calculated the movements of the stars to predict the future.</term>, whose most elegant work remains here, composed in Heroic verse <note>Dactylic hexameter, the meter used for epics like the Aeneid.</note> regarding the discipline of Astrology, and containing both the motion and the *apotelesma*—that is, the stellar influence—flourished in the times of the divine Augustus. He indicates this himself at the beginning of this work, and Pliny testifies to it when he reports in the 36th book of his *Natural History* that a golden ball was added to the summit of a certain Obelisk <note>This refers to the Solarium Augusti, a massive sundial in Rome where an obelisk served as the gnomon.</note> by Manilius the Mathematician to discern the calculations of the hours. He was the first of all the Latins to write about the stars in verse. Therefore, he should be held in high regard, as he boasts of this especially in several places in this work. For it is a task of no small labor and talent to have explained such difficult matters in verse so aptly, in Latin, and so clearly, as our Manilius has done. Even if he had not achieved it, to have wished for it would still be abundantly beautiful and magnificent. Therefore, you may learn from the table written below what we may achieve by the reading of this most elegant work.
